articles.title: Tout ça pour ça ! NVIDIA annulerait la GeForce RTX 5080 24 Go : la GDDR7 est trop chère
articles.text:
Finalement, NVIDIA aurait décidé de laisser de côté cette hypothétique version 24 Go de la GeForce RTX 5080 et conservé le « simple » modèle doté de 16 Go, moins onéreux à produire.
Cruel univers que celui des cartes graphiques. Alors que l'on commençait à vraiment croire que NVIDIA envisageait le lancement d'une version 24 Go de la GeForce RTX 5080, nos espoirs sont douchés par ce qui serait un problème de coût de production. Alors là, quelle surprise !
BenQ iScreenBar : la barre lumineuse qui s’accorde avec l’iMac
Des lignes en harmonie avec celles de l’ordinateur d’Apple, une conception rigoureuse, des matériaux sélectionnés, rien n’a été laissé au hasard, tout comme le service qu’elle rend une fois allumée !
Une RTX 5080 dotée de 24 Go de VRAM…
Les GeForce RTX série 50 en déclinaison « SUPER », on en parle depuis des mois. En réalité, on en parle pratiquement depuis le lancement des RTX 5090 et RTX 5080, c'est dire.
Cela dit, le nombre de rumeurs autour d'un produit est loin d'en faire une réalité et si vous suivez un tant soit peu l'actualité de la carte graphique, vous êtes bien placés pour savoir que les bruits de couloir autour des GPU d'AMD, d'Intel ou de NVIDIA sont loin de tous devenir réalité. Les « SUPER », on les avait ainsi presque oubliées quand la rumeur – seule cette fois – est revenue à la charge alors que NVIDIA semblait retirer les RTX 5080/5090 de sa boutique.
Cette fois, il n'était plus nécessairement question de l'appeler RTX 5080 SUPER, mais simplement « 24 Go » pour insister sur le fait qu'un modèle en chassait un autre. La GeForce RTX 5080 16 Go devait disparaître pour céder la place à un modèle doté de 8 Go de mémoire vidéo en plus. De quoi lui donner un peu plus de peps afin de convaincre les joueurs déçus par l'inaccessibilité de la RTX 5090.
… finalement annulée et retour à la version 16 Go !
Alors que les indices commençaient à se multiplier et que l'on envisageait même une sortie en tout début d'année prochaine, tout porte à croire que NVIDIA a complètement changé son fusil d'épaule.
Relayée par nos confrères du site VideoCardz, la nouvelle de l'annulation de cette version 24 Go de la GeForce RTX 5080 serait à mettre en lien avec le coût de la GDDR7. Remarquez, ce n'est pas franchement une surprise, c'est en partie la raison pour laquelle le prix des cartes gaming haut de gamme et des cartes professionnelles crève le plafond.
À en croire notre confrère, il ne serait donc plus question de se fournir en puces de 3 Go pour concevoir cette variante 24 Go et NVIDIA préfère continuer avec les puces GDDR7 de 2 Go afin de maintenir en vie la GeForce RTX 5080 16 Go telle que nous la connaissons. Nous avons d'ailleurs testé la variante signée ASUS/Noctua il y a seulement quelques jours. Si l'information clarifie un peu la situation, cela ne résout cependant pas les problèmes du prix.
La GeForce RTX 5080 16 Go – et pas seulement le modèle ASUS/Noctua – a effectivement bien augmenté depuis son lancement il y a bientôt deux ans et personne ne voit aucun signe d'amélioration à court terme.
Source : VideoCardz

articles.title: F5 Warns 6 Critical BIG-IP Flaws Can Crash Traffic in Specific Setups, May Allow RCE
articles.text:
Six critical vulnerabilities in F5 BIG-IP allow an attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) without logging in, disrupting traffic until the TMM restarts.
Each flaw needs a specific setup on a virtual server: an iRule that uses a particular command, or an APM policy that includes two particular kinds of agent.
F5, which makes BIG-IP, disclosed the flaws today and says they may also allow remote code execution. The company has released engineering hotfixes and lists no workaround.
The company rates all six 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.3 under CVSS v4.0. They are stack-based buffer overflows in BIG-IP's data plane, the part that processes almost all of its network traffic. The management side is not exposed, according to the company.
None of the company's advisories says the flaws have been exploited. WatchTowr researcher Sina Kheirkhah reported four, and the company found the other two itself.
Five of the flaws are in iRules, a BIG-IP feature that administrators use to manage traffic, and one is in BIG-IP's APM module. Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and BIG-IP CNF, part of the company's BIG-IP Cloud-Native Edition.
Each flaw needs the setup listed below on a virtual server:
- CVE-2026-123637: an APM per-request policy that includes both the Client Information agent and Endpoint Security agents. Affects BIG-IP APM only.
- CVE-2026-121805: an iRule that uses PEM::subscriber on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP PEM, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF.
- CVE-2026-120292: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses MR::message route. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes.
- CVE-2026-120285: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses PSC::ip_address. Affects BIG-IP (all modules), BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF.
- CVE-2026-116953: an iRule that uses GENERICMESSAGE::route on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes.
- CVE-2026-120722: an iRule that uses DNS::scrape on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP DNS and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. The company's advisory lists BIG-IP CNF as not vulnerable, but its CVE record, updated today, lists CNF as affected.
F5's security notification lists the 22 advisories it published today, including 10 for NGINX.
For the six critical flaws, the only fixes are engineering hotfixes, builds that the company issues between its normal software releases. No scheduled release is listed as a fix, and the advisories provide no workaround until a hotfix is installed.
The company warns that "engineering hotfixes do not undergo the extensive QA assessment of scheduled software releases." Its hotfix policy adds that they come with no warranty or promise that they will work.
A system on a custom engineering hotfix needs a new one from the company's support team.
BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes is fixed in BNK-2.4.2-EHF1, BNK-2.3.4-EHF1 and BNK-2.2.5-EHF1, for versions 2.4.0 to 2.4.2, 2.3.0 to 2.3.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.5. BIG-IP CNF, on the same version ranges, is fixed in CNF-2.4.2-EHF1, CNF-2.3.4-EHF1 and CNF-2.2.5-EHF1 for CVE-2026-121805 and CVE-2026-120285.
The company checks only versions that are still within technical support, so an older release missing from its tables has not been shown to be safe.
Today's flaws differ from CVE-2026-94127, an APM flaw that F5 disclosed on September 22 and that was later exploited. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day.
That flaw is a heap-based buffer overflow in APM setups that serve as OAuth authorization servers, allowing attackers to run code without logging in. Today's six are stack-based overflows that need different settings.
Six Other BIG-IP and BIG-IQ Flaws
Today's advisories also cover six lower-rated flaws in BIG-IP and BIG-IQ, each with its own fix. The scores below are CVSS v3.1:
- CVE-2026-125274 (iControl SOAP, 8.8): A user with network access and at least the Guest role can send an unauthorized management request. The company says this may allow them to run system commands, create or delete files, or disable services. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10 and 17.1.3.6, and in BIG-IQ 8.4.2.3. Until then, the SOAP advisory explains how to limit iControl SOAP access to trusted networks and warns that blocking it on self-IP addresses may break high-availability setups.
- CVE-2026-120718 (iControl REST, 8.1): iControl REST tokens may not expire as expected. An attacker who already holds a token may be able to extend how long it stays valid unless its owner deletes it. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.2, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6. As a workaround, scripts that create tokens can be changed to delete them when they are no longer needed.
- CVE-2026-125272 (APM, 7.5): When an APM access profile on a virtual server has a per-request policy with a form-based Logon Page, an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes as the six critical flaws.
- CVE-2026-126822 (APM SAML, 7.5): When an access profile is set up as a SAML Service Provider (SP), an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes. Until then, the company suggests removing the SAML Auth agent if SAML SP is not needed, and limiting access to that virtual server to trusted client networks.
- CVE-2026-126336 (APM SAML, 7.5): A SAML SP agent with encrypted assertions turned on lets an attacker crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6, and the company recommends a high-availability setup to reduce the impact.
- CVE-2026-121812 (APM and SSL Orchestrator, 7.5): A per-request policy with the tmm.access.policytrace database key turned on lets an attacker crash TMM. The key is off by default. APM is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes, and for SSL Orchestrator the advisory lists fixes on the 21.1 and 17.1 branches only.

articles.title: “Me contactó con médicos de Stanford”, empleado de Nvidia reveló que Jensen Huang lo ayudó cuando tuvo cáncer
articles.text:
Jensen Huang, cofundador y exdirector ejecutivo de Nvidia, recibió el reconocimiento público de uno de sus empleados después de que este revelara cómo lo ayudó durante su lucha contra el cáncer. Se trata de John Zedlewski, un alto ejecutivo de la compañía que explicó que Huang utilizó sus contactos en la Universidad de Stanford para facilitarle el ingreso a un ensayo clínico cuando su estado de salud se había complicado.
El testimonio fue publicado en la red social X el 13 de noviembre dfe 2026 y apareció en medio de las críticas y discusiones sobre la personalidad del empresario, quien dejó la dirección de Nvidia después de más de tres décadas al frente de la compañía.
“Tengo un caso de cáncer particularmente grave. Cuando volví a ser hospitalizado en mi peor momento el año pasado, se lo conté a Jensen. Inmediatamente se puso en contacto con sus contactos en Stanford, quienes lograron superar los obstáculos burocráticos y conseguir que me admitieran en un ensayo clínico para el que he resultado ser un candidato perfecto”, escribió Zedlewski.
El ejecutivo también expresó su agradecimiento por la intervención del empresario y cuestionó las versiones que lo describen como alguien indiferente a sus trabajadores.
“Creo que cada uno puede tener su propia opinión sobre los acontecimientos recientes. Pero cualquier afirmación de que a Jensen realmente no le importaban sus empleados es simplemente inexacta. Personalmente, le debo más de lo que puedo expresar”, añadió.
Quién es el empleado de Nvidia que contó su experiencia con Jensen Huang
John Zedlewski ocupa el cargo de vicepresidente de Ciencia de Datos Acelerada en Nvidia y lleva más de una década vinculado a la compañía. Su trayectoria incluye trabajos relacionados con RAPIDS, aprendizaje profundo para vehículos autónomos, imágenes médicas y análisis de datos.
Su publicación no se limitó a contar el episodio relacionado con su enfermedad. También aprovechó para explicar qué aspectos del liderazgo de Huang considera importantes para mantener la cultura de innovación de Nvidia.
Zedlewski sostuvo que la mejor manera de reconocer el legado del empresario es continuar desarrollando tecnología y mantener los principios de trabajo que aprendieron durante años dentro de la organización.
Entre ellos mencionó la importancia de trabajar con rapidez, asumir riesgos calculados y reconocer los errores sin ocultar información. También destacó una filosofía interna conocida como Speed of Light, que busca que los equipos técnicos alcancen el máximo rendimiento posible de sus sistemas.
El estilo de liderazgo de Jensen Huang genera opiniones divididas
El testimonio del vicepresidente de Nvidia contrasta con otras experiencias recogidas por The Wall Street Journal en un reportaje sobre la cultura laboral de la compañía.
El periódico describió un ambiente de trabajo exigente, con reuniones en las que Huang cuestionaba duramente a sus colaboradores cuando consideraba que no tenían suficiente conocimiento sobre sus proyectos o no conseguían los resultados esperados.
Algunos trabajadores señalaron que el empresario podía reprender públicamente a sus subordinados y generar situaciones de mucha presión. Sin embargo, otros destacaron su participación directa en los problemas técnicos y su capacidad para involucrarse en las decisiones de diferentes equipos.
Zedlewski también recordó una reunión relacionada con el desarrollo de vehículos autónomos. Durante ese encuentro, Huang pidió a un ejecutivo que explicara en una pizarra cómo funcionaba un sistema informático para identificar operaciones innecesarias que reducían su velocidad.
Para el trabajador, esa experiencia demuestra que los directivos deben conocer los detalles técnicos de sus proyectos y no limitarse a recibir informes de sus subordinados.

- Un casque léger : 217 g, avec un arceau flexible pensé pour les longues sessions, selon la fiche Amazon.
- À savoir : le prix barré de 229,95 € est le prix conseillé affiché par Amazon, et nous n’avons pas testé ce modèle.
Logitech MX Vertical : 52,50 € de remise sur la souris ergonomique, à 47,49 €
Cette souris verticale sans fil se connecte en Bluetooth ou avec un récepteur USB Unifying, avec un capteur de 4 000 PPP, quatre boutons et une charge rapide, selon la fiche Amazon. Elle fonctionne sur PC, Mac et iPadOS. Clubic l’a testée en 2018 : notre test de la Logitech MX Vertical date donc d’avant cette version vendue aujourd’hui.
✅ Points forts
- Une prise en main verticale : la forme ergonomique vise à soulager le poignet, d’après la fiche Amazon.
- Multi-dispositifs : Bluetooth ou récepteur USB Unifying, sur PC, Mac et iPadOS.
- À savoir : le prix barré de 99,99 € est le prix conseillé affiché par Amazon, et notre test remonte à 2018.
Dreame H12 Pro Ultra : 151 € de remise sur l’aspirateur laveur, à 148 €
Cet aspirateur laveur annonce 16 000 Pa d’aspiration, un lavage des serpillières à 60 °C avec séchage en 30 minutes et un nettoyage automatique à double rotation, selon la fiche Amazon. Nous ne l’avons pas testé.
✅ Points forts
- Un lavage à chaud : serpillières lavées à 60 °C et séchées en 30 minutes, d’après la fiche Amazon.
- Un nettoyage automatique : double rotation avec racleur, annoncé par Dreame.
- À savoir : le prix barré de 299 € est le prix conseillé affiché par Amazon, et nous n’avons pas testé ce modèle.
Ecovacs Deebot T50 Pro Omni Gen3 : 300 € de remise sur le robot aspirateur laveur, à 299 €
Ce robot annonce 25 000 Pa d’aspiration, un lavage des serpillières à 75 °C avec séchage à 45 °C et une station Omni qui se vide seule, selon la fiche Amazon. Nous avons testé le Deebot T50 Pro OMNI, dont ce Gen3 est une déclinaison : notre test louait son aspiration, mais jugeait le lavage perfectible. Nous n’avons pas testé la version Gen3.
✅ Points forts
- Une station tout-en-un : vidage automatique de la poussière et ajout de solution de lavage, selon la fiche Amazon.
- Un séchage à chaud : serpillières lavées à 75 °C puis séchées à 45 °C, annoncé par Ecovacs.
- À savoir : l’offre est vendue par ECOVACS ROBOTICS FRANCE sur Amazon, et notre test portait sur le T50 Pro OMNI, pas sur cette version.
Les meilleures ventes : ce que les lecteurs achètent le plus
EA Sports FC 27, GTA VI, l’Echo Dot, la Kindle Colorsoft et le MacBook Air M5 figurent en haut du classement des ventes de leur catégorie sur Amazon, au moment de notre relevé. S’y ajoutent le Google Pixel 11, noté 8/10 par Clubic, et la TV OLED Samsung 55S85H, déjà achetée par nos lecteurs ces deux dernières semaines.
EA Sports FC 27 : 39,60 € de remise sur le jeu en tête des ventes de la catégorie Jeux, à 40,39 €
Version disque pour PlayStation 5, l’édition standard annonce un gameplay retravaillé, avec des corners dynamiques et une IA offensive améliorée, le mode Carrière Manager avec un marché des transferts repensé, et Football Ultimate Team, selon la fiche Amazon. Nous ne l’avons pas testé.
✅ Points forts
- Un jeu en tête des ventes : n° 1 du classement Jeux d’Amazon au moment de notre relevé du 18 novembre.
- Les modes habituels : Carrière Manager, Clubs et Football Ultimate Team, d’après la fiche Amazon.
- À savoir : c’est un disque pour PS5, non compatible PS4, l’offre court jusqu’au 6 décembre et le prix barré de 79,99 € est le prix conseillé affiché par Amazon.
GTA VI sur PS5 : 19,01 € de remise sur la version en boîte, à 79,99 €
Le jeu sort le 19 novembre. Cette version en boîte contient un code de téléchargement, pas un disque, réservé aux comptes PlayStation enregistrés en France, selon la fiche Amazon. Nous ne l’avons pas testé.
✅ Points forts
- Un jeu très demandé : n° 2 du classement Jeux d’Amazon au moment de notre relevé du 18 novembre.
- Une livraison avant la sortie : l’expédition a commencé le 12 novembre, pour télécharger le jeu à l’avance, d’après la fiche Amazon.
- À savoir : c’est un code et non un disque, valable pour un compte PlayStation français, et le prix barré de 99 € est l’ancien prix affiché par Amazon.
Echo Dot (2022) : 50 € de remise sur l’enceinte connectée, à 39,99 €
Cette enceinte connectée fonctionne en Wi-Fi et en Bluetooth, intègre un hub pour piloter les appareils compatibles et un bouton coupe-micro, selon la fiche Amazon. Elle donne un accès anticipé à Alexa+. Nous ne l’avons pas testée.
✅ Points forts
- Un modèle très demandé : n° 5 du classement des enceintes connectées d’Amazon au moment de notre relevé du 18 novembre.
- Toute la maison : commande vocale des appareils compatibles et routines déclenchées par les capteurs de mouvement ou de température intégrés, selon Amazon.
- À savoir : le prix barré de 89,99 € est le prix conseillé affiché par Amazon, et nous n’avons pas testé ce modèle.
Kindle Colorsoft 16 Go : 135 € de remise sur la liseuse couleur d’Amazon, à 164,99 €
Notre test de la Kindle Colorsoft portait sur la version Signature Edition : il a salué sa gestion de la rémanence, meilleure que celle des autres liseuses couleur testées, avec quasiment aucune image fantôme. La version 16 Go de cette offre est un modèle différent, que nous n’avons pas testé.
✅ Points forts
- Un écran couleur sans fantômes : sur la Signature Edition testée, la rémanence est quasi absente, même sur des livres entièrement coloriés.
- Une liseuse Kindle simple : interface claire et pages qui se tournent presque instantanément, selon notre test de la Signature Edition.
- À savoir : l’écran couleur est à 150 ppp, et notre test jugeait ce format de 7 pouces peu adapté aux BD et aux comics.
MacBook Air 13" M5 : 200 € de remise sur l’ultraportable d’Apple, à 1 199 €
Notre test du MacBook Air M5 retient un ultraportable sans ventilateur, silencieux, avec un SSD doublé et un écran IPS limité à 60 Hz. Nous avons mesuré environ 12 heures d’autonomie, une de moins que le MacBook Air M4. Notre unité de test était la version 1 To, pas cette version à 512 Go.
✅ Points forts
- Un ultraportable silencieux : pas de ventilateur, et des performances solides pour l’usage quotidien lors de notre test.
- Un SSD plus rapide : les vitesses de lecture et d’écriture ont doublé par rapport à l’an dernier, selon notre test.
- À savoir : l’autonomie mesurée est d’environ 12 heures, et l’écran reste à 60 Hz.
Google Pixel 11 : 350 € de remise sur le smartphone noté 8/10, à 649 €
Notre test du Google Pixel 11 lui a attribué 8/10. Son écran OLED de 6,3 pouces à 120 Hz monte jusqu’à 3 000 nits, et il a tenu 17 h 43 au test d’autonomie PCMark, pour 197 g sur la balance. Cette version 256 Go Noir Volcanique est vendue et expédiée par Amazon.
✅ Points forts
- Une autonomie solide : 17 h 43 au test PCMark lors de notre test.
- Un écran très lumineux : OLED de 6,3 pouces à 120 Hz, jusqu’à 3 000 nits en pic.
- À savoir : pas d’écran LTPO, et le GPU perd près de la moitié de ses performances après quelques minutes de jeu intensif.
Samsung 55S85H : un OLED 4K à 120 Hz avec 596,20 € de remise, à 899 €
Ce téléviseur OLED de 55 pouces passe en 4K à 120 Hz, avec une optimisation automatique des réglages selon le jeu, l’assistant Vision AI Companion et le son 3D OTS Lite. Il est livré avec une télécommande solaire. Nous ne l’avons pas testé.
✅ Points forts
- Un OLED pensé pour le jeu : 4K à 120 Hz, faible latence et réglages ajustés automatiquement selon le jeu, d’après la fiche Amazon.
- Un son qui suit l’action : la technologie OTS Lite diffuse un son 3D autour de l’écran, selon Samsung.
- À savoir : le prix barré de 1 495,20 € est le prix conseillé affiché par Amazon, et nous n’avons pas testé ce modèle.
Black Friday 2026 : chez Amazon, les remises ont déjà commencé
Le Black Friday tombe le vendredi 27 novembre, et le Cyber Monday le lundi 30. Amazon n’a pas attendu ces dates : plusieurs offres de cette sélection portent déjà un badge « Offre Pré-Black Friday » ou « Offre à durée limitée ». Les prix ont été relevés le 18 novembre et peuvent encore bouger d’ici la fin du mois. Pour suivre les nouvelles baisses sans y passer vos soirées, notre page Black Friday réunit chaque jour les offres retenues par la rédaction.
Comment lire une promo Amazon avant de cliquer ?
Regardez d’abord le prix barré : sur Amazon, c’est tantôt le prix conseillé par le fabricant, tantôt un ancien prix, et la remise se calcule sur ce repère. Vérifiez ensuite qui vend et expédie le produit, car les conditions de livraison et de retour changent d’un vendeur à l’autre. Comparez enfin la version exacte, avec sa mémoire ou sa taille d’écran, plutôt que le seul nom du modèle. Pour un smartphone, une bonne note en test pèse plus qu’un fort pourcentage, et nos tests de smartphones aident à faire le tri.

articles.title: Critical Apache Roller RCE Flaw Under Active Exploitation, No Authentication Required
articles.text:
A critical security flaw in Apache Roller, an open-source, Java-based blogging platform, has come under active exploitation in the wild, according to the Apache Software Foundation (ASF)
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of unauthenticated deserialization in the XML-RPC endpoint that could lead to remote code execution.
"Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code," project maintainers said. "The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester."
ASF also noted that the vulnerability is the same as CVE-2026-82384 (CVSS score: 9.8), which was patched in September 2026 and listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected.
"This issue is being actively exploited," it added. ASF did not share any details on how the vulnerability is being exploited, or who is being targeted as part of these efforts.
A security researcher named n0mi1k has been credited with finding the flaw, and Matt Raible has been acknowledged for reporting it.
Users are advised to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled.
If immediate patching is not an option, it's recommended to set "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping, and then restart Roller.
"Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting," ASF noted.

articles.title: Qué es Direct, la nueva app de Meta para chatear sin tener cuenta de Instagram
articles.text:
Meta anunció Direct, una aplicación de mensajería independiente que traslada los chats privados de Instagram a un espacio propio y permite registrarse sin tener una cuenta en esa red social.
Basta un correo electrónico o un número de teléfono para crear un perfil. Quienes ya usan Instagram pueden ingresar con las mismas credenciales y sus conversaciones se sincronizan entre ambas aplicaciones.
Cómo funciona el registro con y sin cuenta de Instagram
La aplicación conserva una apariencia cercana a la bandeja de mensajes de Instagram. Quienes inicien sesión con sus credenciales habituales trasladan de forma automática sus chats existentes al nuevo entorno.
Para quienes prefieren prescindir de Instagram, el registro se completa con una dirección de correo o un número telefónico. Sin embargo, esta vía exige un paso adicional: agregar contactos de forma manual mediante el nombre de usuario de Instagram de cada persona o un código QR.
Esa diferencia marca dos rutas de acceso distintas. Una llega con la bandeja ya conectada a la cuenta previa; la otra obliga a construir la lista de contactos desde cero, algo que podría añadir fricción a la experiencia inicial.
Qué funciones tiene Direct en los chats
Direct incorpora herramientas pensadas para hacer las conversaciones más personales. Entre ellas figuran Draw, para dibujar o garabatear dentro de los chats, y Notes, la función que permite publicar actualizaciones breves de estado en la parte superior de la bandeja.
También incluye pegatinas personalizadas para expresarse, efectos de audio como risas de público o sonidos submarinos para añadir a las respuestas de voz, y temas visuales para personalizar el fondo de cada conversación. Según Engadget, el diseño admite tanto chats individuales como grupales.
Esta combinación de herramientas sitúa a Direct dentro de una tendencia más amplia de separación de funciones sociales entre plataformas, en una línea similar a la seguida por otras aplicaciones de mensajería que han reforzado sus opciones para grupos o planificación de encuentros, según el análisis de medios especializados.
Seguridad y controles para menores de edad
Meta afirma que Direct incorpora desde el inicio protecciones ya presentes en Instagram. Solo los contactos previamente conectados pueden iniciar un chat o sumar a alguien a un grupo, y cualquier persona puede reportar, bloquear, restringir o eliminar contactos en cualquier momento.
La compañía también señala que usará tecnología para detectar y actuar frente a interacciones potencialmente inapropiadas con usuarios jóvenes, aunque no detalla qué sistemas aplicará ni qué acciones concretas tomará al identificarlas.
Los padres podrán revisar con quién conversa su hijo adolescente, ajustar configuraciones de seguridad y fijar límites de tiempo diario de uso. Los adolescentes que accedan con su usuario y contraseña de Instagram conservan las mismas protecciones de las Cuentas de Adolescentes de esa red.
En cuanto a la edad mínima, Meta exige tener al menos 13 años para usar Direct. La empresa anunció que empleará tecnología para identificar de forma proactiva cuentas que puedan pertenecer a menores de esa edad y les pedirá verificarla; si no lo hacen, la cuenta será eliminada.
Por qué Meta separa la mensajería de Instagram
El jefe de Instagram, Adam Mosseri, ha señalado con frecuencia que la mensajería es la función más utilizada de la plataforma. Además, se había mostrado reticente a incorporar una bandeja de mensajes directos dentro de Threads, por considerar que podía resultar redundante tener varias apps para comunicarse con las mismas personas y generar problemas en el enrutamiento de notificaciones.
TechCrunch apunta un elemento adicional que Meta no menciona de forma explícita: al permitir usar la mensajería sin abrir Instagram, esos usuarios continúan contando como activos dentro del ecosistema de la compañía aunque nunca accedan a la red social.
Es poco probable que una aplicación centrada en Instagram sustituya a WhatsApp para la mayoría de las personas, según Engadget, aunque podría restarle actividad si usuarios sin cuenta de Instagram la eligen para enviar mensajes a sus contactos.
Meta describe el lanzamiento como una prueba limitada a Turquía y Tailandia y no ha anunciado fechas ni condiciones para extenderla a otros mercados.

articles.title: Cómo jugar GTA 6 antes del lanzamiento en Europa y América Latina: truco de Nueva Zelanda
articles.text:
El estreno oficial de Grand Theft Auto VI está fijado para el 19 de noviembre, pero hay un método conocido como el “truco de Nueva Zelanda” que permite adelantar el acceso al juego. La estrategia aprovecha que Rockstar Games desbloquea el título de forma escalonada según la medianoche de cada país.
El procedimiento consiste en modificar la región de la consola o de la cuenta para que figure como residente de Nueva Zelanda, el primer territorio donde el juego queda disponible. El resultado varía según la plataforma en la que está disponible el título, ya sea en Xbox Series X|S o PlayStation 5.
Cómo funciona el truco de Nueva Zelanda y a qué hora se desbloquea el juego
El mecanismo se basa en la diferencia horaria entre Nueva Zelanda y el resto del mundo. Como GTA VI se habilita a las 00.00 horas según el huso horario local de cada país, los jugadores que figuren registrados en territorio neozelandés ya pueden comenzar antes que el resto.
Esa medianoche neozelandesa equivale a las 12:00 del mediodía del 18 de noviembre en España peninsular. En el caso de América Latina, el horario de desbloqueo varía según cada país: a las 5:00 en México, El Salvador, Guatemala, Nicaragua y Costa Rica; a las 6:00 en Ecuador, Colombia, Perú, Cuba y Panamá; a las 7:00 en Venezuela, Bolivia y República Dominicana, y a las 8:00 en Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay y Chile.
Cómo cambiar la región en Xbox Series X|S
En las consolas de Microsoft, el cambio de ubicación no requiere aplicaciones externas y puede revertirse con facilidad. Los pasos consisten en encender la consola, pulsar el botón del mando para abrir la guía y entrar en “Perfil y sistema”.
Desde ahí, hay que seleccionar “Configuración”, luego “Sistema” y después “Idioma y ubicación”. En ese apartado se elige “Nueva Zelanda” como región y se confirma con la opción “Reiniciar ahora” para que el cambio surta efecto.
Una vez reiniciada la consola, el usuario puede comprobar si el sistema permite iniciar la partida de GTA VI antes de la hora de desbloqueo habitual en su país. El procedimiento es el mismo que utilizaron algunos jugadores con Call of Duty en lanzamientos anteriores, sin que se conocieran consecuencias en sus cuentas.
Por qué el método no funciona igual en PlayStation 5
En PlayStation 5, la situación es distinta porque Sony vincula las compras digitales al país configurado en la cuenta de PlayStation Network y no permite modificar esa región una vez creada la cuenta.
La única alternativa consiste en abrir una cuenta nueva y declarar Nueva Zelanda como país de residencia. Esto obliga a comprar el juego de nuevo en la tienda correspondiente a ese territorio, sin que la compra original quede vinculada a la cuenta principal del usuario.
Las advertencias antes de hacer el truco de Nueva Zelanda
Pese a la ausencia de una confirmación oficial, varios usuarios de PlayStation han reportado en redes sociales haber perdido el acceso a sus cuentas, compras y servicios después de crear perfiles con Nueva Zelanda como país de residencia.
El origen del riesgo está en los términos de servicio de Sony, que piden a los usuarios declarar información veraz, incluido el país de residencia real. Cuando la compañía detecta el uso de datos falsos para obtener un beneficio, considera que existe un incumplimiento que puede derivar en el bloqueo de la cuenta.
Esas restricciones pueden ser temporales o permanentes, y en algunos casos reportados impidieron el acceso a productos que el jugador ya había adquirido con anterioridad. Pero ni Sony ni Rockstar Games han emitido un comunicado oficial sobre baneos vinculados a este método.
Rockstar Games también podría incorporar verificaciones adicionales que bloqueen el acceso anticipado pese al cambio de región, según se advirtió. Ante este panorama, cualquier usuario que decida aplicar el truco de Nueva Zelanda debe asumir el riesgo de sufrir restricciones en su cuenta, sin garantías de que el adelanto de unas horas compense una eventual sanción.

articles.title: New EggStreme Malware Variant Goes Silent to Evade Security Tools in Government Attacks
articles.text:
The suspected Chinese advanced persistent threat (APT) group behind the sophisticated EggStreme malware has rebuilt its toolkit as it continues to target government organizations in the Philippines.
"When attackers are exposed, the cheap response is to rotate," Bitdefender said in a technical report shared with The Hacker News. "A file hash changes with every recompile, a domain costs a few dollars, and a new IP address costs less."
"The EggStreme operators did more than rotate – the agent we now see uses a different network protocol, has an enhanced command set, and comes in a passive variant that never beacons out. The infrastructure appears to be moving away from the one certificate authority that tied its older servers together."
The end result is that the changes allow it to bypass static signatures and heuristic detections built around the EggStreme malware framework when it was first exposed in September 2025.
Delivered via an as-yet-unknown initial access vector, EggStreme's defining characteristic is the use of DLL sideloading to execute payloads. It features multiple components as follows -
- EggStremeFuel (aka RawCookie), which conducts system profiling and deploys EggStremeLoader
- EggStremeLoader, which sets up persistence and decrypts and executes EggStremeReflectiveLoader
- EggStremeReflectiveLoader, which executes EggStremeAgent
- EggStremeAgent (aka Gorem RAT), the core component and a full-featured backdoor that enables system reconnaissance, lateral movement, data theft via an injected keylogger called EggStremeKeylogger, and reverse shell and file upload/download capabilities via a secondary backdoor called EggStremeWizard
It's worth noting that some components of the framework, such as EggStremeFuel and EggStremeLoader, have been put to use by another cluster tracked by Palo Alto Networks as CL-STA-1048 between March and September 2025.
Martin Zugec, technical solutions director at Bitdefender, told The Hacker News that CL-STA-1048's targeting of a Southeast Asian government entity and its associated tooling is "consistent with what we have observed" but emphasized that their research is more focused on the malware's capabilities and its evolution rather than attribution.
As is often the case with Chinese-aligned activity, the same tools can be used by more than one threat actor, Zugec noted, adding they have not compared infrastructure or victim data to determine if the two sets of activity constitute the same threat cluster as CL-STA-1048.
The latest findings from Bitdefender show a significant retooling of EggStreme's capabilities, including removing the keylogger from every agent build observed since then. Within two weeks after public disclosure, the threat actors are also said to have made other changes -
- The method EggStremeFuel uses to protect its configuration
- EggStremeLoader's cryptography and payload format, moving from RC4 to RC5 and to a custom cipher by the end of October 2025
- Added commands in EggStremeAgent that facilitate Active Directory reconnaissance, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) querying, TCP traffic forwarding, and execution of PowerShell, Portable Executable (PE), .NET assembly payloads
- Moving from a single certificate authority to campaign-specific certificate authorities
In addition, where lateral movement previously relied on Impacket-like tooling and on EggStremeAgent itself, newer incidents make use of an unmanaged system that sits outside of the organization's endpoint management but is still reachable by other workstations to stage the payloads and launch them via DLL sideloading using a Visual Basic Script (VBScript) file remotely run over Server Message Block (SMB).
Exactly how the operators gain access to the target is still unclear. "Our first investigation began with a logon script on a network share, and we could not determine how that script got there," Zugec said. "In the later activity we analyzed, the operators used valid credentials and a script staged on a host that the organization did not manage. That tells us how they moved once inside, not how they got in."
Some of the newer builds have been found to run in passive mode by opening a listening port and waiting for the operator to connect in as opposed to contacting an external command-and-control (C2) server.
Bitdefender also noted that there is no evidence at this stage to indicate EggStremeWizard has been discontinued by the attackers.
"The newer EggStremeAgent samples we analyzed do not show whether it is still being deployed because it is not part of the agent," Zugec said. "EggStremeWizard was an additional tool used alongside EggStremeAgent, not the primary implant, and the framework works without it. The keylogger is a separate component. Its absence from the newer agent builds reflects what the operators chose to compile into those builds, so we do not interpret its absence as evidence that the tool has been retired."
There is also some evidence that the attackers have also targeted Taiwan, but it has been treated with low to medium confidence.
"The speed of the loader changes says as much about the operators' maturity as about the cost of exposure," Bitdefender concluded. "The build-time design appears to be what makes rebuilds this fast. What they did not change is how they operate: sideloaded DLLs under system library names, staging through file shares, running from memory, and requiring mutual TLS."
Mustang Panda Targets Philippine Government Using ASEAN Summit Lures
As of late October 2026, Philippine government officials have also been targeted by Mustang Panda, a prolific China-aligned cyber espionage group, using ASEAN Summit lures to deliver PlugX using established tactics like DLL sideloading.
| Mustang Panda attack chain | 
"The package impersonated a Laos–Philippines bilateral meeting agenda from the Lao Ministry of Foreign Affairs," Dream Research Labs said in a report published last week.
"It named five officials and referenced plausible diplomatic priorities, requesting that the reader provide confirmation before the summit. Behind it was a delivery chain that installed PlugX remote-access malware while displaying the decoy agenda."
Earth Alux Uses Stealthy Tradecraft to Strike Southeast Asia
The disclosure comes as a China-nexus threat actor tracked as Earth Alux (aka Ink Dragon, Jewelbug, REF7707, and UAT-11587) has been attributed to a fresh set of attacks targeting Southeast Asian government entities since at least July 2025. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 has assigned the activity the designation TGR-STA-0049 (formerly CL-STA-0049).
"The defining signature of the threat actor behind the activity is the targeting of government entities, combined with the use of advanced custom payloads that are designed for high-stealth intelligence collection operations, with an emphasis on evading security detection tools," Unit 42 researcher Tom Fakterman said.
Attacks mounted by the group have historically deployed an advanced backdoor known as FINALDRAFT (aka Squidoor) since 2023. However, it has since expanded its malware arsenal to include two previously undocumented remote access trojans (RATs) called PerfectPioneer RAT (in July 2025) and KUKURAT (in March 2026).
Initial access to target networks is achieved via exploitation of vulnerable, unpatched Microsoft Exchange servers to deploy web shells like ASPXSpy and Godzilla, which are then used to deploy the RAT payloads. Alternatively, Earth Alux has leveraged phishing emails using decoy PDFs and lookalike domains to compromise victim hosts.
PerfectPioneer RAT is a Go-based malware that's launched via three different methods -
- DLL sideloading to launch a malicious DLL that reads, decrypts and executes XOR-encrypted shellcode containing the RAT
- Decoy installers for Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect that installs the legitimate program but also writes the malware to disk and executes it in the background
- Disguising executable files as PDF documents in phishing emails that, once launched, opens a decoy PDF document while the malware is launched in the background
The malware supports a number of features that enable the operator to gain remote control of the infected host. It facilitates file operations, shell execution, process management, keylogging, SOCKS5 proxy, screenshot capture, Window enumeration and manipulation, and CPU and memory utilization monitoring.
| PerfectPioneer RAT execution chain | 
It also ensures a connection to the C2 server remains active at all times and systematically cleans up temporary files and runs garbage collection if memory usage exceeds 100 MB to minimize forensic traces.
Furthermore, select variants of the malware come with an "isDangerousCommand" feature to avoid running administrative commands that would be highly destructive or noisy, thereby allowing it to be detected by security programs installed on the host. These include rm, curl | bash, wget | bash, and powershell -e, among others.
KUKURAT, in contrast, functions as a modular implant that's executed in networks already compromised by PerfectPioneer RAT. Written in C++, the backdoor implements its functionality as a separate DLL module that's loaded dynamically at runtime directly from the C2 server.
This allows the malware to be highly evasive and adapt its capabilities on the fly in response to shifting operational objectives. It supports the following features -
- Send system information and receive a configuration from the C2 server
- Take screenshots
- Log keystrokes
- Enumerate and terminate processes
- Perform file operations
- Execute shell commands via cmd.exe and PowerShell
- Conduct lateral movement via PsExec
- Carry out SMB credential brute-forcing
- Run Beacon Object Files (BOF)
- Facilitate local privilege elevation
- Ensure the malware remains active by means of a standalone watchdog executable
What's more, KUKURAT initiates bogus, legitimate-looking activity on the endpoint to camouflage and cover up its tracks based on a command issued by the threat actor. This includes -
- Generate 10 decoy HTTP requests per operational cycle to randomly selected domains that are extracted from a hard-coded list of 15 popular websites using randomly generated URL paths with an aim to blend C2 communications
- Mimic legitimate Google Chrome browser behavior by writing random data to the registry path HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\BrowserCrashRecovery, reading the data back, and deleting the key
- Create temporary files with random names and randomized content inside the system %temp% directory, and delete them
"Both PerfectPioneer RAT and KUKURAT use HTTP/3 as the primary method for communicating with C2 infrastructure," Unit 42 said. "While the adoption of HTTP/3 is rare across the broader malware landscape, its deployment in this campaign reflects an emerging trend among advanced threat actors."
The attacks have also been found to leverage established tools like PsExec, WMI, and Windows Remote Management (WinRM) to move laterally across compromised enterprise networks; collect credentials using Mimikatz, ProcDump, and SharpDPAPI; compromise Domain Controllers to deploy KUKURAT on local endpoints; and exfiltrate sensitive data such as files and emails.
"Through the deployment of KUKURAT and the PerfectPioneer RAT, the attackers behind this activity are actively evolving to stay ahead of traditional network defenses by implementing protocol-level evasion via HTTP/3 and QUIC over UDP," Unit 42 concluded.
"What makes this group particularly evasive is the extensive effort invested in maintaining operational security and remaining hidden on compromised endpoints. The group demonstrates a mature understanding of modern defensive ecosystems. They have even gone so far as to embed hard-coded administrative safety switches within their binaries to prevent their own operators from running loud or destructive commands that might trigger security alerts."

articles.title: Hackers target big brands like McDonald’s, Bayer, CarMax in new phishing scam
articles.text:
Hackers target big brands like McDonald’s, Bayer, CarMax in new phishing scam
Typosquatted attacks just became a lot more dangerous
- Attackers rapidly registered lookalike domains matching newly launched brand campaigns to capture mistyped traffic
- Typosquatting targeted major brands including McDonald’s, Bayer, CarMax, and Procter & Gamble
- Researchers warn these domains can enable phishing, credential theft, malvertising, and other scams before detection
Cybercriminals have reportedly found a way to make typosquatted domain scams more convincing, and are already trying out new campaigns, researchers are saying.
Security experts Symantec have outlined how they saw attackers targeting victims with typosquatted names of popular companies such as CarMax, McDonald’s, and Procter & Gamble.
Many people don’t pay close attention to spelling or typos, and threat actors turned it into a criminal enterprise. A malicious executable called Excsel.exe has a higher chance of being launched compared to one called malware-v2.exe. The same goes for websites - Goggle.com or, Facebook.com can be typed and navigated to without a second thought, and visitors who do that often risk losing their sensitive files or infecting their computers with malware.
The practice is called typosquatting and can be found all over the web - on websites, in file names, email addresses, social media profiles, and even mobile applications. But typosquatted domains have a rather short lifespan - they get flagged by users rather quickly and taken down by either domain registrars, or even law enforcement.
Typosquatting with a twist
But what if the victims couldn’t tell if the domain was typosquatted? What if the legitimate one is so fresh that it hasn’t yet established itself in the eyes and the browsers of its target audience? The idea obviously crossed some cybercriminals’ minds, since Symantec recently uncovered just that - typosquatted domains that were registered within a day of the legitimate one.
Symantec says it saw legitimate businesses registering a new domain through a corporate brand-protection registrar, and the crooks following up a day later with a registration of their own - on a Chinese domain registrar.
“Each time a client of CSC (Corporation Service Company) or MarkMonitor registered a new campaign domain, a one-letter lookalike was registered the next day through a China-based registrar. The pattern repeated 27 times, across domains belonging to Abbott Laboratories, Bayer, CarMax, McDonald’s, Procter & Gamble and Sanofi, among others,” Symantec explained.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
“In one case, CarMax registered carmaxclaims[.]com and kmxclaims[.]com through CSC on August 26. The next day, carmaxclaim[.]com and kmxclaim[.]com, each one letter shorter, were registered through a registrar in China. The campaign has not stopped. The same pattern appeared again as recently as November 11, 2026.”
The scam is genius on a number of levels. Not only are these domains infinitely harder to spot as being fake, but visitors who open them expect to hand over sensitive, personally identifiable data. “Most were campaign sites rather than corporate home pages, including patient-savings programs, sweepstakes, rebates, claims portals and legal settlements,” the researchers said.
What's the point?
Some of the names being abused in this campaign include Abbott Laboratories, Arlo Technology, Bayer, Beam Suntory, Bristol-Myers Squibb, CarMax, Greystar, Immunovant, Ipsos, Kroll, McDonald’s, Procter & Gamble and Sanofi.
Another reason why these scams are dangerous is the fact that these addresses are often printed, shown on television advertisements, distributed through pharmacy leaflets, or court-ordered settlement notices. As such, visitors often end up typing the addresses by hand, increasing the chances of landing on the wrong page.
In all 27 examples Symantec observed, the changes were in a single letter. The majority were simply singular versus plural - if the legitimate domain is ‘fyzadasavings’, the attackers would register ‘fyzadasaving’. Same goes for mypgsweeps, or healthspringproducers. Some added a single letter, while others dropped it.
The full list can be found on this link, but since the researchers said the scam was ongoing, it most likely is not exhaustive.
The endgame of the campaign is up for debate. All sites served one of three kinds of content - either a placeholder page that earned money via pay-per-click advertising feeds, scam blogs written around the typosquatted name, or fake search engines. But Symantec believes low-grade scam traffic may not be the end goal, and that advertising networks of this kind can be abused for malvertising and credential harvesting, as well.

articles.title: Fausse réunion Zoom : l'arnaque géante qui a permis de voler des millions dévoilée par le FBI
articles.text:
C'est une escroquerie de grande ampleur qui vient d'être démantelée par le FBI. Elle utilisait des vidéos de gens connus de la victime pour la pousser à télécharger un programme malveillant.
On n'arrête jamais le progrès dans le monde des escroqueries internet. On avait ainsi découvert le mois dernier l'escroquerie au faux support Microsoft, qui opérait depuis quasiment une décennie, et avait permis aux malfaiteurs de générer plusieurs millions de dollars. Mais il y a pourtant beaucoup plus impressionnant encore, comme on peut le voir avec cette annonce du FBI.
Une escroquerie par Zoom volant le visage des proches des victimes démantelée par le FBI
La FBI vient d'annoncer le démantelement d'une vaste infrastructure d'escroquerie, dans le cadre de l'opération « FaceStealer ». Une escroquerie au fonctionnement particulièrement sophistiquée.
Celle-ci commence par le vol de l'identité d'une personne connue de la victime, ou d'un professionnel connu dans son secteur. Cette fausse personnalité sollicite la victime via un message sur LinkedIn ou Telegram, puis l'invite à une conférence Zoom ou Teams. La victime intègre alors une conférence dans laquelle elle voit en vidéo la personne qui est connue, une vidéo prise précédemment par les pirates, avec d'autres participants aussi présents.
À un moment, l'un d'eux explique ne pas entendre le micro de la victime, ce qui est suivi par l'apparition d'un message d'erreur l'invitant à télécharger une mise à jour… qui est en fait un malware.
Quelque 400 millions de dollars volés en dix-huit mois
Et une fois ce programme téléchargé, les pirates ont accès à de nombreuses choses dans l'ordinateur de la victime. Il y a non seulement potentiellement ses comptes en cryptomonnaies, mais aussi les messageries et les réseaux sociaux, ce qui permet de préparer de nouvelles opérations de ce genre avec des proches de la victime (les pirates pouvant accéder à sa webcam et tenter de prendre une vidéo de la cible pour plus part).
Pour le FBI, il s'agit d'une opération très sophistiquée menée par la Corée du Nord. Particulièrement réussie, elle aurait notamment réussi à toucher des développeurs, des experts en cryptomonnaies ou même en cybersécurité. Au total, l'agence fédérale a retrouvé plus de 900 vidéos des victimes dans l'infrastructure démantelée. Le butin est lui estimé à plus de 400 millions de dollars en cryptomonnaie, pour une opération qui n'aura duré « que » dix-huit mois.
Source : France Info

articles.title: Hey, you stuffing cash into your mattress — this series of unfortunate tech outages is not connected, nor is it the end of our digital world
articles.text:
Hey, you stuffing cash into your mattress — this series of unfortunate tech outages is not connected, nor is it the end of our digital world
Fear-mongering isn't helping anyone
"What's going on?!" my commuter friend asked me, wild-eyed. "They told us to start stockpiling water, go to the bank, take out our money!" When I asked her who, she mentioned a mainstream media outlet.
I locked eyes with her to make sure I had her full attention: "Don't do that. This is not a calamity. It's not the end of the tech world."
"But… but… it's all happening. How could it all happen at once?"
"I know, it's an incredible coincidence, but that's also all it is, a coincidence."
She breathed a sigh of relief, and I could actually see the stress leaving her face. For the moment — perhaps until the next outage — she was soothed.
There's no arguing that this has been an unprecedented couple of weeks as we daisy-chained our way through one seemingly massive tech outage after another.
One damn thing after another
It started with Microsoft, and notably Microsoft Outlook, an email platform used by, according to some measures, half a billion people. Considering that Windows is still, according to StatCounter, used by over 76% of desktops, it stands to reason that many would also be using Outlook and other affected Microsoft services like Teams and Copilot.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
A day later, the US Fedral Aviation Authority called a very rare total US ground stop because of a telecommunications issue.
And hours after that, several US banks, specifically Chase (one of the biggest), were reporting that customers could not access their accounts via the app, and sometimes while physically at the bank locations.
But wait, there's more.
United delayed many departing flights while it worked out a tech issue. Then Apple's online services, including iCloud and some access to in-store services, were out for hours.
It's a lot, and people can be forgiven for thinking this all has to be connected.
In a way, they were, but not by a coordinated cyberattack, or even by the growing use of AI. No, they were all connected by the human- and built-in frailties of large-scale digital systems serving millions of people, and because we now live our lives digitally, any disruption is felt instantly by seemingly everyone.
In almost every instance, the companies and governing bodies reported that their hardware and/or software failed because of updates. Apple said its outage was due to an "internal update," while the FAA is now pointing to system-wide updates and one very overactive router.
Chase Bank blamed a software release that broke its own hardware, and United called its outage that impacted flight crews a "technology outage".
Finger, point at yourself
Basically, for all of these outages, the call was coming from inside the building. There were zero signs of cyberattacks or, say, a denial of service attack, where hackers try to overload servers with requests in order to bring down systems and sometimes gain access. No one reported malware attacks or ransomware.
While there's been some conjecture that the FAA outage was related to it trying to apply artificial intelligence to its antiquated system, the real culprit — that router — was far more mundane.
People, however, do not like coincidences. They were raised, after all, on the axiom: where there's smoke, there's fire. It does not help that some media, including TMZ, The New York Post, and the outlet my friend was watching, are stoking these fears with alarming and unfounded headlines.
Look at this front page (below). I honestly feel for the guy they dressed up as a prophet of doom; he looks like he's 15. At least they included the line "...but don't panic, experts say."
Speaking of alarmists, I don't know what TMZ was thinking with this story. Basically, it took a relatively hidden hack of Optimizely, which is apparently used by many sites, and turned it into a massive, global cyberattack. Except no one saw or felt it. As this story was running, I was on a very unhacked Zoom.
Running such a story when tensions, confusion, and anxiety are so high goes well past the point of irresponsible.
If there is a lesson in what's happened here, it's that these systems are fragile, and that we're still doing a poor job of QA testing before releasing updates into the wild.
Microsoft apparently did what it needed to do to test its Outlook update, but those tests didn't account for the scale of activity the patch would face in the wild. The FAA, meanwhile, apparently made the rookie error of applying an update during the busiest working hours.
This isn't the end... it's the beginning
The other lesson I take from this is that we're likely to see more of these outages. After all, infrastructure continues to age, and we have to swap out the old for new.
The age of AI means we'll be deploying powerful new patches that will be more efficient than ever, but, being AI, they may be slightly unpredictable, interacting with systems we didn't expect, or test for.
There's also the concept of shared infrastructure. Over the past few years, we've seen dozens of sites and services go down because a widely shared platform went offline. The best example might be cloud services. Many services do not host their sites and leave it to, for instance, Amazon Web Services. If AWS goes down, so do so many websites.
We've also seen patches that sit between services and widely used platforms like Windows take hundreds of sites and services down with them.
Finally, the power of AI is open to everyone, including hackers, who have been using it to scale up their cyberattacks. What once took a team of hackers now takes one and a legion of AI agents to find previously hidden vulnerabilities in — yes — ageing software.
So, we're not out of the woods. If anything, we're entering the digital age's forbidden forest. But for now, despite the past calamitous tech week, I think we can rest easy. This was not coordinated. This was not an attack. It was just a combination of sloppiness, and some very bad luck.

articles.title: New Attack Bypasses TPM Lockout to Crack Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs in Days, Not Years
articles.text:
On AMD-based PCs and some Intel PCs, the TPM lockout for Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs can be reset by someone who opens the PC's case, researchers at Technische Universität Berlin say.
That leaves short PINs open to guessing. In lab tests, the researchers found a four-digit Hello PIN on an AMD laptop and a 6-digit BitLocker PIN on an Intel laptop this way.
Both PINs were set by the researchers and found within 236 tries. From the speeds they measured, they calculate a worst-case of 40 hours for a four-digit Hello PIN, compared to 69 days with the lockout working as documented. For a default six-digit BitLocker PIN, the worst-case time drops from 19 years to 20 days.
AMD confirmed yesterday that its processor firmware has a flaw that allows the attack on some PCs with its chips. It plans fixes for most of those chips between November and February 2027. For now, the researchers advise adding at least two digits to Hello and BitLocker PINs.
The TPM in these PCs is a firmware TPM, built into the processor. Unlike a separate TPM chip, it has no secure storage of its own, according to the research paper the researchers posted late last week. So it keeps its saved state, including the count of wrong guesses, encrypted on the mainboard's flash chip.
If someone copies that saved state and later writes the old copy back, the count goes back too, unless the PC detects it. Newer PCs try to catch this with counters inside the flash chip, called RPMC, that can only go up.
On AMD PCs that use these counters, the processor's firmware never verifies that a counter actually increased. A small board placed between the processor and the flash chip can block the update and report success, causing the PC to accept the old state.
RPMC chips from flash maker Winbond have a different weakness, the researchers found. A brief drop in the chip's power supply, called a voltage glitch, can cause the chip to reveal the secret key that signs its counter values. With that key, which took about a second to extract with their best settings, the board can forge any counter value.
On the Intel laptop they tested, one glitch was enough: the laptop's firmware feeds the chip the same value at every boot, so the leaked key kept working after each restart.
For the Hello test, the researchers attacked a locked HP OmniBook 3 with an AMD Ryzen AI 5 330 processor and a BitLocker-encrypted drive. Their setup typed PINs from 1000 upward and reached the correct one, 1235, after 236 tries in 57 minutes.
Windows still forced a restart after every 5 incorrect PIN attempts on that laptop, but no lockout delay was applied. Microsoft's lockout defaults lock the TPM after 32 wrong tries and forget one failure every 10 minutes.
The BitLocker test ran on a Framework Laptop 13 with an Intel Core Ultra 5 125H processor and Winbond flash. BitLocker's startup prompt adds no limit of its own, so each reset gave a fresh 32 tries. The setup found the PIN, 123457, after 236 tries in 6 minutes and 55 seconds.
In both tests, the researchers took the flash chip off the mainboard and wired in their own board. A script read the screen, typed PINs, and restarted the laptop through a KVM switch. They also changed firmware settings to slow each laptop's link to the flash chip, because their board could not keep up at full speed.
The researchers make two further claims that their tests did not cover. Either method could be used against either PIN. A recovered Hello PIN can also unlock keys tied to the device and enable Hello-based single sign-on at work, and, in some configurations, pass a multi-factor check.
The researchers have published their attack firmware, board designs, and scripts. They say reproducing the RPMC attacks is not plug-and-play and needs one of their boards. Neither the paper nor the vendor notices published so far describe attacks outside the lab.
Which PCs the Attack Works On and What Vendors Say
Whether the attack works depends on the processor and the flash chip:
- AMD-based PCs with RPMC flash: open to the board that blocks counter updates. The chipmaker has confirmed the firmware flaw behind this and plans to fix it.
- AMD-based PCs without RPMC flash: on two AMD desktops in the researchers' tests, writing an old copy back with an ordinary flash programmer reset the count, requiring no board. They conclude that AMD processors likely have no other protection against this, though two desktops may not be representative of all AMD systems.
- PCs that rely on Winbond RPMC flash: the researchers say these are open to the leaked-key method whatever the processor, and that only a new chip design can fix it.
- Intel PCs without RPMC-like flash: three Intel systems detected the same write-back in those tests.
The researchers expect the AMD firmware flaw to affect AMD PCs that use the Microsoft Pluton security core as their TPM, but did not show this.
On an AMD PC, the owner can boot Linux, for example from a live USB stick, and run the command grep . /sys/bus/pci/drivers/ccp/*/rpmc_* from the researchers' exposure check. The output indicates whether RPMC flash is present and enabled, which tells the owner which of the two methods applies. Missing files do not mean the PC lacks RPMC.
For Intel PCs, the researchers know of no such check. Owners would have to open the PC and look for a Winbond chip marked 25R or 74M.
AMD tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-43613 and assigns it a CVSS score of 5.1 in a security bulletin published yesterday.
The chipmaker says attacks requiring physical access fall outside its product security threat model, but that "RPMC is intended to stop this type of interposer attack." The researchers first told it about the flaw in February.
The chipmaker's fix targets run from November to February 2027 across Ryzen, Ryzen AI, Ryzen Threadripper, Athlon and EPYC chips, and one unnamed product has no date yet. These are planned dates for its own firmware, not updates already out for PCs.
The bulletin does not cover AMD PCs without RPMC flash. It also does not say whether the update will prevent an attacker from installing older, unfixed firmware on the PC, which the researchers say a fix must prevent.
Intel, whose processor was in the BitLocker test laptop, said in a security announcement earlier this week that the research "did not demonstrate a vulnerability in an Intel component". That matches the tests, in which the attack on the Intel laptop needed the Winbond chip's flaw.
According to the researchers, Intel's security team called the reused value a weakness rather than a vulnerability.
The researchers told Microsoft in April. According to them, the company rated the Windows Hello report as "moderate severity" and below its bar for an immediate fix, issued no CVE or bounty, and committed to raising its recommended minimum Hello PIN length to six digits.
At the company's request, the researchers filed the BitLocker finding as a separate report for a different team. The company declined to give them any further written statement for the paper.
Separately, a Windows 11 test build released late last week makes six digits the minimum for personal-account Hello PINs, with an option to use four. The release notes give no reason, and features in that test channel may never reach regular releases.
According to the researchers, Winbond was first told about its chips' weakness to voltage glitches in January 2025 and received a second report in April showing that a glitch also leaks the key. The flash maker is studying the issue, possibly including a new chip design, but has not committed to a fix or a date.
What Owners and Admins Can Do
Two extra digits make a large difference in the researchers' figures:
| Worst-case time to find a numeric PIN |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| PIN length | With the documented lockout | Hello attack (AMD laptop) | BitLocker attack (Intel laptop) | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 digits | 69 days | 40 hours | 5 hours* | 
| 6 digits | 19 years | 168 days | 20 days | 
| 8 digits | 1,903 years | 46 years | 6 years | 
* BitLocker accepts a four-digit PIN only if an admin lowers the six-digit minimum. The times are worst cases calculated from speeds measured on one laptop each.
In May, Microsoft advised moving BitLocker from TPM-only to TPM+PIN to block the YellowKey bypass, as part of its YellowKey mitigation. The same TPM lockout guards that PIN.
Steps for each setup:
- Windows Hello for Business: raise the Minimum PIN length policy, under Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > PIN Complexity. If it is not set, Windows requires six digits, a worst case of 168 days in the table above, and admins can set it as low as four. The PIN policy settings page lists it on the PIN settings tab.
- BitLocker: raise the Configure minimum PIN length for startup policy, which allows 4 to 20 digits and requires six by default. Turning on "Allow enhanced PINs for startup" lets letters and symbols, which the BitLocker PIN guidance recommends for older hardware.
- AMD-based PCs: install the firmware update with the chipmaker's fix when one is available for your PC. Until then, the chipmaker advises keeping PCs under physical control and watching for signs of tampering.
- PCs that rely on Winbond RPMC flash: the flash maker has not committed to a fix, according to the researchers. Intel advises its customers to ask their PC maker about updates.

articles.title: LeBron James demandó a una app de apuestas por un anuncio con su imagen y voz creados con IA
articles.text:
LeBron James demandó a los fundadores de Bron, una aplicación de apuestas deportivas con inteligencia artificial (IA), ante un tribunal federal de Nueva York, Estados Unidos. Los acusa de usar sin permiso su apodo, su imagen y una voz sintética en un anuncio con el que buscaron fama para su producto.
La demanda, de 44 páginas, tiene como acusados a la empresa PlayVision, que opera la app, y a sus cofundadores Anish Gupta y Marc Zoghby. James pide una orden judicial que les prohíba usar su identidad y el nombre “Bron”, además de una indemnización por daños.
El anuncio que mostró a un James creado con IA
El video apareció el 4 de noviembre de 2026 en la cuenta de X de Gupta. Según el escrito, muestra a una versión de James generada con IA en un vestuario, con una camiseta que dice “Bron” sobre el número 23 y sus tatuajes. Habla con una voz que, según la demanda, imita la suya.
En el anuncio, esa figura recorre apuestas sobre otros jugadores de la NBA desde un teléfono y menciona a Kalshi, una plataforma de mercados de predicción. Según la demanda, James tiene un acuerdo de patrocinio con Polymarket, competidora directa de Kalshi, y el anuncio podría perjudicar esa relación.
El escrito sostiene que el video no aclaraba que James no tenía relación con la app, ni que la figura había sido generada con IA, ni incluía un mensaje de juego responsable. Agrega que reunió cerca de un millón de vistas en X en un día.
James afirma que su aval “es único” y que recibe decenas de millones de dólares por asociar su nombre con un producto. Dice que nunca prestó su nombre ni su voz a los acusados.
La carta de advertencia y la respuesta de los fundadores
Los abogados de James enviaron el 5 de noviembre de 2026 una carta para exigir que cesara el uso de su identidad y del nombre “Bron”. Pidieron avisar por escrito a todos los usuarios que apostaron que James no tiene relación con la app. Gupta respondió esa noche que habían retirado el material y que cambiarían el nombre.
Según la demanda, solo se cumplió la retirada del anuncio de las cuentas de la empresa. El 6 de noviembre, Gupta publicó un video que decía que era hora de un nombre nuevo, pero sin revelarlo. El 16 de noviembre, en LinkedIn, volvió a bromear con una posible demanda.
Gupta escribió en redes sociales que el nuevo nombre se anunciaría el miércoles 18 de noviembre, según informó la agencia AP. Hasta el momento de la demanda, la app seguía en la tienda de Apple como “Bron - AI Sports Analysis” y cobraba suscripciones de “Bron Pro”.
La ficha de la tienda describe la app como una herramienta de análisis e información sobre apuestas que no acepta apuestas. En su correo del 5 de noviembre, Gupta dijo que la plataforma “no permite apostar, solo recomendaciones”.
Otro deportista también reclamó
El escrito indica que el anuncio muestra los nombres y fotos de otros jugadores, entre ellos Luka Dončić, Devin Booker y Giannis Antetokounmpo. Según la demanda, ninguno dio su consentimiento. Dončić envió a los acusados un reclamo para que dejaran de usar su imagen.
PlayVision participó en el programa de la aceleradora Y Combinator de otoño de 2025, según CNBC. La app y sus fundadores no habían respondido públicamente a la demanda al cierre de las notas consultadas, según Courthouse News y CNBC.
Los medios señalan que la demanda llega cuando varios jugadores de la NBA enfrentan escrutinio por sus apuestas, entre ellos Damon Jones, excompañero de James, acusado de apostar con información privilegiada. James sostiene que insinuar que un jugador activo apuesta en partidos de la NBA “no es un asunto trivial”.
El caso quedó registrado con el número 1:26-cv-10078 y está en su etapa inicial: no hay sentencia ni acuerdo, y la empresa no había presentado su respuesta al 18 de noviembre.

articles.title: UK government plan to cut EV targets could cost consumers £3bn a year by 2030, critics say — as public EV charging stays on track to hit £1/kWh in 2027
articles.text:
UK government plan to cut EV targets is a ‘truly terrible decision’, critics say — as networks warn public charging could hit £1/kWh in 2027
EV drivers in the UK could soon be hit from all sides
- The UK government could weaken its Zero Emissions Vehicle mandate
- Some critics say that would be a "truly terrible decision"
- Public EV charging could also get more expensive as tariffs spiral
Industry insiders believe the UK government is considering rolling back its Zero Emissions Vehicle (ZEV) targets, as major automotive manufacturers and industry bodies have warned that the supply of EVs is on-track to outstrip demand.
Despite battery electric cars taking 32% of all new car registrations in the UK this October, the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) chief executive, Mike Hawes, warned that support for the transition towards electrification, both by the government and the industry, “cannot be sustained indefinitely”.
Currently, the UK government wants 52% of all new vehicles sold to be electric in 2028, with that figure increasing to 80% by 2030 and eventually 100% by 2035, as combustion engine vehicles are phased out. But Hawes predicts a mere 37.5% share by 2028.
As a result, many corners of the auto industry are calling for a revision to the mandate, with insiders predicting the Labour party could weaken its approach in the coming weeks — something Caroline Lucas, former MP for Brighton and Green Party member, believes would be a “truly terrible decision at a truly terrible time”.
On top of the environmental issues, which could see an extra 7.4 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions in 2030, analysis by The Carbon Brief has also concluded that weakening the EV targets could also cost UK consumers £3 billion a year by 2030, thanks to electric vehicles proving more than £1,000 per year cheaper to own than petrol cars or plug-in hybrids.
To compound matters, there is the risk that billions of pounds worth of committed investment could be put at risk, including huge sums of funding by Charge Point Operators (CPO), as well as battery supply chains and tier one suppliers.
According to industry group Energy UK, the current mandate is “working in the way it was designed to work” and that it is the “single biggest driver of emissions reductions” in government climate plans.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Analysis: The UK government needs to get a grip
Whatever your personal stance on electric vehicles, any indecision from the UK government is likely to rock consumer confidence. This, alongside the introduction of a pay-per-mile tax for EV owners in 2028 is sending mixed messages to anyone thinking of making the switch to electric.
Analysis by charge point provider Zest has also concluded that the price of EV public charging could easily rise above the £1/kWh mark next year, thanks to the spiraling cost of the standing charge rate for the grid connection that network providers have to pay.
For example, electricity and grid costs take 48p of the 58p a driver pays per kWh before VAT at Zest's urban charging hub in Birmingham, leaving just 10p to cover every other cost.
According to the company, various freedom of information requests have revealed that the Treasury has known about the issue for some time.
Zest says it is now down to regulator Ofgem to step in and make the appropriate changes, but proposals to reduce the standing charge have been in discussion for three years without action.
Robin Heap, Zest's founder, called these network charges an “egregious cost burden” shouldered by EV drivers and that any speculation about weakening the ZEV mandate sends the “wrong signal to businesses committing millions to Britain’s electric future”.
While it is understandable that the UK government is trying to appease everyone with its renewed discussions around ZEV mandates, the indecision is not benefitting anyone.
It has been argued for years that both consumers and investors need a clear roadmap for the future, otherwise the country risks being left in transport limbo that’s only going to make motoring more expensive for everyone.

Leon has been navigating a world where automotive and tech collide for almost 20 years, reporting on everything from in-car entertainment to robotised manufacturing plants. Currently, EVs are the focus of his attentions, but give it a few years and it will be electric vertical take-off and landing craft. Outside of work hours, he can be found tinkering with distinctly analogue motorcycles, because electric motors are no replacement for an old Honda inline four.
