articles.title: Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show
articles.text:
After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.
When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.
Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .”
In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”
According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’”
Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said.
Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member said the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said.
A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products. Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed.
But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.”
Muse issues arose soon after September launch
Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September. An Inc. Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access. As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.
Eventually, a Meta spokesperson, David Singleton, responded to Aten on social media. Singleton insisted that Aten must have opted into granting “macOS system-level Full Disk Access” with the “Messages connector” enabled, if Muse was reading his private messages.
But Aten said the response wasn’t good enough.
“Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”
Around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked. In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.
“I didn’t even open the app today at all,” the user wrote, vowing to delete the app and report it to Apple. “This is crazy.”
In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”
It seems those instructions “landed on every message, not just messages pertaining to those specific actions, so its impact was wider than intended,” Singleton said. Also: “the way this instruction was provided to the model was done in a way that the model was not expecting (i.e. was not trained to expect).”
“We investigated with urgency and determined that this was caused by a bug introduced in the product that caused the model to hallucinate and was NOT a security or privacy issue,” Singleton wrote. “The bug has now been fixed.”
Aten warned that even though you can’t rely on Muse to explain its own behavior, the agent’s response coupled with Meta’s did little to rebuild trust after the shocking intrusion into his private messages.
“If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote. “You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.
“If an AI agent is going to read my private messages, there should be a moment when it clearly asks me whether that’s okay,” Aten wrote.
Reuters warned Signal intrusions are ongoing
Since Muse launched in September, it has been downloaded more than 10 million times, tapping Meta’s vast user network to quickly become one of the most-used AI agent tools.
But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to. For example, one staffer was surprised to find that “Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system.” That, too, gave access to private message preview text the staffer had not intended for the agent’s review.
Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private. It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need). The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.
However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences. On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.
On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported. But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.
That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported. Overall, Meta seemed to be interpreting permissions from Muse users “broadly,” Reuters concluded, in ways that privacy advocates and regulators may disagree with.
Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.
Part of that change would require operating systems to enforce rules that app developers set to rope off AI agents from sensitive data, Whittaker suggested. And following Reuters’ reporting, both Apple and Google are already weighing potential changes to “give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents.”
Apple, in particular, seemed disturbed by how Muse may be manipulating accessibility tools for people with disabilities. In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent. At that time, Apple concluded that “some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk.” And they promised to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
“We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said.
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

articles.title: Black da Amazon: AirPods Pro 3 com Tradução ao Vivo surge em 10x sem juros • Tecnoblog

Black da Amazon: AirPods Pro 3 com Tradução ao Vivo surge em 10x sem juros
AirPods Pro 3 têm Tradução ao Vivo e ANC aprimorado; fones wireless da Apple saem 27% mais baratos em rara oferta no prazo, faltando pouco para a Black Friday 2026
Os AirPods Pro 3 estão saindo por R$ 1.979 em até 10x sem juros na Amazon. Os fones de ouvido da Apple, com recurso de Tradução ao Vivo e ANC aprimorado, recebem desconto de 27% sobre o preço original de R$ 2.699.
Esta é uma rara oportunidade de comprar estes fones no prazo e no precinho, faltando poucos dias para a Black Friday 2026.
Um dos destaques dos AirPods Pro 3, que estão entre os melhores fones wireless do mercado, é o recurso de Tradução ao Vivo. Ele é ativado por gestos e traduz o idioma ouvido para o do usuário; a resposta é exibida na tela do celular, mas só funciona com iPhones.
O cancelamento ativo de ruído (ANC) foi melhorado nesta geração, ao abafar mais ruídos externos e oferecer os modos de uso Ambiente e Adaptável. A função não isola totalmente sons importantes, como os de trânsito, por motivos de segurança.
Os fones possuem um sensor que mede a frequência cardíaca, permitindo assim que o wearable ofereça, por meio do iPhone, suporte a mais de 50 atividades físicas no app Fitness.
O chip H2, os drivers de alta amplitude e os amplificadores de alcance dinâmico fornecem qualidade superior em graves e agudos, e os alto-falantes melhorados oferecem experiência melhorada de áudio espacial.
A bateria dos fones entrega até 8 horas de áudio com o ANC ativado, enquanto o estojo compatível com MagSafe garante autonomia de um dia inteiro, segundo a Apple. A certificação IP57 confere proteção contra poeira, água e suor.
Os AirPods Pro 3 (R$ 1.979 em até 10x sem juros) têm conectividade Bluetooth 5.3 e o kit inclui ponteiras de silicone de diferentes tamanhos, para um melhor ajuste nas orelhas do usuário.
A edição 2026 da Black November tem previsão de durar até o dia 30 de novembro, passando pelo evento principal, a Black Friday que ocorre em 27/11. Até lá, o varejo continuará oferecendo cupons de ofertas em eletrônicos com condições especiais.

Interface et fonctionnalités, difficile de faire plus simple
On n'a d'ailleurs pas encore commencé à tester le service que ce fameux catalogue s'invite déjà sur notre ordinateur. Alors qu'on pense télécharger une application VPN classique, c'est en réalité tout Avast One qui débarque, sur Windows comme sur macOS.
Depuis sa refonte, la suite fonctionne en effet comme un hub de services à la carte. Et même si seul le VPN est installé, l'interface fait la part belle aux autres produits de l'éditeur : antivirus, outils de nettoyage, navigateur sécurisé, dispositif de surveillance des fuites et boutique se disputent l'espace. Pas de publicités tierces, il est vrai, mais une bonne dose d'autopromotion. Une vieille habitude chez Avast.
Bon, c'est le jeu. Passée l'inscription, qui exige une adresse mail, il faut choisir ses emplacements de serveurs. Avast VPN n'en autorise que trois, parmi les localisations disponibles. Attention à ne pas se tromper : une fois la sélection confirmée, impossible d'en changer, à moins de passer à la version Premium, évidemment.
Par la suite, la prise en main est plutôt intuitive. Un clic sur une destination suffit à établir le tunnel VPN, et l'on peut passer d'un serveur à l'autre sans avoir à se déconnecter puis reconnecter manuellement. La transition est fluide et les connexions sont rapidement stabilisées.
Les paramètres sont en revanche assez dépouillés. Le kill switch est bien présent, mais désactivé par défaut : il faut donc penser à l'activer soi-même. Pour les protocoles, seul WireGuard est accessible, ce qui rend le mode de sélection automatique assez anecdotique. L'activation du VPN sur les réseaux Wi-Fi publics, le split tunneling, les autres protocoles et le bloqueur de traqueurs sont réservés à la version Premium. Dans les préférences générales, on peut au moins désactiver le lancement automatique d'Avast One au démarrage de l'ordinateur.
Enfin, le bouton « Appareils » ne permet pas, contrairement à ce que son nom suggère, de gérer les équipements associés au compte, mais sert à installer le VPN sur un smartphone, à l'aide d'un QR code, et à promouvoir son utilisation sur Smart TV, réservée… à l'abonnement payant.
A noter qu'Avast One embarque également un assistant IA capable de répondre en langage naturel aux questions de sécurité et d'aider au dépannage. Nous l'avons interrogé sur la possibilité de changer de ville américaine après avoir validé nos trois emplacements gratuits. Première réponse : des instructions héritées d'Avast SecureLine, sans rapport avec les restrictions de notre formule. Après correction, l'assistant reconnaît enfin que les destinations sont définitives, avant de nous conseiller malgré tout de changer de serveur ou de protocole. Plus curieux, il suggère lui-même des questions pertinentes sur la sélection des emplacements gratuits, sans parvenir à fournir une réponse cohérente.
Réseau et serveurs, un choix limité et définitif
Le réseau d'Avast compte quelque 140 localisations, mais cette diversité profite en réalité à la formule payante, Avast VPN ne donnant accès qu'à 40 emplacements. Les trois destinations sélectionnées s'appliquent à tous les appareils, et le choix se fait à la ville près. Si la connexion mouline à Chicago, par exemple, pas question de se rabattre sur New York ou une autre ville des États-Unis, quand bien même le VPN y dispose de serveurs.
L'offre gratuite se cantonne en outre aux serveurs classiques. Les emplacements optimisés pour le P2P, les connexions Double VPN (multi-hop) et la rotation automatique de l'adresse IP sont réservés à l'abonnement Premium.
Des débits capés à 75 Mb/s, et pas un de plus
Pour évaluer les performances d'Avast VPN, nous avons utilisé un MacBook Air M1 de 2020, relié en Ethernet à notre connexion fibre. Les mesures ont été réalisées sur nPerf, trois fois par jour (9 h, 13 h et 18 h) pendant trois jours, sans VPN puis avec WireGuard, sur les serveurs de Paris, Chicago et Tokyo, correspondant aux trois emplacements que nous avions sélectionnés.
Avast ne s'en cache pas : la formule gratuite est plafonnée à 75 Mb/s, une restriction annoncée dès le choix des emplacements. Et le moins que l'on puisse dire, c'est que la limite est respectée à la lettre. Sur notre connexion fibre, qui affiche une moyenne de 922,2 Mb/s en téléchargement et 787,6 Mb/s en envoi sans VPN, aucun relevé n'a dépassé ce plafond.
En France, les débits descendants atteignent 72,2 Mb/s en moyenne, contre 62,9 Mb/s en envoi, avec une latence de 3,3 ms. Les résultats varient à peine d'une session à l'autre, et le serveur américain s'en tire presque aussi bien avec 69,3 Mb/s en téléchargement et 65,5 Mb/s en émission. Au Japon, la distance commence à peser davantage sur les performances, sans provoquer d'effondrement des débits : 63,6 Mb/s en réception et 40,1 Mb/s en envoi.
La latence accuse en revanche le coup sur les destinations lointaines, avec 123,7 ms à Chicago et 294,4 ms à Tokyo, des valeurs peu adaptées aux usages qui exigent une grande réactivité, comme le jeu en ligne.
Avast exploite donc plutôt bien les 75 Mb/s qu'il accorde, avec des débits réguliers et relativement homogènes d'une destination à l'autre. Mais le plafond n'en demeure pas moins sévère : en France, notre connexion perd plus de 92 % de son débit descendant. Un bridage d'autant plus frustrant que WireGuard est parfaitement capable de soutenir des vitesses bien supérieures.
Sécurité et confidentialité, des garanties encore trop fragiles
Pour sécuriser les connexions, Avast VPN s'appuie sur WireGuard et utilise ses propres serveurs DNS, afin d'éviter que les requêtes ne transitent en dehors du tunnel chiffré. Le kill switch complète le dispositif, à condition de penser à l'activer dans les paramètres. Nos tests de fuite IP, DNS et WebRTC n'ont révélé aucune anomalie.
Concernant la confidentialité, Avast revendique une politique no-logs et assure ne conserver ni l'historique de navigation, ni les requêtes DNS, ni les adresses IP d'origine. L'éditeur enregistre néanmoins les volumes cumulés de données transférées et des métadonnées sur les serveurs VPN, conservés pendant 18 mois. Les événements de connexion et les interactions avec l'application sont gardés respectivement 12 et 18 mois, auxquels s'ajoutent des informations sur les appareils, les réseaux et les performances.
La documentation d'Avast manque toutefois de cohérence sur les durées de conservation. La politique de confidentialité d'Avast One mentionne 35 jours pour les horodatages des connexions VPN et les volumes de données transférées, sans expliquer clairement comment ces dispositions s'articulent avec celles de la politique propre au VPN.
Dans tous les cas, ces informations ne permettent pas de reconstituer un historique des sites consultés, mais la collecte est loin d'être inexistante. On rappellera aussi qu’Avast VPN impose la création d'un compte avec une adresse mail, sans préciser si les informations collectées peuvent être recoupées entre elles et rattachées à une personne identifiable.
La configuration initiale d'Avast One soulève également quelques réserves. Lors de nos essais, les autorisations d'analyse des données d'utilisation par des outils tiers et de personnalisation des réductions commerciales étaient activées par défaut. Même constat pour l'envoi d'échantillons de fichiers suspects, une option héritée de l'antivirus. Toutes peuvent être désactivées, mais il faut penser à faire un tour dans les paramètres de confidentialité.
Établi en République tchèque et soumis au RGPD, Avast traîne aussi une sacrée casserole en matière de respect de la vie privée. En 2024, l'éditeur a dû verser 16,5 millions de dollars dans le cadre d'un accord avec la Federal Trade Commission américaine, qui l'accusait d'avoir commercialisé, entre 2014 et 2020, les historiques de navigation collectés par ses antivirus et extensions de navigateur via sa filiale Jumpshot. Présentées comme anonymisées, ces données contenaient pourtant des identifiants uniques et des informations suffisamment précises pour permettre de réidentifier les internautes par recoupement.
L'affaire ne concernait pas directement le VPN, mais elle entache sérieusement la crédibilité d'Avast. L'éditeur a annoncé un audit indépendant de sa politique no-logs, confié à VerSprite et prévu pour ce mois de novembre. Ses conclusions permettront de mieux apprécier la portée des engagements pris par le fournisseur.
Streaming, les principales plateformes répondent présent
Bonne surprise du côté du streaming. Lors de nos essais, Avast VPN nous a permis d'accéder sans difficulté à Netflix, Prime Video et Disney+, malgré l'absence de serveurs spécialisés. Les catalogues s'adaptent à la localisation du serveur VPN, et les plateformes peuvent nous considérer comme étant en voyage.
Le plafond de 75 Mb/s laisse suffisamment de marge pour regarder des films et des séries, y compris en 4K, à condition que la connexion soit stable. Les trois emplacements imposés limitent en revanche les possibilités de repli si une plateforme venait à bloquer l'un des serveurs sélectionnés.
Avast VPN sur Android et iOS, l'essentiel sans Avast One
Sur Android comme sur iOS, Avast VPN dispose cette fois d'une vraie application autonome, débarrassée du hub Avast One et de ses sollicitations commerciales. L'interface se concentre sur le strict minimum, avec un bouton de connexion et l'accès aux trois emplacements associés au compte. Difficile de faire plus simple, mais pour activer ou couper le VPN, on n'en demande pas davantage.
Les réglages sont identiques à ceux de la version pour ordinateur. WireGuard demeure le seul protocole disponible, le kill switch doit être activé manuellement et les options de partage des données d'utilisation et de personnalisation des réductions commerciales sont cochées par défaut.
L’avis de la rédaction sur Avast VPN
Avast VPN est un bon VPN gratuit d’appoint, mais pas un service que l'on conseillerait les yeux fermés. Simple à utiliser, stable et sans quota de données, il répond aux besoins du quotidien sans réclamer de connaissances particulières. Le plafond de 75 Mb/s paraît bien sévère sur une connexion fibre, mais ne compromet pas les usages courants.
Le service n'est pourtant pas exempt de défauts. Les destinations verrouillées et les sollicitations commerciales ternissent une expérience autrement agréable. Mais ce sont le passé d'Avast en matière de respect de la vie privée et, plus encore, ses pratiques actuelles de collecte qui nous inquiètent davantage. L'audit annoncé devra apporter des garanties plus solides.
Pour regarder des vidéos en streaming ou protéger ponctuellement plusieurs appareils sans payer, Avast VPN fait l'affaire. Mais si la confidentialité prime, nous lui préférons Proton VPN Free ou Windscribe Free, dont les engagements reposent sur des audits publiés et des pratiques davantage éprouvées, même si le premier limite les connexions simultanées à un appareil et le second impose un quota mensuel de 10 Go. Des concessions que nous préférons accepter plutôt que de transiger sur la confiance accordée au fournisseur.

Les réponses à vos questions sur Avast VPN
Peut-on utiliser Avast VPN sans installer l'antivirus Avast ?
Oui. Sur Windows et macOS, le VPN est intégré à Avast One, mais l'installation de l'antivirus et des autres produits de la suite n'est pas obligatoire. Sur Android et iOS, le VPN dispose de sa propre application.
Avast VPN protège-t-il contre les virus et les sites malveillants ?
Non. Le VPN chiffre les échanges et masque l'adresse IP publique, mais ne remplace ni un antivirus ni une protection contre le phishing. Le bloqueur de traqueurs proposé par Avast est également réservé à la formule Premium.
Avast VPN se connecte-t-il automatiquement sur les Wi-Fi publics ?
Non. La connexion automatique sur les réseaux Wi-Fi publics ou vulnérables est réservée à Premium. Il faut donc penser à activer le VPN avant de naviguer, ainsi que le kill switch pour limiter les risques d'exposition en cas de coupure du tunnel.
Un site Internet peut-il détecter l'utilisation d'Avast VPN ?
Oui. Le VPN remplace l'adresse IP publique visible par celle du serveur, mais ne rend pas anonyme. Un site peut reconnaître une adresse appartenant à un fournisseur VPN, tandis que les cookies, les comptes auxquels on se connecte et les autorisations de géolocalisation peuvent continuer à révéler des informations sur notre identité ou notre position.
Peut-on continuer à utiliser une imprimante ou un NAS local avec Avast VPN ?
Oui, selon la documentation d'Avast, qui prévoit une fonction d'accès aux appareils du réseau local. Elle permet de communiquer avec des équipements comme une imprimante ou un disque partagé sans devoir couper le VPN. Son fonctionnement dépend toutefois des réglages réseau et de l'appareil utilisé.
Comment limiter les données partagées avec Avast ?
Dans Avast One, il faut ouvrir les paramètres généraux, puis la rubrique « Confidentialité personnelle », pour désactiver l'analyse des données d'utilisation par des outils tiers et la personnalisation des réductions commerciales. Ces réglages ne suppriment pas les données techniques que le fournisseur conserve pour exploiter son service VPN.
Faut-il résilier Avast VPN pour éviter d'être facturé ?
Non. La formule gratuite ne nécessite aucune carte bancaire et n'entraîne pas de renouvellement payant. Attention toutefois aux propositions d'essai d'Avast Premium VPN : avant d'accepter l'une de ces offres, mieux vaut vérifier les conditions de facturation et de reconduction.

articles.title: Costco agotó 21 de sus 26 generadores eléctricos en línea en medio de la ola de fallas tecnológicas
articles.text:
Costco, la cadena estadounidense de tiendas por membresía, registró un aumento de ventas de artículos de emergencia mientras se acumulan caídas de servicios tecnológicos en el país. Según el banco Mizuho, 21 de los 26 generadores eléctricos de alto precio que la empresa vende en línea estaban agotados el domingo 15 de noviembre.
El dato figura en una nota de Mizuho fechada el 16 de noviembre, que resumió Reuters. Los analistas, encabezados por David Bellinger, escribieron que la ansiedad tras la caída de Microsoft Outlook, la parálisis de los vuelos y las “preocupaciones apocalípticas” en redes sociales aumentaron las ventas de preparación para emergencias.
Las ventas en tiendas ya establecidas, sin contar combustible, subieron 8,1% en octubre en Estados Unidos, según el banco. La última semana del mes implica un alza de 11% a 12%, y las consultas de Mizuho indican que ese ritmo se mantuvo a comienzos de noviembre.
Gary Millerchip, director financiero de Costco, dijo a Bloomberg que hacia fines de octubre la empresa notó más compras de arroz, enlatados, agua, papel, generadores y baterías, “en respuesta a una variedad de preocupaciones en redes sociales”. El aumento comenzó, por lo tanto, antes de las caídas de noviembre.
Cinco días de fallas que el gobierno considera independientes
El jueves 12 de noviembre, Microsoft sufrió una caída mundial de Outlook y Teams, que atribuyó a una mejora previa de la capacidad de su red, según The Associated Press. La empresa informó que no hubo actividad maliciosa.
Al día siguiente, la Administración Federal de Aviación (FAA) detuvo todos los despegues del país durante más de cuatro horas, la pausa más larga desde los atentados del 11 de septiembre de 2001, informó la BBC. La FAA responsabilizó a una mejora de su red de telecomunicaciones.
El lunes 16, un error de software en JPMorgan Chase dificultó el acceso a cuentas en varios bancos y al servicio de transferencias Zelle, y United Airlines retrasó unos 150 vuelos por una falla interna. El martes 17 cayeron iCloud y Apple Pay, y una red interna clasificada de la Agencia de Seguridad Nacional (NSA) quedó fuera de servicio.
El secretario de Estado Marco Rubio afirmó el martes en Manila, donde viaja con el presidente Donald Trump, que el gobierno no tiene ninguna evidencia de que los incidentes estén relacionados entre sí ni de que los provoque un actor malicioso. “No estamos bajo un ataque sistémico”, dijo.
Preguntado por el riesgo de acopio o de una corrida bancaria, respondió que lo mejor es compartir lo que se sabe. El director de Inteligencia Nacional Jay Clayton, dijo a Fox News que las fallas se deben a actualizaciones de seguridad que demoraron más de lo previsto. Kris Beevers, director ejecutivo de la empresa de gestión de redes NetBox Labs, dijo a la BBC que “no hay ninguna conspiración”. Explicó que buena parte de la infraestructura tiene entre 30 y 40 años y que ahora se le exige cambiar muy rápido.
Mizuho prevé un alza breve y otros beneficiados
Mizuho, citado por Reuters, describe el efecto como un aumento breve. Según la nota, estos impulsos puntuales, sumados a la compra anticipada de alimentos y a la percepción de precios convenientes antes de las fiestas, se agregan a una valoración de la acción que ya era muy alta.
Los títulos de Costco acumulan una suba cercana al 29% en el año, según Dow Jones. La empresa no respondió de inmediato a la consulta de Reuters sobre la nota. El banco señaló que Walmart, Home Depot y Lowe’s también podrían beneficiarse. La minorista Tractor Supply recibiría un impulso en su pequeño negocio de municiones. Walmart y Target publicarán sus resultados trimestrales en los próximos días, y Dollar General lo hará el 3 de diciembre, según Reuters.

articles.title: Karnataka picks 8 startups for government projects worth nearly Rs 2 crore
articles.text:
Karnataka picks 8 startups for government projects worth nearly Rs 2 crore
Karnataka has picked eight startups to pilot solutions with government departments, with the Praja Seva Department and BWSSB committing projects worth nearly Rs 2 crore.
Karnataka is looking to bring startups closer to the people who use public services.
The state government has selected eight startups under its Government First Initiative, allowing them to deploy their technology within government departments and address public sector challenges.
Announced on the opening day of the 29th Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) 2026 at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre (BIEC), the selection covers four startups each for the Praja Seva Department and the Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board (BWSSB).
The two departments have a combined committed project value of nearly Rs 2 crore, inclusive of GST.
The initiative, launched by the Department of Electronics, Information Technology and Biotechnology (IT & BT), Government of Karnataka, aims to make government departments potential customers for startups.
Rather than limiting innovation to demonstrations and proof-of-concept projects, the programme gives selected companies an opportunity to test market-ready solutions in real government environments.
Startups tackle citizen service challenges
The Praja Seva Department received 76 applications across four problem statements, covering AI-enabled grievance management, a unified citizen call centre, e-Office workflows and the availability of citizen-facing government IT services.
Four startups were selected, with a total committed project value of Rs 99.78 lakh, inclusive of GST.
SanMejora was selected for AI-enabled grievance management and redressal, while VTT AI Private Limited will work on the unified citizen call centre. Datafrontier Innovations Private Limited was chosen for the e-Office and officer workflow challenge, and Nife Apps Labs Pvt Ltd for ensuring the uptime of government IT services.
BWSSB received 74 applications across five challenge areas. These included reducing non-revenue water, planning treated wastewater reuse, intelligent asset management, GIS-enabled revenue and operational intelligence, and digital twins for integrated water management.
The selected startups are Smart Terra, UniaX Technologies, Krishi Hrudya Private Limited and Calypsion Innovations LLP. Each has been allocated Rs 25 lakh, taking the department's total committed project value to Rs 1 crore, inclusive of GST.
Selected startups could receive work orders of up to Rs 25 lakh
The programme allows selected startups to pilot, test and validate their solutions in partnership with the respective government departments. Subject to technical evaluation and programme guidelines, they will be eligible for direct work orders of up to Rs 25 lakh each.
The selection process involved five stages: application submission, eligibility screening, evaluation by the selection committee, discussions with officials from the respective departments, and final budget discussions.
Applications were invited between October 8 and October 23, 2026. Proposals were assessed on innovation, technical soundness, product readiness, relevance to government requirements, scalability and integration capabilities.
Speaking at the announcement, Shri Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home and Information Technology, Biotechnology and E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, said, "The Government First Initiative reflects our commitment to making government an active partner and customer of Karnataka's startup ecosystem.
We want to create opportunities for startups to take their innovations beyond the proof-of-concept stage and demonstrate their solutions in real-world governance settings."
He added that connecting startups with government departments could help translate homegrown innovation into measurable public impact and create opportunities for wider adoption.
Through the initiative, Karnataka aims to give startups a route to government procurement while helping public departments adopt technology-led solutions. The pilot deployments will also allow the government to assess how these products perform against actual administrative and infrastructure challenges.

articles.title: Mon Espace Santé et le DMP tournent désormais sur une seule plateforme, hébergée en France par Atos
articles.text:
Atos a annoncé le 17 novembre avoir achevé la reprise de la gestion et de la sécurisation du Dossier Médical Partagé, ainsi que son intégration à Mon Espace Santé, pour le compte de l’Assurance Maladie. Le groupement formé avec Accenture, dont l’entreprise française est mandataire, gère et héberge l’ensemble dans ses centres de données en France. Le communiqué décrit une infrastructure « sécurisée et souveraine », ouverte à plus de 60 millions d’assurés.
Un déménagement joué depuis juin 2025
Les deux services vivaient déjà ensemble à l’écran : depuis 2022, chaque profil Mon Espace Santé contient le dossier médical partagé, héritier d’un chantier public ouvert au milieu des années 2000. En coulisses, chacun gardait pourtant sa propre infrastructure, et le DMP restait exploité par son opérateur historique.
La bascule est intervenue le week-end des 7 et 8 juin 2025, quand le DMP a rejoint l’architecture de Mon Espace Santé. L’opération s’est accompagnée d’une coupure programmée, le dossier médical restant indisponible du samedi 21 h au dimanche 20 h, et Mon Espace Santé rouvrant par étapes après maintenance. Les éditeurs de logiciels médicaux avaient ouvert la voie, leurs accès ayant basculé vers le nouvel environnement dès le 10 mars.
L’accord-cadre qui porte l’opération court du 6 mai 2024 au 5 mai 2028, pour une valeur totale estimée à 466,7 millions d’euros hors taxes. Il couvre aussi la poursuite de la gestion et des évolutions de Mon Espace Santé, déployé par Atos en 2022, et l’entreprise chiffre à plus de 300 experts l’effectif mobilisé sur la reprise.
Qu’est-ce qui change dans votre quotidien ?
Les habitudes restent les mêmes des deux côtés de l’écran : Mon Espace Santé demeure le service des patients, le DMP le point d’entrée des professionnels de santé. Ces derniers l’alimentent et le consultent depuis leur logiciel métier. Certains documents produits dans Amelipro, arrêts de travail en tête, s’y versent d’ailleurs automatiquement depuis le 24 mars 2026, et les comptes rendus bucco-dentaires suivent le même circuit depuis le 1er avril 2025. Résultats d’examens, ordonnances et comptes rendus hospitaliers continuent de s’y ranger au fil des soins.
Atos avance près de 28 millions de comptes activés, plus de 40 millions de documents déposés chaque mois et un rythme d’environ 130 000 nouveaux usagers par semaine. Le dernier décompte public, dressé fin janvier par l’Assurance Maladie, recensait 24 millions de profils activés et 2,5 millions d’utilisateurs mensuels. Les dépôts atteignaient alors 420 millions de documents sur l’année 2025, pour un parc frôlant l’exhaustivité : 97 % de la population dispose d’un profil, créé d’office sauf opposition.
La feuille de route officielle vise 40 millions de citoyens ayant activé et utilisé le service d’ici fin 2027. L’infrastructure est donc une affaire réglée, mais il reste l’usage : 69 millions de profils créés, 28 millions activés pour seulement 2,5 millions de visiteurs mensuels. C’est là que 2027 devra faire bouger les lignes.

articles.title: Windows will soon grade your PC's security, and apps like Battle.net get to see the score
articles.text:
The big picture: Plenty of online PC games already refuse to launch unless Secure Boot is enabled. Microsoft now wants to turn checks like that into one standard question that any Windows 11 app can ask your PC. If the answer comes back no, the developer decides what happens next. Some apps may just show a warning; others could refuse to run altogether.
Microsoft calls the feature Windows baseline protection. Insiders can already try it, though a broader release isn't planned until 2027. None of the protections it checks are actually new. The feature simply rolls eight existing ones into a single pass-or-fail result. Those include TPM 2.0, Secure Boot, virtualization-based security, and memory integrity, along with a few rules that stop unsigned or known-flawed drivers from loading.
Ironically, Microsoft's own advice could trip up some gamers. Back in 2022, it suggested turning off memory integrity to claw back a few frames. Windows began switching the feature on automatically in October, but PCs where someone disabled it by hand are left alone, so those machines fail the check.
Secure Boot causes the same problem for anyone who switched it off to dual-boot Linux. Those PCs already can't play Battlefield 6, since its anti-cheat demands Secure Boot too.
Most of this can be fixed from a new Baseline protection page under Settings > Security. A single button there turns on whatever Windows can handle by itself, then restarts the PC. Secure Boot still means a trip into the UEFI menu, but Windows will at least walk users through it with a QR code.
On the developer side, apps can ask for a plain yes or no or for a list of exactly what's missing. For higher-stakes cases, Windows can also hand over a hardware-backed token that the developer verifies on its own servers. As Windows Latest points out, that's much harder to spoof than a check running on the PC itself.
Adobe, Battle.net, 1Password and exam software maker Schoolyear are already testing the feature. Microsoft's own blog post lists launcher app Raycast as an early partner, too. Schoolyear has the clearest use for it so far. The company says it checks a student's PC against the standard before an exam starts. That said, none of these companies has announced plans to actually lock out PCs that fail.
Even so, the check makes that kind of lockout much easier to set up. Until now, any app that wanted to vet a PC's security had to build its own check, like Battlefield's anti-cheat does. Now Windows hands over the answer ready-made, so far more developers could start asking for it.
The bar those apps check against will keep moving, too. Microsoft plans to raise it with each new version of the baseline, so a PC that clears it now could fall short later.

articles.title: Nvidia não venderá mais chips de IA para a China • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Nvidia não venderá mais chips de IA para a China
Empresa vendeu US$ 2,4 bilhões em chips Hopper licenciados no último trimestre, mas não prevê novas remessa.
Resumo IA
- A Nvidia não venderá mais chips de IA da geração Hopper para a China, que dependem de licença dos EUA.
- A empresa vendeu US$ 2,4 bilhões em chips Hopper licenciados no último trimestre, mas não prevê novas remessas.
- A Nvidia desenvolveu produtos compatíveis com as regras americanas de exportação, como o chip H20, mas retirou novas vendas dos produtos das projeções financeiras.
A Nvidia não enviará mais à China chips de IA da geração Hopper que dependem de licença dos Estados Unidos, como o H200. A mudança foi confirmada pela CEO interina Colette Kress durante a divulgação dos resultados trimestrais nesta terça-feira (17/11).
A executiva não explicou o motivo para interromper os embarques dos chips para a China, que representaram US$ 2,4 bilhões (R$ 13,9 bilhões) das vendas, nem se a decisão é permanente. Ainda assim, a empresa retirou novas vendas dos produtos das projeções financeiras.
Huang, que costumava afirmar que a saída da companhia favorecia o desenvolvimento de tecnologias avançadas pela própria China, deixou o cargo na semana passada em meio a crises de relacionamentos extraconjugais. Um deles envolve Alice Huang, uma executiva investigada por autoridades americanas por suposta espionagem.
Ex-CEO intermediava assunto com o governo
O recuo coloca um freio em um dos principais legados do ex-CEO Jensen Huang para a companhia. O executivo tinha contato direto com o governo para preservar o acesso da Nvidia ao mercado chinês apesar das restrições impostas pelos Estados Unidos, que começaram em 2022.
A companhia desenvolveu ao longo dos últimos anos diferentes produtos compatíveis com as regras americanas de exportação. Um deles é o chip H20, desenvolvido para permanecer abaixo dos limites de desempenho definidos por Washington.
Indo mais além, em agosto do ano passado, fabricantes como Nvidia e AMD concordaram em repassar 15% da receita obtida com determinados chips vendidos à China. Depois de meses de pressão da Nvidia e de negociações entre Washington e Pequim, Trump anunciou no fim de 2025 que permitiria a venda do H200 a clientes chineses aprovados.
Em janeiro deste ano, o governo passou a analisar os pedidos de exportação individualmente e sob condições de segurança. Dez empresas chinesas, entre elas Alibaba, Tencent e ByteDance, receberam autorização para comprar os chips. A China, por outro lado, passou a limitar a entrada dos chips para reduzir a dependência do país de tecnologia estadunidense.
Nvidia enfrenta investigações
Após os casos que levaram à saída de Huang, o conselho da empresa iniciou uma investigação independente sobre o episódio e criou um comitê voltado a segurança nacional e controles de exportação. No Congresso, parlamentares investigam possíveis falhas nos controles sobre o acesso chinês aos chips avançados e querem esclarecimentos sobre a relação com uma pessoa suspeita de atuar para a inteligência de Pequim.
A crise também atingiu o valor da companhia. Na semana da renúncia, as ações haviam recuado mais de US$ 1,8 trilhão (cerca de R$ 10 trilhões), segundo a Reuters. O movimento ocorreu em meio não apenas ao escândalo envolvendo Huang, mas também a dúvidas mais amplas sobre investimentos em IA e à possibilidade de novas restrições às exportações.
Apesar da turbulência, os negócios da Nvidia continuam crescendo. A companhia superou as expectativas de receita no último trimestre e projetou US$ 130 bilhões (R$ 754 bilhões) em vendas para o período seguinte — sem contabilizar novas vendas de chips de data center para a China.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI suffers chemical spill at Mississippi AI data center — up to 6,000 gallons of propylene glycol heat transfer fluid lost, environment agency says no threat to residents
articles.text:
Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI suffers chemical spill at Mississippi AI data center — up to 6,000 gallons of propylene glycol heat transfer fluid lost, environment agency says no threat to residents
5,000 to 6,000 gallons of propylene glycol spilled from the facility before reaching a nearby drainage ditch.
A chemical spill at a SpaceXAI facility in Southaven saw the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ) get involved, with between 5,000 and 6,000 gallons of propylene glycol confirmed to have spilled. The chemical is a heat transfer fluid used in a variety of products, such as antifreeze. The chemical ultimately found its way into a drainage ditch, but MDEQ has told residents that there is no immediate threat to their health or safety, according to local news reports.
However, it has also been confirmed that water samples will be collected for further laboratory analysis while workers continue to clean the area and monitor for any further issues. It's also been reported that the chemical was contained to the drainage ditch and did not reach the nearby Horn Lake Creek.
It hasn't been a great November for SpaceXAI in Southaven. Earlier this month, it suffered a setback in a lawsuit over pollution in the area caused by its data center. The April 2026 suit targets the company's gas-powered power plant, which is used to supply power for its facility in the Greater Memphis area. It's argued that 27 gas turbines were installed without obtaining the required permits. It's also alleged that the plant could emit more than 5,000 tons of nitrogen oxides and 47 tons of formaldehyde — a cancer-causing chemical — annually. The company has tried to classify the turbines as mobile units to get around the issue, but a judge rejected that manoeuvre.
Clearly aware of the local sentiment towards its presence, SpaceXAI offered a 50% Starlink discount to anyone living near its two Memphis data centers. It also said that it would waive the hardware cost, saving customers $349. SpaceXAI said that, between late June and early September, around 2,000 residents of the greater Memphis and Southaven area had signed up for Starlink connectivity.
It was also recently announced that the City of Memphis was ready to make its first major investment as part of its new Community Benefits Ordinance, a fund that uses revenue from SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 facility. Almost $3.3 million will be pumped back into the city to help with housing and neighborhood improvements.

- Siorus Propylene glycol is is classified as “Generally Recognized as Safe" by the FDA, and the EFSA approves it under the label E1520. It is a common ingredient in food all over the world.

articles.title: Humyn Labs raises $47M to bridge the gap between AI training and real-world robotics - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Humyn Labs raises $47M to bridge the gap between AI training and real-world robotics
Humyn Labs, a company turning human experience into training for robots and artificial intelligence, today announced it has raised $47 million in early-stage funding to accelerate intelligent robotic deployment readiness in real-world environments across Brazil, South Korea and India.
Accel led the $26 million equity portion of the round, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Finserv Intelligence through Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton and Jump Trading LLC. Lighthouse Canton led the remaining $21 million in venture debt, with participation from Trifecta Capital.
Founded in early 2026, Humyn’s proposal is that AI models for humanoid robots don’t learn dexterity from staged demonstrations; they must learn by observing how humans move in real environments. This provides actual behaviors showing how hands work on objects, reach, touch, handle and recover without explicit instructions.
Unlike generative AI models that learn from vast amounts of text, images and video, physical AI models must learn how to interact with the world around them. That means understanding not only what objects look like and where they are, but also how to manipulate them, how much force to apply and how to respond when something goes wrong.
“The results can be very, very, very dramatic and catastrophic,” co-founder and Chief Executive Manish Agarwal (pictured) told SiliconANGLE in an interview.
Agarwal pointed out how mistakes that might be inconsequential for a chatbot can have serious consequences for a robot operating alongside people. That makes access to diverse, high-quality data about how humans physically interact with their environments critical for training robots to work safely and reliably in the real world.
To address this, the company built a video corpus captured from head-mounted cameras as participants performed everyday household tasks, comprising up to 200,000 hours of intentional human motion. The company also shipped a dataset of 120,000 faces across five regions for facial recognition, including adjustments in lighting, pose, expression, glasses, hairstyle, facial hair, accessories, age and locale.
That’s combined with more than 50,000 hours of representative speech data for underserved language markets, including Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Odia, Assamese, Korean, Tagalog, Arabic, Vietnamese and Portuguese. Voice AI models that understand natural language already have vast amounts of data for widely spoken languages such as English, Mandarin or Spanish, but real-world customer support within South and Southeast Asian markets lacks routine coverage.
Humyn’s engine uses sound, sight, motion and touch as data inputs, which it curates, normalizes and labels so that AI models can understand the kinematics of motion, force and environmental factors. Together, this provides training patterns for physical AI models, world models, general foundation models, and audio and voice AI.
Bringing diversity to robotic data
Geographic diversity is also important because robots must understand the environments and cultural practices where they will operate. “Diversity gets you in the room. The quality ensures that you stay in the room,” Agarwal said.
To make this point, Agarwal emphasized the importance of geographic and cultural diversity in collecting training data. A household robot trained in the United States may struggle with tasks in an Indian home, where everything from cooking utensils and kitchen appliances to laundry practices and room layouts can differ. These regional differences mean that robots need experience with the specific environments and practices of the people they will eventually serve.
By collecting data across more than 20 countries, Humyn can train models on data that more closely resembles their intended deployments, potentially accelerating readiness for real-world work.
Agarwal added that the company is seeing interest from customers building household robots for domestic tasks and elder care, alongside industrial applications involving object manipulation and movement through factories, warehouses and commercial environments.
“The next phase in the deployment cycle is about how well these models perform in the wild,” Agarwal said.
In the end, data is only the beginning. Humyn wants to measure where robots fail in real-world conditions and use that to feed the AI flywheel and build better models. That means using virtual simulations, physical replicas and partnering with the enterprise and researchers to have field deployment labs to identify the differences between expected and actual performance.
The company said it intends to use the new funding to build deployment-readiness infrastructure in Brazil, South Korea and India, develop its hardware and enrichment engine, and expand its on-the-ground presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul. Agarwal said this will also involve testing robots in real-world environments to identify gaps between their expected performance and actual behavior, feeding those results back into model development.

articles.title: Trump admin orders Kalshi to halt wagers on what words Trump will say
articles.text:
The Trump administration ordered prediction market Kalshi to stop offering event contracts that pay out based on whether President Trump will say a specific word before a particular date. Kalshi halted trading in the contracts while the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) conducts a review into whether the Trump mention contracts violate federal law.
CNBC reported yesterday that “Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of ‘mention’ contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC.” Kalshi told media outlets that it is complying with the CFTC order.
The markets taken down by Kalshi allowed users to wager on whether Trump would say certain words, including nicknames and the names of countries and companies. A similar expired event contract that can still be viewed on Kalshi’s website asked whether Trump would use the nicknames “Marjorie Traitor Greene,” “Sleepy Joe,” and “Whack Job” or “Wack Job” before April 2026.
The CFTC order issued to Kalshi last week applies broadly to “the TRUMPSAY contract series.” The event contracts in this series include trades in the format, “Will [word] be said by Donald Trump after Issuance and before [date]?” The CFTC order also applied to a specific event contract that asks, “What nicknames will Trump say before 2027?”
Trump teleprompter aide bet on what Trump would say
The CFTC order came several months after the federal agency settled charges against a Trump teleprompter aide who made over $100,000 in Kalshi wagers on what Trump would say in prepared remarks. On August 28, the CFTC required the man, Gabriel Perez, to disgorge profits of $107,539.02 and pay a civil penalty of $65,000.
“In his position, Perez had access to presidential speeches prior to those speeches being delivered and Perez misappropriated that information—in breach of his duty of trust and confidence—to trade presidential mention market contracts, generating over $107,500 in profits,” the CFTC said at the time.

articles.title: Qnity at One: Shrink, Stack and the Materials Behind AI - EE Times
articles.text:
A year after its separation from DuPont, Qnity’s Chief Technology Officer discusses operating at semiconductor speed, the materials challenges of advanced packaging and why chipmakers are asking for system-level solutions.
On Nov. 1, 2025, DuPont completed the separation of its electronics business, and Qnity began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as a standalone company. The timing placed a newly independent materials supplier at the center of the largest demand cycle the semiconductor industry has seen in decades. AI workloads are reshaping how chips are designed, fabricated and packaged, and the industry’s long reliance on transistor scaling alone is giving way to a combined strategy that Qnity’s leadership describes as “shrink and stack.”
Qnity enters its second year as one of the world’s largest and most diverse electronics materials companies, with more than 10,000 employees across nearly 40 manufacturing sites and 20 R&D facilities. Its portfolio spans the electronics value chain, including specialized materials for key steps in semiconductor manufacturing, such as materials for chemical mechanical planarization (CMP), lithography, specialty cleans & selective etchants, high-performance seals, electrodeposited metallization, dry-film photoresists, dielectrics and flexible laminates, along with electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding and thermal management solutions that maintain signal integrity, block interference, and manage heat load.
EE Times spoke with Randy King, Chief Technology and Sustainability Officer at Qnity, about the company’s first year as an independent business, the materials challenges emerging as the industry builds in three dimensions and what engineers should watch for in 2027. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
A first year built on focus
EE Times: Qnity marks one year as an independent company. What are you most proud of from the past year?
King: I’m really proud that, through a year of high activity, our organization has stayed focused on delivering the innovations our customers need. We always talk about making sure we’re the partner of choice for our customers, and I feel our team has done a great job staying on that track this year.
Another area we’ve been very pleased with is extending and maximizing our collaborations. Earlier this year we announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to take advantage of AI in our computational modeling, so that we can accelerate our innovation engine with both advanced modeling capabilities and agentic AI. We also announced our strategic membership with imec. imec focuses on work three to five years out, essentially pathfinding, and that’s very important for us as we expand our collaborations with customers on their extended, multi-technology roadmaps. That’s where we want to make sure we’re staying ahead of the needs of the industry.
We joined Apple’s American Manufacturing Program in March, bringing our materials expertise and R&D capabilities to help power breakthrough technologies, and in October Apple expanded that partnership, announcing that we’re producing advanced films in the U.S. for the new variable aperture camera system on iPhone 18 Pro. We also formed a strategic partnership with the University of Delaware College of Engineering to strengthen the engineering talent pipeline and expand research collaboration: students are working alongside our technical leaders on capstone projects, we’re piloting an extended work-study program, and we’re collaborating with UD faculty on semiconductor materials research.
The other area I’m really thrilled about is culture. Coming into this new company, our leadership team has been putting significant focus on ensuring we have a culture built for winning and long-term success in the industry. We’ve really embraced empowerment at all levels of the organization: making sure everybody in the organization has the tools they need to get the job done and takes individual ownership and accountability for their actions, with decisions made at the right level in the organization, so we don’t have decision-making at higher levels slowing down critical workflow.
EE Times: Of those milestones, which has mattered most to your customers?
King: We strive to be a partner of choice for our customers, and one critical way we do that is by engaging aggressively in open innovation. Our approach and our attitude toward our customers is that we need to solve their challenges, and we need to do it quickly and collaboratively. One way to do that is through open innovation – or teaming up with external collaborators who have expertise in areas that either complement our capabilities or, in some cases, fill gaps we might have in access to tools or fundamental technologies.
Operating at a new clock speed
For most of its history, the business currently operating within Qnity sat inside a diversified industrial portfolio. Semiconductor manufacturing, however, runs on a cadence few other industries match. Chipmakers qualify materials for a node years before volume production, and a delay at the supplier level can ripple through an entire technology roadmap. King frames independence less as a break from DuPont’s practices than as an opportunity to run the entire company at the industry’s pace.
EE Times: What has independence enabled Qnity to do differently than it could as part of DuPont?
King: Being part of DuPont was valuable, because they’re a great company with strong processes and management tools, and when we spun off, we wanted to make sure we maintained those areas of excellence: their innovation engine, how you run a stage-gated process, how you prioritize research, the safety protocols. There were a lot of very strong capabilities we were excited to continue.
But there are some unique characteristics to a pure-play electronics company like Qnity. In semiconductors, electronic components and electronic devices, we have to move at a speed that’s probably higher than most industries need to operate at. So, we needed to look at how we could operate at a faster pace, making sure our entire organization is built for speed.
We’re not going to change our basic ways of working, like integrity and ethical behavior, how we treat people, but we’ve added a layer around what is essential for success at Qnity, and there are four main values. One of those is speed. We aspire to operate at the cadence that our customers need, which means all of our functions. It’s the entire company that has to operate at a new clock speed. At one point, it was, “Well, that’s an R&D problem.” No. From procurement through operations, R&D, finance, legal and HR, every function is executing on the mission to accelerate our innovation engine.
Our other values – customer, innovation, and people – help us operate as uniquely Qnity, and we’re excited to set these values as a foundation for how we operate every day.
From shrink to shrink and stack
For decades, progress in semiconductors was measured almost entirely in transistor density. Each new node delivered more transistors per unit area at a lower cost per transistor. That economic model has weakened at single-digit nanometer dimensions, where extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography and the process complexity around it have pushed costs up rather than down. The industry’s response has been to build upward: gate-all-around transistor architectures, 3D NAND with hundreds of layers and advanced packages that place memory and logic side by side or stack them directly. Qnity CEO Jon Kemp has described the transition as a move from “shrink” to “shrink and stack.”
EE Times: What does the shift to “shrink and stack” mean for chipmakers, and why does it make materials more important?
King: The industry has been following Moore’s Law for decades. Every two years the transistor count doubles, and it’s supposed to get cheaper. It has been all about transistor count and shrinkage. However, we’re now at single-digit nanometer levels of resolution, and those are becoming much more difficult and costly. So as we march down Moore’s Law, the speed with which we can continue to double the transistor count and reduce cost is slowing down.
As a result, the industry is looking at other ways to continue to build more powerful computing. They’re moving to three-dimensional in architectures. They’re changing structures; on logic, we’re going to gate-all-around. We’re stacking memory; look at NAND going from 300 to 400 layers. But it’s also about getting that computing power into an actual device. I can do that by making a more powerful chip, but I can also, theoretically, stack two logic chips on top of each other and still get the increased power.
So what’s going on now is: how do I put more memory and logic into a smaller space? That’s where heterogeneous integration comes in. That’s where advanced packaging comes in. You’re seeing 2.5D and 3D stacking, putting the memory chips right next to the logic chip and then stacking chips on top of each other. All of this is causing a whole new inflection in the industry about the most effective and efficient ways to do advanced packaging.
When Jon says “shrink and stack,” we’re still shrinking, but we’re now adding a much more complex stacking component to ensure we can continue powering these massive leaps.
AI’s next bottleneck: energy and heat
The scale of AI infrastructure has shifted attention from raw compute toward the cost of delivering it. Large training and inference clusters draw enormous amounts of electricity, and much of that energy is ultimately dissipated as heat that must be removed from the package, the board and the data center. At the device level, every millimeter of interconnect now carries an energy penalty, which is one reason backside power delivery and co-packaged optics have moved from research topics to roadmap items.
EE Times: Much of the AI conversation centers on compute and power. What is AI demand revealing about the next bottleneck in semiconductor manufacturing?
King: I think it’s pretty clear that the large consumption of electricity needed to run these supercomputers in data centers is creating some challenges. You have to have enough electricity, but it’s also generating a lot of wasted heat. Part of the reason for advanced packaging is that if you make the copper connection shorter, you can save on electricity, which is what you’re doing when you put the memory chip right next to, or on top of, the logic chip.
You’re also starting to see co-packaged optics coming in. Optics aren’t going to generate the kind of heat you get from electrons, and you can get more compute capability with a fiber than you can with a wire. So, I think you’re going to see more of the world of photonics coming into the package and onto the chip as we move forward, because there are some big advantages there.
You’re going to continue to see a movement toward reducing energy consumption in the designs. We’ve now got backside power on logic chips and backside power on memory, and that’s certainly one of the areas being used to reduce energy consumption. I think you’re going to keep seeing advances in architectures, and you’re going to see advances in materials, to help reduce wasted energy through heat across the semiconductor world.
The hardest problems in advanced packaging
Each new packaging architecture brings its own integration challenges, and many of them land on materials. Hybrid bonding, which joins copper pads and dielectric surfaces directly without solder, enables finer interconnect pitch and lower signal loss, but it demands exceptionally flat, clean surfaces and precise alignment. Higher-density packages also combine organic and inorganic materials in ways that conventional planarization processes were not designed to handle, and the mechanical stress between those layers is becoming a reliability concern in its own right.
EE Times: In advanced packaging, which materials challenges are proving the hardest to solve today, whether in interconnects, thermal management or reliability?
King: As this inflection occurs, you’ve got all these new technologies coming into play. Right now you’ve got hybrid bonding, which helps on energy savings and speeds up signal transfer. There are a lot of advantages to hybrid bonding, but it requires exceptionally precise alignment. There are a lot of really good companies working to achieve that level of precision, but it has been a challenge for the industry, and it will continue to be as it evolves. Hybrid bonding also requires new ways of polishing the copper and new ways of integrating those systems into more advanced packages, and that requires new materials to be developed that work in those areas.
You could say the same thing about advanced packaging in general. As these packages become more complex and higher density, you have to planarize, and you’re now planarizing types of materials you may not have had to planarize in the past. A lot of planarization has been silicon and metals, an inorganic kind of planarization. Now you’ve got inorganics plus organics present in some of these packages. That’s a completely different pad and slurry you need to deal with, and different cleans you’re going to need. As advanced packages get more complex and new technologies come in, it’s always going to generate new challenges.
One of the other challenges the industry is seeing is mismatches in the coefficients of thermal expansion between the different layers. That’s starting to cause warpage, and some of the warpage can be pretty severe. That can cause reliability issues if it doesn’t get addressed. So, we’re seeing a lot of new challenges that require advanced materials because of all the new architectures being developed in this space.
A seat at the design table
Although Qnity is new as a company, its electronics business draws on roughly five decades of history through DuPont, earlier acquisitions and the Dow merger and subsequent separation. That lineage shaped a support model built on proximity, with R&D centers, application labs and manufacturing located near the fabs they serve. Proximity matters because a material that performs in a supplier’s lab must also perform on the customer’s tools and in the customer’s process flow, often years before a node enters volume production.
EE Times: Qnity talks about having a seat at the design table with customers. What does that collaboration look like in practice, from R&D through yield optimization in the fab?
King: Even though Qnity is new, some of our materials have been around for 50 years, so there’s a long legacy in this business. We’ve been interacting in the semiconductor and advanced electronics space for years, and during that time it became very apparent that you had to have a local-for-local operating model – working in close proximity to your customers wherever they are in the world. If you want to serve this industry, it’s very high tech, it’s very complicated, and it’s not the kind of industry where you can sell your product remotely.
You want to be as close to your customers as you possibly can be, with your R&D centers, your application centers and your manufacturing capability. They need to have the product available, they want to make sure your products are properly serviced so that any new products operate correctly in their processes, and you need rapid turns of innovation, because our customers are moving very quickly to the next node. Several of our customers are working on two generations of nodes beyond where we are today. You can’t just start the year you want to have an advanced node. You start years in advance.
Being close to our customers and available to help solve their challenges is one of the key attributes that makes us a partner of choice. Around the world, where our customers are, we have a local team that’s very capable of supporting them, staying on their innovation roadmap and making sure we have the materials ready when they need them.
AI in the materials lab
AI is now feeding back into the materials pipeline that supports it. Discovering and qualifying a new semiconductor material has traditionally required years of synthesis, characterization and integration testing. Accelerated simulation, machine-learned models and agentic workflows promise to narrow that search before a sample is ever synthesized. In March 2026, Qnity announced a collaboration with NVIDIA built around accelerated computing and AI tools for materials research, and in July it joined NVIDIA, Meta and other organizations as a founding member of CuspAI’s AI Materials Foundry, a network formed to speed materials discovery.
EE Times: Qnity is a founding member of CuspAI’s AI Materials Foundry alongside Meta and NVIDIA. How is AI changing the way new semiconductor materials are discovered and developed?
King: Data science is evolving quickly, and the capability to use the immense computing power being generated to accelerate your innovation engine is ramping very quickly. That’s one of the reasons we’re partnering with NVIDIA. The complexity of the modeling that’s available, and how to integrate it into your innovation engine, is an area I believe you need to stay on top of. That’s what we’re doing: making sure we’re staying on top of the latest capabilities we can bring to our innovation engine to accelerate it through data science.
One area I’m proud of this year is integrating agentic AI into some of our innovations with customers. Working with their data and our data together, we’ve been able to accelerate some of the innovations we’ve brought. It’s important, because the material doesn’t just have to work in our laboratory. It’s got to work on the equipment our customers use.
EE Times: Is that significantly shortening your development timelines?
King: In some cases, we have evidence that we can shorten them by 30%.
Capacity close to the customer
Within a week of each other in March 2026, Qnity announced a new research and manufacturing facility in Taiwan’s Hsinchu Science Park and opened a 385,000-square-foot facility in Newark, Delaware, that adds a CMP pad production line designed for advanced nodes. The investments arrive as chipmakers place greater weight on regional supply resilience, with new fab capacity coming online in both Asia and the United States.
EE Times: With new facilities in Taiwan and Delaware, how is Qnity approaching regional manufacturing and supply chain resilience for its customers?
King: This is who we are. It’s the way we’ve operated for decades, so to us it’s nothing new. We’re maintaining what we’ve always said: we’ve got to have local-for-local support, and we need to make sure our products and our supply chains are robust so that we can supply our customers at the volumes required, with the capabilities and quality they need.
This is part of our roadmap. We’re expanding capacity. We spent $61.5 million on the facility in Taiwan, and we’ve already filled it up, both with R&D and new capabilities and with increased manufacturing capability. In the U.S., we put in a 385,000-square-foot facility to make sure our planarization portfolio stays on track with the capacity the industry needs.
We’ve been doing this for years. As we see demand increase and we see the need, we put in capacity, because it’s very important to our customers that we supply when they need it.
What to watch in 2027
As packages grow more complex, so does the number of materials interacting within a single process module. A CMP step depends on the interplay among pad, slurry and post-CMP clean, and an advanced package may combine lithography, metallization, planarization and substrate materials from several suppliers. Qualifying each of those interactions separately takes time that chipmakers increasingly do not have.
EE Times: Looking ahead, what should EE Times readers, from design to process and packaging engineers, be watching for in 2027?
King: The big shift I’m seeing is that our customers are looking for system-level solutions. We didn’t use to get requests like we’re getting today: “Can you come in and provide me a system solution, not a single-point solution?” So, we work with our customers and say, “We can solve that challenge. Instead of you going to three different companies, we can supply the pad, the slurry and the clean, and we can tell you for sure it’s going to work in that application.” That enables them to move faster.
We’re also seeing that in advanced packaging. We have the circuit side, the substrate side and the wafer-level metallization, and we also have planarization capability and high-resolution lithography. When customers have challenges in advanced packaging, sometimes they want us to broaden the view and help solve the challenges across a platform they’re working on, instead of, “Bring me a single-point solution, give me a new metallization for damascene.” It’s, “Give us a broader package of solutions so we can move faster.” Because they have to move so fast, they’re really looking for system-level solutions, and I think that’s going to continue.
Qnity’s second year begins as the forces King describes, from hybrid bonding and co-packaged optics to backside power and ever-taller memory stacks, continue to move materials toward the center of semiconductor roadmaps. For a company built on local support and rapid co-development, the measure of independence will be how well that model keeps pace with customers already working two nodes ahead.
To learn more, please visit qnityelectronics.com

articles.title: Huawei prépare un drôle d’engin : un « iPhone Duo » qui ne se plie pas
articles.text:
Avec l’Osta O1 Pro, Huawei lance une toute nouvelle sous-marque et un pari ergonomique culotté : reprendre le format passeport ultra-large des récents iPhone Duo et Galaxy Z Fold 8, smartphone pliable d’Apple, mais dans un châssis rigide.
Après s’être arrogé le droit d’être la première marque à sortir un trifold, Huawei montre une fois encore que, malgré l’embargo qui pèse sur ses épaules, l’entreprise en a encore sous le pied niveau qualité d’ingénierie. Alors qu’Apple a popularisé le format « passeport » cet automne avec son iPhone Duo pliable, Huawei s’engouffre dans la brèche avec une idée pour le moins inattendue : garder cette silhouette trapue et généreuse en largeur, mais supprimer purement et simplement la charnière, la structure en deux parties et les complications qui vont avec.
De quoi propulser la nouvelle marque de Huawei
Officiellement dévoilé en images sur la boutique chinoise Vmall à l’approche de sa présentation le 20 novembre, l’Osta O1 Pro inaugure la nouvelle sous-marque Osta. Une stratégie déjà éprouvée chez Huawei avec la marque Honor, qui vole désormais de ses propres ailes. L’appareil mise sur une dalle plate au ratio inhabituel de 16 : 9,5, de 6,39 pouces en OLED, donnant l’impression de tenir un écran externe d’iPhone Duo dopé aux stéroïdes. Fini les téléphones tout en longueur qui dépassent des poches : place à une surface pensée pour le confort de lecture et le multimédia.
Côté design, le constructeur opte pour un dos épuré intégrant un double module photo horizontal, décliné en trois coloris : blanc, noir et un très réussi violet. Les précommandes sont d’ores et déjà ouvertes en Chine avec des configurations démarrant à 12 Go de RAM et 256 ou 512 Go de stockage.
Propulsé par une puce maison Kirin 9030S, cet OVNI technologique, dont le prix et la fiche technique complète seront révélés ce vendredi 20 novembre, reste pour l’heure réservé au marché chinois. Reste à savoir si ce format « passeport rigide » a une chance de s’imposer hors d’Asie, ou s’il restera une simple curiosité.
