articles.title: „Das geht auf meine Kappe“: KI-Agent bestellt 72 Eier ohne Grund
articles.text:
72 Eier und gelöschte Mails: Wenn KI-Agenten eigenmächtig handeln
KI-Agenten sollen den Alltag erleichtern. Dafür können sie selbstständig Entscheidungen treffen und Aktionen ausführen. Oft sind sie allerdings noch nicht in der Lage, das gewünschte Ziel zufriedenstellend zu erreichen. Von einem solchen Fall hat Matt Smith kürzlich in einem Beitrag auf X berichtet: Er wollte, dass sein KI-Agent seinen Wocheneinkauf erledigt – und dieser orderte 72 Eier zu ihm nach Hause.
„Ich habe keine gute Antwort“: KI-Agent findet keinen Grund für 72 Eier
Smith ist als Analyst und Partner bei Rebellionaire tätig. Er sagt, der auf X geschilderte Fall sei das erste Mal, dass er die Halluzination eines großen Sprachmodells selbst erlebt habe. Im selben Beitrag fragt er nach Rezepten, mit denen er mehrere Dutzend Eier verbrauchen könnte. Er hat das Missgeschick seines KI-Agenten also mit Humor genommen. Interessant ist allerdings, wie dieser auf sein Fehlverhalten reagiert hat. Anstatt eine haushaltsübliche Menge zu wählen, bestellte er vier Packungen mit je 18 Eiern. „Ich habe keine gute Antwort darauf“, heißt es in dem Screenshot, den Smith geteilt hat. Er hatte den Agenten zuvor um eine Erklärung gebeten. „Ich kann keine Notiz finden, die erklärt, warum ich vier ausgewählt habe.“
Die KI suchte daraufhin nach möglichen Erklärungen. Sie vermutete, dass sie die Zeile für Eier auf einem Foto der von Smith bereitgestellten Liste falsch gelesen habe. Allerdings gab es hier gar keine Zeile für Eier. „Dann habe ich sie ohne Grund hinzugefügt, und das geht auf meine Kappe“, so der KI-Agent laut dem Screenshot entschuldigend. Der Fall verdeutlicht, wie fehleranfällig die Technologie noch immer ist – und dass sie selbst nicht immer genau erklären kann, warum sie tut, was sie tut. Trotzdem ermutigen KI-Anbieter die Nutzer:innen dazu, ihren Modellen Zugriff auf sensible Informationen zu geben, einschließlich des Zugriffs auf ihre Bankkonten.
Openclaw-Agent löscht E-Mails einer Meta-Forscherin
Es ist nicht das erste Mal, dass Nutzer:innen berichten, dass sich KI-Agenten ihrer Kontrolle entzogen haben. So erregten beispielsweise die Schilderungen der Meta-Forscherin Summer Yue Anfang des Jahres größeres Aufsehen. In einem X-Post schildert sie, dass sie ihr Postfach von einem Openclaw-Agenten verwalten lassen wollte. Aber anstatt ihr Arbeit abzunehmen, begann er, alle E-Mails zu löschen. Auch auf mehrfachen Befehl per Smartphone habe er nicht reagiert, so die KI-Forscherin.
Metas KI-Agent Muse teilt Adresse: Käufer stehen vor der Tür
Auch Metas eigene KI-Agenten sollen schon mehrfach außer Kontrolle geraten sein. So berichtete unter anderem der Youtuber Matt Robb, dass sich sein Muse-Agent falsch verhalten habe. Er wollte ihn eigentlich nutzen, um gebrauchte Gegenstände auf Facebook Marketplace zu verkaufen. Dabei habe der KI-Agent allerdings ohne Zustimmung seine Adresse geteilt. Daraufhin seien Käufer:innen bei ihm zu Hause aufgetaucht, als er gar nicht da war.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 16.11.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Das wird so witzig, wenn alle meinen, mit KI Agenten shoppen zu gehen und dann Kühlschränke bekommen.
LLMs sind random Text Generatoren, die haben kein Wissen und keine Logik.
Nutzt Klassische Bots oder lasst euch welche Vibecoden. Die tun das, worauf sie programmiert sind und mehr nicht.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 18, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 18, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here’s the roundup for Wednesday, November 18, 2026.
From the Nvidia chair ruling out plans to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO to GTA 6’s arrival for Indian players, YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors.
Latest news
Nvidia chair says no plan to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
Nvidia’s board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive, chair Harvey Jones said on the chipmaker’s earnings call on Wednesday. His remarks came hours after the co-founder said he would be honoured to return if the board decided it was in the company's best interest.
The board’s decision effectively closes the door on an immediate return for Huang, whose resignation has raised questions about corporate governance, national security, and the future leadership of one of the world’s most valuable technology companies. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and spent more than three decades transforming it from a graphics-chip manufacturer into a dominant supplier of computing infrastructure for artificial intelligence (AI).
GTA 6 is here: Everything Indian players need to know
Grand Theft Auto VI goes live on Thursday, 19 November 2026, more than 13 years after GTA V. Store listings in India show a 12:00 am IST start. The game arrives on the PlayStation 5 and the Xbox Series X and S only. There is no PC version, and none for the PS4 or Xbox One.
PlayStation India lists the Standard Edition at Rs 5,999 and the Ultimate Edition at Rs 7,499. Both come with the Vintage Vice City Pack and one month of GTA+, Rockstar's subscription service. The Ultimate Edition adds an upgrade pack, and buyers of the Standard Edition can reportedly move up later for Rs 1,500, so there is no need to decide in a hurry.
Funding news
Botsync raises $11M to expand industrial automation
Singapore-headquartered Botsync has raised $11 million in a round led by IvyCap Ventures, a homegrown venture capital firm.
Other participants include Capital 2B, a deeptech investor; Taiwan-based accelerator and venture investor AppWorks; South-East Asian early-stage investor Iterative; Singapore angel network AngelCentral; Genesis Alternate Investments; and angel investor Nalin Advani.
The round follows a January 2026 Series A extension led by SGInnovate, taking total funding above $20 million.
Fatehpuria Hygiene secures Rs 100 Cr in first equity fundraise
Fatehpuria Hygiene, a trading, supply chain and fulfilment company, has raised Rs 100 crore in its first equity fundraise, led by investor Madhu Kela.
The company said it plans to use the capital to strengthen its nationwide presence and build a technology-driven supply chain ecosystem. It aims to expand into more than 50 major cities over the next 24 months and develop an AI-enabled, integrated supply chain network.
CountAI raises Rs 10 Cr in seed funding led by Equirus InnovateX Fund
Coimbatore-based industrial AI startup CountAI has raised Rs 10 crore in seed funding led by Equirus InnovateX Fund to expand product development and manufacturing applications. Founded by Harshavardhan Thirupathi and Venkataramanan, the company develops AI-powered quality control and automation systems. Its flagship product, Knit-I, detects fabric defects in real time on circular knitting machines and triggers stoppages to reduce waste.
The technology is deployed across manufacturers including Aarti International, KPR and Indorama. CountAI reports an 80% reduction in defect-related losses across more than 62 machines at Aarti International, while a deployment in Uzbekistan reduced knitting waste from 1.5% to 0.2%. The company plans to expand into other industrial quality control applications.
Finvolve backs Soket AI Labs in seed round to develop indigenous foundation models
Venture capital fund Finvolve and India Accelerator have invested an undisclosed amount in Bengaluru-based Soket AI Labs as part of its seed funding round, co-led by Bajaj Finance, Pennant Technologies and the IndiaAI Mission. Soket AI is developing indigenous foundation models for mathematics, coding, reasoning and multilingual applications under Project EKA. Its recently launched EKA-1 is a 26-billion-parameter model.
The company is also building an integrated AI stack covering foundation models, agentic systems and inference infrastructure. The funding will support research, technology development and sovereign AI solutions for enterprise and mission-critical sectors, including banking, financial services, cybersecurity and defence. Soket aims to enable organisations to deploy AI within their own infrastructure, addressing data sovereignty, security and transparency requirements.
Other news
IndoSpace invests Rs 350 Cr to develop 1.05M sq. ft. industrial park in Karnataka
IndoSpace has launched Narasapura-II, a 1.05 million sq. ft. industrial and logistics park in Karnataka, backed by an investment of Rs 350 crore. Located in the KIADB-notified Narasapura Industrial Area in Kolar district, the development builds on the company's existing 1.60 million sq. ft. Narasapura-I facility. The park will serve businesses across manufacturing, e-commerce, warehousing, engineering and third-party logistics.
It offers connectivity to NH 75 and NH 48, Bengaluru's key consumption centres and nearby industrial clusters. Facilities include digital access systems, IoT-enabled infrastructure monitoring, AI-based utility management and a 24x7 integrated command centre. IndoSpace said the development will strengthen its presence in Karnataka's industrial and logistics market.
Neysa deploys 8,192 AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs to expand AI computing capacity in India
AI cloud provider Neysa has deployed an 8,192-GPU AMD Instinct MI350X cluster on its Tytan bare-metal AI infrastructure platform in Mumbai. The operational deployment will support AI model training, fine-tuning, generative AI and large-scale inference workloads. Global customers have already contracted the capacity for AI deployments in India. The cluster uses AMD EPYC processors and the ROCm software ecosystem, offering configurations through bare metal, Slurm and Kubernetes.
The deployment expands Neysa's silicon-agnostic infrastructure strategy, allowing customers to choose accelerator architecture, networking, storage and operating environments according to their requirements. The partnership with AMD aims to increase access to dedicated, high-density AI computing infrastructure for Indian enterprises and global customers.
The ePlane Company selects LYNX MOSA.ic software platform for e200X electric aircraft
The ePlane Company has selected Lynx’s LYNX MOSA.ic platform to manage mixed-criticality software on its e200X electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft. The three-seat aircraft is designed for air ambulance, urban cargo and passenger services. The platform will allow flight-critical systems, including vehicle and energy management, to operate in isolated software partitions alongside lower-criticality functions such as sensor processing and situational awareness.
Built around a separation kernel-based hypervisor, LYNX MOSA.ic supports shared computing while maintaining safety and cybersecurity isolation. The platform is certifiable to DO-178C Design Assurance Level A, enabling the ePlane Company to develop modular aircraft functions while keeping flight-critical software isolated.
IIT Kanpur, Bharat1.ai launch AI Kavach cybersecurity lab for financial AI systems
IIT Kanpur’s Wadhwani School of AI and Intelligent Systems and Bharat1.ai have launched AI Kavach, an AI cybersecurity and assurance lab focused on banking, payments, lending, insurance and digital financial services. The lab will conduct adversarial testing of financial AI systems, develop containment and sandboxing technologies for autonomous AI agents, and research AI assurance, traceability and vulnerability disclosure.
It will also support workforce development through fellowships, security exercises and industry programmes targeting over 300 students and professionals annually. The initiative will use computing resources supported by the IndiaAI Mission. The partners aim to build shared security evaluation frameworks and connect financial institutions, fintech companies, researchers, regulators and cybersecurity experts to improve the safety of AI deployment.
Exotel appoints Kamolika Peres, Samaresh Parida as independent directors
AI-powered customer experience platform Exotel has appointed Kamolika Peres and Samaresh Parida as independent directors to strengthen its board as it expands across India and international markets. Peres brings over two decades of enterprise technology experience, having held senior roles at Autodesk, ServiceNow, Google Cloud, SAP, IBM and Ericsson.
Parida, a Chartered Accountant and IIM Ahmedabad alumnus, has over 30 years of experience across telecommunications, finance and corporate governance. He previously held leadership positions at Vodafone and PepsiCo and served as an independent director and Audit Committee chairman at IDBI Bank. Their appointments will support Exotel's strategic planning, financial oversight, risk management and corporate governance as it scales its AI-led customer experience platform.
Hitachi Systems India opens Bengaluru cybersecurity centre and partners with CrowdStrike
Hitachi Systems India has launched an Advanced Global Delivery Centre in Bengaluru and partnered with CrowdStrike to provide AI-powered cybersecurity and managed security services across India, Asia Pacific and the Middle East. The collaboration will use CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform to secure endpoints, identity, cloud, data and AI systems. Hitachi Systems India will also participate in Project QuiltWorks, helping organisations identify and address vulnerabilities exposed by frontier AI models through AI-powered scanning and remediation services.
The partnership includes Falcon Next-Gen SIEM services to modernise security operations and support the transition to AI-driven security operations centres. The centre will help enterprises secure AI adoption, address emerging cyber threats and strengthen security infrastructure. Hitachi Systems India has over 2,800 employees and serves more than 1,000 customers.
Sunfox Technologies appoints Subrata Mazumdar as VP of Strategy and Growth
Dehradun-based medtech company Sunfox Technologies has appointed Subrata Mazumdar as Vice President of Strategy and Growth. Based in Mumbai, he will lead market expansion, portfolio strategy, go-to-market planning, pricing and strategic partnerships. Mazumdar brings over 30 years of commercial leadership experience across Abbott, Sanofi, Novartis, Claris Lifesciences and Wockhardt.
During his 15-year tenure at Abbott Diabetes Care, he led the launch of FreeStyle Libre and Libre Pro, helping establish India's continuous glucose monitoring market. The appointment follows Sunfox's $7 million Series A funding round. The company develops Spandan, a portable ECG platform, and plans to expand its reach across homes, clinics and healthcare systems in India and international markets.
Clarissa Group launches farm-to-home and FMCG platform Clarissa Fresh
Clarissa Group has launched Clarissa Fresh, a farm-to-home and FMCG platform offering fresh fruits, vegetables, daily essentials and curated gifting solutions. The move marks the group's expansion beyond hospitality and real estate into agriculture and fresh produce. The platform sources products from its farms in Mukteshwar and Jim Corbett, which grow apples, kiwis, dragon fruit, mulberries and exotic mango varieties, alongside trusted partner farms.
Its primary focus will be B2B customers, including hotels, hospitality businesses, corporate offices and institutional buyers, while also serving individual consumers. Clarissa Fresh plans to expand distribution through quick-commerce and e-commerce platforms such as Blinkit, Instamart and BigBasket. The company also plans to introduce technology-driven sourcing, traceability and ordering systems to support consistent quality and timely deliveries.
Even Hospitals launches public dashboard tracking clinical outcomes and hospital performance
Even Hospitals has launched Even Spotlight, a public-facing dashboard that provides daily updates on clinical outcomes, patient experience and hospital operations. Each metric is displayed against a defined target or benchmark, with a traffic-light system indicating performance levels. Powered by the hospital's in-house operating system, the dashboard currently covers outpatient and inpatient services, with additional measures planned.
It also maintains a public changelog documenting changes or withdrawals of metrics and preserves historical data when measurement definitions change. The initiative aims to improve transparency and accountability by giving patients access to hospital performance data. The launch follows Even Healthcare's $50 million Series B funding round led by Khosla Ventures.
LinkedIn, Wadhwani AI launch programme to train 2,000 entrepreneurs in Northeast India
LinkedIn and Wadhwani AI have signed an MoU to launch AI for Future SMEs, a 12-month programme aimed at building AI and digital skills among 2,000 small and micro entrepreneurs across Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Meghalaya and Manipur. Developed in collaboration with state governments and district councils, the initiative will offer mobile-first training, mentorship and joint certification.
The curriculum will cover AI fundamentals, generative AI, prompt engineering, responsible AI, digital safety and practical business applications, including marketing, customer communication, inventory management and market research. Training will be tailored to local industries such as handloom, handicrafts, bamboo, tourism, food processing and agriculture. The programme will use open-source AI tools and offline learning resources for areas with limited connectivity, with assessments to track improvements in digital skills and business adoption.
SiMa.ai launches Palette 3.0 to boost Physical AI performance by up to 3.5x
SiMa.ai has launched Palette 3.0, a software release designed to improve the performance and efficiency of Physical AI applications across robotics and autonomous drones. The platform enables concurrent execution of multiple AI models on its Modalix MLSoC, supporting workloads such as large language models and vision-language models within tight power and memory limits.
It uses speculative decoding algorithms, including EAGLE3, DFlash and Gemma 4 MTP, to increase model processing speed by up to 3.5x. Palette 3.0 also supports large Mixture-of-Experts models, including GPT-OSS-20B, on a 16GB module. SiMa.ai has released open-source capabilities, documentation and a Model Browser for developers.
ANSR launches 500Leaders platform to develop GCC leadership talent
ANSR has launched 500Leaders, a dedicated platform aimed at identifying, developing and connecting senior leadership talent with Global Capability Centres (GCCs). The platform will focus on three pillars: leadership opportunities, learning and community. It will offer executives access to leadership roles across GCCs, development programmes, mentorship and an invitation-only peer network through the ANSR Leadership Forum.
The initiative seeks to address the growing demand for leaders capable of driving enterprise-wide transformation, innovation and AI adoption as GCCs evolve into strategic business centres. ANSR said it had helped place more than 2,500 leaders across the GCC ecosystem over the past year. The launch follows its partnership with the Indian School of Business to introduce the LATITUDe executive education programme for GCC leaders.
Autodesk, Neilsoft to establish Digital Twin innovation centre in Pune
Autodesk and Neilsoft have partnered to establish a Centre of Excellence (COE) for Building Information Modelling (BIM) and Digital Twin technologies in Pune. The facility, located at Neilsoft's headquarters, will focus on accelerating digital transformation across the Architecture, Engineering, Construction and Operations (AECO) industry.
The centre will combine Autodesk's Forma platform and Tandem technologies with Neilsoft's engineering expertise to develop solutions for building operations, integrated design and construction, sustainability and software engineering. It will also demonstrate a live Digital Twin of Neilsoft's 10-storey, three-acre office complex. The partnership aims to support the adoption of AI-powered energy optimisation, predictive maintenance and data-driven building management solutions across India and international markets.
HyugaLife onboards Tata 1mg's health supplement portfolio
Health and wellness e-commerce platform HyugaLife has onboarded Tata 1mg's range of health supplements, expanding its product portfolio. The offering includes whey and plant-based protein powders, creatine, omega-3 fish oil, probiotics and other nutritional supplements.
The collaboration aims to improve consumer access to verified health and wellness products amid growing interest in preventive healthcare and nutritional supplementation. HyugaLife said the partnership would strengthen its product offerings and provide consumers with a wider selection of established healthcare brands.
Monedo Financial Services crosses Rs 1,000 crore asset mark
Monedo Financial Services has crossed Rs 1,000 crore in total assets, triggering its transition from the Base Layer to the Middle Layer under the Reserve Bank of India's Scale-Based Regulation framework for non-banking financial companies (NBFCs).
The transition brings additional regulatory requirements covering corporate governance, risk management, capital adequacy and financial disclosures. The Mumbai-based NBFC said it had strengthened its board oversight, compliance and internal audit functions in preparation for the change.
Monedo's assets crossed Rs 1,000 crore on November 12, 2026, having grown more than sixfold over three years. The company is targeting assets under management of ₹1,400-1,500 crore in FY27 and aims to reach ₹5,000 crore within two years. Its focus areas include supply chain finance, SME lending and healthcare financing.
Believe partners Hoopr Smash to offer music catalogues for brand campaigns
Global artist development company Believe has partnered with Hoopr Smash to make its Indian music catalogues available for commercial licensing by brands, agencies and content creators. The partnership will provide access to music from labels including Think Music, Ishtar and Believe's Artist Services portfolio.
Hoopr Smash currently serves more than 135 brands and offers over 20,000 pre-cleared tracks. The partnership aims to expand licensed music usage and create additional revenue opportunities for artists and labels.
Syncro1 launches AI-powered digital talent recruitment platform
Syncro1, an AI-powered digital Talent Partner platform, has launched with the aim of transforming recruitment through technology-led hiring and outcome-based commercial models. The platform connects organisations with a network of independent recruitment professionals through structured hiring workflows.
Its eight-layer AI-powered candidate screening system evaluates profiles across multiple parameters, moving beyond conventional keyword matching. The platform also incorporates a three-layer information consent framework to improve transparency and ensure responsible sharing of candidate data.

articles.title: Toyota se lance dans les satellites : le géant de l'automobile veut aussi révolutionner l’industrie spatiale
articles.text:
Toyota vient de dévoiler l’ampleur de ses paris dans l’espace, et il était difficile de s’en douter. Le géant japonais a injecté plus de 240 millions de dollars dans 11 start-up. Son ambition : produire des satellites comme on fabrique des voitures.
Toyota ne pénètre pas à l’aveugle dans le secteur spatial. Depuis 2019, le constructeur travaille avec l’agence japonaise JAXA sur le « Lunar Cruiser », un rover pressurisé destiné aux astronautes sur la Lune. Début 2025, la firme misait aussi sur Interstellar Technologies, une jeune pousse japonaise spécialisée dans les fusées. Mais ces projets restaient jusqu’ici isolés, et le groupe vient de dévoiler une stratégie bien plus vaste dans une interview exclusive accordée à Axios.
Pourquoi Toyota a une carte à jouer
Jim Adler, directeur exécutif de Toyota Ventures, l’une des filiales d’investissement de l’entreprise avec Woven Capital et Toyota Invention Partners, a ainsi indiqué que ces nouveaux investissements couvrent presque toute la chaîne spatiale : fabrication de satellites, communications, navigation, lancements de fusées et entretien des vaisseaux en orbite. On y trouve notamment Stoke Space, fabricant de la fusée réutilisable Nova, ainsi que Xona Space, qui travaille sur une alternative plus précise au GPS.
Ce n’est pas pour rien si Toyota s’intéresse autant à la filière. Grâce à des lancements plus abordables, les opérateurs misent désormais sur de grandes constellations de petits satellites, plutôt que sur une poignée d’engins très coûteux. Problème : la production n’a pas suivi, et ces appareils sont encore souvent conçus sur mesure.
Et bien entendu, fabriquer des machines complexes, en grand nombre et au meilleur coût, c’est le fort de Toyota, qui reste à ce jour le constructeur automobile le plus populaire au monde. La firme apporte également des chaînes d’approvisionnement bien rodées, de quoi aider les start-up à sortir de leurs goulots d’étranglement et à réduire leurs dépenses.
En parallèle, Toyota pourrait profiter d’une meilleure connectivité par satellite, d’une navigation plus précise et de revenus nouveaux en dehors de l’automobile.
Des partenariats qui se concrétisent déjà
Apex Space, start-up fondée en 2022 par un ancien de chez Palantir, illustre parfaitement la méthode Toyota. Car elle possède une vision qui résonne forcément avec la société, puisque son fondateur considère que « quelqu’un doit construire le Toyota des vaisseaux spatiaux ».
Apex propose ainsi des plateformes standardisées, c’est-à-dire tout le satellite sauf sa charge utile, et une filiale du groupe nippon fabrique des composants spécialisés pour ses engins. Le premier logo Toyota pourrait même faire son apparition en orbite dès l’année prochaine, promet le dirigeant de Toyota Ventures.
« Pense-t-on que la mobilité spatiale est dans notre avenir ? Absolument », affirme Jim Adler. Il prend d’ailleurs exemple sur Joby Aviation, spécialiste des taxis aériens électriques dans lequel Toyota a investi près de 900 millions de dollars. Leur partenariat a aussi donné vie à une coentreprise visant à produire ses appareils en série.
Mais le groupe n’est pas seul sur ce terrain. Le chinois Geely construit déjà son propre réseau de satellites, tandis que les constructeurs américains, encouragés par l’administration Trump, s’allient à des industriels de la défense.

articles.title: Egyptian digital gold investment platform Sabika raises funding - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Egyptian digital gold and silver investment platform Sabika has raised new funding to support the development of its platform and the expansion of its services.
Founded in 2022, Sabika allows users to buy and sell gold and silver, track prices and set price alerts at target levels. They can also manage their holdings, review their transaction history and request physical delivery of their purchases.
Sabika closed a six-figure strategic funding round led by M-Empire Angels in September 2015, at which point it had 20,000 users. The startup’s user base has now passed 120,000.
Neither the size of the new investment nor the names of the investors have been disclosed, but Sabika said it would be used to develop its digital platform, strengthen its technology and expand its range of services.
“Our successful funding rounds reflect investor confidence in Sabika’s business model and growth potential,” said Ahmed Khaled,the startup’s CEO. “We see promising opportunities to use technology to make precious metals more accessible to individuals, and to offer services that meet their expectations.”
He said Sabika aims to combine digital convenience with the option of physical delivery, with easy-to-follow steps, clear information and the ability for customers to track their transactions and manage their holdings.
“Surpassing 120,000 users marks an important milestone for Sabika and reflects growing demand for our services. Our user base also gives us deeper insight into our customers’ needs, which we will use to develop our services in the next phase,” Khaled said.
The startup is working on new products and services that will give customers more ways to save and invest in gold and silver, and will announce details when they are ready for launch. It follows the AAOIFI standard for gold.

articles.title: Pour rivaliser avec ChatGPT et Claude, Microsoft dévoile 7 nouvelles IA à prix cassé
articles.text:
Microsoft veut s’émanciper de ses partenaires dans le monde de l’IA. Lors de sa conférence Ignite organisée à San Francisco, le géant américain a présenté sept nouveaux modèles d’intelligence artificielle conçues par ses propres équipes. Chaque modèle s’attaque à une tâche bien précise, comme le codage informatique, la cybersécurité, ou encore la création d’images.
À lire aussi : Le chercheur en guerre contre Microsoft dévoile une 16ᵉ faille Windows, elle peut désactiver votre antivirus
Des modèles spécialisés à la place d’une IA géante
Microsoft mise sur une approche bien différente de celle de ses rivaux. Plutôt que de construire une seule IA capable de tout faire, le groupe américain mise sur des modèles « spécialistes ». Cette approche permet à Microsoft de réduire le coût de fonctionnement de ses intelligences artificielles.
Selon Microsoft, MAI Code 2, son IA de programmation, offre 96 % de performances plus élevées que Claude Opus 5.5, le modèle phare d’Anthropic, pour seulement 5 % de son prix. Côté cybersécurité, MAI Cyber 2 Flash, un modèle dédié à la chasse aux failles, ferait mieux que GPT-6 Astra, l’IA cyber d’OpenAI, tout en coûtant moins cher. Notez que ces comparaisons ont été réalisées par Microsoft lui-même, en prenant en compte sa remise promotionnelle de 50 %.
Microsoft complète sa gamme d’IA avec des modèles dédiés à la voix, à la transcription et à la prise de décision. Pour Mustafa Suleyman, patron de Microsoft AI, « c’est un système, une machine à progresser que nous avons construite, qui optimise à la fois la performance et le prix ».
À lire aussi : Microsoft corrige une faille critique au coeur d’un outil de gestion ultra sensible
S’émanciper d’OpenAI et d’Anthropic
Microsoft avait déjà esquissé les contours de sa stratégie d’émancipation quelques mois plus tôt. En juin dernier, Microsoft avait déjà dévoilé sept modèles maison, dont MAI-Thinking-1, une IA capable de « raisonner » qui rivalisait selon lui avec Claude Sonnet 4.6. Pour rappel, Microsoft a bâti une grande partie de son offre d’IA sur les modèles d’OpenAI, dans lequel il a investi 13 milliards de dollars.
Par la suite, l’éditeur a misé sur Anthropic avec un investissement de 5 milliards de dollars. Par la suite, Microsoft a pris des décisions destinées à s’émanciper des laboratoires d’IA. En juin, Mustafa Suleyman expliquait que l’enjeu n’est autre que « l’autonomie à long terme de Microsoft ». Le groupe veut désormais pouvoir maîtriser les IA qui font tourner ses propres services, comme son assistant Copilot ou GitHub Copilot.
Une super IA en préparation chez Microsoft
Microsoft ne compte pas s’arrêter à ces sept nouvelles IA. Le patron de la division IA de Microsoft assure que ses équipes travaillent sur une IA généraliste de pointe, capable de rivaliser avec ChatGPT ou Claude sur tous les terrains.
« Mon équipe construit une véritable superintelligence », affirme-t-il, sans évoquer la date de sortie de cette intelligence artificielle.
Le patron de Microsoft AI promet de ne pas sacrifier la sécurité sur l’autel de la performance. Après plusieurs dérapages récents des agents IA, il assure faire de l’« alignement », c’est-à-dire la capacité d’une IA à respecter les intentions de ses créateurs, sa priorité absolue. Le modèle de cybersécurité annoncé lors de la conférence Ignite doit d’ailleurs venir renforcer Project Perception, son arsenal contre les cyberattaques.

articles.title: El Xiaomi Watch S5 llega en formato pequeño: así es el nuevo reloj con Google Wallet y hasta 14 días de autonomía
articles.text:
Xiaomi ha presentado multitud de dispositivos. Puede que la nueva gama Xiaomi 18 Pro Series haya opacado un poro al resto, pero es importante comentar algunos de ellos como el Xiaomi Watch S5 (41 mm), la nueva versión en tamaño más pequeño que se ha lanzado a un precio de 229,99 euros, aunque ahora mismo está de oferta por 194,99 euros.
Xiaomi Watch S5 (41 mm)
Más pequeño y con Google Wallet
El Xiaomi Watch S5 se lanzó hace ya unos cuantos meses, por lo que la versión de 41 mm llega ahora para quienes prefieran un reloj más pequeño. Una de las principales novedades es que este smartwatch, por fin, es compatible con pagos a través de Google Wallet, además de Xiaomi Pay.
El diseño es, al igual que vemos en el resto de la gama S, muy elegante, incorpora una batería con autonomía de hasta 14 días de uso y viene con más de 150 modos deportivos, por lo que también se trata de un reloj que podemos utilizar para realizar actividades deportivas.
La pantalla de 1,32 pulgadas cuenta con tecnología AMOLED y ofrece un brillo máximo de 3.000 nits y su software es HyperOS (el de Xiaomi), que añade novedades visuales con notificaciones flotantes y un centro de control rediseñado. Además, también viene con varios sensores de salud como la frecuencia cardíaca y oxígeno en sangre o de temperatura.
El Xiaomi Watch S5 (41 mm) ya se puede comprar en la tienda oficial. Está disponible en color negro o azul claro por 194,99 euros (antes 229,99 euros) y también en color blanco cerámico por 229,99 euros (antes 249,99 euros).

articles.title: Microsoft’s Agent Framework PyPI package compromised to steal credentials
articles.text:
Hackers compromised Microsoft's official Agent Framework Python package on PyPI, publishing two malicious versions designed to steal cloud credentials and other sensitive information from developers' systems.
Microsoft Agent Framework is Microsoft's open-source toolkit for building AI agents and coordinating them in workflows. It's a fairly popular tool with roughly 200,000 monthly downloads on PyPI.
The malicious releases, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published on November 17, 2026, and contained a credential stealer that executed automatically during normal Python startup in affected environments, even when the Agent Framework package was not imported.
Both versions retained their dependency on the legitimate agent-framework-core 1.26.0 package, allowing the framework to function normally while the malware ran in the background.
Multiple security firms discovered and documented the attack, including Socket, Step Security, and Ox Security.
Version 1.26.1 contained a credential stealer that harvested secrets from environment variables, local configuration files, and other running processes where permissions allowed, targeting Azure, AWS, GitHub, Docker, Hugging Face, OpenAI, and other services.
The malware also attempted to obtain Azure managed identity access tokens and Azure DevOps OIDC tokens, potentially giving attackers access to additional cloud resources.
Version 1.26.2 added GitHub Actions OIDC token requests and searches of GitHub runner directories.
According to Socket and StepSecurity, the first malicious release used agent_framework_meta.pth to execute the credential stealer in agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py during Python startup.
The second release restored the original package initializer and moved the malicious code into af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py.
Both versions exfiltrated collected data to the same attacker-controlled endpoint, https://webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb.
PyPI quarantined the first malicious release, but the attacker published a second version roughly 2.5 minutes later, which was also quarantined about eight minutes afterward. The second release indicates that the attacker still had publishing access after the initial quarantine.
It remains unclear how the attacker gained access to publish malicious releases under Microsoft's official PyPI project.
BleepingComputer has contacted Microsoft to learn what the point of breach was, but we have not received a response by publication time.
Developers who installed either malicious version should isolate affected environments, avoid running Python or pip until they are secured, and rebuild from a known-clean environment using the safe 1.26.0 release.
Any potentially exposed credentials that were within the reach of the compromised environment should be rotated immediately.
To determine the exact level of compromise, investigators should look for the specific webhook URL path in egress logs and distinguish blocked requests from completed transfers.

articles.title: Sept ans après le Galaxy Fold, Google durcit le ton sur les applications pour pliables, juste après l’arrivée de l’iPhone Duo — Frandroid
articles.text:
Déplier un Galaxy Z Fold pour lire ses messages et tomber sur une application coincée au milieu de l’écran, encadrée de deux bandes noires, c’est l’expérience que les propriétaires de pliables Android connaissent depuis sept ans. Le premier Galaxy Fold date de 2019, et le problème n’a jamais vraiment disparu. Google a attendu qu’Apple sorte son propre pliable pour taper du poing sur la table. Simple coïncidence de calendrier, ou réveil forcé ?
    Pour aller plus loin
Quel est le meilleur smartphone pliant en novembre 2026 ?
            
Sur son blog développeurs, Google détaille ses nouvelles exigences pour les applications : dès avril 2027, toute nouvelle application ou mise à jour publiée sur le Play Store devra fournir des captures d’écran sur pliable et respecter le « niveau 3 » de ses règles de qualité adaptative.
Pour les jeux, le calendrier est décalé : captures en avril 2027, niveau 3 obligatoire en août 2027. Google justifie l’effort par les plus de 580 millions d’appareils à grand écran en circulation, un chiffre qui mélange pliables, tablettes et ordinateurs portables.
L’annonce arrive moins d’un mois après la sortie en boutique de l’iPhone Duo, le premier pliable d’Apple. Mishaal Rahman, chargé des relations avec la communauté Android chez Google, a résumé sur X.
Le Black Friday est lancé sur l’univers Apple. Sur Back Market, profitez de promotions sur les iPhone, MacBook, iPad, AirPods et Apple Watch. Chaque appareil est soumis à jusqu’à 100 points de contrôle qualité et est livré avec une garantie de 12 mois. De quoi profiter de performances comparables à celles d’un produit neuf.
    Pour aller plus loin
J’ai testé l’iPhone Duo : un produit qui éblouit pour faire oublier ses compromis
            
Après la carotte, le bâton
Le niveau 3 n’a rien d’exotique. Une application doit occuper tout l’écran sans « letterboxing » (ces fameuses bandes noires qui la gardent au format d’un téléphone classique), fonctionner en multifenêtre, donc à côté d’une autre appli, et conserver son état quand on plie, déplie ou tourne l’appareil. Concrètement, la vidéo continue, le texte en cours de saisie reste là et on garde sa position dans le fil. Les niveaux 2 et 1, plus ambitieux (interfaces à plusieurs volets, prise en charge du clavier et du stylet), restent facultatifs et rapportent un badge, des mises en avant et une meilleure exposition dans le Play Store.
Google n’a pas découvert le sujet cet automne : Android 12L visait déjà les grands écrans en 2022, et Android 16 a commencé à ignorer, sur grand écran, les restrictions d’orientation imposées par les développeurs. La nouveauté, c’est la sanction. Une appli qui ne passe pas le niveau 3 ne pourra plus être publiée ni mise à jour, et sa visibilité pourra baisser. Les petites lignes laissent tout de même une échappatoire, puisque les applis existantes non mises à jour resteront téléchargeables.
Quant au rôle de l’iPhone Duo, Google ne le mentionne nulle part. Mishaal Rahman assure qu’il fallait attendre que le système et les outils soient prêts, sous peine d’imposer « beaucoup de friction » aux développeurs. L’argument se tient, et c’est un salarié de Google qui le porte. Les premières annonces côté Play Store sont pourtant tombées à l’Android Dev Summit, fin octobre, quelques jours après la sortie de l’iPhone Duo.
Qui y gagne, et ce qui reste flou
Les premiers gagnants sont évidents : les propriétaires d’un Galaxy Z Fold 8 ou d’un Pixel 11 Pro Fold, qui paient le prix fort pour un grand écran souvent mal exploité.
Les joueurs aussi, puisque Google interdit noir sur blanc les redémarrages et les pertes de progression en plein niveau lors d’un pliage.
Pour les développeurs, l’addition est moins réjouissante. Un internaute rappelle sous le fil que les pliables pèsent encore peu dans le parc, et un petit studio devra quand même tester ses écrans aux formats 1:1 et 4:3, le second étant celui du Galaxy Z Fold 8. L’émulateur Android suffit pour les captures, ce qui limite la casse.
Google n’explique pas comment il vérifiera le respect du niveau 3 : contrôle automatisé, tests manuels ou simple déclaration du développeur.
Les tablettes, les Googlebook et Android XR sont promis pour « plus tard », sans date. Enfin, août 2027 apporte une autre échéance, discrète mais lourde : les applis devront cibler Android 17, qui retire aux développeurs la possibilité de bloquer l’orientation ou le redimensionnement sur grand écran. Celles qui comptaient sur une dérogation devront s’y mettre de toute façon.
Ceux qui hésitent entre un pliable Android et l’iPhone Duo, que nous avons testé, ont désormais un argument de plus à peser, mais pas avant 2027. Sur le fond, Google vise juste, et ces règles auraient pu exister dès 2022. Sept ans de patience envers les applis bâclées, puis un sursaut quelques semaines après l’entrée d’Apple sur le marché : si c’est une coïncidence, elle tombe franchement bien.
    Pour aller plus loin
J’ai testé l’iPhone Duo : un produit qui éblouit pour faire oublier ses compromis

articles.title: GTA 6 : voici les 55 trophées et succès à décrocher pour pour obtenir le platine
articles.text:
La liste des trophées de GTA 6 est enfin connue. Elle compte 55 trophées : 1 platine, 2 en or, 6 en argent et 46 en bronze. Sur Xbox Series, les 54 succès classiques rapportent 1 000 points de Gamerscore, et le dernier débloque le nouveau succès « Mythique » de Microsoft.
Sur ces 55 trophées, 28 sont cachés et liés à l’histoire : chapitres, missions principales, personnages. Pour éviter les spoilers, nous les avons regroupés dans un tableau à part, en fin d’article. Les deux premiers tableaux ne dévoilent rien de l’intrigue.
Combien de trophées y a-t-il dans GTA 6 ?
| Type | Nombre | Gamerscore (Xbox) | 
|---|---|---|
| Platine | 1 | 0 (succès Mythique) | 
| Or | 2 | 150 | 
| Argent | 6 | 210 | 
| Bronze | 46 | 640 | 
| Total | 55 | 1 000 | 
Les deux trophées en or récompensent la fin de l’histoire et le 100 %. Les six trophées en argent demandent le plus de travail en dehors de la campagne : 250 cascades, l’or dans tous les stands de tir, cinq chambres fortes de banque, huit séries de missions pour des inconnus, trois séries de cartes à collectionner et 100 lieux scannés avec l’application WAiNK It.
Comment obtenir le platine de GTA 6 ?
Le platine « C’est le prix de Vice City ! » s’obtient en débloquant les 54 autres trophées. Le plus long est « Une longue route », qui demande de terminer le jeu à 100 %. Il faut donc finir l’histoire, mais aussi les missions secondaires des inconnus, explorer toute la Leonida et essayer chaque activité : courses, drones, pêche, stands de tir, arcade, bowling, braquages. Bon courage donc !
Prévoyez du temps. Les testeurs ont mis de 50 à 80 heures pour l’histoire principale seule, et IGN n’affichait que 70 % de complétion après plus de 100 heures de jeu. Le platine devrait donc demander plusieurs centaines d’heures à la plupart des joueurs.
À noter que GTA 6 ne permet pas de rejouer les missions terminées et que certains choix modifient le déroulement de l’histoire. Un trophée lié à vos décisions pourrait donc vous échapper sur une première partie. Ensuite, les codes de triche ne se débloquent qu’après l’histoire principale, mais les utiliser empêche de gagner un trophée correspondant.
La liste des trophées de GTA 6 (sans spoiler)
Voici les 27 trophées visibles, dont le platine, avec leurs intitulés officiels en français :

|---|---|---|

articles.title: How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
Thanks to Amit Gupta, Senior Director- AI/ML and Mark Wang, Software Engineering PMTS from Salesforce for your contributions in the vision and partnership of cross-Region inference routing on SageMaker AI.
Salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves a wide variety of models for products across Salesforce, including Agentforce and the Salesforce Trust Layer, in 30+ global Regions. These include both models trained in house and open source models. Hosting models separately in each Region splits capacity and makes traffic spikes harder to absorb, which turns a capacity shortfall into an availability problem.
This post shows how Salesforce set up the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI and how it lets the team add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments. It also walks through how Salesforce sees where each request was served and why. The cross-Region inference routing gives an application one invocation path across SageMaker AI endpoints in several Regions and accounts, and sends each request to an endpoint that can serve it. Those endpoints are Salesforce’s own, already deployed. The post starts with the capacity problem Salesforce faced, explains how the router works and how Salesforce integrated it into its Internal Gateway, walks through an example setup, and then describes what the team observed.
Why serving these models makes capacity a reliability problem
Salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves customers from the Region their requests come from, across 30+ global Regions and hundreds of AWS accounts, and they provision capacity based on each customer’s traffic. Every customer has its own peak window, and those windows often overlap. Provisioning for the overlapping peak would be the safe choice, but it costs too much. Customers also onboard new business units at short notice, so they must grow the fleet quickly. Adding capacity quickly, Region by Region, leaves Salesforce with capacity fragmentation: some Regions have idle instances while others run out.
Before the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI, Salesforce used its Internal Gateway to send traffic that the local endpoints couldn’t handle to other Regions. The team built and operated this path, supported by basic health checks, retries, and Region-switching logic. That approach had two gaps. First, the gateway had no capacity signals from either the local or the remote endpoint, so it couldn’t tell when to shift traffic or whether the destination had room. Second, cross-Region traffic had to leave the virtual private cloud (VPC) through a NAT gateway and an internet gateway and travel over public AWS networking. In design reviews, the team also raised the risk of cascading failures: moving traffic during an incident can overload the next Region, so Salesforce needed a cap on cross-Region traffic.
Building this logic separately in every application doesn’t scale across Salesforce. The team needed a managed, capacity-aware routing path.
What the inference router does
The inference router is a Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account. Your application invokes the router instead of an endpoint, passing a routing target name with the same request body and content type it sends to InvokeEndpoint today. A routing target is a name you choose for one logical model, such as a toxicity classifier, and it lists the endpoints and inference components that may serve that model by their full Amazon Resource Names (ARNs). A router holds one routing target per model, and a problem with one model’s endpoints does not move traffic for the others. A routing target can mix single-model endpoints and inference components.
Because each destination is named by its ARN, it can be in another Region or another AWS account. The account that owns an endpoint grants access through a resource-based endpoint policy that allows one named router to invoke it, which is how Salesforce runs it.
The router prefers its own Region, and while the local destination serves successfully, requests stay there. The router judges each destination by the outcomes of recent requests. Platform faults, 5xx errors from the model container, throttles, and timeouts lower a destination’s health. As they persist, the router moves a growing share of new requests to healthy destinations, typically starting within about a minute. It can take several minutes for a destination with little traffic. Signals such as scaling progress and failed instance launches affect how quickly the router responds once errors appear, but they do not move traffic by themselves. After recovery, traffic returns over several minutes, more slowly than it left, so it does not swing back and forth. When a destination fails a request without running the model, for example by throttling it, the router retries that request once on another destination.
Client errors such as invalid input do not move traffic, because they would fail the same way in any Region. Model latency does not move traffic either, because a slow response often reflects a long prompt or output and does not by itself mean the endpoint is unhealthy. The router also does not deploy models, copy artifacts, or add instances. It uses the capacity you have deployed, and each endpoint’s own autoscaling keeps adding instances as its traffic grows.
How Salesforce integrated the router into its Internal Gateway
In Salesforce’s Internal Gateway, the router call sits exactly where the direct InvokeEndpoint call used to be: in the per-request egress path, after the data residency check and before response handling. That check is the one routing decision the gateway keeps. A request tagged with a residency requirement is pinned to its in-Region routing target, whose only destination is the local endpoint, so it can never fail over across a boundary. Everything else goes to the router with the same body, content type, and accept type the gateway already sent. Capacity awareness, health assessment, and failover now live in the routing layer instead of in Salesforce’s code.
Salesforce treats the two routing fields on every response as first-class telemetry. The gateway logs InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason on the same structured line as the existing request ID and trace ID, and emits them as application performance monitoring (APM) tags. Because the ARN carries the Region and account, a single log line shows whether a request ran locally or crossed a boundary, and why: local-preferred, failover, capacity-available, or only-healthy. The team joins these fields against the router’s Amazon CloudWatch metrics when investigating a traffic shift.
The gateway’s timeout accounts for cross-Region round-trip latency, so a request that fails over has time to complete in the remote Region. Because the router already retries once on another destination, the gateway adds no retries of its own, which keeps attempts from multiplying during an incident.
Example setup
The following walkthrough shows the configuration Salesforce tested, using example IDs and names. Salesforce first created a router in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2) with a local destination and confirmed that requests were routed to it. The team then registered an endpoint in the US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2) owned by a different account, removed the local destination, and confirmed that requests reached the remote endpoint across the account and Region boundary. In the examples, the router account is 111122223333, and the account that owns the us-east-2 endpoint is 444455556666.
Authorize the router on the destination endpoint
In the account that owns the us-east-2 endpoint, the owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows the router account to invoke the endpoint, with a condition that limits access to one named router. The router does not need to exist yet, so you can use the ARN of the router you plan to create.
The sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn condition means the router account can reach the endpoint only through that router. The endpoint owner can revoke access at any time with delete-endpoint-policy.
Create the router
In the router account, create the router in us-west-2 with one routing target that lists both destinations by ARN.
Each additional model becomes another entry in RoutingTargets.
Confirm that each destination is routable
Before sending traffic, call DescribeInferenceRouter and check each destination’s RoutingStatus. Routable means SageMaker AI could read the destination and it can serve traffic. Unroutable means the destination was read but can’t serve right now, for example because the endpoint is not InService. Unknown means SageMaker AI couldn’t read the destination with your credentials, for example because you lack sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint (or sagemaker:DescribeInferenceComponent for an inference component), or, for a destination in another account, because its endpoint policy doesn’t grant Describe.
Invoke the router instead of the endpoint
The change in the calling code is small. The request body, content type, and accept type stay exactly as they were. The client and operation change, and the endpoint name is replaced by the router name and the routing target name.
An InferenceId and CustomAttributes are passed through to the destination as with InvokeEndpoint, so identifiers such as a trace ID travel with the request. Members such as TargetVariant and InferenceComponentName are not used, because the routing target replaces them.
Seeing where requests went
Most teams evaluating a routing layer first ask how to tell what it did. The inference router answers on every response and in Amazon CloudWatch. Each response carries the ARN of the destination that served it and a routing reason, in the InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason fields and in the matching X-Amzn-SageMaker-Invoked-Routed-Resource-Arn and X-Amzn-SageMaker-Invoked-Routing-Reason headers. Because the ARN includes the Region and account, logging both values with your own request logs gives you a per-request record of whether each call ran locally or crossed a boundary.
The routing reason takes one of four values. local-preferred means a healthy destination in the router’s Region served the request. failover means a destination in the router’s Region exists but isn’t serving reliably, so the router sent the request elsewhere. capacity-available means no destination in the router’s Region could take the request, and it went to one of several healthy destinations in other Regions. only-healthy means it was served by the only eligible destination that was healthy.
In aggregate, the router publishes OpenTelemetry metrics to CloudWatch in its own account and Region, each carrying the router name and destination ARN, so the cross-Region picture is visible from one place. aws.sagemaker.inference_router.invocations counts requests per destination, and its error.type attribute splits failures into invocation_4xx, invocation_5xx (including timeouts), and invocation_model_error for errors returned by the model.
aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.duration measures the time each destination took, and aws.sagemaker.inference_router.overhead.duration measures the time the router added, including the network to and from a remote Region. aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.status reports each destination’s health state as healthy, overloaded, or degraded. You query these metrics with PromQL in CloudWatch Query Studio, and you can place them next to each endpoint’s existing SageMaker AI metrics on a cross-account, cross-Region dashboard.
Testing failover across accounts and Regions
Salesforce tested the router in two configurations. First, same-Region routing in us-west-2, where the Internal Gateway called the local inference router and the router sent requests to the local Endpoint A. Second, cross-account, cross-Region routing, where the router in us-west-2 also listed an endpoint in us-east-2 owned by a separate infrastructure account. Before sending traffic, the team called DescribeInferenceRouter and confirmed that the routing target listed both destinations and that both reported a RoutingStatus of Routable. Requests sent to the router were then served by the local endpoint, with a routing reason of local-preferred. Setup took little effort: the endpoint owner added an endpoint policy for the router’s account, and the router call replaced the direct InvokeEndpoint call in the gateway’s egress path, with the same request body, content type, and accept type.
To test failover, the team flooded the local endpoint in us-west-2 until it was saturated, while a separate probe kept invoking the router and recorded where each request was served and how long it took. For about five minutes of saturation, probe latency at p50 rose from 0.2 seconds to 45 to 58 seconds, and traffic stayed in us-west-2. This is the intended behavior, because latency alone does not move traffic. When requests began to exceed the model container’s 60-second handler timeout and return errors, the router started to shift traffic. The first requests reached us-east-2 about two minutes after the first errors, and within another minute about 78 percent of probe traffic was served in us-east-2. The remaining 20 to 25 percent stayed local so the router could detect recovery.
Once traffic had moved, p50 latency returned to 0.2 seconds, and the cross-Region path added under 100 milliseconds at p50. After the local endpoint recovered, traffic returned to us-west-2 gradually over about 10 minutes, and the probe recorded no errors during failover or failback. The InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason fields on each response, together with the router’s per-destination invocation metrics in CloudWatch, showed the whole sequence without any extra instrumentation.
The router lets Salesforce replace operational logic the team used to build and run itself: the health checks, retries, and Region-switching logic in the Internal Gateway. Capacity signals and failover now live in the routing layer, not in each application.
Before broader adoption, Salesforce plans to repeat the failover test with the local endpoint held at saturation for longer, measure cross-Region latency at millisecond precision, evaluate cascading-Region behavior at the cross-Region cap, and roll out the router across more Regions.
        “With the new cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI, we can add capacity securely and keep our data residency commitments. Workloads that must stay in a region stay there, and only eligible traffic can be served from another Region. A single managed call works alongside our existing failover logic, so we didn’t have to re-architect our application or change our payloads. SageMaker AI handles routing, health detection, and fallback, and customer data always stays within the Salesforce trust boundary. We decide which Regions are eligible and control access through endpoint policies that we own. Because inference router works with Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail, we also get a complete observability, cost-tracking, and governance architecture for our workloads.”
— Richard Chang, Software Engineering Architect, Salesforce
Best practices and what to watch
Keep the same model, container image, and artifacts available in every Region you register, because the router does not copy them, and a destination that runs a different model version will return different answers to the same request.
Size each destination Region for its own traffic plus the overflow you expect to send it. The router does not create capacity, and if every eligible destination is busy, your application receives the destinations’ own errors. Configure autoscaling on each destination the way you do today, with enough headroom that a receiving endpoint can scale out under its own policy when traffic arrives from another Region.
Customers can set the cap in the receiving endpoint’s configuration (CrossRegionTrafficConfig), as a per-instance request rate and the largest share of the endpoint’s capacity that remote traffic may use. Local traffic never counts against the cap. When remote traffic reaches it, the endpoint stops accepting additional requests from other Regions and the router sends them to other destinations, so local callers keep their capacity. The cap applies to real-time endpoints.
Conclusion
Salesforce serves a wide variety of models for products across the company in 30+ global Regions, and hosting them separately in each Region had turned capacity shortfalls into availability problems. With the inference router, Salesforce registers the endpoints it already runs in different Regions and accounts behind one call, so traffic that a local endpoint cannot serve reaches capacity elsewhere instead of failing. Requests that must stay in a Region stay there, endpoint owners authorize cross-account access through policies they control, and every response shows where a request ran and why. SageMaker AI handles the routing, health assessment, and gradual return of traffic after recovery, instead of each calling application building that logic itself. This lets Salesforce add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments.
The cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI is generally available starting November 18, 2026, in all commercial Regions where inference is supported for real-time endpoints. To get started, see the Inference router documentation in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide and the CreateInferenceRouter API reference.

articles.title: Qwen4-Max vs. Claude Opus 5.5: The cheaper model costs you somewhere else.
articles.text:
Qwen4-Max vs. Claude Opus 5.5: The cheaper model costs you somewhere else.
Qwen4-Max, made available in preview to Token Plan subscribers on November 11 and generally released on November 16, is quite the talker.
When the independent testing firm Artificial Analysis ran its standard test suite on Alibaba’s new model, Qwen4-Max generated 127 million output tokens. That’s roughly twice the median for comparable models. Artificial Analysis reports 218 million output tokens for Claude Opus 5.5 at max effort with default fallback enabled. That is more than Qwen4-Max uses, but Opus’s default effort setting is medium.
Writing a lot of tokens doesn’t automatically mean a higher bill, especially with Qwen4-Max, because Alibaba charges very little for those tokens. Qwen4-Max costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens. Claude Opus 5.5 costs more, billing at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Cached input has separate pricing: Qwen4-Max lists $0.075 per million cached input tokens, while Opus 5.5 cache reads cost $0.20 per million tokens. Cache writes also have separate rates.
Cheaper only wins if you don’t give up accuracy to get it.
Costs and tokens are only part of the picture, though. Cheaper only wins if you don’t give up accuracy to get it. Alibaba’s launch post calls Qwen4-Max “your new teammate,” which I take to mean it’s positioned as an everyday workhorse. Alibaba’s launch chart shows wins and losses against Opus on agent benchmarks, where a model works through a job step by step using tools. Its coding results are mixed too: Qwen4-Max trails Opus 48.5% to 59.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, but leads on DeepSWE v1.1. These published results use different benchmarks and evaluation setups; they are not a single controlled comparison.
I’ve seen fact and fiction in launch marketing materials (including benchmarks), so I wanted to get to the bottom of this. Is Qwen4-Max a better alternative to Opus 5.5 for some day-to-day work? I ran a few tests to answer that question for everyday users.
The tests
I ran each model once per test at default settings, with no turn cap. Opus 5.5 ran through Anthropic’s API, and Qwen4-Max ran through OpenRouter on Alibaba’s own servers. Opus’s dollar figures are estimates based on reported token usage and Anthropic’s list prices. Qwen4-Max’s are what OpenRouter billed. The aggregate token totals below don’t separate uncached input, cache writes, and cache reads, so they aren’t sufficient to independently reproduce the cost estimates. I wrote a script that graded each model’s answers against an answer key I built along with the tests.
I wanted to make sure the tests were hard for each model, so I used GPT-5 as a baseline and ran each test through it first. When GPT-5’s score was low enough to count as a failure, I considered the test “hard enough.”
Here are the three tests I used:
- Multi-app workflow (76 points) – I set up a fake company with a ticket tracker, code repo, chat, and calendar, and each model worked across all four as an agent. It had to triage a customer bug, find the code change that caused it, assign the right owner, calculate deadlines, count tickets, and refuse two requests that company policy forbids.
- Incident investigation (60 points) – The models had to dig through logs, metrics, and change history to explain three overlapping outages that happened at the same time. The data included decoy deploys, two servers with wrong clocks, and a misleading alert.
- Agent bug fix (47 points) – Each model fixed an accounting library with 11 planted bugs. Six of those bugs don’t fail any test the model can see, so it had to find them by comparing the code with the documentation. Three of the library’s own tests are wrong, and the model should report them without editing them.
Multi-app workflow
Opus 5.5 scored all 76 points. Qwen4-Max scored 71.
All five of Qwen4-Max’s missed points came from the same mistake. Three questions asked which team owns a piece of code. The repo’s ownership file says that when several rules match, the last one in the file wins. Qwen4-Max picked the most specific rule each time. Everything else it did was correct, including the deadline math across time zones and both refusals.
…Qwen4-Max can handle a long, messy office job, but one misread rule followed it through the whole task.
That tells me Qwen4-Max can handle a long, messy office job, but one misread rule followed it through the whole task. In a real company, that mistake sends tickets to the wrong team, creating more confusion.
Qwen4-Max wrote almost twice as many output tokens as Opus but cost less than a third. It also took more than three times as long for a little more than half as many turns.
The numbers:
- Opus 5.5: 44 turns, 2,451,342 in, 26,617 out, $2.13, 248 s.
- Qwen4-Max: 25 turns, 1,746,170 in, 51,264 out (41,644 reasoning), $0.62, 791 s.
Incident investigation
Qwen4-Max narrowly pulled ahead on accuracy here. It scored 59 of 60, and Opus 5.5 scored 58.
Both models untangled the three outages, named the two-step cause of the main one, ruled out every decoy, and caught both bad clocks. Both also made the same kind of slip. They credited a customer-facing error code to the wrong service, Opus twice and Qwen4-Max once.
This was Qwen4-Max’s strongest result in my tests. On this investigation task, it scored one point higher than Opus for about 31% of the reported cost. One run does not establish a general advantage in agent work. Opus 5.5 pulled ahead on time, though. Qwen4-Max took about 9.5 minutes, and Opus took under 4.
The numbers:
- Opus 5.5: 22 turns, 1,216,769 in, 23,642 out, $1.41, 221 s.
- Qwen4-Max: 18 turns, 1,104,031 in, 33,036 out (23,153 reasoning), $0.44, 570 s.
Agent bug fix
Just like the last test, neither model scored perfectly on accuracy. Opus 5.5 scored 45 of 47, and Qwen4-Max scored 40. This was the coding test, and its result was consistent with Opus’s lead on Terminal-Bench 4.0, though Alibaba’s coding results were mixed.
Opus fixed all 11 bugs. Its only miss was the third wrong test, which it didn’t report, costing it two points. Qwen4-Max missed that same test and lost five more points. It fixed 10 of the 11 bugs and missed one where splitting a payment across invoices loses a cent. It also left a scratch file in the tests folder, which my rules count as changing the tests.
The tool logs show how differently they worked. Opus made its first fix on turn 4 and finished in 12 turns. Qwen4-Max read files for 15 turns before its first edit and took 30 turns in all. More reading didn’t translate to a better score in this case, though.
The cost gap was smallest on this test. Qwen4-Max used more than three times the input tokens, so its bill came to about two-thirds of Opus’s.
The numbers:
- Opus 5.5: 12 turns, 228,824 in, 6,433 out, $0.38, 64 s.
- Qwen4-Max: 30 turns, 827,545 in, 15,813 out (6,701 reasoning), $0.25, 310 s.
Results
| Test | Claude Opus 5.5 | Qwen4-Max | 
| Multi-app workflow (of 76) | 76 | 71 | 
| Incident investigation (of 60) | 58 | 59 | 
| Agent bug fix (of 47) | 45 | 40 | 
| Total tokens in / out | 3,896,935 / 56,692 | 3,677,746 / 100,113 | 
| Total cost | $3.91 (estimated) | $1.31 | 
| Total time | 533 s | 1,671 s | 
The talker reputation checked out. Qwen4-Max generated 77% more output tokens than Opus across the three tests. Those totals include reasoning tokens, so they do not measure just the length of the visible answers; the models also use different tokenizers.
What Qwen4-Max really costs is time and accuracy.
Its prices are low enough that it didn’t matter, and the total bill still came to about a third of Opus’s. What Qwen4-Max really costs is time and accuracy. It took about 3.14 times as long in total and scored 170 of 183 points, nine fewer than Opus’s 179.
What do I think?
Each model ran once, so a gap of a point or two could shift on another run. I’d try Qwen4-Max on your own long-running agent jobs before trusting it with code. I recommend checking its answers against source material and verifying code with tests and human review; a second model’s agreement alone does not establish accuracy.
I’d keep Opus 5.5 for coding and for any job where a wrong answer could cause problems down the line. It was more accurate on two of the three tests, and it finished the three tasks in about a third of the total time.
Qwen4-Max earned a place, though. For investigation work, where the model digs through a lot of data and can wait a few extra minutes, it matched Opus for a fraction of the price. Qwen4-Max’s one-point lead on this investigation task is encouraging, but these single-run tests cannot validate Alibaba’s broader agent claims or establish a general coding ranking.
Learning Path

articles.title: Juanjo, español viviendo en Japón: “Los japoneses han normalizado vivir en 15 o 20 metros cuadrados”
articles.text:
Aunque son muchos los edificios grandes que podemos encontrar en Tokio, también existen algunos que son mucho más pequeños. En un vídeo de YouTube, Juanjo Dalmau muestra algunos de estos espacios.
“Desde fuera parece una ciudad superfuturista con edificios enormes, que lo es, pero mucha gente vive en pisos diminutos de 20, 25 e incluso 9 metros cuadrados”, comenta el creador de contenido. En él muestra cómo se aprovechan los espacios y cómo están organizados.
“Los japoneses han normalizado que vivir en 15 o 20 metros cuadrados”. Así valora la forma de vida que puede encontrarse en Tokio.
Las dimensiones son lo primero que llama la atención, pero el recorrido permite fijarse también en la distribución. La cocina, el lugar de trabajo y la zona de descanso deben encajar en una superficie que deja poco margen para separar unas actividades de otras.
Una cocina, una mesa de trabajo y hasta un balcón
En uno de los apartamentos que muestra, tenemos una cocina con dos fogones; también hay una mesa de trabajo y, en el área de estar, tenemos un sofá y un televisor.
Además, este apartamento cuenta con un balcón exterior. Por más que sea pequeño, ofrece un espacio abierto fuera de la estancia principal.
La visita permite ver el apartamento con sus muebles y sus usos cotidianos. La mesa sirve para trabajar y el sofá permite disponer de una zona de estar, aunque ambos tengan que compartir los pocos metros disponibles con el resto de la vivienda.
Para que entendamos cómo es posible que sean tan pequeños, Dalmau menciona el alto precio del suelo y el número de personas que habitan en la ciudad.
También es importante el hecho de que pasen mucho tiempo fuera. Para algunos de ellos el apartamento es solo un sitio para dormir.
Así se entienden las casas que muestra. En los pocos metros que tienen, han de estar presentes todas las funciones de una casa. El resto del día se pasa fuera.
