articles.title: Tesla’s $30,000 Cybercab comes with a $299 monthly catch
articles.text:
There is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla’s self-driving Cybercab, several.
Last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet’s Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox, offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks, but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s “limited release” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December.
From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.
The business model raises questions about what people will actually get when they buy a Cybercab. “You’ll never really own the car,” says Ivan Drury, the director of insights at Edmunds. “It’s more like $30,000 to buy into a franchise.”
According to documents posted on Tesla’s website, the vehicle “will not operate” without what Tesla is calling an “autonomy subscription,” a monthly fee that will start at $299. If owners don’t pay on time and in full, their self-driving cars won’t work. If they try to operate the vehicles in areas that don’t support the service—right now, they’re restricted to portions of cities in Florida and Texas—their self-driving cars won’t work. (That area can expand, contract, or “relocate” at any time.)
If owners do anything that Tesla deems “unauthorized or inappropriate,” the company says it can suspend or cancel the subscription—and their self-driving cars won’t work. If the vehicle loses connectivity, the self-driving cars won’t work. (“Tesla is not responsible for carrier, spectrum, environmental, or other external outages,” its “autonomy agreement” says.)

articles.title: Behind Booking.com's AI Evolution: The Unpolished Story
articles.text:
Transcript
Jabez Eliezer Manuel: Today, Booking.com impacts billions of travel decisions, and behind each of those travel decisions is actually a bunch of ML platforms working behind the scenes. I'm here to talk about them. In the spirit of QCon's 20th anniversary, we are going to go back in time by two decades and take on a journey and then see how these platforms evolve.
To make it easier for you to follow along, I've structured my talk into three layers, the data management layer, the ML engineering, and domain intelligence. In the data management layer, we will see the evolution of our databases, and some of the scale challenges that we had, and the cloud migration that we undertook to actually better our data. In the ML engineering layer, it'll be model serving at scale, and our feature engineering atoms there. In the domain intelligence layer, it'll be a high-level tour of all the machine learning platforms that we have. I'll pick one of them and then do a deep dive, so you get a full evolution of that specific platform, and you'll also have something tangible to take.
The World in 2005
Let's go back to 2005. This was how the world looked like in 2005, if you remember these camera phones. Web 2.0 was taking off as a platform, and Booking.com was just like 9 years old. It had still not joined the Priceline group. Inside Booking, something fascinating was happening. We had run our first A/B experiment. Today everything goes through experimentation. It doesn't matter if it's a simple CSS change or an infrastructure change, everything goes through experimentation. At any point in time, if you're visiting Booking.com, you are subjected to 1,000-plus experiments, literally. Over the period of time, we have run 150,000 experiments or more until now. One thing that's certain is that most of our experiments fail, our success rate is just less than 25%. The goal isn't to get it right, but it is to learn fast. If you see that golden star on the top right, it's my little takeaway marker.
It's my way of hinting to you that there might be a lesson in this slide that is reusable for you. Continuing on experimentation. Experimentation built our data-driven DNA. It gave us a lot of technical benefits, which is sure. The ones that I like are that it eliminated HIPPOs. There were no endless debates internally. You just say, ok, let's go and build, test it, and done. The last is like, no, it created a culture of humility. There were no experts in the room, meaning that nobody could pinpoint and say, yes, let's experiment and then figure it out.
Data Management Layer
Experiments needed data, and that's where we are going to begin our journey in data management. In this part, I want to talk about our MySQL, our Hadoop, and our move to cloud. These are the three topics that I want to cover. This was our original tech stack when Booking.com started. It was just Perl and Postgres. Quickly, we replaced Postgres with MySQL, primarily because of its asynchronous replication capabilities and for other reasons as well. In 2005, our setup was just a single master and four slaves. Fast forward 15 years, we were operating one of the largest clusters in the world. You might be wondering, how do you manage so many instances? Three things. We have a single writer setup, and we have replication chains, which I'll show you. Then we have a lot of automation. Let's make it real with an example, with an image. What you're seeing is a single master topology.
On the left, orange is the master, and then there are replicas or slaves. The colors indicate different data centers out there. As you can see, we minimize the replication across DCs by having intermediate masters. This whole topology is managed by a replication management tool called Orchestrator. If anybody is using MySQL, you might be aware of it. Automation was a necessity. For example, every 60 days, we take these 7,000 instances or so out, deprovision them, and reprovision them again. That meant that for every three minutes, there is some action that is going on. It is not humanely possible for some engineer to sit and do it. We have plenty of automation to do that.
There are a few things that makes our MySQL setup a little bit different. One is we don't use any specialized hardware. It's like simple frontend blades that are used for MySQL. No stored procedures, no UDFs, no views, not even a cache layer. Yes, no cache layers. The secret sauce, what we do is we actually create smaller DBs. The soft limit is 2 terabytes. The hard limit is 10 terabytes. We try to keep everything small. The reason is we want this database to fit into the fast storage of that server blade that we are using. In this example, we were normally using server blade 7 or 9, if you are aware of its configuration. What that meant is our point queries were less than 350 microseconds, which was roughly in the order of some of the memory engines out there. We were effectively using MySQL as a cache.
It also provided several side benefits. It was faster backups, quicker failovers, and primarily also lower cost, because if you're moving away from fast storage to iSCSI, it's expensive. We didn't just use MySQL. We actually helped shape it. What do I mean by that? In the early days of Booking, we had expertise in-house to fork MySQL, but we made a conscious decision to say that we're not going to fork, we're going to contribute upstream. Many of the features that you see today exist because we wanted it. Like, for example, GTID-based replication is because we actually proposed it. We made the case. We shaped the design of MySQL.
I want to sidestep a bit and then give you a picture of how machine learning looked in that era. It was Perl scripts and statistical and scientific computing libraries from CPAN and just cron jobs. The deployment strategy was simple. Copy the script and pray. It solved real business problems. We were able to do fraud detection. We were doing demand forecasting with regression. We were doing recommendations with KNN and a few other things. Even in those days, we were able to solve that. This MySQL setup helped us a bit. As data grew large, we needed something more. Hadoop came to the rescue. In 2011, we actually built two on-premise clusters. This was a configuration that was there. It was redundant clusters. The setup looked like this. There was MySQL on bare metal. Then there was this classic Hadoop stack, HDFS, YARN, MapReduce. Then we layered it with Oozie for orchestration, Spark for workflows, and Hive for SQL, and Sqoop for moving data between Hadoop and MySQL.
On top of it, we had some self-serve tooling, a classic setup. Data came into Hadoop via two means. From MySQL, it came as nightly jobs into Hadoop. Then from Kafka, it was Kafka Connect that was bringing in data. This data was used for machine learning purposes. This is how prediction training was happening back then. What you see is two workflows, the training workflow on the top and an inference workflow. A scientist would actually write a workflow where they would train a Python model. Then they call it as pickling the model, which is just serializing the model, storing into Hadoop. Then another workflow loads that model, does the prediction that it wants. Then it actually stores it into MySQL in some cases, but not in all cases. Basically, the whole prediction was happening completely offline. In some cases, we want real-time. In those cases, what we did was we just faked it.
This is how we faked it. The top is the offline workflow, and the bottom is a web request. We wanted the real-time prediction to happen in the web request. All we did was we trained the model. I'll give you an example how we did it. Let's take an example of a model that we want to train, like device and country is the feature, and probability to book is the output that we want to do. In those cases, what we did was we just enumerated all the input features. We just created all possible devices, all possible countries. Then we just predicted on that upfront. That gave us a table. All we did was store that table into the MySQL. Then when the request came in, we just queried the table as if we were predicting, and then went on to do our job. Obviously, it doesn't work for most cases, but that was our earlier real-time prediction with faking it with lookup tables.
That worked for us in most cases. Hadoop powered for us most of our pipeline for many years, but there were some problems. One was it was a shared environment, so every training, production workloads, everything was running in a single cluster. There was mono-version. If you are a data scientist, you cannot use a version that you want. You just have to use a version that is possible, like now it is shared. The second thing was there was no GPU support. That limited our ability to train a bigger model, larger model. We were using two different DCs for redundant setup. Then you need to keep the data in sync between this, and that was becoming a headache. Capacity issues, like at peak times, we were operating very close to max capacity. Noisy neighbors, like some NOOB who's writing a query can actually clog the entire production cluster.
Most importantly, there was no discovery or ownership, even though people depended on each other's data. That was the biggest headache for us. This is what it looked like. Like now somebody might think that this is a Rorschach psychological test, but it is just a dependency graph for our workflows. If you zoom in closely, you can see Hadoop screaming in binary there.
2011, we introduced Hadoop. 2018, we realized the limitation of Hadoop, but then it took us until 2022 to put it into maintenance mode, and another three years to go into sunset. Like now what was going wrong? Why did it take so long, that hairball that you saw earlier? Why was it difficult? We were operating with hundreds of petabytes of data. We had about 190,000 Hadoop tables, 7,000-plus workflows, hundreds of teams, and then we want to keep everything up and running. Our goal was move everything, stop nothing, align everyone. Everybody knows that that last part is already a moonshot. We were like, why pick one impossible thing? Pick three. We had four problems to solve. One was, we wanted to actually modernize our compute and scale it, obviously, because we were operating at max capacity. Then we want segregation of workflows, because we wanted isolation at least between dev and production.
Governance and ownership, which was a mess, we wanted to fix that. The last was, we wanted to enable discovery of workflows and datasets so that people can reuse things. Saying goodbye to Hadoop was hard, and this is why. This is what happened in those gap years. 2018, when we realized the mistake, or realized the problem, we actually attempted to move into one of the cloud providers. Quickly, the product got shelved. The reason was, depending upon who you ask, it is either cost or a strategy shift. We quickly pivoted to building something internally to help us. Like now we actually built assistant application along with Hadoop to have a data catalog. Then we also had built Kubernetes clusters to do Spark. That eased us a little bit, so we could continue on. A short bit later, we started the modernization project, where we focused on three things, like quality, ownership, and governance of data.
We were trying to fix that with that modernization project. During that time period, we actually piloted another cloud, and that showed promise, but we didn't actually make enough to move the needle to actually do a full migration. In 2023, leadership actually made the call, and they said, guys, we're going to do it all in, no plan B. That actually helped, we made progress, and we succeeded. Just within one and a half years, we migrated everything that you saw. This is how we did it. Maybe there is something in there for you. We actually built a tool that mapped every possible table, every dependency into a graph. That was our first effort, map the universe. Second thing that we did was, we looked at the usage analysis of all the tables and the workflows, and the lineage as well, and said, which of this is business critical?
Then we tried to trim it down. You'd be surprised that 92% of the workflows didn't pass the test, someone cares, it was easy. The best architectural tool is Delete key. What we then did is, we actually did graph analysis on those workflows that passed, and we actually prioritized it by centrality and impact. We took a few, and after that it was simple. Group them into batches, do the migration, and slowly phase out the legacy system.
If you look back, one key thing that made the difference was this unified command center, which held that graph data, and that became the central place for anybody to look at it during the migration. If I had a workflow that I had to migrate, but then I depended on a few other workflows, I could go in there and then see, ok, when is my dependency migrating, and when can I migrate. I could plan things easy. Anything, status, dependencies, blockers, everything was in there. This replaced spreadsheet tracking, and also it replaced tribal knowledge. Everybody knew what exactly was happening. The second thing we already saw was, we removed plan B out of the equation. Leadership said, just go in. We all know that this is not always the best plan. The best strategy is prevention. If we had a time machine, these are the four messages that we would send to our past self. First, catalog every asset that you have. Data workflows doesn't matter. Catalog it. Establish clear ownership. It can be business ownership and also technical ownership of the data. Build quality gates before you share that data. Track lineage end-to-end. That concludes our data layer.
ML Engineering Layer
Next in the ML engineering layer, I want to talk about two things. One is how we industrialized ML model serving. Second, our attempts at feature engineering and the problem that still remains. Before I do that, I want to give you a 30-second overview of evolution of our ML stack. In 2005, we actually were using Perl libraries and the MySQL, which was still doing the job. Hadoop came into the picture that brought in big data analysis and reporting, that was good. True machine learning kickstarted with the introduction of Oozie and Python, like the sklearn era, because we were able to do things easily. When Spark came in, that changed the game or changed the pace of the game. Now we were able to do more things faster and we were able to crunch more numbers. H2O took it to another level. Now we were able to do faster training.
Also, we were able to deploy models directly in any Java environment. That was a big thing. In 2017, deep learning came in. Deep learning started as a very simple hackathon project, where a group of developers wanted to improve the image stacks, which was of low quality. From then on, it is widely adopted across the company. 2023, LLM wave took off and we built a bunch of generative products, which we'll touch upon a bit later. 2025, we started laying the foundations of the agentic systems, which we'll also touch later.
Going back, if you look at the timeline, 2015, in my opinion, was a pivotal year, because we were solving two problems. One was real-time predictions. Until then, we were solving real-time predictions with fake lookup tables that you saw earlier. In a hackathon, we actually built a small Scala service, which was backed by a storage. It was actually used to do model serving. Machine learning scientists could upload the model. Back in those days, the model was just classical problems, like logistic regression, classification, and so on. Uploading a model is nothing but uploading a CSV file with all the features that was used, what type of those features, and some weights and coefficients. In real time, when a user landed on the website, some backend service collected the features necessary to invoke the model. Then they used the Perl SDK, because we were still in Perl back then, to invoke the Scala service.
Over a period of time, this Scala service has evolved into a platform. Now it supports 12-plus different model formats. You can think of all the major ones are in here. This is how the setup looks like today. That service is deployed in multiple clusters. Why multiple clusters? We have some general-purpose shared tenant clusters, some dedicated clusters for very critical workloads, and then also some clusters for batch. Either these clusters actually host their model, or they actually can interact with externally hosted models, so like SageMaker. They can also contact feature store, which we'll cover later. To hide the complexity from the end users, these clusters are fronted by a custom proxy. Every prediction that these clusters make, is logged. Then those logs go into data lake and also to our monitoring platforms. Let's take an example how a flow of machine learning scientists uploading a model and inference happens.
Machine learning scientists upload the model artifact into something like S3, and then they notify an ML portal to say, I've registered this new model. That triggers a pipeline. The coordinator goes and picks up that model that the ML scientist uploaded, and then comes back, versions it in its own storage. Also, what it does is, it finds the right cluster to deploy, and then allocates enough space, and triggers that upload. In addition, it'll also upload that, update the proxy that you saw earlier to say that the proxy knows which cluster to route to. Serving was simple. When a web request came in, backend servers just invoked the custom proxy with this client SDK. This was one of our success stories. There was no problem, and it was a clear success. Two years back, this is what that system that you just saw handled. It has 480-plus models. It can do 400 billion predictions per day. All of those predictions within less than 20 milliseconds on an average. Those are impressive numbers.
Second problem that we started solving in 2015 was feature engineering. Back then, 80% of the time was spent on just data preparation. Two pain points emerged. One was duplication. Each team was trying to build the feature by themselves in a different way. The second was there was skew. The models that behaved one way in training was behaving another way in inference. We set out to solve the problem by solving the duplication and to bring consistency. We thought, let's build reusable computations. We decided to tackle the problem separately for offline and for online, because offline was targeted at machine learning scientists. Online was targeted for engineers. I'm going to sidestep here to give you the context so you can better understand the decisions that the team made. What you're seeing on screen is just an initial dataset. You have a user ID, what the user searched and when.
Then also the label that we are predicting on to say that did the user eventually book or not. That's the initial dataset. That's how an ML scientist starts their work. What they do is they try to add more features into this dataset. They keep looking for other feature tables. Feature tables look like this, which is just a time series representation of a feature. In this case, the feature represented is what is the number of searches that the user did in the last seven days. That is the series that you're seeing. Once they found such a feature table, all they do is a point-in-wise join, wherein they take a unique ID, in this case, user ID, and some timestamp, and they do a time-wise join on it. Then they get a training set, wherein they have the feature that they were looking for, which in this case is the count of last seven days.
When we looked at this, we said, we can help in two places. One is building that feature table, and the other is doing the time-wise join. That is what we set out to achieve. That was a feature table. That feature table is built by another fact log or an immutable log. This is just the searches that have happened over a period of time. By looking at this, it is just very clear that there is one data frame and the other data frame. We figured out we can actually just use Spark ML transformer, which did the feature translation between.
This is how it looked in its entirety. There were immutable fact logs, which is just log of search events that have happened in the past. We asked people to write reusable feature encoders that converted into a feature table. Once we had that, all anybody has to do is just go look at the initial dataset and do a time-wise join on it. We tried to do something similar to online as well. There were event streams. We asked people to write feature mappers in Scala, and that became enriched streams. From there, there was a centralized team which took all these features, put it into Cassandra, and then served it via an API. There were a couple of problems with this approach. One was parity. Data was different between online and offline. The computation was different from online and offline. Then there were performance issues because of the amount of data that we were processing in offline.
Backfilling or recomputation was hard. In the second attempt, we decided, let's fix data and computational parity together. The way we fixed data parity was we introduced the concept of timelines. Timelines is nothing but a time-ordered sequence of events for a user. User searched, user clicked, user booked, things like that. The idea was, let's build this timeline equally or approximately in the same way for both online and offline. Then that way, once we have that, we can just write computation once and then use the timeline. That was a big picture. This is how the timelines were built. Those are the search, clicks, and immutable events. They got materialized into Hadoop. We built timeline builders separately. It's a duplicate effort, but it was managed by a central team. That timeline was operating separately for online and offline. They synced the data or the timelines into Cassandra and HDFS. The only difference between these two timelines were the Cassandra timelines were trimmed. Unlike the MVA, TVA, we actually didn't trim timelines for saving the universe. We trimmed timelines in Cassandra for saving the space.
This is how we used timelines for computational parity. We had a full timeline in HDFS, a trimmed timeline in Cassandra. We asked people to write centralized shared feature libraries. These are things that can be used to compute features, things like sum, count, large scale, and all those typical things was written by a centralized team. It also allowed extension. Anybody could come in and write in the feature that is not already there. In online or in real time, when an application wanted some inference, they would go to a feature store API and ask, can you give me this feature? What it would do is go into Cassandra, pick up the timeline for that specific user or use case, and then build that feature on the fly with these shared libraries. The same happened on the training side or on offline. That stack was Python, because scientists were using Python.
We had a wrapper, which had a feature computation library wrapper. What it did was, whenever the scientist wanted a feature, it submitted a Spark job. In that Spark job, we actually did the same thing. We typically achieved what we wanted to do, both data and feature parity. The problem was, ML scientists were not familiar with writing features in Java, and that created a dependency between engineering and ML science. Secondly, in the previous one, the Cassandra timelines, computing features on the fly was costly, expensive, because it took more than 90 milliseconds or so to actually just fetch the data. It was not suitable for most of the use cases. Then we said, ok, third attempt. Forget feature computation, we'll just focus on feature storage and serving. Let people deal with feature computation. We didn't care how features are computed, as long as we knew where to pick the features from.
If it was pre-computed, ok, we'll go to a data lake of sorts. If it is real time, we'll go to Kafka. Then we built a feature store. In the feature store, there was an ingestor component, which knew about these multiple data sources, and pulled that data, and stored it into an online store, and served it via an API. In this API, there was no on-the-fly computation. It was just a simple lookup, because features were already computed. The same pipeline, what it also did was sync data into offline, so that MLS can use it for retraining purposes, and for also other analysis. This feature store also had other benefits, like it had feature registry, feature monitoring, and so on. In essence, after three attempts, this is what we learned. It's a multidimensional problem, and we don't have an answer. Currently, for the pre-computation and real time, we currently have three systems, and we are always looking for one more system. That wraps the second layer.
Domain Intelligence Layer
Now in that third layer, we are moving away from infrastructure to business impact. I want to give you a high-level tour of all the ML platforms that we have, and then dive into one of them. This is the platform that we have. One is GenAI platform. It's the newest kid in the block. What it does is it enables any team to actually safely build generative AI experiences. It provides tools and infrastructure and foundational capabilities like guardrails, evaluation, orchestration out of the box. Things like PII detection, PII masking, everything comes out of the box. The product teams can focus just on product innovation and not on LLM plumbing. Let's look at a few use cases there, what we have. The trip planning, which is just a conversational experience where someone can go talk in natural language and get recommendations, that's powered by GenAI. We have smart filters.
If you were ever on Booking.com, you would see hundreds of filters on the left, and it is hard for anyone to know which to pick. We have a text box where you can type it, and that translated into the right filters and sorters. The third is review summaries. That provides, based on the last reviews, a quick snapshot of pros and cons. The next is property Q&A. This actually enables instant answers to any property-specific questions, and it is grounded on reviews, past Q&A, and that is also powered by GenAI. We also have a booking support, wherein we have AI that can do basic customer support on payments, cancellation, and things regarding your booking. These are the use cases. There are many interesting things under the platform, but we are not going to cover it today.
GenAI is good, but to generate data, we actually want good content. That's where content intelligence comes in. What it does is it provides surfaces like good, high-quality content that are usable. This platform analyzes every image and text. It actually adds metadata or enriches that metadata. For example, if it is images, it adds themes, tags, and looks for any harmful content. If it is text, it looks for, for example, sentiments or topics that have been discussed. This also supports the reviews. Because most of the things happen in the background, like fraud detection is also taken care of by this content intelligence. One example that you see, anytime you see a gallery on Booking.com, it is probably powered by this content intelligence. Picking up the right photo to put up front and the order, which photos to highlight and so on. The other thing is, it autogenerates all text for screen readers.
There's a platform for that. It also does reviews. It detects topics on the reviews and summarizes it at the property level. This is what it enabled was, not just getting intelligence at content level, but going one level higher. For example, if property had all the images and all the summaries, we can actually create intelligence at the property level to see what is happening. That kind of aggregation level, this platform enabled. The third is ranking. Ranking's responsibility is to order millions of products so that any time a customer comes in, they see the most relevant results for them, like something personalized. This is a platform that we are going to dig in, so I'll park it here. Recommendations is a self-serve platform wherein you can build any kind of recommendations across the funnel, from discovery to post-booking. It has more than 40, 50 use cases. I picked a few to give you a flavor of what it looks like.
The pushcards that you might see on Booking.com is powered by recommendations. There's multi-vertical recommendations. When I say multi-vertical, I'm referring to accommodations, flights, attractions, and so on. Those kinds of recommendations come from this platform. Unique stays, team-based recommendations for you, and attraction carousels that you might see on the page, and any flight recommendations. All of these are examples that are powered by recommendations platform. The last platform is value intelligence. The responsibility of this platform is to measure and optimize promotions. By promotions, I mean anything like vouchers, discounts, things like rewards that's being optimized by value intelligence. The goal of this platform is to say, maximize value for travelers, partners, and the business. That wraps all the platforms.
Let's jump into ranking platform. Ranking is a three-way optimization problem. We need choice and value for customers. We need exposure and growth for the partners. We also need efficiency and revenue for business. If we show irrelevant results, the travelers are going to be annoyed. If we show poor visibility, partners are going to be frustrated. If any one of them is annoyed for too long, I'm going to get my salary re-ranked. It's a three-way optimization problem. Back then in 2005, we had the formula for ranking hotels look like this. It was simple. It was just a simple function, which took bookings and views, and a random tiebreaker in case there were two hotels which had the same rank. The formula evolved over time. We introduced cancellations. It was taking consideration of seasonality. What is the distance of the hotel from the center? What is the number of views the hotel is getting?
Availability of the hotel. The average ranking in the locality. What is the visitor traffic? Guest reviews. These are just some flavors of what are the factors we considered. Back then, ranking actually was computed offline using simple Perl cron scripts every night, and then the scores were dumped into MySQL, and we used it in real time. Around 2016, we actually tried to replace the ranking formula with machine learning, and we failed miserably. The handcrafted formula was undefeatable. We could not beat it for a long time, like one and a half years or so. This formula cannot be beaten. The reasons were many fold. The primary reason was that the ideal model that we wanted to train the model on, and the massive amount of data that we had was not actually helpful when Spark kept exploding. The memory of Spark was not sufficient. What we did was we cut corners, we made some approximations, and we succeeded. In true Booking sense, we ran an experiment, and it was successful.
Next, we wanted to tackle personalized ranking, and there was a problem. This is what it looked like. The ranking scores was calculated offline until then. It was put into MySQL, and an availability engine read that MySQL data, loaded it into memory. The responsibility of this availability engine was that it needs to search the availability and prices of millions of properties. Because of the amount of data that this engine had, it used a scatter-gather pattern. It had a coordinator and 24 shards. Each of those shards actually worked on a subset of the data. When a request came in from the user, it came to the availability engine via a search orchestrator, and the request landed there. The request contained something like this. Where does the user want to search on? When? Then, what is the party size? Then, what are the filters and preferences of the user?
The coordinator accepted that request and then distributed the work to the workers. Workers went on to do their job. They actually looked into the subset of the data that they had, took the data out, and then they used the ranking scores that were preloaded into memory to do the sorting. After they did the sorting, they supplied the results back to the coordinator. Coordinator aggregated all the information from the workers and re-sorted the results and gave the results back to the search. This is what was happening. If you wanted to personalize, meaning that every user gets a specific set of results, what we had to do was take the ranking logic out of this availability engine, get rid of those static scores at the bottom, and then replace it with a service. Then have that service invoke actually a model which is deployed in the model serving platform that we saw earlier.
That's what we wanted to do. There were two problems. The first problem was, if there were 1,000 requests for the availability engine, it meant that the new service is going to get 24,000 requests because it was sitting behind the fanout, behind the shards. Secondly, the availability engine was operating at super low latency, and that also meant that this new service plus the network hop to the model and the model's time all needs to be well within the time of that service. It's basically a high throughput, low latency problem, and we managed to crack it. These are the numbers from 2024. That ranking service that you saw in the previous slide, that green box that was introduced new, is able to solve 100,000 requests per second with a p99.9 latency of 100 milliseconds. The average is way low. It's like 40, 50 milliseconds or so.
I want to share one more thing before I wrap up the evolution story. Experiments at Booking typically run for two to four weeks, but this meant that we couldn't actually train or run models. We were limited in the number of models that we can run every year, because we just had 53 weeks. We wanted to move faster, knowing well that if we actually put in a bad ranking model upfront, it is going to cost all of us, like travelers, partners, and business. What we did was we introduced interleaving. This is how it worked. Typically, for an A/B testing, we actually take the users and split them across two groups, and then we show different search results for them, which was coming from different ranking models. In interleaving, what we did was we didn't show two groups, we didn't split the groups, we just showed the same results for all users.
Those results were coming from merged data, meaning we would train a couple of models, in this case, two models, red and blue. We trained the model, and each of these models gave a list of results. Then we would somehow need to merge it. One simple example could be, take the top one from here, top one from here, merge it. Then keep alternating it. It's just a team draft approach. Then once you have done, you present that to all users across the service. Then you check offline, ok, from which list did the user interact more? Was it from model A or from model B? That gives us the answer. Why it was useful was we could suddenly run more variants. On the right side, it doesn't have to be two. We can even run eight different models that are actually interleaving the results for search. That is, we can run more variants that was like 10 times speed-up than what we are used to with A/B testing.
We could use it with less traffic because interleaving is super sensitive to customer preferences, and we can get signals faster. The way we use it now, interleaving and A/B, is that we train a bunch of models, we pre-select it with interleaving, we pick up a winner, and then we take the winner and then do proper A/B testing. We have optimized both speed, while not losing scientific rigor.
I started the talk by saying that experiment laid the foundation in general for data-driven decision-making. You can see that, still, it continues to underpin what we do every day. With that, that concludes the evolution story.
What's Brewing?
Next, I want to tell you where we are going. These are the five platforms that you saw. What we started doing last year is that we started building the foundations of agentic systems. By agentic systems, think about memories, all kinds of memories, episodic, semantic, procedural, and think about agent serving, like access control for those agents, delegation controls for the users to those agents, agent-to-agent communication. Those are the things we started working on last year. Parallelly, what we are also doing is unifying all these platforms under a single umbrella and then having a single orchestration layer. Why? Because we foresee a possible fragmentation and we wanted to avoid it earlier. Like for cross-domain use cases, we want a single, centralized, unified experience for the customer, and this platform can do that. Secondly, we wanted to centralize all kinds of AI-related governance, security, quality, and all those things. We wanted to centralize that.

articles.title: Mira el genial tráiler final de 'Las nuevas desventuras de Cliff Booth', la secuela de 'Érase una vez en Hollywood' con Brad Pitt
articles.text:
La secuela de Érase una vez en Hollywood, titulada Las nuevas desventuras de Cliff Booth, está a punto de estrenarse y acaba de lanzar su esperado tráiler final. La película volverá a contar con Brad Pitt como el intrépido protagonista. Un papel que, recordemos, le valió el Oscar en la cinta de Quentin Tarantino. Esta vez, el que no regresa es el propio director, que cede el testigo a nada menos que a David Fincher.
Tal y como vemos en el avance, esto no es más que otro verano en Hollywood. Estamos en 1977, ocho años después de que Cliff Booth se cruzara con la familia Manson en el Hollywood de 1969 de Érase una vez en Hollywood. Ahora, en el tráiler de Las nuevas desventuras de Cliff Booth, el cuento de hadas ha terminado. Los Ángeles ya no necesita a un doble de acción que se encargue de los hippies como antes.
Pero Hollywood siempre tendrá problemas, y algunos solo puede resolverlos alguien con las habilidades únicas (y, en ocasiones, al margen de la ley) de Cliff. Cuando no se gana la vida como camarero o proyeccionista, Cliff Booth es todo un solucionador de problemas: se ocupa de los conflictos de los peces gordos de Hollywood. Y, a veces, también de los que no lo son tanto.
Mira el tráiler de Las nuevas desventuras de Cliff Booth
David Fincher dirige Las nuevas desventuras de Cliff Booth pero, eso sí, lo hace a partir de un guion del propio Quentin Tarantino. Tampoco regresan Leonardo DiCaprio ni Margot Robbie, por lo que el filme será más bien un spin-off centrado exclusivamente en la vida del personaje de Brad Pitt ocho años después.
El reparto lo componen, además del propio Pitt, nombres de la talla de Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Peter Weller, Matt Groove, JB Tadena, Corey Fogelmanis, Karren Karagulian. La película se estrenará en exclusiva durante dos semanas en salas IMAX el 25 de noviembre de 2026, antes de llegar a Netflix el 23 de diciembre de 2026.

articles.title: Industry leaders want Canada to choose whether it builds its own fusion future, or buys it from abroad | BetaKit
articles.text:
As the global race to develop commercially viable nuclear fusion power intensifies, a trio of the field’s leading Canadians entrepreneurs says it is time for the country to prioritize investment in the industry.
Daedal Systems founder and CEO Henry Gould, General Fusion CEO Greg Twinney, and Stellarex Energy co-founder and CEO Spencer Pitcher made the argument on stage yesterday at the MaRS Climate Impact conference in Toronto during a panel on commercial fusion.
Many global players are competing to harness fusion, the same physical process that powers the sun, to generate abundant, carbon-free energy. Pitcher, who leads the fusion-focused and Toronto-based Princeton University laboratory spinoff Stellarex, argued that Canada now needs to follow the same path it took when it began investing heavily in nuclear energy after World War II.
“If we don’t make this decision now, we’ll buy our devices from other countries for a very long time.”
Spencer Pitcher, Stellarex
“Seventy-five years ago, our grandparents—in some cases, your great-grandparents—made a decision that Canada would have a clean source of nuclear energy based on heavy water, moderated reactors, and unenriched uranium,” Pitcher said. “This was a really bold decision made by politicians, engineers, bankers, and investors … It [has been] the foundation of energy supply in [Ontario] for two generations, and will probably continue for another few generations.”
Pitcher thinks Canada would benefit from adopting the same “can-do attitude” today. “Fusion is the ultimate source of energy,” he added. “It’s the primary source of energy in the universe. Nothing comes after it; it’s the end game. If we don’t make this decision now, we’ll buy our devices from other countries for a very long time.”
Twinney and Gould agreed. “We need Canada to acknowledge this opportunity in a real way,” Twinney said.
Gould noted that the last two decades of fusion and plasma development in Canada “have been lacklustre, basically non-existent, with the exception of General Fusion,” his previous employer.
He thinks the path forward entails focusing on tritium systems, where he said Canada has a competitive advantage. Canada is a global leader in the production, processing, and handling of tritium, a radioactive isotope of hydrogen and a key ingredient in the fuel for nuclear fusion, which could soon become a key strategic resource.
“Do we only sell fuel-handling systems to this emerging industry for value to be captured elsewhere, or do we leverage that competitive advantage, do more with it, bolster reactor developers and other parts of the supply chain?” Gould asked.
RELATED: Ex-General Fusion employee raises $4 million USD for fusion diagnostics startup Daedal
Gould believes a three-pronged approach is in order: doubling down on tritium systems, supporting fusion developers, and filling tech gaps in the industry, such as in measurement instruments like the ones Daedal is building.
Twinney said Canada lags the United States and United Kingdom on a regulatory framework for fusion, and ought to follow in those countries’ footsteps.
Though Canada recently launched a national nuclear energy strategy that listed fusion as one of the innovative forms of power the federal government intends to support, Twinney thinks the country could use a dedicated national fusion strategy, something General Fusion advocated for but did not receive in the federal government’s latest budget.
“We have some of the best fusion companies—even though there’s a small group of us—in the world … These companies are going to be successful one way or the other, and we should keep them in Canada,” he added.
An open approach to combat “Theranos-type risk”
Moderator Zoltan Tompa, partner and team lead of BDC Capital’s Climate Tech Fund, noted that establishing credibility is “critical” when it comes to fusion development. Tompa asked the panellists whether they see potential “Theranos-type risk” in the sector, highlighting that some unnamed firms have been making “extraordinary claims” lately that they may not be able to support and could ultimately chill market interest in fusion.
“In the scientific community, we’ve been worried about this for several years,” Pitcher said.
Gould also sees potential for fraud to create a chill in fusion. “It’s deep tech,” he said. “There’s long development cycles. There [are] these thorny physics and science problems that are difficult for the investment community to understand … It’s a long path to revenue.”
RELATED: General Fusion “pleased” with public-market debut after redemption-heavy SPAC deal
With capital providers investing in fusion based on tech development milestones rather than actual sales, assessing true value creation can be more difficult, especially for the less technically savvy.
To build trust, Pitcher argued that companies could disclose two key performance metrics, their “fusion triple product” and their recirculating power requirement, without threatening their intellectual property or “special sauce.”
Twinney agreed with the sentiment. “Sharing the science basis of your approach and what you’ve achieved, and allowing peers and industry [to evaluate it], this is common practice and a great way to establish your own credibility, to get feedback from [third parties], and also make sure that you are bringing the people along that you need to bring along.”
“We believe an open approach is the best approach,” he said.

articles.title: Sam Altman warns against a future where AI, not humans, calls the shots | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman believes that people should stay in charge of the future when it comes to how AI technology impacts the world and everyone’s lives. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the AI executive referred to discussions in Silicon Valley about whether there will be a gradual handover to AI — meaning AI will eventually become the decision-making authority across every major industry and institution.
“One thing we’ve been talking a lot about recently is there’s been this thing in Silicon Valley that seems almost ridiculous to have to fight against, but we both believe very deeply that people need to stay in control of the future, and there’s increasing talk about, well, there is either going to be or there should be this sort of gradual handover to AI. And I — we both — agree that that’s a terrible idea,” said Altman, who was sharing the stage with OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman.
The hand-off theory stems from the idea that as AI models become increasingly more powerful, they will learn to improve themselves — a concept known as “recursive self-improvement” or RSI. As existing AI technology builds newer, smarter generations, those will eventually become a superintelligence that humans can no longer control, the belief goes.
Altman explained that he and Brockman only disagree over how to best accomplish the goal of keeping humans in control, or what sort of challenges we should expect to face along the way. However, Altman characterized this as more of a debate between two people who share the same larger views.
“The question of how to actually prevent [handover] from happening — how to actually ensure that we will, given all of the various pressures and given what other companies may try to do — that we are going to actually ensure that people stay in control of the future in a very deep way, and we don’t have this either accidental or intentional handover — I think we can both agree on that,” Altman said.
Brockman added that, as the models improve, there’s an increasing responsibility for alignment, safety, and security, which may require changes in how things are currently done.
“Monitoring is a good example of something where I think we are going to need new … technology,” he said.
Today, AI researchers monitor the model’s chain of thought, where the AI writes out what it’s thinking as it works through problems and performs tasks. But in Brockman’s view, that may not always be the best way to monitor more advanced AI that’s being built now.
“As the models have gotten more capable, they can do more within just the forward path without having to actually write out that thinking, which means we need a new approach to monitoring,” Brockman said. “We’re going to need to deliver that, and I think that there will be points where we need to really think about, as the capabilities get to a certain point, chain-of-thought monitorability is degraded,” he continued, adding that all the problems were technical ones to be solved.
OpenAI had committed to increased chain-of-thought monitoring after the incident where an OpenAI model escaped containment and hacked into the AI model repository Hugging Face. In Wednesday’s interview, Brockman noted that the company told 25% of its production engineers to stop building things and work on securing the AI technology after the hack.
But despite the high-profile breach, he argued that forward progress was still critical to fight bad actors.
“I think to realize that if you look to the level of capabilities of models in the world, and you see cyber models that are coming from that are now … in the hands of threat actors everywhere, that I think that it’s really important that defenders use the most capable models to defend,” he said.

articles.title: Robotaxi-Premiere in München: So kommst du jetzt in ein selbstfahrendes Uber
articles.text:
Robotaxi-Premiere in München: So kommst du jetzt in ein selbstfahrendes Uber
Im Rennen um selbstfahrende Taxis in Deutschland liefern sich zwei Regionen – München und Berlin – einen spannenden Wettlauf. Während der US-Elektroautohersteller Tesla vor den Toren Berlins eine Milliardenfabrik für künftige Robotaxis hochziehen will, rollen in der bayerischen Landeshauptstadt bereits die Testflotten durch den Stadtverkehr: Heute starteten der Fahrdienstvermittler Uber und der chinesische KI-Spezialist Momenta in München ein gemeinsames Pilotprojekt für autonome Fahrten.
Bei der Premiere an der Straße „Am Oberwiesenfeld“ nördlich des Münchner Olympiaparks gaben die Partner den Startschuss für den Testbetrieb für Kunden mit Sicherheitsbegleitung. Fahrgäste in München können sich ab sofort über die Uber-App auf eine Interessentenliste setzen lassen.
Ausgewählte Nutzerinnen und Nutzer, die im Münchner Norden eine Fahrt über die Optionen UberX, Electric oder Comfort buchen, können nun ein autonomes Fahrzeug vermittelt bekommen – Ein- und Ausstieg erfolgen an festgelegten Haltepunkten.
Das Angebot ist zunächst kostenlos, bei jeder Fahrt sitzt eine Sicherheitskraft mit an Bord, die aber nur in Ausnahmen steuernd eingreift. Grundlage sind Level-4-Erprobungsgenehmigungen des Kraftfahrt-Bundesamts.
München ist Europas Testlabor – im Raum Berlin entsteht die Fabrik
Mit dem Start festigt München seine Rolle als wichtigstes europäisches Testlabor für den praktischen Einsatz autonomer Fahrzeuge. Neben Uber und Momenta erprobt Uber in der Stadt bereits ein zweites Robotaxi-System mit dem KI-Unternehmen Autobrains und dem Chipkonzern Nvidia.
Zudem kartiert die Google-Schwesterfirma Waymo seit dem Herbst das Münchner Stadtgebiet, um Ende 2027 einen regulären fahrerlosen Fahrdienst in Betrieb zu nehmen. Und im öffentlichen Nahverkehr sind im Rahmen des Projekts MINGA bereits erste Testfahrgäste auf der regulären MVG-Buslinie 178 in einem autonom fahrenden Elektrobus unterwegs.
Während in München der Alltag im komplexen Stadtverkehr trainiert wird, setzt die Hauptstadtregion einen industriellen Kontrapunkt: Am Montag hatte Tesla angekündigt, drei Milliarden Euro in den Ausbau seines Werks im brandenburgischen Grünheide bei Berlin zu investieren. Dort soll ab 2029 das eigene, komplett lenkrad- und pedallose Robotaxi «Cybercab» in Großserie vom Band rollen – mit einer Zielkapazität von bis zu einer Million Fahrzeugen pro Jahr.
Technik-Wettstreit: Teure Laser-Sensoren gegen Kamera-Systeme
Hinter den Projekten steht zugleich ein grundlegender Systemstreit der Entwickler, wie sich ein Auto überhaupt sicher durch den Verkehr navigieren lässt: Sowohl Momenta als auch der US-Pionier Waymo setzen auf maximal abgesicherte Technik. Ihre Fahrzeuge kombinieren hochauflösende Kameras und Radarsensoren mit sogenannten Lidar-Sensoren, die die Umgebung mit Hilfe von Laserstrahlen dreidimensional und zentimetergenau abtasten.
Momenta verknüpft diese Technik zudem mit Daten aus mehr als 1,4 Millionen Serienfahrzeugen von Herstellern wie Mercedes-Benz, BMW, Audi und Volkswagen, für die das Unternehmen bereits Fahrerassistenzsysteme liefert.
Einen radikal anderen und deutlich günstigeren Weg verfolgen Tesla sowie Ubers zweiter Münchner Partner Autobrains. Beide verzichten komplett auf teure Lidar-Sensoren. Während Tesla bei seinem «Cybercab» ausschließlich auf acht Kameras und neuronale Netze setzt, nutzt das System von Autobrains lediglich sechs Kameras und gleicht deren Bilder in Echtzeit mit Luftbildern ab.
Internationaler Wettlauf: USA, China und Golfstaaten sind voraus
„Deutschlands strenger Regulierungsansatz, bei dem Sicherheit an erster Stelle steht, hat einen der weltweiten Maßstäbe für autonomes Fahren gesetzt“, sagte Momenta-Manager Shuo Xie zum Start in München. Während hierzulande allerdings noch mit Sicherheitsfahrern geprobt wird, gehören komplett fahrerlose Taxis in anderen Teilen der Welt längst zum regulären Straßenbild.
Vorreiter sind die USA und China: In US-Metropolen wie San Francisco, Phoenix, Los Angeles und Austin betreibt vor allem die Google-Schwester Waymo kommerzielle Flotten ohne Sicherheitsbegleitung.
In chinesischen Millionenstädten wie Peking, Wuhan oder Guangzhou bieten Tech-Konzerne wie Baidu (mit dem Dienst Apollo Go) sowie Spezialisten wie Pony.ai und WeRide längst reguläre App-Fahrten ohne Mensch am Steuer an.
Auch am Persischen Golf schreitet die Kommerzialisierung rasant voran: In den Vereinigten Arabischen Emiraten, insbesondere in Abu Dhabi und Dubai, sind bereits vollautonome Robotaxis – teils ebenfalls in Kooperation mit der Uber-Plattform – im regulären Fahrgastbetrieb unterwegs, um den öffentlichen Nahverkehr zu ergänzen.
Innerhalb Europas sorgte zudem ein Projekt in der kroatischen Hauptstadt Zagreb für Aufsehen: Dort bietet das vom Elektro-Supersportwagen-Pionier Mate Rimac mitgegründete Start-up Verne seit diesem Jahr über Uber erste kostenpflichtige Robotaxi-Fahrten an und erprobt auf einer Teststrecke zum Flughafen bereits Fahrten komplett ohne Sicherheitsfahrer – greift dafür nach Verzögerungen bei der eigenen Fahrzeugentwicklung allerdings auf umgebaute chinesische Elektroautos und Software des Anbieters Pony.ai zurück.

articles.title: Koduri’s Oxmiq Offers IP, Tools for Indian Teams to Design AI Chips - EE Times
articles.text:
In an exclusive interview, Raja Koduri, founder and CEO of Oxmiq Labs, discussed the company’s India initiative, the role of memory hierarchy in AI computing systems, custom silicon economics, and India’s infrastructure requirements.
Oxmiq Labs has developed tools and intellectual property (IP) to help teams in India design their own AI chips. The company is also working on an India initiative that it expects to detail in December, Koduri told EE Times.
“We have built tools to enable teams in India to make their own chips,” he said. “We are working on an initiative in India, and hopefully, when I return to India in December, I will be able to share some of those initiatives publicly.”
The aim, Koduri said, is to develop state-of-the-art chips designed to produce AI tokens as efficiently as possible.
Separately, Oxmiq is an architecture and engineering partner to AM Intelligence Labs, the AI compute division of AM Group, the parent company of Greenko, India’s renewable energy producer with a portfolio target of 50 GW by 2030. The partnership covers site selection, compute design, and partner selection. The initial build will use Nvidia GPUs, with locally developed designs to follow.
“To begin with, we are bringing the best technology available today, which is Nvidia GPUs,” he said. “But as we move toward 2030, we will also leverage designs developed in India.”
Koduri said India must develop its own designs, chips, and infrastructure to bring down the cost of converting electricity into AI output, even if manufacturing remains overseas.
“Chips designed in India can be manufactured in Taiwan or South Korea,” he said. “That is perfectly fine. But the products should be owned by India.”
From megawatts to intelligence
Koduri said the main constraint in AI computing is how efficiently a data center converts power into AI output. At the technical level, he said, the memory hierarchy matters more than floating-point operations and compute.
“It is all a memory hierarchy problem, from NAND flash storage to double data rate [DDR] memory attached to the central processing unit [CPU], high-bandwidth memory [HBM] attached to the GPU, and static random-access memory [SRAM],” he said.
A startup might focus on one type of memory, such as SRAM, and position it as the answer to a particular computing problem. But Koduri said the system-level requirements are broader.
“We look at the problem as a memory hierarchy and exploit each level as efficiently as possible,” he said.
Asked what changes when energy, compute, cooling, networking, and software are designed together, Koduri said the industry has traditionally operated in separate layers. Chipmakers typically design and sell a chip to a systems company, which builds a system. Another company builds the rack, while a data center operator handles installation, thermal management, and cooling.
“There are multiple layers in the ecosystem before everything comes together,” he said.
However, the scale of AI data center expansion is changing how companies approach the design process. Koduri said engineers must consider the entire data center rather than optimize an individual chip in isolation.
“We have to think about the whole system,” he said. “Not just the system, but the entire data center.”
The objective, he explained, is to convert incoming electricity into tokens as efficiently as possible while managing the heat generated by the chips.
Koduri described this as an optimization problem that will continue to evolve as AI models and computing architectures change. Over the past five years, he said, the industry has moved from basic transformers to mixture-of-experts models, DeepSeek optimizations, and decision-making models. GPU optimization is also continuing.
“The real constraint is that we have megawatts coming in and intelligence coming out,” he said. “How efficiently can we transform those megawatts into intelligence?”
Customers, Koduri said, care about the output of the complete system. “They want to plug in electricity, provide cooling, and get tokens they can sell. That is all.”
Oxmiq’s role at AM Intelligence Labs
Oxmiq’s work with AM Intelligence Labs covers data center planning and the selection of technology partners, Koduri said.
The company’s support begins with site selection and data center design. It then works on compute design, rack placement, networking and storage requirements, thermal management, cooling, and software stack operations.
“We provide all that expertise,” he said.
“We do not necessarily solve every problem ourselves,” Koduri said. “For example, we may select a suitable partner to provide the system, such as an original equipment manufacturer. That is the kind of support we are currently providing to [AM Group], because we come from the technology world, while they come from the energy world.”
Koduri pointed to AM Intelligence Lab’s first AI factory in Hyderabad, which he described as probably the first such deployment in Asia. The company has ordered about 9,000 Nvidia Rubin GPUs for the 30-MW facility, with delivery of Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale systems scheduled for the first quarter of 2027. It has since placed an additional order for 20,000 Rubin GPUs for sites in India and Malaysia.
Custom silicon economics and India’s infrastructure needs
Koduri said companies can potentially improve computing efficiency by designing the silicon, systems, and infrastructure for a specific data center rather than relying entirely on components designed for a wide range of customers.
Traditionally, a chipmaker had to sell its product to many data centers to generate revenue. That required designing a flexible product that could accommodate different customer requirements, standards, and features, even if those compromises reduced efficiency.
“If I am designing for one data center and its specific constraints, I can build something that is twice as cost-effective,” he said.
For a 1-GW data center, which Koduri estimated could cost around $55 billion to build, he said custom-designing the system could potentially deliver twice the compute by using power more efficiently.
He said this approach could change both the engineering mindset and the business model. A company developing silicon could now target the data center problem itself, with a single customer potentially generating multibillion-dollar revenue.
Koduri said custom silicon, systems, and software begin to make economic sense for customers planning at least 100 megawatts (MW) of computing capacity.
He put the cost of 100 MW of computing capacity at approximately $5.5 billion using off-the-shelf hardware. By comparison, R&D for a state-of-the-art chip manufactured by TSMC could cost around $100 million to $150 million. Developing a complete custom system could cost up to about $500 million, even with generous spending, he said.
If a custom system roughly halved that cost, a customer could save more than $2 billion even after spending $500 million on development, he said.
However, customers need the IP, tools, and technical know-how to develop custom systems, and Koduri said Oxmiq is building a solution to that problem.
Koduri said Oxmiq’s customers fall into three categories. The first comprises infrastructure companies such as AM Intelligence Labs, which are building computing capacity and need support across the system. The second includes companies designing silicon for applications such as data centers, physical AI, and enterprise AI.
Oxmiq can provide hardware and software IP to startups developing products such as chips for robots, allowing them to focus on their customers’ requirements, Koduri said.
The third category includes companies developing new materials and new physics, such as new forms of memory, silicon, silicon photonics, and photonics-based interconnects. They can license Oxmiq’s IP rather than develop the computing technology alongside their research.
In India, Oxmiq is engaging with customers in the infrastructure and silicon design categories. In the U.S., it works across all three categories, with most customers in infrastructure and new-physics applications, he said.
India’s installed data center power capacity stood at 1.57 GW in August 2026, up from about 375 MW in 2020, and is projected to reach nearly 8 GW by 2030, according to the Indian Press Information Bureau. About $70 billion of investment is underway, with a further $90 billion in announced projects.
Koduri said a 1-GW data center costs approximately $55 billion to build. By comparison, he said capital expenditure per gigawatt in China was moving toward $10 billion. “They can get things done at one-fifth, and perhaps one-tenth, of the cost of the rest of the world,” he said.
He estimated that India would need at least 6 GW of infrastructure to provide intelligence to its entire population, adding that the actual requirement would be much higher. The combined GPU capacity currently available in India, including planned deployments by AM Intelligence Labs, would not reach 100 MW, he said. That suggests India would need to increase that capacity at least 60-fold before the end of the decade.
For Koduri, the opportunity is not limited to building more data centers. It also includes developing the chips, systems, and software that convert electricity into AI output. “The opportunities for design teams, systems teams, and software teams in India are tremendous,” he said. “This is a build-out that India should participate in.”

articles.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says it's 'hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The AI industry is entering a new era, and not just because of its constant stream of new model releases and discoveries. The AI community must now push forward without one of its most influential figures, Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang stepped down last week amid several scandals involving affairs with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy, raising potentially far-reaching national security concerns.
Speaking onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman each revealed that they had spoken privately with Huang as the embattled former CEO’s public image continued to unravel.
“Jensen took one of the earliest big bets on us. We took a big bet on Nvidia,” Altman said. “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.”
OpenAI has worked closely with Huang over the years. Nvidia invested $30 billion in the company earlier this year and designs the chips that power OpenAI’s technology.
Brockman added that he and his wife are friends with Huang’s family, so the couple had reached out “personally, just to be there for him and his family at this time.”
“I think it’s obviously a tough time for everyone, but again, I think Nvidia is such an incredible company,” Brockman said. “I think that… what Jensen has built there, it clearly is built to last, and so we’re excited to keep partnering and looking to the future.”
Huang’s impact on Nvidia and the broader AI industry has been so profound that nearly 200,000 people, including Elon Musk and other influential CEOs, have signed a petition calling for the chipmaker to reinstate him. Nvidia executives said during the company’s earnings call on Tuesday that they do not have plans to reappoint Huang, even though the founder offered to return.
Altman was reticent to weigh in on Huang’s future at Nvidia. When asked whether he thought Huang could return, Altman replied, “One thing I did not appreciate was everybody on Earth speculating with some random theory.”
“I will say, I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best,” Altman said. “I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here.”

articles.title: US-IT-Chaos: Wie du erkennst, ob es sich um Ausfälle oder Cyberangriffe handelt
articles.text:
Nach IT-Chaos in den USA: Wie du erkennst, ob es sich um Ausfälle oder Cyberangriffe handelt
In den USA häufen sich seit Mitte November 2026 IT-Ausfälle, von denen Millionen Nutzer:innen weltweit betroffen sind. So fielen mehrere Cloud-Dienste von Microsoft aus, darunter Outlook und Teams. Auch bei der US-Luftfahrtbehörde FAA, dem US-Geheimdienst NSA oder Online-Diensten von Apple kam es zu Störungen.
USA sehen keine Belege für Cyberangriffe
Beobachter:innen spekulieren aufgrund der Häufung und vor dem Hintergrund von tatsächlichen Cyberangriffen auf Supermärkte, Dienstleister und Behörden in Europa über entsprechende Attacken von Hacker:innen. US-Außenminister Marco Rubio erklärte dagegen am 17. November 2026, dass es „keinerlei Belege oder Gründe für diese Annahme“ gebe, wie das ZDF berichtet.
Die Kolleg:innen von Wired haben einen Guide mit verschiedenen Fragen erstellt, die sich Nutzer:innen stellen können. Die Beantwortung soll dann dazu beitragen, besser einschätzen zu können, ob es sich um Ausfälle oder Cyberattacken handelt.
Suche nach technischen Fehlern
Zunächst einmal sollte die Suche nach technischen Fehlern Priorität haben. IT-Expert:innen gehen jedenfalls davon aus, dass fehlerhafte Softwareupdates, Änderungen an der Konfiguration oder beschädigte Kabel oder Geräte deutlich häufiger vorkommen als Cyberangriffe.
Doug Madory vom IT-Sicherheitsunternehmen Infoblox schätzt gegenüber Wired, dass bei den von ihm beobachteten Netzwerkausfällen nur einer von tausend auf einen Hackerangriff zurückging. Danach sollten Nutzer:innen die Statusseiten und offizielle Mitteilungen von Betreibern betroffener Dienste prüfen. Je mehr Firmen auf große Cloud-Anbieter wie AWS setzen, desto mehr Dienste und Kund:innen können von einem dort auftretenden Problem betroffen sein.
Mithilfe von Diensten wie Cloudflare Radar lässt sich zudem einfach ermitteln, ob nur ein Anbieter oder mehrere Netzwerke in der Region von Ausfällen betroffen sind. Daran kann man ablesen, ob es sich um ein fehlerhaftes Update bei einem Betreiber oder etwa um ein beschädigtes Glasfaserkabel handeln könnte.
Bekennerschreiben von Ransomware-Gruppen
Hinweise auf Cyberangriffe liefern dagegen mögliche Bekennerschreiben, etwa von Ransomware-Gruppen. Diese sind allerdings mit Vorsicht zu genießen, da solche Behauptungen übertrieben oder erfunden sein könnten, wie Wired warnt. Eine Bestätigung können Mitteilungen der betroffenen Organisation, von Behörden oder unabhängigen Sicherheitsforscher:innen liefern.
Einen weiteren Anhaltspunkt kann auch die Dauer des Ausfalls liefern. Geht es um ein fehlerhaftes Update, ist das oft innerhalb von Minuten oder Stunden geregelt. Bei einer Ransomware-Attacke kann es dagegen Tage, Wochen oder Monate dauern, bis ausgefallene Dienste wieder normal funktionieren.
Technik wird immer komplexer
Im Fall der aktuellen IT-Ausfälle in den USA kommt noch ein weiterer Punkt dazu, der eine genauere Betrachtung verdient: die zeitliche Nähe der Angriffe. Experte Madory erklärt allerdings, dass die Serie an Störungen auch schlicht zeigen könnte, wie komplex die Technik geworden sei.
„In unserer Gesellschaft läuft alles über internetbasierte Dienste. Und die fallen von Zeit zu Zeit aus“, so Madory gegenüber Wired. Solche Ausfälle ließen sich nie ganz verhindern. Wichtig sei zu verstehen, was jeden einzelnen Ausfall ausmache und was man daraus lernen könne.

articles.title: Voyager 1 spacecraft crosses milestones distance of one-light day from Earth 49 years after launch — now 16.09 billion miles away, signal takes full 24 hours to travel home
articles.text:
Voyager 1 spacecraft crosses milestones distance of one-light day from Earth 49 years after launch — now 16.09 billion miles away, signal takes full 24 hours to travel home
It has been traveling for nearly 50 years to reach this milestone and continues into the unknown.
NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today. A countdown at Orbital Radar confirmed that Voyager cruised past the threshold at a leisurely 37,844 mph just after 5 am ET on Wednesday, November 18. It means that Voyager is now more than 16 billion miles away, and that a signal from the spacecraft now takes fully 24 hours to travel the distance.
There are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat. Sci-fi shows casually mention light-years as if they are like a trip to the local convenience store. One light-day isn’t a distance to be derided, though. Over the last half century, hurtling through space at a cruising speed of 38,000 mph, the Voyager spacecraft has clocked about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers).
These are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming. So NASA has kindly provided some context with the distances of various heavenly bodies in miles and light-speeds. For example, the Moon is 238,855 miles distant, or about 1.3 light seconds away from Earth. Due to Mars’ independent orbit around the Sun, it can take between three minutes and 22 minutes for light to travel between the red and the blue planet. Meanwhile, the Sun’s rays reach Earth, about 93 million miles away, in 20 light seconds. Now let us remind you that Voyager 1 is on the brink of being a whole light-day away.
On Wednesday, with this major milestone passed, Voyager 1’s journey will be far from over. NASA says that it is on course for an obscure star called Gliese 445, now in the constellation Ursa Minor. We’ll have to keep the champagne on ice for another 40,000 years to celebrate the fly-past of that star, though.
Voyager 1 carries a copy of the Golden Record. Like sending a message in a bottle, NASA scientists launched Voyager with the hope that someone, somewhere will eventually read the message. Moreover, the receiving aliens will need to source tech to play the record, which contains sounds, music, and the data needed to reconstruct photos that showcase the diversity of life and culture on our planet.
If an alien got hold of the record on Wednesday and managed to rustle up a gramophone player to listen to it, a message sent to Earth via radio waves would take a full 24 hours to be received.
Space enthusiasts are also invited to participate in a global event “by creating a wave of golden light.” It sounds rather pointless, but enthusiasts are asked to flash the three-letter call sign for NASA's Voyager mission, VGR, into the night sky - Morse Code style - using their phone flashlights. There’s a website you can open to flash your screen appropriately.

articles.title: Microsoft is giving agents their own Cloud PC capabilities to help you with crucial tasks
articles.text:
Microsoft is giving agents their own Cloud PC capabilities to help you with crucial tasks
You can prescribe an AI agent its own Cloud PC
- Companies can now give AI agents their own Windows Cloud PC, just like a human worker
- They'll be managed through Intune and Entra with unique identities and permissions
- General Cloud PC performance and reliability are also on track to see improvements
Taking the idea of giving AI agents their own identity even further, Microsoft has announced that it will be giving them their own managed Cloud PCs so that they can operate Windows apps and perform tasks just like any other human workers.
This follows the launch of Windows 365 for Agents earlier this year, and comes as part of sweeping updates for "people, agents and IT" to the company's Cloud PC portfolio.
Under the updates, Microsoft is using Direct Stream to improve responsiveness, reliability and performance, boasting that users can now connect to their Cloud PCs within seconds, making them feel much more like conventional, local machines.
Cloud PCs updated to support AI agents
The reason for granting AI agents access to their own Cloud PCs is because many apps lack APIs that allow agents to interact with them directly, so Microsoft wants to give users deeper system-level access instead. It means that automation can be opened up for legacy and unsupported apps, rather than companies being forced to rebuild or migrate apps entirely.
"Our AI agents can interact with real Windows applications, perform QA testing and generate documentation, all within a secure, enterprise-governed Windows 365 for Agents environment," one early customer shared.
Windows 365 for Agents will also be eligible for Copilot Credits, which Microsoft describes as a 'common currency' that's applicable across its AI offerings, for easier billing and spend visibility.
The company noted that Cloud PCs are controlled through Microsoft Intune and Entra – in other words, they're managed just like earlier Cloud PCs for humans, taking on their own identities which can be set up to be more restrictive than human identities.
