articles.title: Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
articles.text:
Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
- Date:
- November 16, 2026
- Source:
- University of Innsbruck
- Summary:
- Scientists have developed a new way to determine whether quantum simulations can be trusted, solving a growing problem as quantum computers become too powerful for conventional machines to check. Demonstrated on a 51-qubit system, the technique measures uncertainty and provides verifiable error margins that could help unlock the full potential of quantum computing.
- Share:
As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.
The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.
Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.
A New Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy
The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.
Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.
But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," says Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties."
Rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify important interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.
"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy."
Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator
To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.
After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.
This represents an important step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.
Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems
The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.
"This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important."
The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.
Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.
"After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," says Peter Zoller.
This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.
The findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Innsbruck. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Tristan Kraft, Manoj K. Joshi, William T. Lam, Tobias Olsacher, Florian Kranzl, Johannes Franke, Lata Kh Joshi, Rainer Blatt, Augusto Smerzi, Daniel Stilck França, Benoît Vermersch, Barbara Kraus, Christian F. Roos, Peter Zoller. Bounded-Error Quantum Simulation via Hamiltonian and Lindbladian Learning. Physical Review X, 2026; 16 (3) DOI: 10.1103/s96t-n8tx

articles.title: AWS PrivateLink Tunnel Endpoints Open a Whole CIDR Range to Another Account
articles.text:
AWS has published a technical walkthrough of tunnel endpoints, a VPC endpoint type launched in September that lets an application in one VPC reach every address in a CIDR range shared from another account, instead of one resource at a time. The provider shares a CIDR-type resource configuration through AWS Resource Access Manager and the consumer creates a tunnel endpoint against it. From then on, anything inside the range is reachable, including resources that did not exist when the share was made.
Bruce Pinsky and Ashish Kumar of AWS frame it as a vendor-access problem, for "a vendor or service provider whose software must reach applications and resources in a customer's network." Until now, that meant a separate PrivateLink resource configuration per database or host, which breaks down when the resources are ephemeral, or the customer does not want to enumerate them. With a CIDR configuration, the customer defines a perimeter in address ranges, and "resources located outside the perimeter can't be reached by the vendor." Two further properties come with the design: the consumer and provider VPCs can use overlapping CIDR blocks, and connections "can start only from the consumer VPC, not from the provider network."
(Source: AWS Networking & Content Delivery blog)
On the r/aws thread about the September launch, the first question was what this does that VPC peering does not, from a self-described veteran of AWS's advanced networking components. The answers that followed are the use cases: a peering connection exposes the whole VPC in both directions, while a tunnel endpoint shares a subset of the address space in one direction only; one commenter at a bank wrote that "peering with unregulated partners is a massive no-no, the auditors will rip you to shreds for it." Another pointed to clusters that do client-side load balancing, such as self-managed Kafka or Aerospike, which until now needed port-based routing on a Network Load Balancer and a separate port-mapping horizon for connections arriving over an interface endpoint. The same thread drew the line against VPC Lattice itself: Lattice services work at layer 7, tunnel endpoints at layer 4 without a resource configuration per target.
The unusual part is on the consumer side: the application's traffic has to arrive at the tunnel endpoint wrapped in GENEVE, the encapsulation protocol defined in RFC 8926, over UDP port 6081 and in the same Availability Zone. The endpoint strips the header, checks that the inner destination falls inside the shared range, rewrites the source to a resource gateway address, and forwards a plain packet into the provider VPC. Linux can do the wrapping in the kernel. The walkthrough creates an ip link add ... type geneve id 0 device inside its own network namespace with a default route through it, which sends the provider's ranges into the tunnel and leaves the instance's other traffic alone. On the far side, the resources see the resource gateway as the client, so the post advises security groups that reference the gateway's security group or subnet rather than a single address.
The documentation lists the constraints. Inner traffic must be TCP, with UDP permitted only for DNS, so ICMP and ping do not work, and IP fragments are dropped. Private DNS names are not supported on tunnel endpoints. The endpoint's subnets must sit in Availability Zones that overlap with the resource gateway's, or the association shows as inaccessible. A resource gateway's DNS setting cannot be changed after creation. And the access logs identify the consumer's endpoint but carry no field for the inner source address, so a provider can attribute traffic to a vendor and not to a workload behind that vendor's endpoint. The post also warns that sharing 0.0.0.0/0 grants access to everything the provider VPC can route to, including networks behind VPC peering, Direct Connect or a Site-to-Site VPN, and recommends sharing the narrowest ranges that work.
Both points have been tested in practice. Ryo Suzuki of the Japanese consultancy Classmethod connected two VPCs that both use 10.0.0.0/16 and got HTTP through, but only by running a GENEVE relay as root on the client, by routing a /32 per destination host, or by putting an HAProxy or NAT instance in front, each of which adds a hop or a single point of failure; his conclusion was that "route management according to the number of destinations is required." In a second experiment, he shared 0.0.0.0/0 from a VPC with a NAT gateway and reached the internet from a VPC with no gateway at all, which confirmed AWS's warning from the other side; he judged it workable as a temporary path and "difficult to use in a permanent production setup."
Pricing is an hourly charge per tunnel endpoint plus a per-GB charge for data processed, under PrivateLink pricing, with the provider side billed per GB through the resource gateway under VPC Lattice pricing, and the feature is available in 28 regions. Terraform support followed from the community: a contributor request opened two days after launch was implemented by another contributor and shipped in version 6.71.0 of the AWS provider, as a Tunnel endpoint type on aws_vpc_endpoint and a cidr_resource block on the Lattice resource configuration.

articles.title: How Orkes ParticleDB turns an impressive demo into a remarkable application
articles.text:
How Orkes ParticleDB turns an impressive demo into a remarkable application
Building an AI agent that performs an impressive demonstration is one thing. Building one that can reliably process financial transactions, handle customer refunds, or make business decisions without compromising sensitive data is quite another.
That distinction is becoming increasingly important as enterprises move from experimenting with generative AI to deploying agentic applications in production. Developers need more than powerful language models. They need dependable access to enterprise data, orchestration, security, fault tolerance, and a way to explain what an AI agent actually did. Orkes believes its newly previewed ParticleDB can help solve a significant part of that problem.
In an interview last month with The New Stack Editor-in-Chief Nick Lucchesi at AgentCon and MCPCon 2026 in San Jose, California, Orkes co-founder and CEO Jeu George discussed how the company’s emerging database technology and established Conductor orchestration platform are designed to make enterprise AI development simpler and more dependable.
Why ParticleDB matters to developers
At its recent Orkes Shift developer conference in San Francisco, the company previewed ParticleDB, an agentic database designed to bring together data capabilities that conventionally require multiple systems. Enterprise developers frequently work with relational databases, key-value stores, vector databases, and analytical systems. Connecting these technologies often means building complex extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipelines, managing data movement, and maintaining infrastructure that becomes increasingly difficult to operate.
ParticleDB’s premise is that these capabilities should work together within a common engine, reducing the integration burden on development teams. George contends that the need becomes especially pressing when AI agents enter the picture.
“When do AI agents and LLM models become useful? When they have data.”
—Orkes CEO Jeu George
“When do AI agents and LLM models become useful? When they have data,” George told The New Stack. That data, however, often resides within tightly controlled enterprise environments. Companies cannot simply expose sensitive customer information, financial records, or proprietary business processes to autonomous agents.
George envisions a different approach: Rather than allowing agents to roam freely through enterprise systems, a trusted platform supplies the specific information and context they need. Combined with Orkes Conductor, ParticleDB is intended to keep applications, agents and their underlying data closely integrated within customers’ cloud boundaries.
Reliability is still the hardest problem
Beyond data integration, George emphasized a familiar challenge for distributed-systems developers: Things inevitably break. Network outages, software bugs, infrastructure failures, and security incidents are unavoidable. With AI agents potentially executing workflows for hours or even days, recovering from failure without duplicating transactions becomes essential.
“If you design systems from the ground up that things are always going to fail, you simulate failures all the time, and that’s how you get to a robust application.”
“If you design systems from the ground up that things are always going to fail, you simulate failures all the time, and that’s how you get to a robust application,” George said. Orkes Conductor addresses that problem through workflow orchestration, recovery mechanisms, security controls, and audit trails. Developers can combine deterministic business processes with AI-driven decisions while retaining visibility into individual actions.
For regulated industries such as banking and insurance, that visibility is particularly valuable. Organizations need to reconstruct an agent’s decisions, identify which models and systems were involved, and explain outcomes to customers or regulators.
Knowing when to use an agent
One particularly useful part of the conversation examines a straightforward e-commerce refund. George explains why AI agents should handle ambiguous tasks, such as interpreting customer complaints, while predictable operations – issuing refunds, updating financial records and generating receipts – remain conventional workflows. Unusual or high-risk cases can be escalated to humans.
“…successful agentic applications aren’t necessarily the most autonomous. They’re the ones that combine intelligence with dependable execution.”
The broader message for developers is that successful agentic applications aren’t necessarily the most autonomous. They’re the ones that combine intelligence with dependable execution.
Watch our full interview with Jeu George to learn how Orkes is approaching enterprise data integration, agent orchestration, security, and explainability – and why George believes the next generation of AI applications will require a fundamentally different production infrastructure.

articles.title: VeroSecurity Raises $11 Million for AI Security Engineering Platform
articles.text:
VeroSecurity, founded in 2025 by IDF 8200 alumni Elad Tessler (CEO) and Daniel Meirov (CTO), has raised $11 million in a seed funding round led by TLV Partners. The firm is building a platform for AI Security Engineering (ASE) – the process of securing AI tools and agents – and will use the funding to advance the platform and grow its go-to-market presence in the United States.
AI Security Engineering is a new, and as yet ill-defined, security discipline. Its purpose is to secure the AI tools and agents that are increasingly being adopted, used, and modified in-house by company employees. This is happening at pace and volume – so the object of ASE is a moving target; and is a security requirement that is different to and separate from cybersecurity.
ASE policy is defined by security teams. Vero turns these policy definitions into enforced controls, automatically updates them as the AI tools evolve, and refers only those enforcement decisions that require a human judgement to the security team.
Vero’s idea is to bring a new approach to securing AI. “CISOs have seen enough dashboards and tables that tell their teams what’s wrong and leave the work to them. AI Security Engineering deserves a better operating model, designed for AI rather than borrowed from other areas of security,” commented Elad Tessler, Co-Founder and CEO of VeroSecurity. “We’re working alongside the first generation of AI security leaders and building Vero around what they actually need: a platform that does the work, keeps protections current as AI changes, and brings them only the decisions that require human judgment.”
The core technology within the platform is Vero’s AI Runtime Governor. It puts security decisions into effect as AI operates, enforcing approved policies and blocking agent actions that trigger unauthorized behavior. If a change requires a new risk decision, Vero brings the analysis and recommended action to the responsible security professional.
In parallel with developing its AI Security Engineering platform, Vero is establishing AISecurityEngineering.org, an open community and knowledge center featuring practical field guides, workshops and the ASE credential track. ASE is new, rapidly growing, and different to existing mainstream cybersecurity.
“Our own weekly count of open roles titled ‘AI Security Engineer’ went from 367 on 25 October to 451 on 14 November, up 23% in three weeks,” Tessler told SecurityWeek. “Demand is arriving before the discipline has been written down.”
He added, “Security disciplines that have lasted, like AppSec and detection engineering, grew a shared body of knowledge before they had standard job titles. AI Security Engineering needs that too, and right now!”
Vero is bringing order to the evolving and disorganized security requirement of AI Security Engineering. While the new open community will help to define and establish the discipline, Vero’s own platform will assist the ASE role to perform the operational work.
“The Vero platform undertakes the impossible part of the ASE work, leaving the human engineer in situ to make judgement calls where necessary,” explained Tessler. The impossible part is the volume (dozens of tool changes every week, each one mapped to every control they touch), and tempo (agents act in seconds, so defenses must be in place before the action, not reviewed after it) of AI tool changes. “The human part is deciding what the business will accept, which exceptions make sense, and when a new tool is worth the risk.”
“We’re betting on more AI security engineers, not fewer,” said Tessler, “which is why we’re building AISecurityEngineering.org to train them. Without Vero, keeping up with AI in a large company takes a team. With it, one person, or a security leader taking it on alongside their job, can stay ahead.”
Vero is adding flesh to a newly emerging security requirement: AI Security Engineering. The Vero platform and AI Runtime Governor automates much of the mechanics of securing AI tools and agents used in-house, by continuously discovering, assessing and securing enterprise AI. Additionally, launching the separate AISecurityEngineering.org open community will help establish a body of subject knowledge to sustain and grow the new discipline.

articles.title: Ireland's Disseqt AI raises €7.3 million to safely deploy AI agents | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Disseqt AI, a Dublin-based AI assurance platform, has raised €7.3 million ($8 million) to help enterprises deploy AI agents safely, at scale and enable them to meet regulatory requirements.
Gresham House Ventures led the round, with participation from Sure Valley Ventures (SVV), Delta Partners and Enterprise Ireland, alongside angels including senior leaders from OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, Salesforce and Meta, and cricket legend Rahul Dravid.
Apoorva Kumar, CEO and co-founder of Disseqt AI, says, “Every enterprise is handing real work to AI agents, but very few can prove those agents are safe, fair and within policy. That gap is what stops AI from going live, and it is what we built Disseqt to close. We test before launch, control in real time and keep the audit trail, independently of the model providers.
“When your agent is talking to 80 million people, or processing thousands of banking transactions, ‘good enough’ isn’t an option. This funding lets us bring that standard to many more enterprises. AI governance and assurance needs to become a standard part of how every enterprise runs AI.”
Disseqt’s funding follows several European investment rounds in AI-agent assurance, governance and security during 2026.
In the UK, Geordie AI raised €25 million to strengthen AI-agent governance, Trent AI secured €11 million for agentic cybersecurity, and AI Score received €4.6 million to support safer enterprise AI adoption. Spain also recorded investments in NeuralTrust (€17.2 million) and AI evaluation platform Galtea (€2.7 million).
Closer to home, Irish-founded Evervault raised €21 million for adjacent encrypted-data infrastructure.
Together with rounds secured by Mindgard, Overmind and Hybridity, these announcements represent approximately €111.8 million in 2026 funding, excluding Disseqt’s investment.
Rohit Mathur, Partner, Gresham House Ventures, adds, “We see AI governance and assurance becoming essential infrastructure as enterprises put AI into live operations. Companies need to test and control their AI with tools that sit apart from the model providers they rely on. Disseqt does that across the full life of an AI application, and its early customers include some of the most demanding regulated buyers in Europe.
“Enterprise AI deployment spend scaled to £130 billion by September 2026, up from £25 billion last year, and this will accelerate many-folds in a short span. However it won’t happen without proper governance and assurance which is what Disseqt AI is built for.”
Disseqt was founded in late 2025 by Apoorva Kumar (CEO), Manish Atri (CTO) and Cyril Treacy (COO). Between them they have held senior roles at Microsoft, AWS and Salesforce across enterprise software, AI and cybersecurity.
According to the company, AI agents are moving from answering questions to doing real work, handling requests, accessing company data and taking actions inside business systems. McKinsey’s 2026 State of AI survey found that 40% of respondents at companies with more than $1 billion in annual revenue were scaling AI agents in at least one business function, up from 27% a year earlier.
However, agents do not always behave as intended and can introduce risks even while pursuing assigned tasks. In October 2026, OpenAI disclosed two internal incidents in which coding agents weakened safety monitoring, with one falsely denying the change. As businesses give agents greater access to data, tools and customer interactions, ensuring they operate within company policy is becoming increasingly important.
This is where AI assurance comes in. It provides ongoing testing and monitoring to ensure AI systems behave as intended.
Disseqt enables enterprises to test applications and agents before launch, enforce company policies once live and monitor their behaviour continuously, blocking outputs that breach those policies while maintaining evidence for audit and oversight.
For example, enterprises can test whether an agent can be prompted to reveal confidential customer data, address vulnerabilities before deployment and retain a record of the results for audit.
The approach has already been applied at scale and across multiple customers. In a project for a global sports league’s fan engagement agent, used by 80 million fans, Disseqt reportedly improved the safe-response rate from 80% to 99% across tests covering safety, bias and privacy risks. Disseqt reports that no unsafe outputs were detected when the original failing tests were repeated following fixes. Similarly, Disseqt’s provide assurance for a large European Bank credit card services programme.
Kara Owen, British Ambassador to Ireland, says, “Huge congratulations to Apoorva and the Disseqt AI team on this fantastic milestone. It is great to see an innovative Irish AI company expanding its presence in the UK and tapping into the UK’s deep technology, investment and AI ecosystem. Their expansion into London is a great example of the opportunities for ambitious Irish tech companies to use the UK as a platform to scale, grow internationally and reach new markets. I’m delighted to see Disseqt AI strengthening the already vibrant technology links between Ireland and the UK.”
The funding will help Disseqt win more enterprise customers and expand internationally, as it works towards its goal of becoming the assurance layer enterprises rely on for every AI agent they deploy. The company is hiring across sales, operations and technology.

articles.title: Voyager 1 at one light-day: Historian revisits Golden Record's forgotten details
articles.text:
In the one light-day that humanity’s most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again.
Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter’s moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a “commemorative phonograph record,” in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whoever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space.
About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson. While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs’ overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago.
“So much has been written about the contents of the record—the message in the bottle, so to speak—whereas I was more interested in the hardware, the bottle itself, because so very little is known about that,” Swanson, former chief historian for NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston and founding editor of Quest: The History of Spaceflight Quarterly, said in an interview.
Historian Glen Swanson (right) with his wife, anthropologist Deana Weibel (center), and Jon Lomberg, space artist, science journalist, and design director for the Voyager Golden Record.
Historian Glen Swanson (right) with his wife, anthropologist Deana Weibel (center), and Jon Lomberg, space artist, science journalist, and design director for the Voyager Golden Record.
Credit:
Glen Swanson via collectSPACE.com
With the 50th anniversaries looming for the launches of both Voyager probes, Swanson and Jon Lomberg, the design director of the Golden Record, recently set about writing Voyager’s Golden Record: An Enduring Reflection, which will be released by the University of Chicago Press in August 2027.
“There isn’t a whole lot of information, and some of the information is somewhat contradictory,” said Swanson of the existing resources and publications. “So it is kind of refreshing to look back and see what exactly went on.”
Meanwhile, the Voyagers continue to travel outward, still communicating with Earth. On November 18, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth—the distance a particle of light travels in 24 hours—giving Swanson an occasion to share details from his and Jon Lomberg’s pending book.
Under cover
Within the immense scale of the Universe, Voyager 2 is barely even a block from its home. Were an intelligent species to find it today—some 16 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) away from Earth—they might not need anything contained on the Golden Record to trace its origins back to our planet.
But that was never the intention of the Golden Record’s designers, who created the archive to last and be relevant for a much more distant encounter.
“They are pretty confident that it’s going to last a long, long, long time based on the data; the probabilities of the impacts from micrometeorites and things like that,” Swanson said.
Historian Glen Swanson rediscovered that the designers of the Voyager Golden Record repeated the operating instructions on the inside of its protective cover.
Historian Glen Swanson rediscovered that the designers of the Voyager Golden Record repeated the operating instructions on the inside of its protective cover.
Credit:
Glen Swanson via collectSPACE.com
When most people think of the Golden Record, says Swanson, what often comes to mind is not the disc itself, but its protective cover. In addition to being inscribed with the now-iconic Pulsar map of the location of our Sun as earlier flown on the Pioneer 10 and 11 probes, hieroglyphs lay out how to play the record and access the data (e.g., photos) also contained on the disc.
The cover also shields the record from possible damage, but nothing protects the protector.
“The designers recognized that the outside of the cover was going to wear down. It just would,” Swanson told collectSPACE. “Even small amounts of dust are eventually going to wear down the inscriptions to the point perhaps where they are not going to be readable.”
It is a catch-22: The instructions needed to be on the outside so whoever finds Voyager easily finds what to do. But if the hieroglyphs are damaged or are eroded away, the disc inside might forever go unplayed.
The solution may seem obvious, but it’s unclear whether the designers thought of it back then.
“It makes a whole lot of sense that they repeated the instructions on the inside of the cover, because when someone or something finds Voyager, they might only be able to make out a little bit on the outside,” said Swanson.
There were hints that this backup existed in photographs of the covers taken before the Voyager probes were launched, but they were either not clear enough or had other objects (e.g., a bag) in the way to make out what was there. It was not until Swanson found and referenced the original blueprints that he could confirm the instructions were on the inside, too.
The schematics for the Voyager Golden Record’s protective cover confirmed the “reduced size” instructions to be added to the interior side, just as Glen Swanson found.
Credit:
Glen Swanson/NASA/JPL
The schematics for the Voyager Golden Record’s protective cover confirmed the “reduced size” instructions to be added to the interior side, just as Glen Swanson found.
Credit:
Glen Swanson/NASA/JPL
There is another reason why the record’s designers may have felt they needed to repeat the instructions, according to Swanson.
“What’s the best way to convey the importance of those instructions? You repeat them,” he said. “You have them on the outside, and you have them on the inside.”
Limited edition
Initially, the Voyager Golden Record was a limited edition of just three—one to fly on each spacecraft and a flight backup.
“Later, meaning maybe a month or so after the launches, there’s correspondence indicating that NASA said to go ahead and make 10 extras,” said Swanson, noting that the count included the spare. “How they came up with that number, I am not 100 percent sure, other than maybe they were to make as many as they could based on the hardware and funding available.”
Over the years, various reports have either lowered the total number to as few as six or raised it as high as 14, for reasons unexplained. What is for certain—as Swanson also verified—is that the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Pasadena, California, retained and displays the flight spare.
In the process of his research, Swanson was also able to verify that original duplicates are held today at the United Nations in New York; the US Library of Congress, NASA Headquarters, and Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in Washington, DC; the Johnson Space Center in Texas; the Kennedy Space Center in Florida; Langley Research Center in Virginia; Glenn Research Center in Ohio; and Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland.
“Interestingly enough, NASA Headquarters was not given one originally, so how they obtained their copy is not certain,” said Swanson. “It may be that President Carter turned his copy over to NASA HQ since records indicate that he had one. Archivists at the Carter Presidential Library and Museum confirmed that they never received a Golden Record, so Carter most likely gave it back to NASA at some point.”
In 2024, SpaceX founder Elon Musk replied to a social media post, saying, “I have one,” without offering any other details. It is believed he was referring to a replica, not one of the NASA-produced duplicates.
This duplicate of the Voyager Golden Record was transferred to the National Air and Space Museum in 1978. (Smithsonian)
Credit:
Smithsonian
This duplicate of the Voyager Golden Record was transferred to the National Air and Space Museum in 1978. (Smithsonian)
Credit:
Smithsonian
Due to rights issues and material challenges, no complete versions have been offered for sale. The audio tracks have been collected on vinyl, CD, in playlists, and even a CD-ROM, which was produced for the visuals. Full- and smaller-size replicas of the cover have also been made.
Swanson and Lomberg are working on a full-size replica of the copper record to be released in conjunction with their book. But even that, as now planned, will not be playable.
“I think humanity is delighted that there were 10 spares made, because now we have those to study and look at, as the two that were flown are now well out of our reach,” said Swanson.
Robert Pearlman is a space historian, journalist and the founder and editor of collectSPACE, a daily news publication and online community focused on where space exploration intersects with pop culture. He is also a contributing writer for Space.com and co-author of "Space Stations: The Art, Science, and Reality of Working in Space” published by Smithsonian Books in 2018. He is on the leadership board for For All Moonkind and is a member of the American Astronautical Society's history committee.

articles.title: Connect Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to private APIs in a hub-and-spoke network with centralized inspection | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Connect Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to private APIs in a hub-and-spoke network with centralized inspection
In many enterprises, a central network team owns every virtual private cloud (VPC) and subnet, and every flow between VPCs must pass a central firewall in both directions. Agents that call internal REST APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, must meet the same two requirements. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model.
This post shows a pattern that meets both requirements. The network team keeps ownership of every subnet, and traffic between the Gateway and your private APIs and MCP servers crosses the central firewall in both directions. It covers where to place the Amazon VPC Lattice resource gateway that the Gateway uses to reach private targets. It also covers who owns each piece, six configuration decisions, and the checks that confirm the pattern works.
We built and tested the pattern in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region (us-east-1), in a lab with three member accounts and a management account in AWS Organizations. The AWS CloudFormation templates, test scripts, test evidence, and reference material (address plan, full validation checks, troubleshooting, quotas) are in the companion repository. Use the pattern as a guideline and adjust it to your own account architecture.
Terms used in this post
- Resource gateway: The Amazon VPC Lattice entry point into a VPC: elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in subnets you choose. Backends see its addresses as the source of each connection.
- Resource configuration: A VPC Lattice object that names one backend (here, an internal load balancer or VPC endpoint DNS name and port) behind a resource gateway. You can share it with other accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).
- Managed mode and self-managed mode: The two private endpoint options for Gateway targets. In managed mode, AgentCore creates the resource gateway for you. In self-managed mode, you create it and give the target a resource configuration.
When to use this pattern
Use this pattern when all of the following are true:
- A network account owns every VPC, subnet, and AWS Transit Gateway attachment, and shares application subnets through AWS RAM.
- A central firewall in an inspection VPC must inspect traffic entering and leaving every VPC.
- Application teams manage only their own resources and security groups.
Otherwise, one of the options in Table 1 fits better.
Table 1: When another option fits better.
| Your environment | Use | 
| The Gateway account can own subnets that reach your tools | Managed mode | 
| Traffic between the Gateway and the tools doesn’t need central inspection | Self-managed mode, as documented | 
| Tools are reachable on public endpoints | A standard Gateway target | 
We also considered managed mode in subnets that AgentCore owns, a resource gateway in each tool VPC or in the central endpoints VPC, and internet-facing load balancers with AWS WAF per tool. The alternatives write-up explains why each falls short under these constraints.
Design requirements for centralized inspection
- The network account owns every subnet. The Gateway and application accounts build only in subnets shared to them through AWS RAM.
- Every flow between VPCs crosses the central firewall, in both directions. The central firewall in the inspection VPC inspects the traffic between the Gateway and your private APIs and MCP servers.
AgentCore Gateway reaches private targets through a VPC Lattice resource gateway, and the two private endpoint modes place it differently. Managed mode creates it in the Gateway account, which fits environments where that account can own the subnets it runs in. Self-managed mode, as documented, places it in subnets with direct access to the backend, which fits environments that do not require inspection between the Gateway and the tool. This environment needs both conditions at once, so the pattern uses self-managed mode with one change. The network account owns the resource gateway and places it in subnets routed through AWS Transit Gateway, so every request and reply passes the inspection VPC.
Solution overview
Give the resource gateway its own VPC and subnets in the network account. Don’t share them, and keep backends out of them. Route them through the transit gateway so every request and reply between VPCs crosses the firewall. Share one resource configuration per backend with the AgentCore account through AWS RAM. Figure 1 shows the accounts, VPCs, and traffic path.
Traffic path
- The agent, in a shared subnet with no internet route, calls the Gateway URL. Private DNS on the Gateway interface endpoint resolves it inside the agent’s VPC.
- AWS WAF, if attached, evaluates the request. The Gateway checks its resource policy and the inbound JSON Web Token (JWT), then picks the target and tool.
- The Gateway gets an outbound OAuth token for the tool account and sends the request through VPC Lattice to the resource gateway in the network account.
- The resource gateway subnets route to the transit gateway, which sends the traffic through the inspection VPC to the tool account’s internal Application Load Balancer (ALB) or execute-api endpoint. (Crosses the firewall.)
- The ALB or Amazon API Gateway validates the token and forwards the request to the backend.
- The response returns the same way. (Crosses the firewall.)
How does Gateway traffic enter the network account’s VPC without a transit gateway attachment in the AgentCore account? When you create a target, AgentCore associates the shared resource configuration with its own VPC Lattice service network. VPC Lattice then delivers connections from that service network to the resource gateway’s network interfaces in your VPC. AWS operates that hop, and from there your routes and firewall take over.
What this pattern doesn’t do. Check these limits against your requirements before you adopt it:
- No payload inspection – Traffic is TLS end to end from the Gateway to the ALB, with a certificate the Gateway validates. The firewall sees flow metadata and the TLS Server Name Indication (SNI), not payloads. Request content is in the Gateway, AWS WAF, and ALB logs.
- Some legs skip the firewall – The agent-to-interface-endpoint leg and the Gateway-to-resource-gateway leg don’t cross it. Neither do the token requests that AgentCore makes to each identity provider.
- No end-user identity at the tool – With the client credentials grant, every call that reaches the tool carries the Gateway’s client identity. To trace a call to a caller, use the inbound JWT claims in the Gateway application logs.
Who owns what
Table 2: Who creates what.
|  | One time | New API on a connected ALB | New ALB or tool account | 
| Network team | Resource gateway and its VPC, subnets, and routes. Firewall rules. A default route from the tool VPC to the transit gateway for the ALB’s signing-key fetch. Gateway interface endpoint and policy. AWS RAM share | Nothing | One resource configuration added to the share. A firewall rule if the range is new | 
| Tool team | An ALB certificate whose subject alternative name matches the target host name that the AgentCore team uses | A listener rule (with jwt-validation) on their ALB | An internal ALB and security group, and an app client for the Gateway (client credentials grant, with a scope such as tools/invoke) | 
| AgentCore team | Gateway, inbound authorizer, resource policy, optional AWS WAF | One Gateway target per API or MCP server | A target, plus an OAuth credential provider for a new identity provider | 
A new operation or tool on an existing target needs no new target: update the OpenAPI spec with UpdateGatewayTarget, or call SynchronizeGatewayTargets for an MCP server. The repository’s build order lists the steps in each account and the values the teams pass to each other.
Prerequisites
- An organization in AWS Organizations with resource sharing in AWS RAM enabled.
- AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) 2.37.7 or later, or the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) 1.43.106 or later, for the certificateConfigurations parameter.
- For the role that creates Gateway targets: vpc-lattice:GetResourceConfiguration, vpc-lattice:CreateServiceNetworkResourceAssociation, vpc-lattice:GetServiceNetworkResourceAssociation, vpc-lattice:ListServiceNetworkResourceAssociations, and vpc-lattice:AssociateViaAWSService, plus the bedrock-agentcore target actions. Check your service control policies (SCPs) if your organization doesn’t use VPC Lattice today.
- A firewall in a central inspection VPC attached to the transit gateway with appliance mode enabled.
Key design decisions
The snippets are excerpts from the lab templates and use the lab’s address plan. RGW_NET is the resource gateway subnets (10.0.1.0/24–10.0.3.0/24), TOOL_NET is the tool VPC (10.12.0.0/16), and ALB_NET is the ALB subnets in it.
Decision 1: Put the resource gateway in a dedicated VPC in the network account
Create a dedicated VPC in the network account for the resource gateway, with subnets you don’t share and no central endpoints or backends. Route those subnets to the transit gateway. Keep one resource gateway per trust zone.
Used only with AgentCore, the resource gateway consumes one IP address per subnet, so small subnets are enough. Two settings can’t be changed after creation, Ipv4AddressesPerEni and ResourceConfigDnsResolution, so choose them up front. Use Availability Zone IDs that VPC Lattice and your AgentCore features support. The lab layout lists them for us-east-1.
Decision 2: Create one resource configuration per load balancer, and share it through AWS RAM
Point the resource configuration at the internal ALB DNS name and share it with the AgentCore account. Don’t start the name with rcfg-, which VPC Lattice reserves.
VPC Lattice delivers the connection to the resource configuration’s domain. AgentCore sends the target URL’s host name (for example tools.example.internal) as the SNI and checks the ALB certificate against it. The certificate’s subject alternative name must match that host name. The host name doesn’t need to resolve in DNS.
For private API Gateway REST APIs, point one resource configuration at the network account’s execute-api interface endpoint. Each API’s target uses its own URL, and each API’s resource policy must allow that endpoint through aws:SourceVpce. In our tests, a second API in another account worked through the same resource configuration with no network change.
Decision 3: Pass only the flows you need through the firewall
Your firewall needs two stateful allows: from the resource gateway subnets to the tool VPC on port 443, and from the ALB subnets to the identity provider’s host name on port 443. Session-based firewalls pass replies of an allowed flow. In the lab we used AWS Network Firewall with strict rule order and the default actions Drop established and Alert established. With these defaults, the firewall drops client-to-server packets that no rule passes, and lets replies through unless a rule drops them. The rule-order notes explain the semantics.
The first rule allows only the resource gateway subnets to reach the tool VPC on port 443. The second allows the ALB to fetch its identity provider’s signing keys (JSON Web Key Set, or JWKS), only from the ALB subnets and only to the identity provider’s host name. The tool VPC needs a default route to the transit gateway for this fetch to reach central egress. If your identity provider isn’t Amazon Cognito, replace the host name. Without this rule, in our tests, the ALB returned HTTP 500 and the agent received MCP invocation failed.
To prove replies cross the firewall, we added a drop rule for the reply direction preceding the pass rule:
Tool calls then hung until timeout, and the firewall logged to_client drops for sid 100098. Removing the rule restored the calls. Run the same test on your own firewall.
Decision 4: Validate the tool account’s token on the internal ALB or private API
The tool account keeps its own identity provider (Amazon Cognito in the lab) and creates an app client for the Gateway. Validate that client’s token on every path to the backend.
Internal ALB – Make the listener’s default action a fixed response, and put a jwt-validation action on every rule that forwards. Pin client_id to the Gateway’s app client so that other clients in the same user pool are rejected.
In our tests, a target with no token, one with another identity provider’s token, and one with a different app client’s token were all rejected with HTTP 401 before the backend ran. The agent saw only An internal error occurred, so use the ALB access logs to diagnose token problems.
Private REST API – An API key doesn’t authenticate the caller, so add an authorizer to every method, such as a Cognito user pool authorizer with a required scope (as in the lab). Also attach an endpoint policy to the execute-api endpoint that limits it to APIs owned by approved accounts. It controls which APIs the endpoint reaches, not who calls it. The authorizer controls the caller.
The ALB or endpoint security group allows only the resource gateway subnets, so the resource gateway is the only network path in. If your firewall applies source NAT, the security group must allow the firewall’s addresses instead, and it then admits anything the firewall forwards. The firewall rule and the token validation become the controls.
Decision 5: Create Gateway targets that reference the shared resource configuration
Create the Gateway with a JWT authorizer and, optionally, an AWS WAF web access control list (web ACL), which inspects the tool-call arguments for every target. AWS WAF inspects only the first 16 KB of the body by default (adjustable to 64 KB), so decide how each rule handles larger bodies. Add AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet to the common rule set. See the AWS WAF notes.
Gateway targets with a private endpoint can’t use NO_AUTH for inbound authorization unless you configure an interceptor function.
Each target needs an OAuth credential provider that holds the tool account’s app client ID and secret and the identity provider’s discovery URL:
If the ALB uses a certificate from a private certificate authority (CA), also store the CA certificate as a PEM string in an AWS Secrets Manager secret. The Gateway execution role (the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role you give the Gateway when you create it) needs permission to read that secret and the credential provider.
An OpenAPI target uses the same blocks with openApiSchema in place of mcpServer. To rotate the CA, update the secret and call UpdateGatewayTarget. Open connections can keep the old trust material for up to 15 minutes.
Keep the Gateway the only consumer of the shared resource configuration. The AWS managed permission for AWS RAM also grants ec2:CreateVpcEndpoint, so the AgentCore account could reach the backend through a resource VPC endpoint or service network of its own. A customer managed permission can’t fix this: AWS RAM rejects vpc-lattice:AssociateViaAWSService in one, and without it Gateway targets fail. Attach an SCP to the AgentCore account instead:
With this SCP, our attempts to create a resource VPC endpoint and a service network association of its own were denied, and a new Gateway target still reached READY. SCPs don’t apply to the management account, so don’t run AgentCore there. In the network account, alarm on unexpected associations with an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches the AWS CloudTrail event CreateServiceNetworkResourceAssociationBySharee.
Revoke access by deleting the Gateway targets (or the service network resource association) first, then removing the resource configuration from the share. Removing it from the share alone doesn’t remove existing associations.
Decision 6: Reach the Gateway privately, and close the public endpoint
Create the Gateway interface endpoint in the shared agent VPC with private DNS enabled, and attach an endpoint policy that lists the approved Gateways. The principal must be *, because the Gateway authenticates callers with bearer tokens. The Resource list is the control.
In our tests, a second Gateway called through the same endpoint returned JSON-RPC error -32002 Insufficient permissions, but still answered on its public endpoint.
The interface endpoint doesn’t close the Gateway’s public endpoint. Attach a resource policy that allows bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway only when aws:SourceVpce is your endpoint and denies it otherwise (the full policy is in the repository). In our tests, internet calls returned -32002 about 30 seconds after we applied it, while endpoint calls kept working. AWS notes policy changes can take up to 15 minutes.
An agent with no internet route still needs its inbound JWT. Give it a path to its identity provider’s token endpoint, such as a route to the transit gateway and a firewall rule scoped like the JWKS rule in Decision 3. Alternatively, use a private identity provider.
Validate the pattern in your environment
Before you rely on the pattern, run these checks in a non-production copy of your network account, with your own firewall. The full list of 14 checks, with how to run each and the results we saw, is in the repository, along with a log source for every hop.
- Requests come from the resource gateway – The ALB access log shows a source IP in the resource gateway range (or your firewall’s range, if it applies source NAT).
- Requests cross the firewall – Firewall flow logs show TLS flows from resource gateway addresses to the tool account on port 443.
- Replies cross the firewall – With a reply-direction drop rule in place (Decision 3), calls fail and the firewall logs to_client drops.
- The ALB and private API are token boundaries – Targets with no token, or another client’s token, get HTTP 401 and the backend isn’t invoked.
- The public Gateway endpoint is closed – With the resource policy attached, internet calls get -32002 and endpoint calls succeed.
If a check fails or the agent gets a generic error, the troubleshooting guide maps each symptom to the log that shows the cause.
Considerations
- Cost: Each VPC Lattice service network resource association carries an hourly charge plus data processing. See VPC Lattice pricing. Plan for one association per target. To see how many associations your targets create, compare the resourceAssociationArn that GetGatewayTarget returns for each target, and prefer one target per API or MCP server over many small targets.
- Traffic to public endpoints: Three calls leave the private path: the ALB’s JWKS fetch, the agent’s inbound token request, and AgentCore’s outbound OAuth token requests to each identity provider.
- Account layout and quotas: Gateway tool-call quotas apply per account as well as per gateway. Use one AgentCore account per environment, and split gateways by domain or agent group well before the limits. VPC Lattice closes idle connections, so use keepalives for long-lived MCP streams. The repository lists the other quotas.
- Scope of our tests: We used AWS Network Firewall, no source NAT, and us-east-1 only. Source NAT, multiple Regions, private identity providers, and OpenAPI limitations are covered in the other considerations.
Conclusion
When your network team owns every subnet and every flow between VPCs must pass a central firewall, place the VPC Lattice resource gateway in the network account and route its subnets through the transit gateway. The network team sets up the entry point once and adds one resource configuration per backend load balancer. Application teams keep owning only their load balancers, security groups, identity providers, and Gateway targets, and AWS WAF moves from per-tool public load balancers to the Gateway. Run the validation checks in your own environment before you rely on the pattern.

articles.title: GTA 6 sur PS5 : le PSN a flanché, mais Sony annonce un retour à la normale avant minuit — Frandroid
articles.text:
Treize ans d’attente depuis GTA V, plus de 200 Go préchargés depuis une semaine, et c’est finalement l’écran de connexion qui fait des siennes. Une partie des joueurs PS5 s’est retrouvée face à des messages d’erreur en tentant de rejoindre le PlayStation Network ce mercredi soir. Ce genre d’incident passe inaperçu un jour ordinaire. Il prend une autre dimension quand GTA 6 doit se débloquer à minuit et que toute l’Europe a les yeux rivés sur sa console.
Les signalements ont commencé à grimper vers 18 h 30 sur Downdetector, un site qui agrège les plaintes des utilisateurs, avec un pic autour de 19 h. Vers 19 h 40, la moitié des signalements portaient sur la connexion au serveur, 41 % sur des échecs de connexion et à peine 5 % sur les achats : autrement dit, le problème n’était pas de payer, mais d’entrer.
Le Black Friday est lancé sur l’univers Apple. Sur Back Market, profitez de promotions sur les iPhone, MacBook, iPad, AirPods et Apple Watch. Chaque appareil est soumis à jusqu’à 100 points de contrôle qualité et est livré avec une garantie de 12 mois. De quoi profiter de performances comparables à celles d’un produit neuf.
Sony a fini par déclarer un incident à 19 h 58 sur sa page d’état des services, évoquant des « difficultés pour lancer des jeux, des applications ou des fonctionnalités réseau ». Vers 20 h 30, la même page affichait de nouveau tous les services comme opérationnels, sans que Sony précise la cause. On suit l’évolution minute par minute dans notre direct consacré à la sortie de GTA 6.
    Pour aller plus loin
Sortie de GTA 6 : suivez le lancement du jeu en direct
            
Minuit, le vrai crash-test du PSN
Sony n’a pas officiellement relié l’incident à GTA 6, mais le calendrier parle de lui-même. Le jeu se débloque à minuit heure locale, région par région, et la Nouvelle-Zélande a ouvert le bal à midi, heure de Paris. Selon Cloudflare Radar, l’observatoire du trafic Internet de Cloudflare, les requêtes DNS vers les domaines de téléchargement de PlayStation y ont été multipliées par 15 au moment du lancement. Ces requêtes, c’est l’annuaire que consulte une console avant de contacter un serveur : quand elles explosent, c’est que des milliers de machines frappent à la même porte au même instant.
La France et l’Europe continentale, elles, basculeront toutes ensemble à minuit pile. Sans disque, même l’édition physique n’étant qu’un code dans une boîte, chaque joueur passera forcément par les serveurs de Sony. Le réseau avait d’ailleurs déjà connu des ratés pendant l’ouverture du préchargement, le 12 novembre, avec un PlayStation Store et une gestion de compte partiellement hors service. Sony a de la mémoire en la matière : la panne de 2011 avait coupé le PSN pendant 23 jours.
Que faire avant minuit
Ceux qui ont tout préchargé sont les moins exposés, même si ni Sony ni Rockstar n’ont dit si GTA 6 peut démarrer sans connexion au PSN. Les retardataires qui comptent lancer 200 Go de téléchargement ce soir prennent en revanche le plus de risques. Quelques réglages valent la peine d’être vérifiés pendant que le réseau respire, et les mises à jour de dernière minute sont relayées dans notre suivi en direct de la sortie.
- On installe la mise à jour système de la PS5 : PlayStation l’a annoncée comme obligatoire pour jouer à GTA 6.
- On active « Partage de console et jeu hors ligne » dans Paramètres, Utilisateurs et comptes, Autre. La console devient alors la machine principale du compte, ce qui permet en principe de lancer ses jeux numériques même si le PSN tousse.
- Si un cadenas reste affiché après minuit, on passe par « Restaurer les licences », comme le recommande la page d’aide officielle de PlayStation.
- Avant de tout supprimer et réinstaller, on jette un œil à la page d’état de Sony : si une alerte s’affiche, le problème ne vient pas de la console.

articles.title: Meet two Mississauga founders rethinking the way money moves | BetaKit
articles.text:
Two FinTech founders in Mississauga are taking aim at the complicated infrastructure behind international payments.
Gharsa Amin, founder and CEO of Kavodax, and Gezim Ramabaja, founder and CEO of Zpayd, are approaching the problem from different corners of the financial industry. One is using blockchain technology to speed up international transfers, while the other is building the connections that allow financial institutions to offer bill payments globally.
Both companies have tapped into Mississauga’s startup ecosystem for mentorship, industry connections, and support in bringing their products to market.
BetaKit spoke with the founders about what it takes to break into the financial industry, bring new payment technologies to market, and build a business in Mississauga.
Taking international transfers from days to minutes
When Gharsa Amin’s grandmother fell ill in Germany, she sent money from Canada to help support her. The transfer took five days, passed through multiple banking clearances, and incurred foreign exchange fees of approximately three to four percent. Her grandmother also had to visit the bank in person to access the funds.
“Having worked in digital banking, compliance, and technology, I knew there had to be a better way,” Amin said.
“You don’t necessarily need to build the next major financial institution. Sometimes the biggest opportunity is building the infrastructure that allows those institutions to do more.”
She founded Kavodax in 2025 to tackle the delays and costs of international payments, particularly for small and medium-sized businesses that regularly pay overseas suppliers and contractors.
Kavodax uses blockchain-based settlement and stablecoin technology to move money between countries. Customers fund payments through their bank accounts, and recipients receive funds in their local currency. Kavodax aims to complete transfers in under 30 minutes, avoiding some of the intermediaries involved in conventional international banking.
Amin said customers are generally less concerned with the technology itself than the cost and reliability of the service.
“We don’t lead with blockchain; we lead with the business problem,” she said. “Most business owners care about how much a payment costs, how quickly their supplier receives it, and whether they can trust the process.”
Conversations with prospective customers revealed frustration with foreign exchange fees of three to five percent, long settlement times, and difficulty tracking international transfers.
Kavodax has expanded its payment capabilities to more than 70 countries and 30 currencies. It has also secured approximately $400,000 in non-dilutive funding and $100,000 in investment. The company has turned its attention to getting businesses onto the platform, particularly those making regular payments to overseas suppliers and contractors. It’s also pursuing partnerships with other FinTech providers that could integrate Kavodax’s technology into their own services.
Kavodax has secured registrations with FINTRAC and the Bank of Canada, and is pursuing further security and compliance certifications as it expands its banking relationships.
Amin also sought help with the business side of Kavodax. She participated in IDEA Mississauga’s 2025 EmpowHER Tech Launchpad, a 12-week accelerator delivered in partnership with York University’s YSpace, that helps women-led tech companies grow through mentorship, business training, and investor-readiness support.
The program helped sharpen Kavodax’s customer focus, validate market demand, and identify where to concentrate its efforts. “One of my biggest takeaways was that commercialization cannot wait until product development is finished,” Amin added.
Mississauga’s international business community has also helped Amin better understand her prospective customers. Companies that rely on overseas suppliers face precisely the payment problems Kavodax is trying to address.
Kavodax’s next priorities include increasing transaction volumes, strengthening banking partnerships, and closing a $2-million financing round.
“Longer term, our ambition is to help businesses save billions in unnecessary international payment costs and expand access to financial services for 500,000 people,” Amin said. “We want to build globally relevant financial infrastructure right here in Canada.”
A borderless bill payment network
Gezim Ramabaja was just 18 when he opened his first business: a coffee shop in his native Kosovo. By the time he found his way into FinTech, he had also run a restaurant and a construction company in Canada.
It was through those latter businesses that Ramabaja stumbled across the problem that would inspire Zpayd. Many of his employees were students who relied on their parents for help paying bills. For international students in particular, arranging payments from overseas could involve technical difficulties and high fees.
“While the financial world had become increasingly connected, bill payment remained fragmented,” he said. “Payment networks, billers, and financial institutions operated largely within their own domestic ecosystems, making it difficult to pay bills across borders or access billers outside a particular country.”
He began developing Zpayd in 2021 with the goal of helping people pay bills across borders.
“I knew there had to be a better way.”
Gharsa Amin,
Kavodax
Zpayd initially offered the service directly to consumers, and finding interest wasn’t the problem. At one point, Zpayd was attracting as many as 20 sign-ups a day, and the demands of onboarding and supporting individual customers were beginning to stretch the business.
At the Money20/20 FinTech conference in Las Vegas, Ramabaja met executives who suggested offering Zpayd’s services directly to their companies. Through a single institutional relationship, Zpayd could potentially reach thousands of existing customers.
“This changed our business model but not our underlying vision,” Ramabaja said.
Today, Zpayd provides the infrastructure that allows financial institutions to offer domestic and international bill payments through their existing services. A customer could, for instance, pay a utility bill overseas through a participating payment provider, with Zpayd handling the connections to the local biller and payment network behind the scenes.
The company also supports creditor payments and loan disbursements. A lender could use Zpayd to send money directly to a creditor, for example, without relying on cheques or manual processing.
But getting banks and other financial institutions to adopt new technology is no small undertaking. Ramabaja said prospective partners have lengthy procurement processes and want assurances around security, compliance, reporting, and settlement.
“We’ve learned that credibility in this industry is built through execution,” Ramabaja said. “You have to demonstrate reliability, security, and consistency before institutions are comfortable making you part of their financial infrastructure.”
Ramabaja has been involved with IDEA Mississauga since 2023 and is an alumnus of ICUBE, the startup incubator at the University of Toronto Mississauga. He credits both organizations with helping him connect with mentors, industry professionals, and other entrepreneurs during Zpayd’s development.
Ramabaja also sees Mississauga’s proximity to Toronto’s financial sector as an advantage for a company seeking relationships with banks and payment providers.
“I also think it’s important to recognize that successful technology companies don’t need to be built exclusively in traditional technology hubs,” he said. “Mississauga has the talent, business community, and resources to support companies developing solutions for global markets.”
Ramabaja is now looking at opportunities to expand Zpayd’s services into new markets and payment categories, including loan repayments and emerging payment methods such as stablecoins. His longer-term goal is to build a global network that financial institutions can use to offer bill payment services, wherever their customers need them.
“You don’t necessarily need to build the next major financial institution,” he said. “Sometimes the biggest opportunity is building the infrastructure that allows those institutions to do more.”
PRESENTED BY
Mississauga’s startup ecosystem offers opportunities to access mentorship, develop industry connections, and work through the challenges of commercialization.

articles.title: Actualiza ya tu PS5 o 'GTA 6' no arrancará, confirma Sony
articles.text:
GTA 6 ya está llegando a los países que cruzaron la barrera de la medianoche y ya transitan el tan anhelado 19 de noviembre. Para muchos otros, todavía faltan algunas horas para que puedan poner sus manos sobre el anhelado juego de Rockstar Games, cuyas primeras reseñas son tan positivas como se esperaba (y tal vez más). Pero mucho ojo si planeas jugarlo desde una PS5, pues antes de ejecutarlo tendrás que instalar sí o sí una actualización de sistema.
Sony ha lanzado un parche de software para la PS5 que es obligatorio si quieres acceder a GTA 6. Se trata de la actualización de firmware 26.07-14.23.00, que pesa casi 1,3 GB. La misma inició su despliegue en la mañana de ayer. No obstante, no fue hasta bien entrada la madrugada europea de hoy que se confirmó que su instalación era un requisito ineludible para acceder a Grand Theft Auto VI.
Los motivos oficiales detrás de la actualización de la PS5 antes del debut de GTA 6 apuntan solamente a la resolución de fallos de seguridad. Se especula con que Sony en realidad está tratando de cerrar cualquier puerta a posibles intentos de hackear el software de la consola y de piratear lo nuevo de Rockstar Games.
Si quieres jugar GTA 6, actualiza tu PS5 al firmware 14.23
La PS5 se ha convertido en noticia últimamente por los avances en jailbreaking que se han dado con el apoyo de IA generativa. En los últimos días, un hacker presumió de supuestamente dumpear el binario de un juego en una consola usando la versión 14.22 del firmware. ¿Esto qué significa? Que aparentemente pudo extraer los archivos originales de un videojuego, un paso crucial para piratearlo. Si bien no se brindaron más precisiones sobre la veracidad del caso, es lógico pensar que Sony ha tomado recaudos para evitar sorpresas desagradables con GTA 6.
Pese a la falta de detalles, se cree que Sony está cortando el acceso a PlayStation Network a las PS5 con firmware anterior a 14.23. De modo que si quieres acceder a GTA 6, no tienes otra alternativa más que instalar la actualización en cuestión en tu consola.
"Sony Interactive ha lanzado una actualización del software del sistema de PS5 que es necesaria para jugar a Grand Theft Auto VI. Los jugadores deben descargar esta actualización antes de la medianoche del 19 de noviembre para estar listos para jugar el día del lanzamiento", dice el escueto mensaje compartido en X (Twitter) a través de un perfil de soporte. La cuenta principal de PlayStation lo republicó con un emoji de ojos para llamar la atención de cualquier jugador desprevenido.
Si bien en buena parte de Occidente todavía restan algunas horas para que GTA 6 llegue a manos de los jugadores, muchos han optado por el viejo "truco de Nueva Zelanda" para reducir al mínimo posible la brecha de disponibilidad. Se espera que el 19 de noviembre tenga una de las tasas de ausentismo laboral más altas de la historia reciente. Un dato acorde con el lanzamiento más importante alguna vez visto en la industria de los videojuegos.

articles.title: Waymo pulls cars off U.S. highways following California ban
articles.text:
Autonomous driving company Waymo has temporarily pulled all its driverless cars from U.S. freeways following a ban from California.
The California Department of Motor Vehicles ordered the driverless vehicles to stop driving on all of the state’s freeways on Nov. 11, citing what it called an “imminent hazard to public safety.”
In a statement provided to the New York Times, the department cited an incident in which three Waymo vehicles entered a construction closure on Highway 101, and another in which the vehicles tried to get around a police blockade on Interstate 280 in San Francisco.
“Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state,” said Waymo spokesperson Chris Pappas. “In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance.”
The DMV says that the restrictions in California will remain in place until the company makes “effective corrective actions” to fix the problem.
Now, this ban comes just as Waymo cars are starting to hit Toronto streets, with a planned launch for 2028. Hopefully Waymo can improve its highway performance before vehicles hit the busiest highways in North America.
From my perspective, this is not a good look for the self-driving automotive industry. If one of the industry’s leaders is scaling back operations after multiple dangerous incidents, then other companies could have trouble gaining trust with local authorities, the public, and the federal government. However, for now, it is only a temporary ban.
Source: The New York Times

articles.title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
articles.text:
The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
MIT Technology Review’s highly subjective take on the latest buzz about AI
Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack.
You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey. You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.
