articles.title: SSDs, laptops, and phones may get cheaper as consumer NAND spot pricing drops 20% — Bank of America expects contract price drops, report cites oversupply in consumer market amid declining demand and growing Chinese competition
articles.text:
SSDs, laptops, and phones may get cheaper as consumer NAND spot pricing drops 20% — Bank of America expects contract price drops, report cites oversupply in consumer market amid declining demand and growing Chinese competition
A small but welcome potential reprieve for PC builders and consumers.
Solid-state drives, phones, laptops, and tablets have all gotten substantially pricier in the last couple of years. Beyond the stratospheric prices of DDR5 memory, prospective PC builders and consumer electronics buyers have had to deal with upcharges on SSDs of all sizes thanks to the AI boom. That may be changing soon, as spot pricing for consumer NAND chips is reportedly dropping, according to a new report from Seoul Economic Daily (SED).
The report observes a 20% drop in spot pricing for NAND chips over just the last month. Its conclusions are bolstered by information from a Bank of America note from Nov. 13, wherein industry sources tell that institution that NAND is due for a market correction.
SED says that according to that note, 512 Gb NAND wafers saw a 32% drop to $14.30 apiece on the spot market, while 1 Tb wafers fell 19% to $24.90. SED quotes another industry source that says: "NAND cannot sustain the steep price gains seen so far."
Those decreases may be hard to square in a time when enterprise SSDs are getting pricier by the day, but SED notes that the rise in phone and PC prices has led customers to delay upgrades, resulting in a 20% year-on-year decline in shipments for phones alone and making for the lowest third-quarter volumes in 14 years. Meanwhile, PC shipments have also fallen 22.5% year-on-year, according to a Gartner report.
In the face of those consumer decisions, device makers are letting their existing stock drain out and are presumably stocked with NAND chips for the short term, thus resulting in lower prices for new fab shipments on the short-term spot market.
Another factor in the consumer NAND market is that not all flash is equal. Both RAM and NAND makers have been redirecting their chip output to serve the ongoing AI boom, converting their consumer-grade production lines to make higher-spec silicon. Memory factories have been converting DDR5 capacity to HBM at a steady pace, as parts of the process are shared across both types.
But according to the Bank of America note that SED cites, things are different in the NAND world. High-density flash now sits at around 300 layers, and its production requires substantially different tooling compared to the lower-grade silicon deemed suitable for us mere mortals. So the continuing growth in NAND demand from AI data centers may not translate directly into reduced consumer supply.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Beyond those factors, added supply from Chinese NAND maker YMTC is creating additional downward price pressure in the NAND market. SED notes that YMTC has taken a 14% chunk from major players in the NAND market in the second quarter of this year alone.
On net, these forces could result in a bit of relief for consumer tech. SED says Bank of America expects consumer NAND prices for PCs and smartphones to fall 5% to 10% on the longer-term contract market in the first quarter of 2027, while enterprise NAND contract prices are expected to hold more or less steady.
Whether those declines translate to lower prices for finished devices and components like SSDs will remain to be seen, and products with those chips inside will require some time to reach the market. But in the ongoing AI supply crunch, any potential relief is worth celebrating.
Download the Tom's Hardware app for up-to-the-minute updates on iOS and Android. Also follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.
- M Lopez 20% is peanuts. The price needs to drop entirely by 50% at a minimum for consumers to begin to feel relief.
Prices have been sitting at an inflated high for the last year now. Look at the prices of GPUs versus MSRP and that should give you a tiny indication of how completely screwing the pricing is today. Reply
- jabliese M Lopez said:20% is peanuts. The price needs to drop entirely by 50% at a minimum for consumers to begin to feel relief.Hmm. That makes a 20% drop 40% of your total goal of 50%. Does not sound like peanuts to me. Reply
- usertests If there's a 20% drop, there could be more coming. The supply/demand game is on.
DDR6 looks crazy, btw:
https://videocardz.com/newz/jedec-announces-ddr6-memory-modules-are-44-shorter-than-ddr5-speeds-up-to-14-4-gt-s Reply
- thestryker It's not surprising that NAND would see the first reversal in demand. Each server brought online needs fewer NAND packages than any other type of memory. There's also many different NAND performance levels which means the consumer reduction is probably hurting since not all NAND can go in enterprise parts unlike DDR5.
Specifically regarding the article:
Memory factories have been converting DDR5 capacity to HBM at a steady pace, as parts of the process are shared across both types. There is no publicly available evidence to backup this statement so it probably shouldn't be in an article here. A lot of people certainly seem to think that's the case, but the available information points towards HBM capacity being expanded while DDR5 capacity stagnated. Earlier this year DDR5 was more profitable than HBM on a per bit basis so it stands to reason they absolutely would not be cutting it at all. Reply

articles.title: British hackers face prison for GTA 6 data breach and crypto thefts | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Two British hackers are facing lengthy prison sentences for separate hacks as part of their roles in long-running, prolific cybercriminal hacking groups. The two are accused of hacks that stole millions of dollars in cryptocurrency and leaked pre-release footage from Grand Theft Auto VI.
Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, Scotland, has been sentenced to six years by a U.S. court after he was extradited to the United States in 2025. Buchanan was accused of stealing at least $11 million in cryptocurrency from dozens of companies as part of a phishing scheme. The attacks would impersonate IT helpdesks and call up unsuspecting employees and trick them into giving over their credentials, which the hackers would use to break in and steal cryptocurrency.
Meanwhile, Arion Kurtaj, 21, from Oxford, England, has pleaded guilty to several cyberattacks that he carried out while a teenager. One hack included the theft of data and extortion of Rockstar Games, the maker of Grand Theft Auto VI, which was released Wednesday after several delays.
Kurtaj was previously ordered by a U.K. court to be detained indefinitely after deeming him unable to stand trial due to his autism diagnosis and his perceived high hacking risk to the public. But U.K. authorities, tasked with charging Kurtaj with cybercrime offenses, confirmed Monday that he had admitted to several hacks, including leaking footage of the long-awaited video game, and would subsequently face a public trial.
U.K. authorities confirmed earlier reporting that Kurtaj hacked several companies, including while he was confined to a hotel amid police protection from rival criminal gangs. The authorities said Kurtaj used an Amazon Fire TV stick to hack the companies, which breached his bail conditions.
Both Buchanan and Kurtaj were members of overlapping cybercriminal groups, dubbed 0ktapus, Lapsus$, and later Scattered Spider. These prolific hacking gangs mostly consist of teenagers and young male adults, lending to the term “advanced persistent teenagers,” whose focus and motivations were to steal as much money as possible through various cyberattacks.
Over the years, the hackers were collectively responsible for hundreds of cyberattacks targeting big companies, including Coinbase, DoorDash, Mailchimp, and Nvidia.
By late 2024, both U.K. and U.S. authorities say they had indicted five of the hackers whom they believed were key members of the hacking groups, including Buchanan. The U.S. Department of Justice said this week that Buchanan is the fifth and final defendant to be sentenced in this case.

articles.title: Java hit by major security flaw — here's what we know about Java4Shell so far
articles.text:
Java hit by major security flaw — here's what we know about Java4Shell so far
Java4Shell enables data exfiltration and remote code execution
- Researchers disclosed a critical OpenJDK memory-corruption flaw that could enable information disclosure or remote code execution
- The vulnerability affects multiple Java distributions and several widely used enterprise applications
- Oracle released patches for the issue, and organizations are urged to update immediately or apply temporary mitigations
Security researchers discovered a critical vulnerability in the Java runtime, potentially allowing malicious actors to reveal sensitive information or run malicious code remotely.
Researcher Quang Long from Calif disclosed finding a memory corruption flaw in OpenJDK, the open-source implementation of the Java platform, which he dubbed Java4Shell. OpenJDK provides the tools users need to run Java apps, so any vulnerabilities found there could impact a wide range of software built on Java.
“Java is the world's third most popular programming language, powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies,” he said. “It is the beating heart of the modern economy. Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems.”
A memory corruption flaw happens when software incorrectly writes to, or modifies, areas of a computer’s memory, allowing attackers to overwrite data, access sensitive information, or run malicious code. In this case, the flaw affects OpenJDK’s Base64, a decoding functionality that converts binary data (images, files) into text using a set of 64 characters, making it easier to transmit or store data in text-based systems.
Enterprise apps at risk
The bug is now tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and, according to the National Vulnerability Database (NVD), has a severity score of 8.1/10 (high). Calif ranks it 9.2/10 (critical). “Difficult to exploit vulnerability allows unauthenticated attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition,” NVD says in its advisory. “Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition.”
OpenJDK versions 17.0.6 and later were said to be affected, as well as all Java distributions built from that code. That includes Oracle Java SE, Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, and Red Hat OpenJDK.
It also means that some of the applications running on these distributions could be exploitable as well. So far, researchers have tested Jenkins, Atlassian Jira, Confluence, and Keycloak, and confirmed them to be vulnerable in some versions, but the list is by no means extensive.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
For Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, the researcher managed to perform unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). For Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, he managed to pull off authenticated RCE.
If you’re not using any of the abovementioned products, that doesn’t mean the vulnerability should be ignored. Calif managed to trigger the memory corruption vulnerability with just 64 “A” characters followed by a single equals sign (=). On older OpenJDK 17 versions, 128 “A” characters were necessary to trigger the bug. Honestly, if someone was screaming at me like that, I would probably be triggered, as well. It’s also worth mentioning that there is no universal exploit for Java4Shell - attackers must find a way in for each individual app.
How to fix Java4Shell
It was added that the bug affects only hardware-accelerated decoding functions used on some x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 instructions.
Luong said he was inspired to look for a Java bug after the PHP2Shell discovery. Just as then, he used OpenAI’s Codex AI coding assistant to find the bug, and it only took him an hour and some $200 in tokens. AI agents also assisted with building application-specific exploitation chains, it was said.
Oracle patched CVE-2026-114938 on November 17, when it released its November Critical Security Patch Update. Users are advised to install that update without delay, but those that cannot do that are advised to disable hardware-accelerated Base64 functionality by launching OpenJDK with the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics option.
They can also use -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512 instructions if they’re running Java on x86-64 systems. Still, these are considered workarounds and temporary mitigations and are, by no means, a permanent solution to Java4Shell.

articles.title: Weitreichende Systemausfälle: Warum KI nur indirekt das Problem sein könnte
articles.text:
Weitreichende Systemausfälle: Warum KI nur indirekt das Problem sein könnte
In den vergangenen Tagen legte eine Reihe schwerer Ausfälle mehrere kritische Systeme in den USA lahm. Die Auswirkungen gingen aber weit über die Vereinigten Staaten hinaus. Teilweise waren Nutzer:innen weltweit betroffen. Laut einem Bericht der Washington Sun, der sich auf drei anonyme Quellen beruft, wurden Abgeordnete des US-Kongresses inzwischen über die Gründe informiert. Demnach seien die Ausfälle darauf zurückzuführen, dass mithilfe von KI entdeckte Schwachstellen geschlossen werden sollten.
Nutzer:innen weltweit von Ausfall betroffen
Ein Beispiel ist die Störung von Outlook. Laut Microsoft wurde diese aus einem Zusammenspiel mehrerer Faktoren ausgelöst. Am Abend des 12. Novembers hätten auf dem Höhepunkt der Störung mehr als 80 Prozent der zuständigen Rechner nicht mehr reagiert. Grund war eine im Juli aufgespielte Software-Änderung an einer zentralen digitalen Eingangstür für den Datenverkehr von Microsoft 365, die mehr als drei Monate unauffällig lief. Die Tests hätten den Fehler nicht angezeigt, da sie vorwiegend ältere Technik nutzten. Er trat aber vor allem auf neueren Servern auf.
Zwei zusätzliche Belastungen ließen den Fehler am vergangenen Donnerstag zur US-Hauptnutzungszeit ausbrechen. Einerseits hatte Microsoft kurz zuvor Teams planmäßig auf dieselbe Hauptinfrastruktur umgeschaltet, was den Datenverkehr erhöhte. Andererseits fielen wegen eines anderen Problems knapp 14 Prozent der Server-Kapazitäten vorübergehend aus. Als die ersten Server unter der Last ausfielen, wurden Anfragen automatisch auf die verbliebenen Rechner umgeleitet. Das löste denselben Fehler auch dort aus. Dieser Dominoeffekt erfasste innerhalb von unter zwei Stunden fast das gesamte System.
KI zwingt veraltete Systeme in die Knie
Microsoft war nicht das einzige Unternehmen mit einem solchen Ausfall. Auch Wells Fargo, die Bank of America und der gesamte US-Flugverkehr waren betroffen. Die Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) verhängte am Freitagabend ein landesweites Startverbot. Grund dafür war eine Störung der Radar- und Telekommunikation der Flugsicherung. Laut dem Wall Street Journal fielen mehr als 20.000 Flüge aus. Markwayne Mullin, Minister für Innere Sicherheit, erklärte am Dienstag gegenüber CNBC, er sei zu 98 Prozent überzeugt, dass hinter den Störungen keine Cyberangriffe steckten.
Öffentlich wollten die betroffenen Unternehmen und Behörden die KI-bezogene Software-Problematik aber nicht als Ursache bestätigen. Das gilt unter anderem für die FAA. Auch Microsoft führte die Störung bei Outlook offiziell auf einen technischen Defekt zurück. Die NSA, die ebenfalls betroffen war, räumte am Dienstag ein, dass es in einigen ihrer Netzwerke zu einer Beeinträchtigung infolge geplanter Wartungsarbeiten gekommen sei, wie Politico berichtete. In der öffentlichen Erklärung der Behörde wurden KI-generierte Patches ebenfalls nicht als Ursache genannt.
Weitere Ausfälle sind wahrscheinlich
Laut Washington Sun installieren Unternehmen, Behörden und Finanzinstitute eilig Software-Patches, nachdem KI-Modelle potenziell schwerwiegende Schwachstellen in ihren Systemen aufgedeckt haben. Dies habe einige Systeme überlastet und Ausfälle ausgelöst. „Diese Modelle identifizieren massive Schwachstellen, und das erhöht die Dringlichkeit, sofort Patches zu installieren“, erklärte ein über die Angelegenheit informierter Kongressbeamter gegenüber der Washington Sun. „Sie versuchen, eine Vielzahl von Patches auf einmal durchzusetzen – mehr, als das System bewältigen kann.“
Der Einsatz von KI zur Aufdeckung von Schwachstellen stellt Unternehmen und Behörden vor eine neue Herausforderung. Die Verantwortlichen müssen diese schnell beheben – zumal Angreifer:innen möglicherweise ähnlich leistungsfähige KI nutzen. Auch Mullin vermutet, dass neue Technologien in veralteten Computersystemen unerwartete Probleme verursachen könnten. „Sie setzen neue Technologien auf wirklich alte Computersysteme ein, und das scheint das System einfach zu überfordern“, sagte er gegenüber CNBC. „Wir werden noch mehr davon sehen, wenn neue Technologien eingeführt werden.“

articles.title: Gemini-Nutzer können jetzt KI-Training untersagen, aber Verlauf behalten
articles.text:
Mehr Datenschutz bei Gemini: Nutzer können jetzt KI-Training untersagen, aber Verlauf behalten
Gemini-Nutzer:innen, die ihre Chats länger behalten wollten, stimmten damit bisher auch zu, dass Google diese Inhalte zum Training seiner KI-Modelle nutzt. Die entsprechende Einstellung ließ sich unter dem Menüpunkt „Aktivitäten speichern“ aktivieren.
Googles Datenschutz-Update bei Gemini
Wer dem KI-Training nicht zustimmen wollte, konnte die eigenen Chats nicht länger als 72 Stunden speichern lassen. Diese Zeit nahm sich Google für Antworten und „Sicherheitsmaßnahmen in Gemini“. Mit einem Update der Datenschutzeinstellungen der Gemini-App ändert Google diese Vorgehensweise jetzt grundlegend.
Auf der einen Seite sollen temporäre Chats und Chats mit deaktiviertem Verlauf künftig statt 72 Stunden etwa zwei Monate lang im Konto der Nutzer:innen gespeichert bleiben. Google erklärt das in seinem aktualisierten Privacy-Hub mit dem Schutz von Nutzer:innen und Öffentlichkeit sowie der Möglichkeit, zu antworten und Feedback zu verarbeiten.
Die längere Speicherzeit soll etwa sicherstellen, dass die Chats „im Falle eines Systemausfalls verfügbar sind“. Zudem soll Gemini sie bei Antworten als Kontext verwenden können. Warum dafür eine deutliche Ausweitung der Speicherzeit notwendig sein soll, erklärt Google nicht.
Datennutzung für KI-Training untersagen
Dafür schließt Google in seinen aktualisierten Datenschutzeinstellungen jetzt aus, temporäre Chats oder jene mit deaktiviertem Verlauf automatisch für das Training seiner KI-Modelle zu verwenden. Geben Nutzer:innen allerdings Feedback, kann Google die Chats der vergangenen 24 Stunden verwenden, um die Gemini-App entsprechend zu verbessern.
Dabei greift das Unternehmen nicht nur auf in den Chats enthaltenen Text, sondern auch auf mögliche Uploads oder Daten aus verbundenen Apps zu. Ähnliches gilt für die Speicherfunktion bei aktiviertem Verlauf. Die gespeicherten Chats enthalten dann etwa auch Audioaufnahmen, Gemini-Live-Videos und Bildschirmfreigaben, Prompts, Tasks und Toolaufrufe sowie Daten von besuchten Websites.
Außerdem geht es auch um den ungefähren Ort des für die KI-Chats genutzten Geräts, die IP‑Adresse sowie die im Google-Konto hinterlegten Privat- und Arbeitsadressen. Bei eingeschalteter History-Funktion (Verlauf) speichert Google die Daten bis zu 18 Monate. Mit der Aktualisierung ermöglicht es Google Nutzer:innen jetzt, selbst zu entscheiden, ob sie diese Daten für das KI-Training bereitstellen wollen oder nicht.
ChatGPT und Claude speichern kürzer
Die Konkurrenz setzt übrigens auf deutlich kürzere Speicherzeiträume, wie Techcrunch berichtet. Bei OpenAI werden temporäre Chats in ChatGPT für bis zu 30 Tage gespeichert. Denselben Zeitraum gibt auch Anthropic für Inkognito-Chats bei Claude an. Es ist allerdings möglich, dass beide KI-Anbieter einige Daten aus rechtlichen Gründen länger aufbewahren, etwa um Verstöße von Richtlinien zu untersuchen.

The MSI Crosshair sports a 16-inch IPS display with a sharp QHD resolution that's powered by an Nvidia RTX 5060 graphics card with 8GB of fast VRAM. Other specs include a 20-core Intel Core Ultra 7 255HX processor, 16GB of memory, and a 1TB SSD. Windows 11 operating system comes preinstalled.
MSI's Crosshair 16 comes with an 80 Wh lithium-polymer battery for plenty of power and uptime when you're not next to a mains socket, although for the best gaming performance, the laptop will always run best when connected to mains power. This is definitely a laptop designed for gamers, with a bright 4-zone RGB backlit keyboard, complete with 99-key anti-ghost rollover.
For connectivity, the Crosshair comes complete with Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3, and for external ports, there are 2x USB 3.0/3.1 Gen1 ports, 3x USB 3.1 Gen2 ports, and USB-C Power Delivery (PD). An HDMI port for video connectivity and a 3.5mm audio port.

articles.title: The MeOut Summit 2026 ultimate guide: Networking, side events and more | EU-Startups
articles.text:
On 25–26 November, Budapest will welcome the first edition of The MeOut Summit 2026, bringing together over 1,000 founders, investors, corporate innovators, and ecosystem builders for two days of meaningful connections and new opportunities.
Organised by MeOut Group in partnership with EU-Startups, the Summit will take place at Akvárium Budapest, right in the heart of the Hungarian capital.
With just days to go, here’s everything you need to know about networking opportunities, exciting side events, and the practical details to make the most of your Summit experience!
Networking app is live
One of the best ways to make the most of The MeOut Summit is to start connecting before you even arrive.
Our official networking app is now live, allowing registered attendees to discover fellow participants, explore profiles, exchange messages, and schedule valuable one-on-one meetings in advance.
Whether you’re looking to meet potential investors, discover promising startups, find future business partners, or connect with ecosystem leaders, the app will help you identify the right people and make every conversation count.
Already have your ticket? Check your inbox for instructions on accessing the app. We recommend completing your profile and starting to book meetings ahead of the Summit, so you can arrive in Budapest with valuable conversations already on your calendar.
Networking opportunities around every corner
At The MeOut Summit, some of the most valuable conversations will happen beyond the stages. Throughout both days, you’ll find plenty of opportunities to connect with fellow attendees, whether through pre-arranged meetings or spontaneous introductions over coffee.
To make networking as easy as possible, the venue will feature several dedicated meeting spaces:
- Meeting Room: Numbered tables for scheduled one-on-one meetings.
- Networking Area: A central space to meet participating organisations, ecosystem representatives, and fellow attendees.
- Lounge Room: A relaxed setting with comfortable sofas and tables for more informal conversations.
- Terrace: Additional space for casual meetings and networking.
These locations will also be available to select when arranging meetings through the Summit app.
Side events you not to miss
The MeOut Summit experience goes beyond the main programme. A selection of side events will bring the startup community together in more informal settings, offering even more opportunities to meet, connect, and exchange ideas.
Here are some side events worth adding to your calendar:
Tuesday, 24 November | 17:30–20:00
Budapest Connect (3rd Edition)
Arriving a day early? Kick off your Summit experience at Budapest Connect, hosted by Pronto Ventures. Taking place at the Akvárium Terrace, this informal gathering will bring together founders, investors, operators, and startup enthusiasts. No pitches, no panels, just meaningful conversations and a great opportunity to start building connections before the Summit officially begins.
Wednesday, 25 November | 07:30–08:30
MeOut Summit Warm-up Run
Start your Summit day with fresh air, movement, and new connections! Organised with Startup Hungary Running Club and DSZA Legal, this relaxed morning run along the Danube welcomes participants of all levels. Enjoy an easy pace, friendly conversations, and coffee and pastries afterwards.
Wednesday, 25 November | 17:30–20:30
Official Networking Drinks by MeOut Summit
After an exciting first day, the conversations continue at the Akvárium Terrace! Join founders, investors, speakers, and fellow attendees for the official networking drinks. It’s the perfect opportunity to reconnect with people you’ve met throughout the day, make new introductions, and enjoy a relaxed evening with the startup community.
Please note: Some side events require separate registration, so make sure to check the details and secure your spot in advance.
Where to find us
Everything is almost ready to welcome you to Budapest! Here are the essential details to help you plan your visit:
- Venue: Akvárium Klub, Erzsébet tér 12, 1051 Budapest, Hungary
- Dates: Wednesday, 25 November and Thursday, 26 November 2026
- Programme start: 10:00, with networking opportunities throughout the day
- Getting there: Akvárium is located just steps away from Deák Ferenc tér, where metro lines M1, M2, and M3 intersect.
- Registration: Upon arrival, head to the registration area at the main entrance to check in and collect your badge.
Before arriving, don’t forget to check your emails for event updates, activate your networking app, schedule your meetings, and explore the side events you’d like to attend.
See you in Budapest
With The MeOut Summit 2026 just around the corner, now is the perfect time to start planning your networking experience. Make sure your app profile is ready, your meetings are booked, and your favourite side events are on your calendar.
Whether you’re hoping to meet your next investor, discover a future business partner, or simply connect with inspiring people from across Europe’s startup ecosystem, we look forward to welcoming you on 25–26 November at Akvárium Budapest!
Still haven’t secured your spot? Get you tickets here.

articles.title: Console portable PC : Lenovo préparerait une Legion Go Beam pour faire oublier ses prix fous — Frandroid
articles.text:
Payer une console portable plus de 3 000 euros, c’est désormais possible, et il ne s’agit pas d’une édition collector plaquée or. C’est le prix affiché par Lenovo France pour la Legion Go 2 en version 2 To, une machine dont l’entrée de gamme démarrait à 999 euros au lancement. Pendant que la mémoire vive part alimenter les centres de données de l’IA, la marque chinoise semble préparer une sortie de secours. Les premières images viennent de fuiter, et elles ressemblent furieusement à une console qui a fait des économies.
L’appareil s’appellerait Legion Go Beam, selon Windows Latest, qui en a obtenu trois clichés en exclusivité et les a relayés sur X. On y voit une coque blanche à liserés vert citron (très Xbox), des sticks à anneaux verts et des haut-parleurs tournés vers l’avant au bas de chaque poignée.
À l’arrière, on trouve des gâchettes classiques, deux boutons baptisés Y1 et Y2 et une large grille d’aération. Le site n’a obtenu ni fiche technique, ni prix, ni système d’exploitation. Lenovo n’a rien confirmé.
Sécurisez vos achats durant Black Friday avec la meilleure offre de l’année. Dénichez les bonnes affaires, Bitdefender s’occupe des arnaques.
Une Legion Go S repeinte, avec moins d’options
De face, la Beam ressemble beaucoup à la Legion Go S sortie en 2025, une console à manettes intégrées proposée sous Windows 11 ou SteamOS. Il lui manque toutefois le petit pavé tactile placé sous le stick droit, celui qui sert de souris pour naviguer dans le bureau Windows. Elle n’aurait aussi qu’un port USB-C sur la tranche supérieure, là où la Go S en a deux, ce qui complique la recharge quand un accessoire est branché.
Selon Windows Latest, les manettes ne se détachent pas. Exit donc le mode souris pour les jeux de tir et la béquille, deux marqueurs de la gamme Legion Go.
Le détail le plus parlant reste l’écran, entouré de bordures assez épaisses pour loger un logo Legion en dessous. Pour Abhijith M B, auteur de la fuite, ces bordures sont « l’indice qui trahit tout » : Lenovo rabote les coûts. Il faut dire que le prix de la Legion Go 2 est devenu délirant.
Lenovo n’est pas seul à subir ce que les joueurs appellent le « RAMageddon », la flambée des prix de la mémoire et du stockage aspirés par l’IA. Valve a relevé le prix de ses Steam Deck OLED. Ayaneo a même suspendu les précommandes de sa Next 2 en mars, estimant que continuer à la vendre n’était « plus tenable », avant de les rouvrir à un tarif nettement plus élevé. Une Legion Go sans fioritures viserait donc le joueur qui veut emporter sa bibliothèque Steam sans payer le prix d’un PC portable gamer.
Le problème, c’est que l’essentiel manque encore. On ignore la puce, la quantité de mémoire vive (le composant qui fait justement grimper la facture) et la nature de l’écran, OLED ou LCD. Le système reste aussi un mystère. SteamOS, le système de Valve basé sur Linux, est pensé pour la manette et souvent plus fluide, mais certains jeux en ligne protégés par un anti-triche refusent d’y tourner. Windows 11 lance à peu près tout, au prix d’une interface encore peu adaptée aux petits écrans, même si Microsoft affirme l’améliorer avec son mode Xbox.
Lenovo tiendra sa conférence Tech World au CES 2027 le 6 janvier à la Sphere de Las Vegas, soit à 2 h du matin le 7 janvier à Paris. La marque n’a pas évoqué le jeu vidéo à cette occasion, donc rien ne garantit que la Beam y soit présentée.

articles.title: The Download: AI learns to smell and hydropower struggles
articles.text:
The Download: AI learns to smell and hydropower struggles
Plus: The wave of outages has reached the US government and Apple.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”
Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents. But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases. Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver.
How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us?
—Amit Katwala
Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.
Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region's two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure.
Find out how climate change is threatening a vital source of renewable power.
—Casey Crownhart
MIT Technology Review Narrated: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping move power efficiently across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.
As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, plans are emerging to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses. The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 The wave of outages has reached the US government and Apple
The agency’s classified communications network has gone down. (CNN)
+ An update disrupted Apple Music, App Store, and AppleCare. (AP)
+ The issues join a recent flood of outages at critical services. (CNBC)
+ Marco Rubio says they’re unrelated and not hostile acts. (Guardian)
+ But AI is accelerating the discovery of vulnerabilities. (Vox)
+ And making online crimes easier. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Measles is officially endemic again in the US
Scientists blame persistent gaps in vaccination coverage. (Guardian)
+ This year’s outbreak is the deadliest since 1991. (Nature)
+ Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status. (DW)
+ Other infections could be next. (MIT Technology Review)
3 Only nine countries have backed COP31’s AI climate pledge
The voluntary pledge doesn’t include binding targets. (Reuters $)
+ Plans for carbon removal tech have divided COP31. (New Scientist $)
+ For all its flaws, the annual climate meeting still matters. (Axios)
+ What to know about this year’s talks. (MIT Technology Review)
4 Nvidia has delivered blowout results and rejected Huang’s return
Revenue more than doubled amid booming AI chip sales. (Axios)
+ Nvidia has stopped shipments of H200 chips to China. (Gizmodo)
+ China has threatened countermeasures over new chip curbs. (Reuters $)
5 More than a third of Gen-Z relies on AI for friendship
Those who do have higher odds of loneliness. (Wired $)
6 Ukraine says Starshield speed limits remain in occupied territory
Zelenskyy said the restrictions hamper air defences. (CNBC)
7 San Diego has dumped Flock cameras and smart streetlights
It’s shutting down more than 500 surveillance cameras. (Ars Technica)
+ What Flock’s defenders are missing. (MIT Technology Review)
8 Waymo has pulled its driverless taxis from US freeways
The move comes after California banned freeway trips. (NBC News)
9 Lakes are becoming strangely synchronized
Scientists warn this could lead to ecological collapses. (404 Media)
10 “Human” has won the Cambridge Dictionary’s word of the year
The dictionary says the word has gained importance in the AI age. (BBC)
Quote of the day
“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”
—Donald Trump shrugs off a week of outages that grounded flights, locked customers out of their banks, and knocked out an NSA network, NPR reports.
One more thing
What’s next for IVF
IVF has brought millions of babies into the world over the last four decades. But the process can still be slow, painful, and expensive—and far from guaranteed to work. Now, a wave of new technologies aims to change that.
Researchers are using AI to identify promising sperm and embryos, developing robotic systems that could automate parts of the IVF process, and even exploring controversial genetic editing techniques designed to prevent inherited disease.
The technologies could make IVF more effective and accessible. But they’re also raising difficult ethical questions about how far reproductive medicine should go.
—Jessica Hamzelou
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ One man's mom has made him a magnificent Monty Python and the Holy Grail quilt.
+ An origamist has folded an astonishing mechanical typewriter from a single sheet of paper.
+ The Techno-Optimism Archive is a fascinating history of hype surrounding new technologies.
+ This richly illustrated travelogue traces the curious journey of citrus from the Himalayan foothills to the heart of Sicily.

Plus: 22 nations have called for a new global body to oversee AI.

articles.title: 200 OK is dead as an AI agent health signal. Here’s what comes next.
articles.text:
200 OK is dead as an AI agent health signal. Here’s what comes next.
A customer asks whether they can swap unworn boots for a size 10. The agent replies, in under a second, that it cannot help with that topic. The web service returns 200 OK. Latency is nominal, error counters are flat, and the Datadog dashboard stays solid green. A customer has just left, and nothing in the APM stack knows.
That is the failure this article is about: the kind that looks like success.
In lean manufacturing, this exact category of silent defect is solved using two twin principles: Poka-Yoke (mistake-proofing stations so bad parts cannot pass) and Jidoka (autonomation—building machines that detect anomalies themselves and automatically halt the line via an Andon emergency cord rather than waiting for downstream customer complaints).
“A customer has just left, and nothing in the APM stack knows. That is the failure this article is about: the kind that looks like success.”
Modern AI agent engineering needs to adopt this exact control-loop architecture, replacing passive health checks with active station barriers.
1. Error analysis: Finding what to watch
When we retrospectively ran an offline evaluation benchmark script against three weeks of archived Datadog logs, we found our primary intent classifier had silently dropped 4.2% in schema-valid classification accuracy—masked entirely by default fallback handlers returning 200 OK.
We started by conducting a manual, single-day audit of 100 randomly sampled 200 OK production traces pulled directly from our archived Datadog logs. Two engineers read the raw customer text and manually categorized every routing decision against a ground-truth spreadsheet rubric.
When we bucketed those 100 manual traces, the breakdown was stark:
- 62% Explicit schema violations / API timeouts: Caught by standard error boundaries or handled by fallback defaults.
- 11% False negatives: Let spam or out-of-scope queries pass downstream (wasting LLM tokens).
- 27% False-positive blocks: Valid customer inquiries incorrectly classified as OUT_OF_SCOPE.
This manual audit revealed our critical blind spot. A false negative wastes a few cents in tokens; a schema crash raises a 500 error and pages on-call; but a false-positive block turns away a customer while returning a clean 200 OK. That audit gave us both our core metric to guard—the False Positive Block Rate (FPBR)—and the foundational insight needed to design our observability layer.
2. Why the intent classifier is the blast-radius bottleneck
In our production customer support agent architecture, requests are rarely handled by a monolithic, generalist LLM. Instead, our deployments rely on a multi-agent orchestration pattern (router-specialist topology). An inbound user prompt first hits a triage router agent, which parses the query and dispatches it to downstream domain specialists (Billing, Account Access, Returns), or short-circuits it if it falls outside support bounds (OUT_OF_SCOPE).
Of all the components in this multi-agent stack, we evaluate the Intent Classification Agent first because it sits at the front door.
“An intent classifier false positive has the highest cascading blast radius in the multi-agent topology because it causes a silent, permanent customer drop-off that bypasses all downstream observability.”
If the intent classifier makes a false-positive error—misinterpreting a legitimate exchange or warranty claim as OUT_OF_SCOPE—it triggers an immediate short-circuit. Downstream specialists are never invoked, tokens are saved, and the system cheerfully returns a 200 OK refusal. An intent classifier false positive has the highest cascading blast radius in the multi-agent topology because it causes a silent, permanent customer drop-off that bypasses all downstream observability.
3. Jidoka: Measuring the judge (RoBERTa vs. LLM-as-a-judge)
While the industry frequently defaults to “LLM-as-a-judge” frameworks (using models like GPT-4o or Llama 3) for agent monitoring, we deliberately deployed a fine-tuned encoder model (RoBERTa-base NLI cross-encoder).
To judge an intent classification output, you aren’t asking a model to generate free-form text; you are asking it to evaluate context, verify constraints, and output a strict classification label. Encoders are native classification architectures that look at the entire prompt context multidirectionally rather than predicting the next token autoregressively. This makes them faster, entirely deterministic, free of token-generation overhead, and natively suited for semantic entailment tasks.
Why RoBERTa-base (and when to use DeBERTa instead)
We chose RoBERTa-base specifically for its infrastructure footprint: at ~1.5 GB RAM, it dropped onto our existing c7i.xlarge nodes with zero new cloud cost overhead.
If your customer queries frequently exceed 256 tokens or you are hunting for marginal accuracy gains across enterprise-wide clusters, DeBERTa-v3-base is a better option. DeBERTa’s disentangled attention mechanism yields a 1–2% bump in semantic entailment accuracy. However, that comes at the cost of a heavier CPU compute profile requiring careful thread pinning if co-hosted on legacy nodes alongside core routing services.
Before loading our evaluator in production, we lock PyTorch execution to a single dedicated core and run a container warmup pass to eliminate cold-start latency penalties:
Python
import os
from typing import Any, Dict
from enum import Enum
import torch
from transformers import pipeline
# Lock PyTorch math engine to 1 CPU core before model initialization
torch.set_num_threads(1)
torch.set_num_interop_threads(1)
os.environ["OMP_NUM_THREADS"] = "1"
os.environ["MKL_NUM_THREADS"] = "1"
class AllowedIntent(str, Enum):
    RETURN_POLICY = 'RETURN_POLICY'  # Exchanges classified here
    ORDER_STATUS = 'ORDER_STATUS'
    ACCOUNT_ACCESS = 'ACCOUNT_ACCESS'
    OUT_OF_SCOPE = 'OUT_OF_SCOPE'
class RoBERTaEvaluator:
    """Local, thread-bounded NLI Cross-Encoder Evaluator."""
    def __init__(self, model_path: str):
        self.pipe = pipeline("text-classification", model=model_path, device="cpu")
        self.id2label = self.pipe.model.config.id2label
        
        # Engineering scar: Run dummy inference to force graph compilation during container startup
        self.pipe("warmup prompt")
    def check(self, query: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        res = self.pipe(query[:2000])[0]
        raw_label = res["label"]
        
        if raw_label.startswith("LABEL_"):
            idx = int(raw_label.replace("LABEL_", ""))
            label_name = self.id2label.get(idx, raw_label)
        else:
            label_name = raw_label
        try:
            matched_intent = AllowedIntent(label_name)
        except ValueError:
            matched_intent = AllowedIntent.OUT_OF_SCOPE
        return {"top_intent": matched_intent, "score": float(res["score"])}
To construct our training and validation datasets, we combined our 100 manually audited production traces with 20 synthetic edge cases, yielding a 120-query evaluation dataset partitioned into train, dev, and held-out test splits.
An evaluator is a second opinion, not ground truth. To validate our RoBERTa judge, we evaluated it against our held-out test split of 40 hand-labeled queries (20 positive, 20 negative):
- True Positive Rate (TPR): 91.5% (sensitivity in catching actual false-positive blocks).
- True Negative Rate (TNR): 94.0% (specificity in passing valid agent choices).
- False Alarm Rate (1 – TNR): 6.0% (the baseline overhead sent to the operator queue).
4. The latency budget
Adding inline evaluation on the hot path introduces an immediate engineering anxiety: compute cost and latency.
We ran our classifier on a co-hosted c7i.xlarge instance (4 vCPUs, 8 GB RAM) capable of handling an average baseline of 100 requests per minute (~1.6 req/sec). To ensure our quality gate did not degrade our p95 SLA or starve adjacent services, we constrained the engine using PyTorch CPU optimization guardrails:
- Model footprint: Fine-tuned RoBERTa-base cross-encoder (~1.5 GB RAM footprint).
- Thread capping: Bounded to exactly 1 CPU core via torch.set_num_threads(1).
- Maximum peak load: 480 inference calls per minute (~8 classifications per second). This represents the maximum velocity a single modern Intel thread on the c7i instance can achieve for matrix multiplication on standard-length text prompts (~256 tokens).
- Latency profile: Evaluator execution takes p50 = 42ms and p95 = 88ms (measured via PyTorch benchmark scripts running synthetic 256-token runs on our co-hosted instance).
- Financial cost: $0.00 in added cloud infrastructure by reclaiming idle CPU headroom on existing nodes.
5. Control Poka-Yoke: The software limit switch at the station boundary
To fulfill our first Lean requirement, we implement a Control Poka-Yoke as the software equivalent of a manufacturing limit switch that intercepts malformed outputs before downstream tokens are wasted.
Before invoking any classifier, we establish our schema contract:
Python
from typing import Any, Optional, Tuple
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError
class IntentResult(BaseModel):
    selected_intent: AllowedIntent
    confidence: float = Field(ge=0.0, le=1.0)
def validate_schema(raw: Any) -> Tuple[Optional[IntentResult], Optional[Exception]]:
    if not isinstance(raw, dict):
        return None, TypeError('Raw output is not a dictionary')
    try:
        return IntentResult(
            selected_intent=raw.get('intent'),
            confidence=raw.get('confidence', 0.0)
        ), None
    except ValidationError as exc:
        return None, exc
validate_schema() acts as the station sensor: nothing crosses this line unvalidated. If an agent emits a malformed structure, execution immediately branches to an operator handoff without executing downstream steps.
6. Instrumenting the turn: Telemetry, traces, and what an alert looks like
Knowing our judge’s error profile allows us to mathematically derive our trip conditions. Below a 0.9 confidence score, the evaluator’s false-alarm rate spikes above 18%, causing operator fatigue. Therefore, we set our Andon page floor at 0.9.
A single agent turn ties together our previously defined schema validator and RoBERTa evaluator inside a nested OpenTelemetry trace tree. The parent span (intent_agent_turn) encompasses the primary interaction (primary_agent_interaction) and its downstream execution child spans (context_retrieval, prompt_render, llm_inference), followed synchronously by the local judge (nli_evaluation). When the judge detects a semantic mismatch, it triggers an andon_pulled event acting as our digital emergency stop cord:
Python
import hashlib
from typing import Any, Dict
from opentelemetry import trace, metrics
tracer = trace.get_tracer('intent_gate', '1.0.0')
meter = metrics.get_meter('intent_gate', '1.0.0')
disagreements_counter = meter.create_counter('intent_gate.disagreements')
def run_turn(conversation_id: str, query: str, prompt_version: str, agent, evaluator: RoBERTaEvaluator) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    turn = {'prompt_version': prompt_version, 'disagreement_type': None}
    
    with tracer.start_as_current_span('intent_agent_turn') as root:
        root.set_attribute('gen_ai.conversation.id', conversation_id)
        root.set_attribute('app.prompt.version', prompt_version)
        root.set_attribute('app.query.sha256', hashlib.sha256(query.encode()).hexdigest()[:16])
        with tracer.start_as_current_span('primary_agent_interaction') as s1:
            with tracer.start_as_current_span('context_retrieval'): pass
            with tracer.start_as_current_span('prompt_render'): pass
            with tracer.start_as_current_span('llm_inference'):
                raw = agent.classify(query=query, prompt_version=prompt_version)
            result, error = validate_schema(raw)
            s1.set_attribute('app.intent.schema_valid', result is not None)
            if result is None:
                s1.set_status(trace.Status(trace.StatusCode.ERROR, 'schema_violation'))
                turn['action'] = 'HANDOFF_SCHEMA_FAILURE'
                return turn
        with tracer.start_as_current_span('nli_evaluation') as s2:
            verdict = evaluator.check(query)
            agent_intent, eval_intent = result.selected_intent, verdict['top_intent']
            
            dtype = None
            if agent_intent != eval_intent:
                if agent_intent == AllowedIntent.OUT_OF_SCOPE:
                    dtype = 'SUSPECTED_FALSE_POSITIVE'
                elif eval_intent == AllowedIntent.OUT_OF_SCOPE:
                    dtype = 'SUSPECTED_FALSE_NEGATIVE'
                else:
                    dtype = 'INTENT_MISMATCH'
            turn.update({
                'agent_intent': agent_intent.value,
                'evaluator_intent': eval_intent.value,
                'evaluator_score': verdict['score'],
                'disagreement_type': dtype
            })
            
            if dtype:
                disagreements_counter.add(1, {'prompt_version': prompt_version, 'type': dtype})
                s2.add_event('andon_pulled', {'type': dtype})
                turn['action'] = 'HANDOFF_EVALUATOR_DISAGREEMENT'
                return turn
        turn['action'] = 'PROCEED_TO_GENERATION'
        return turn
What the telemetry stack monitors
To maintain complete visibility across the agent’s lifecycle, our telemetry watches four distinct layers across the trace hierarchy:
| Signal | Source span/counter | Action trigger | 
| Schema compliance rate | primary_agent_interaction | Instant operator handoff on Pydantic ValidationError. | 
| Suspected False-Positive Block Rate (FPBR) | nli_evaluation counter | Andon alert at > 0.9 score; anomaly detection triggers incident workflow. | 
| Refusal step-changes | Root span outcome (app.outcome) | Monitored on deploy dashboard; step-changes trigger prompt rollback review. | 
| Downstream task resolution | Product analytics trace join | Weekly review of whether passed queries resulted in human escalation or re-asks. | 
The first incident: What caught the regression
The first time this observability gate ran in production was during the deployment of prompt version v1.2.0, shipped to tighten return abuse policies. The failure stemmed from a single un-audited prompt modifier that interpreted sizing exchanges as abuse vectors:
Diff
[System Prompt Diff: v1.1.0 -> v1.2.0]
- Handle customer return requests in accordance with standard 30-day policy windows.
+ Zero tolerance for policy circumvention. Intercept all ambiguous customer inquiries 
+ regarding item modification, sizing swaps, or exchanges as potential return abuse vectors.
When a quality regression fires, the alert payload received on the #andon-agent-alerts Slack channel contains the exact trace ID, prompt version tag, candidate classification, and the evaluator’s confidence verdict:
JSON
{
  "event": "QUALITY_REGRESSION_SUSPECTED",
  "trace_id": "37a886864e32af95d4012a30acbda366",
  "prompt_version": "v1.2.0",
  "reason": "EVALUATOR_DISAGREEMENT",
  "disagreement_type": "SUSPECTED_FALSE_POSITIVE",
  "agent_intent": "OUT_OF_SCOPE",
  "evaluator_intent": "RETURN_POLICY",
  "evaluator_score": 0.9412
}
The incident timeline unfolded in under three minutes:
- 00:00:00: v1.2.0 deployed globally.
- 00:12:02 (t = 0): The boots query fails 12 minutes after deployment. Agent returns OUT_OF_SCOPE; evaluator flags RETURN_POLICY (score 0.9412).
- 00:12:04 (t + 2s): #andon-agent-alerts Slack channel receives trace webhook with debug link.
- 00:14:38 (t + 156s): Traffic auto-drains and reverts to stable v1.1.0 following operator intervention. Total detection-to-reset time: 2m 36s.
The offline evaluation suite missed this failure because its 250 static test cases contained zero colloquial variants for apparel or shoe sizing swaps.
7. Limitations and release provenance protocol
- Correlated failure blindspots: If both the primary LLM agent and the RoBERTa evaluator misinterpret a novel phrase identically, no alert fires.
- Cold-start vulnerability: The first 30 requests of a new prompt version are unguarded by monitoring thresholds to prevent small-sample noise trips.
- Operator dependency: Pulling an Andon cord when no human operators are on duty creates queue backlogs without resolving customer friction.
- Prompt version provenance: To prevent unannounced semantic drift, treat prompt text with the same CI/CD immutability as compiled bytecode. Every prompt revision is hashed into deployment manifests, and release notes explicitly log every semantic instruction modifier.
Summary
- The problem: Production AI agents fail silently by returning confident, well-formed 200 OK refusals that pass passive APM health checks while turning away legitimate customers.
- The solution: We applied Lean Poka-Yoke (inline schema validation) and Jidoka (a local, thread-bounded RoBERTa-base cross-encoder judge acting as an automated Andon cord) to evaluate intent classifications synchronously.
- The economics: By locking the evaluator to 1 CPU core (torch.set_num_threads(1)) on co-hosted c7i.xlarge nodes, we achieved p50 = 42ms / p95 = 88ms latency with $0.00 in added cloud infrastructure cost.
- The incident: When prompt v1.2.0 accidentally flagged product sizing swaps as out-of-scope, the inline judge caught the regression at t=0, alerted #andon-agent-alerts via Slack webhook at t+2s, and enabled a full rollback to v1.1.0 within 2 minutes and 36 seconds.

articles.title: Absolute Batman can save DC Studios
articles.text:
With James Gunn and Peter Safran out as the co-heads of DC Studios following Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, it’s unclear what will become of the cinematic universe that was building around movies like last year’s Superman. Though Gunn’s Man of Tomorrowfeature might still come out, it seems like his larger vision for the DC Universe may be tossed out by DC Studios’ newly appointed CEO, Jeremy Latcham. Gunn was taking his time fleshing out the DCU with relatively less high-profile characters like Peacemaker, Supergirl, and Clayface. But Latcham has reportedly received a mandate from Skydance CEO David Ellison to fast-track a new version of the Justice League featuring more popular heroes like Wonder Woman and the Green Lantern.
Absolute Batman can save DC Studios
Skydance’s cinematic superhero universe could get back on track through DC’s progressive Absolute Universe comics.
This drastic shift in priorities will likely change what the DCU looks like in the coming years as Skydance attempts to parlay its comics IP into projects that can help it get on top of the $80 billion of debt the company is now responsible for after acquiring WBD. Ellison’s instinct to whip out the A-list superheroes is probably right from a business perspective. Most casual DC movie fans are more interested in stories about the Trinity than obscure characters like Gorilla Grodd. But after two iffy attempts at creating interconnected DC movie franchises, that audience might not have much of an appetite for yet another full-on reboot.
Rather than starting from scratch, DC Studios should probably keep some of the things that worked well during Gunn and Safran’s tenure, like presenting Superman as a compassionate person with a strong moral compass. But if the studio really wants to take this franchise in a new direction that gets people excited, it should also be thinking about tapping into the energy of some of DC’s most successful recent comics. Though the WBD merger prompted Skydance to begin laying off almost 2,000 employees last month, DC Comics — which Skydance gained control of as part of the deal — was reportedly left unscathed because the publishing arm’s business has been performing surprisingly well. Much of that success seems to have been driven by strong sales of comics created by DC’s Absolute Universe imprint.
Launched in 2024, the Absolute Universe comics reimagine DC’s heroes and villains as wildly different versions of their classic selves. Absolute Wonder Woman is a witch raised in Hell, Absolute Superman first arrives on Earth as a teenager who remembers his childhood on Krypton, and Absolute Batman is a working-class civil engineer rather than a socialite born into immense wealth. The Absolute characters’ worldviews and approaches to enacting justice are all distinct from their mainstream universe counterparts. But as much as the Absolute comics diverge from established canon, they each capture the essence of what makes their central characters iconic pillars of the DC brand.
Wonder Woman aside, there have been so many cinematic portrayals of DC characters based on their classic selves that it has often seemed like Warner Bros. was stuck in a kind of rut. There have been slight stylistic differences between the various big-screen iterations of Superman and Batman over the years, but for the most part, they have all come across as the products of a studio that’s averse to trying new things.
Absolute Batman is compelling because it inverts the established power structures that define most classic Batman comics.
That’s part of what made Matt Reeves’ The Batman— which didn’t bother to rehash Bruce Wayne’s tragic origin story — feel somewhat like a breath of fresh air when it debuted in 2022. Robert Pattinson will reprise his role as the Dark Knight in The Batman Part II, but it’s not really clear whether that version of the character will have any bearing on the DCU’s future.
Between Reeves’ Batman films existing in their own universe (similar to Todd Phillips’ Joker features) and Pattinson presumably being busy now that he’s been cast as Amazon’s new James Bond, it doesn’t seem likely that that version of the character will be incorporated into the DCU. Ellison obviously intends to put out more projects featuring Batman, though, and DC Studios could tell a riveting story if it took some cues from the hero’s Absolute incarnation. What makes Absolute Batman such a compelling series is the way it inverts the established power structures that define most classic Batman comics. In those books, Bruce Wayne is part of Gotham’s marginalized underclass, while the Joker is a moneyed elite whose villainy is highlighted in the way he manipulates various industries.
This inversion puts Absolute Batman in a position to operate as a vigilante with a much deeper connection to the ordinary people he has sworn to protect. Monstrous supervillains like Poison Ivy and Bane are still major threats, but the comics also spend time pitting Absolute Batman against more ordinary evils like corrupt police departments infested with white nationalists fixated on terrorizing minorities. Absolute Batman’s progressive political overtones might not align with Ellison’s personal sensibilities, and the comic’s brutality probably doesn’t align with Latcham’s approach to making films. But Absolute Batman’sphenomenal sales have made it abundantly clear that readers are enjoying these stories, which is likely a big part why DC Studios announced earlier this year that it has plans to produce an animated series based on the comics.
Those plans might change in the wake of Skydance acquiring WBD, but an Absolute Batman series would give DC Studios an organic way to introduce the character into its tentpole films. Having characters jump back and forth between TV and the big screen was one of the stronger ideas Gunn introduced to the DCU, and it’s a strategy that could continue to benefit DC Studios under Latcham’s leadership. Turning Absolute Batman into the next flagship Bruce Wayne would be a bold move on Skydance’s part. But if the studio really wants to prove that this megamerger was the right decision, it needs to show the public that it has the guts to take exciting chances.

articles.title: Ethiopian Airlines reports cyberattack a week after Air Botswana
articles.text:
Ethiopian Airlines on Wednesday warned customers that some of their information may have been exposed in a recent cyberattack, weeks after Air Botswana disclosed a suspected ransomware incident on its internal systems.
In an email notice sent through its frequent-flyer programme ShebaMiles, the Addis Ababa-based carrier said the incident was “of limited scope” and said there was “currently no evidence” that customers’ financial information was accessed.
Ethiopian Airlines did not provide the date of the intrusion or the customer data and gave no estimate of how many people might be affected. It also did not say whether the breach was confined to the loyalty programme or whether bookings and flight operations were affected.
The breach at Ethiopian Airlines underscores the risks facing carriers as they rely on third parties to handle everything from customer enquiries to airport check-in. An intrusion can expose millions of passenger records without grounding a flight, as Qantas found last year, while an attack on a shared check-in provider can disrupt operations at several airports at once.
“We are treating this matter with the utmost seriousness and are working closely with our cybersecurity partners and relevant authorities to investigate the incident and assess its full impact,” the airline said. “As a precaution, we encourage you to remain vigilant against any suspicious or unsolicited communications.”
ShebaMiles had more than 5.38 million members when Ethiopian Airlines announced a partnership with Etihad Airways’ loyalty programme in 2025. The airline group carried about 19 million passengers and generated $7.6 billion in revenue in its 2024/25 financial year.
Aviation attacks
The Ethiopian Airlines disclosure follows a series of incidents that have exposed the aviation business, from employee records and loyalty accounts to the software airports use to check in passengers.
Air Botswana said it detected unauthorised access on November 3 to systems containing employee and internal information. The state-owned carrier described the incident as suspected ransomware and said passenger bookings, aircraft systems and flight operations were not affected. It has yet to disclose whether any data was copied.
At Qantas, an attacker gained access to a third-party customer service platform used by one of the airline’s call centres in 2025. The Australian carrier said the breach compromised some personal information belonging to 5.7 million customers, including names, email addresses and frequent-flyer details. Qantas said the incident had no impact on its operations.
An attack on Collins Aerospace two months later showed how disruption at a single supplier could spread across airports. The ransomware attack knocked out automated check-in and baggage drop at several European airports, including Heathrow, affecting dozens of flights.

articles.title: AMD teases mystery CES 2027 announcement: Zen 6, RDNA 5, or yet more AI?
articles.text:
What just happened? CES 2027 is a little over a month away, and AMD has already teased an announcement it has planned for the event. But the mysterious A-shaped/peaked motif that the company published doesn't give much away. It could be the RDNA 5 GPUs, the upcoming Zen 6 processors, or maybe even new laptop CPUs. Sadly, it could also be another AI-related announcement that almost nobody cares about.
Jack Huynh, AMD's SVP and GM of Computing and Graphics, posted the teaser on his official X account. He's certainly building up the reveal as something special, talking about "the next era of computing" and "creating a future filled with possibilities we once only dreamed of."
 – Jack Huynh (@jackhuynh) November 17, 2026
A lot of speculation points to this being an RDNA 5 announcement. That presumes that the A-shaped image is a reference to AT, or Alpha Trion, the codename for AMD's next-gen graphics chips: AT0, AT2, AT3 and AT4.
But most people think the post relates to Olympic Ridge, the codename for the Zen 6-powered Ryzen desktop CPU. That does seem possible, given that AMD announced general availability of the Zen 6 EPYC SP7 processors only a few weeks ago.
It could be that AMD is hinting at an unveiling of the new Zen 6 laptop processors. The way the line in the video swings around and opens like a hinge does suggest this is the case, and AMD is developing Medusa Point and Gator Range mobile processors that are expected to arrive next year.
Then there is the final, and sadly most likely, explanation. The symbol in the clip does start as a single line, like an "I," before opening into an "A." Yes, this could be yet another AI-related announcement, possibly something to do with AI agents. The language Huynh uses in his post certainly aligns with the hyperbole we so often hear when companies talk about AI, unfortunately.
AMD certainly had plenty to say about AI at CES this January. Alongside the Ryzen AI 400 chips for Copilot+ laptops, the company showed off Ryzen AI Halo, a mini PC that AMD said could run AI models with up to 200 billion parameters locally. Lisa Su also gave attendees a look at Helios, a server rack pairing Instinct MI455X GPUs with Zen 6 Epyc processors.
AMD's recent financial report showed its gaming revenue had crashed 40% while data center revenue jumped 97% to $8.5 billion, prompting CEO Lisa Su to declare that "we are a data center-first company." A few days later, AMD Gaming posted a message asking gamers to remember Radeon loyalty.

articles.title: Yelp Migrates Cassandra to EKS by Moving EBS Volumes
articles.text:
Yelp has moved its Cassandra fleet from legacy self-managed Kubernetes clusters to Amazon EKS by re-pointing existing EBS volumes at new pods, rather than streaming data between nodes. A blog post by the site reliability team details a migration. It covered about 90 production clusters. There was zero downtime for customers and no data loss. The largest cluster, a 54-pod user-data store, took about 12 hours end to end.
Yelp had already moved its stateless workloads to EKS through its PaaSTA deployment layer, but Cassandra stayed behind. Kubernetes has no built-in way to migrate StatefulSets and their persistent volumes across clusters. The usual approach is to add nodes to the new cluster and shut down the old ones. This would temporarily double compute capacity but also lead to data transfer costs. For the largest clusters, streaming alone could have taken weeks. Yelp also considered a regional failover and rebuild, and a new Cassandra datacenter in EKS, but rated both as less transparent to customers.
Yelp's "Rolling PV Transplant" relies on the fact that an EBS volume is bound to an Availability Zone, not to a Kubernetes cluster, and that a PersistentVolume is effectively a pointer to a volume ID. The team pre-creates PVs and PVCs in EKS that reference the existing volume IDs, then creates an identical StatefulSet there, whose pods wait in ContainerCreating. The automation then deletes one pod at a time on the legacy cluster, waits for the volume to detach, and lets the EKS pod claim it. The pod rejoins the ring with the same data and token range, and the process repeats for the next pod. Cassandra's replication tolerates the few minutes each node is offline.
Yelp set a skipReconciliation: true flag on the custom resources in both clusters. This was done because two operators managed the same logical ring during the migration. The flag helped prevent them from conflicting over pod state. The flag was cleared on the EKS side at the end.
Across roughly 1,000 pods, about 1,000 TiB moved by pointer rather than over the wire. No node was ever decommissioned from the ring, so rollback was the same operation in reverse. Yelp used it a handful of times, for a missing subnet definition and a certificate mismatch, and restored pods within minutes. After a week of manual dev runs and a week of automation, one engineer ran the production rollout in about three weeks, migrating three to six clusters on a typical day.
The team had Claude generate the orchestration script, roughly 800 lines of bash, from its validated manual runbook, rather than asking it to design the procedure. The script needed minor adjustments after two days of testing.
The approach relies on a previous Container Storage Interface migration by Yelp's Compute Infrastructure team. This work gave the Data Infrastructure team confidence in the volume detach and attach process. Yelp also used the technique for Kafka clusters, and says it applies to any AZ-pinned stateful workload on Kubernetes. The legacy clusters are now retired.
The one failure specific to this technique was a stale VolumeAttachment object left behind by the AWS CSI controller after pod deletion. The EKS pod sat in Pending with no error, and deleting the object on the legacy cluster fixed it. Yelp advises building explicit timeouts for stalled detach and attach operations into any automation. Two other findings were unrelated to the mechanism. Backups failed with IAM AccessDenied errors for 48 hours because a new -eks role was not yet being assumed by scheduled jobs, and the alert only filed a ticket instead of paging. Pausing repairs for the migration also exposed one cluster whose repairs had been silently disabled for three months, leaving accumulated data inconsistencies. Teams planning a similar move should audit repair state, backup IAM roles and alert severity before starting.
Yelp's approach is not the only way to move Cassandra between EKS clusters. Monday.com's engineering team describes a different one in a post on zero-downtime Cassandra migration between EKS clusters. K8ssandra-managed clusters had to move without any downtime or data loss. So, the team created a workflow to add new Cassandra data centers, safely transfer data, and remove the old ones. That is the streaming model Yelp considered and rejected. The new cluster is brought up alongside the old one and receives data over the network, and the original is retired only afterwards. The team believes success relied more on control, automation, and handling failures than on speed. They automated long tasks like rebuilds and planned the migration in stages based on operator behavior.
The two migrations differ in what they trade away. Yelp's disk transplant skips data transfer and extra compute. It allows for a rollback by swapping the pointer. However, it relies on EBS volumes being linked to an Availability Zone, not a cluster. Monday.com's approach does not rely on that property, and it keeps the old environment intact until the end. The cost is a longer migration and the capacity to run both sides at once, which Yelp calculated would have taken weeks for its largest clusters.
Despite the different mechanics, the post-migration lessons are similar. Monday.com devotes part of its write-up to verifying that backups work after the migration, along with monitoring, dashboards and alerts. Yelp's own backups failed on an IAM role mismatch within 48 hours of its first production clusters landing in EKS. Teams planning either approach should treat those checks as part of the migration plan, not as cleanup afterwards.

France Is Blaming Iran for the Fridge Cyberattack
U.S. intelligence agencies have recently reached a “”ow confidence” assessment that Iran was responsible for the attacks in France, according to three U.S. officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence. A “low confidence” assessment generally means that there is some intelligence that points in a certain direction but is fragmented, and that the assessment could change as more information is collected.
The agencies’ judgment on the French incidents linked those attacks to Iran generally and not to a specific group such as the Revolutionary Guards, two of the officials said. They added that Iran was also seen as probably responsible for other similar attacks around Europe, but that those investigations were in their early stages.
