En Xataka Homa | Tengo la calefacción puesta a la temperatura "ideal" y paso frío: esta es la clave para solucionarlo

articles.title: S3 vs. ScyllaDB for tiny telemetry: What Red Canary learned the hard way
articles.text:
S3 vs. ScyllaDB for tiny telemetry: What Red Canary learned the hard way
At Red Canary, storing large amounts of small data is a big deal.
Their Linux Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) sensors run on hundreds of thousands of endpoints (VMs, laptops, EC2 instances, etc.) They continuously generate small payloads with telemetry details (file changes, process launches, and network connections), as well as self-reported health checks. Uploading all these small payloads to S3, which charges per PUT operation, became quite costly at scale.
The logical approach – merging data into larger chunks before uploading them to S3 — did cut costs. However, it also introduced file-size limits, delayed data freshness, and complicated debugging of specific endpoint records. After some experimentation, they cut latency and costs with an unexpected approach: storing large amounts of small data in a write-optimized database, ScyllaDB.
“After some experimentation, they cut latency and costs with an unexpected approach: storing large amounts of small data in a write-optimized database, ScyllaDB.”
Andres Medina, a staff software engineer on the LinuxEDR team, took the Monster Scale Summit stage to share their journey from S3 and Postgres to a Firehose buffer to ScyllaDB – and the lessons learned along the way. You can watch his complete talk or read the highlights below.
Checking the health check data flow
Medina’s team decided to start pipeline optimization with the health check data. As a lower-risk part of the pipeline than the actual telemetry data, it seemed like the safest spot for experimentation.
Problem 1: cost
The cost problem was the most pressing pain that they wanted to address. “S3 charges a flat fee per S3 PUT, which occurs for every payload upload,” Medina explained. “So if we have hundreds of thousands of endpoints, we’re being charged for hundreds of thousands of S3 PUTs.”
They hoped that creating a buffer would provide a short-term fix, at least. Using AWS Firehose and Kinesis, they combined small data streams into larger files and wrote them to S3 once they reached a defined threshold. It did reduce costs – but at the cost of introducing new issues:
- Firehose and Kinesis impose a strict one-megabyte-per-shard limit, and the larger files just didn’t fit.
- Visibility into the health data was delayed. Before, it was passed over to S3 immediately. With the change, they had to wait until the designated threshold was met.
- Debugging specific endpoints became difficult. When lots of endpoint IDs are mashed together, it’s much harder to find a particular endpoint in a large customer fleet.
Problem 2: database scalability
Another issue: Postgres was used to store endpoint metadata, and it was just overwhelmed at their scale. “Sometimes a large customer might restart a chunk of their fleet,” Medina shared. “That means that many endpoints will try to check in at very similar times, causing a spike of writes in the database.” They also had to throttle their incoming database requests, as sudden bursts could take down the database.
Yes, they could have tweaked and tuned their existing database for yet more short-term solutions. But the team wanted a longer-term fix.
Looking for a longer-term solution
The team set the following criteria for a new approach:
- Ability to sustain their large and growing throughput
- Improve time-to-visibility in their portal
- Minimal admin burden
They ultimately chose ScyllaDB Cloud, with the Bring Your Own Account (BYOA) deployment option. Medina explained, “We installed it in our own AWS account, in a separate account from our remaining data to reduce any risk there. That way, ScyllaDB can still manage that cluster without having access to our data.”
Their shift to ScyllaDB involved two phases: replacing Postgres, then replacing S3.
Replacing Postgres
Replacing Postgres was simpler than replacing S3. Each sensor event appends a single row, and the web portal always queries it in a time series manner – asking for a customer’s active endpoints over a given period of time. Still, Postgres and ScyllaDB are very different databases, which pushed the team to learn a few lessons regarding tombstones and uneven data volumes.
When you delete data in ScyllaDB, it isn’t just removed. ScyllaDB leaves a timestamped marker called a tombstone. This prevents data resurrection, which occurs if a node misses a deletion (e.g., due to a network error) and later restores the old data during a cluster repair.
Tombstones were particularly troubling for Red Canary’s ephemeral endpoints, which are online only for a short time. Medina said, “Some clusters might scale up for an hour and then scale back down, which means an endpoint is alive for a very small amount of time. That meant some customers had partitions that were mostly just tombstones. When you query it, ScyllaDB has to iterate through all these tombstones, making our latency worse than it should be.”
The fix here was simple. Since they don’t need to delete any data, they didn’t need tombstones. They cleared them from the read path by setting a short TTL on the table and tuning tombstone garbage collection to evict tombstones faster. The latency improved as a result.
“Some clusters might scale up for an hour and then scale back down. That meant some customers had partitions that were mostly just tombstones. When you query it, ScyllaDB has to iterate through all these tombstones, making our latency worse than it should be.”
The second issue was that their data volume varied wildly across customers. Some customers have a few dozen endpoints, while others have hundreds of thousands. To avoid creating hot partitions in ScyllaDB, Medina and the team developed a bucketing strategy.
They split each customer’s data into smaller numbered “buckets,” which ScyllaDB distributes across shards. When fetching a customer’s data, the system checks how many buckets they have and queries them all at once (in parallel) for faster responses.
The following diagrams compare the short-term solution to the long-term one. In the After diagram, the Postgres endpoint database is gone. Instead, the service forwards sensor health data to ScyllaDB, and the portal queries the service for the metadata needed for recently active endpoints.
Replacing S3
The next challenge was the unconventional move to replace S3 usage with ScyllaDB. Throughput was higher, and access patterns were less predictable. Medina explained, “It’s not a service trying to query in one way. Instead, it’s developers debugging.” They could predict one thing at least: developers would debug one specific sensor at a time. So, they defined “sensor ID” as the partition for their queries.
There was an ulterior motive here. Medina shared, “One of our biggest reasons for wanting to do this was to see if ScyllaDB could also be used for our detection data in the future.” Since the health data had similar throughput and was less critical to their operations, it was a safe way to test the waters for a broader shift to ScyllaDB.
The first complicating factor in the S3 replacement was that their events contain very large arrays used to track a given process’s memory consumption at a given endpoint. Some endpoints have thousands of processes running at the same time, which could create rather large rows. The solution was to unnest the array and store it in an auxiliary table, tracking each process’s memory usage separately from the primary table. “We can still put every row in the same partition so that our querying is still easy enough, as long as the partition doesn’t get too big (too many rows),” Medina added.
Next up: batching. They wanted to batch rather than write each health event individually to avoid multiple network round trips to the database. However, batching is more efficient if every statement in a batch belongs to the same partition. Ideally, they split each health payload’s statements by partition when they receive it. The ScyllaDB Rust driver wasn’t designed for this, though.
Wrangling the Rust driver
More specifically, the Rust driver doesn’t expose a prepared statement with values already serialized (a bound statement). To get a partition for a statement with values, you would have to serialize it once to get the corresponding hashed token, then serialize it again to execute the statement.
If you try to keep these values unserialized together with the statement, it’s difficult to put them into collections in Rust (a Rust collection like a vector or hash map requires everything to be the same type). If different statements have different types, it’s complicated. However, once you serialize them, those values are just a stream of bytes. You can keep all that data in the same collection.
Medina detailed his workaround like this: “To get around this, I forked the Rust driver to add the idea of a bound statement and then a bound batch, which is just a collection of statements. With this now in place, we can ask the bound statement what its token is without having to reserialize it, and then execute it again without reserializing it. A second benefit is that we can separate CPU work from I/O work. In Rust, you mostly use Tokio for I/O operations, and doing CPU work there can block the runtime and reduce efficiency.
“When we made this change, our average time to process a file dropped from about 150 milliseconds to 50 milliseconds — a drop of about 60%.”
So now we can do all of the CPU work in a CPU-bound worker using Rayon, and then we send it back to Tokio when we’re done. Then in Tokio, you can just do the I/O for the batch execution. When we made this change, our average time to process a file dropped from about 150 milliseconds to 50 milliseconds — a drop of about 60%. Of course, this is for our use case, so your mileage may vary.”
Did it work?
Here’s the final system architecture.
The LinuxEDR services now own the health data for the LinuxEDR product, and that data no longer goes to the engine. ScyllaDB stores all the check-ins and health metrics. There’s a separate metrics database for now, but that might be replaced soon. The portal can query the services to get the list of active endpoints, and any developer can query ScyllaDB for debugging.
So far, the team has significantly reduced their per-endpoint cost. Batching has boosted their I/O per second, with a ~20X reduction in writes versus rows inserted (~670K rows/second, but only ~36K writes/second due to batching). And the portal now retrieves endpoints in seconds instead of minutes for its largest customers. “Each query to ScyllaDB is in the double-digit millisecond range,” Medina noted.
Next steps
Medina wrapped up with this:
“Since the transition has gone fairly smoothly, we’re now exploring using it for data that is more critical. One of my team’s main goals is to store our detection data in ScyllaDB to avoid sending data that doesn’t need to go to the engine. Also, we’re looking at ways to use it outside my team to replace some uses of OpenSearch, which has been giving us issues with cost, performance, and sometimes paging…no one likes being paged. Ideally, I would also like to merge the fork at some point so I don’t need to rebase the driver on every new release.”

articles.title: How Stretto built an AI voice agent with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Stretto built an AI voice agent with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic
This post is co-written with Danya Gordin from Stretto and Marcelo Wzorek from CI&T.
Before Stretto built an AI voice agent, consumers considering bankruptcy on its Bankruptcy.com site filled out a web form with a few fields: debt amount, attorney status, and contact information. These form-generated leads carried thin margins.
The gap between a web form lead and a fully qualified lead is significant. Bankruptcy attorneys place more value on a lead that includes detailed financial data: debts, assets, vehicles, real estate, employment history, and prior filings. The web form could have been extended to capture that detail, but the longer it got, the more visitors abandoned it partway through. A phone interview would have drawn the information out naturally, because people are more willing to share financially sensitive details in conversation, but staffing and training a human intake team to run those interviews was cost-prohibitive.
Stretto saw an opportunity: replace the web form with an AI voice agent that conducts the intake interview by phone. The agent would guide callers through the full bankruptcy questionnaire conversationally and extract structured data in real time. It would then sort leads against attorney-defined rules to support attorney decision-making.
The challenge was finding a voice AI solution that could handle sensitive financial conversations naturally, with low latency, clean interruption handling, and emotional awareness, at a cost that made the unit economics work.
In this post, we walk through how Stretto worked with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center and CI&T (an AWS Partner) to build Tara, an AI voice agent powered by Amazon Nova 2 Sonic, a speech-to-speech model in Amazon Bedrock. Tara conducts multi-phase bankruptcy intake interviews and sorts leads against attorney-defined rules. We cover the architecture, the phased build from validation through production deployment, and how the team tested voice quality for sensitive conversations.
Solution overview
Tara is an AI voice agent that conducts bankruptcy intake interviews over the phone. When a caller dials the Bankruptcy.com number, Tara picks up, introduces herself, and guides the caller through a structured conversation. She collects personal information, financial details, asset inventories, and employment history while adapting her tone to the caller’s emotional state. At the end of the call, Stretto’s system applies attorney-defined rules to sort the lead as qualified, disqualified, or needs-more-information for attorney review.
The solution is built on Amazon Nova 2 Sonic, a speech-to-speech foundation model (FM)available through Amazon Bedrock. It processes speech input and generates speech output natively in a single model rather than chaining separate speech-to-text, language model, and text-to-speech components. This architecture is designed to reduce latency and produce more natural-sounding conversations, both critical for the sensitive nature of bankruptcy intake calls. Building on Amazon Bedrock gave the team both Amazon Nova 2 Sonic and Anthropic’s Claude through one managed service, with no model infrastructure to run. It also brought AWS security and governance controls to a workload that handles sensitive financial data. Access to both models is governed by AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Traffic to Amazon Bedrock stays on the AWS network through virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints (AWS PrivateLink). Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use prompts or model outputs to train models (for details, see Data protection in Amazon Bedrock). Because the models run in the same AWS environment as the voice bridge, the database, and Amazon CloudWatch monitoring, the team could secure and operate the whole solution with one set of tools. Amazon Nova 2 Sonic and Amazon Bedrock are not available in all AWS Regions. For current Region availability, see Amazon Bedrock supported Regions.
The team chose Amazon Nova 2 Sonic over the previous voice solution for three reasons:
- Cost: Stretto reports a 95 percent reduction in per-minute voice cost compared to its previous solution, based on Amazon Bedrock on-demand pricing in us-east-1 as of April 2026.
- Latency: In Stretto’s testing, the previous solution exhibited time-to-first-audio latency above 500 milliseconds, creating awkward pauses. Amazon Nova 2 Sonic is designed for low latency to support natural conversational flow.
- Interruption handling: Callers in stressful situations need to interject, correct themselves, and ask clarifying questions. The previous solution handled barge-in poorly, often breaking the conversation flow. Amazon Nova 2 Sonic is designed to handle interruptions without breaking the session.
The following figure shows the end-to-end architecture.
A caller reaches Tara through Twilio, which opens a WebSocket connection into AWS. Traffic passes through AWS WAF and an Application Load Balancer to the voice bridge on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate, which streams audio with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic (accessed through Amazon Bedrock). After the call, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) with a dead-letter queue hands the transcript to an asynchronous processor. The processor uses Anthropic’s Claude 3 Haiku on Amazon Bedrock to extract structured fields, which persist in Amazon Aurora Serverless v2. Qualified leads route to attorneys by jurisdiction. Supporting services include NAT gateways, VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink), Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), AWS Secrets Manager, and Amazon CloudWatch.
Stretto used Twilio for telephony because Tara’s intake is fully automated, with no human agents taking calls, and because Stretto wanted a direct integration with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic that kept its existing AWS backend in place. Twilio Media Streams delivers the caller’s raw audio over a WebSocket, which is the input the voice bridge needs, and CI&T had already integrated it with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. For contact center workloads that route calls among human agents, Amazon Connect also supports Amazon Nova 2 Sonic.
The architecture uses the following AWS services:
- Amazon Nova 2 Sonic (through Amazon Bedrock): The speech-to-speech foundation model that powers Tara’s voice conversations. It handles both speech recognition and response generation in a single pass, supporting tool calling for structured data collection during the interview.
- Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate: A serverless compute engine that runs the voice bridge containers connecting the telephony layer to Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. The voice bridge tasks run continuously across three Availability Zones for high availability.
- Amazon Aurora Serverless v2: A PostgreSQL-compatible serverless relational database deployed in Multi-AZ configuration. Stores caller profiles, intake responses, qualification results, and session metadata. The serverless scaling of Aurora matches the variable call volume patterns.
- Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic’s Claude 3 Haiku): Handles structured data extraction from conversation transcripts. After Amazon Nova 2 Sonic generates a transcript, Claude 3 Haiku extracts typed fields (names, dollar amounts, addresses, vehicle details) into the relational schema.
- Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) with dead-letter queues: Manages asynchronous webhook processing for post-call events, preserving failed messages for retry.
- AWS WAF, VPC Endpoints, and Application Load Balancer: Security and networking layers that help protect API endpoints, route traffic across Availability Zones, and provide private connectivity to AWS services.
Building and validating the voice agent
The team took a phased approach: validate voice quality first, build the production integration, then expand the questionnaire scope after proving the system worked with real callers.
Validating voice quality for sensitive conversations
Bankruptcy conversations are emotionally charged. Callers are often stressed, hesitant, or embarrassed. The voice agent needs to sound empathetic and natural, not robotic or transactional. Before writing any integration code, the team spent a dedicated week testing the voice quality of Amazon Nova 2 Sonic against several caller scenarios.
The validation covered:
- Voice quality across caller emotional states (calm, stressed, hesitant, frustrated).
- Time-to-first-audio latency benchmarks against the previous solution’s over 500 ms baseline.
- Barge-in and interruption handling: can a caller interject mid-sentence without breaking the conversation?
- Emotional tone adaptation: does the agent adjust its pace and tone when a caller sounds distressed?
This validation step produced a comparison report documenting the performance of Amazon Nova 2 Sonic against the previous solution across each dimension. The report became the go/no-go gate for proceeding to integration.
Deploying to production with real callers
With voice quality validated, the team built the end-to-end integration over three weeks. The call flow works as follows:
- A caller dials the Bankruptcy.com number. Twilio’s telephony layer receives the call and opens a WebSocket connection to the voice bridge running on Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate.
- The voice bridge streams audio bidirectionally between the caller and Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. Tara introduces herself, collects consent, and begins the intake interview.
- After the call, the full transcript feeds into an extraction pipeline powered by Anthropic’s Claude 3 Haiku on Amazon Bedrock. The pipeline extracts the fields from the conversation and stores them in Amazon Aurora.
The full attorney-designed intake can run 15–20 minutes, which is longer than the maximum duration of a single Amazon Nova 2 Sonic streaming session (for the current value, see Getting started with speech-to-speech). The team treated that session duration as a design parameter and implemented the session continuation pattern, an approach that carries conversation context across session boundaries. The voice bridge tracks how long each bidirectional stream with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic has been open. Shortly before the limit, it opens a new stream with the same system prompt and tool configuration and sends the conversation so far as text history. When Tara finishes her current response, the bridge switches the caller’s audio to the new stream and closes the old one, so the conversation continues smoothly for the caller.
The initial deployment covered the existing 13-field intake form, collecting the same data points the web form captured but through natural conversation. This gave the team a production baseline to measure against before expanding scope.
Expanding the intake and lead qualification
With the production pilot running, the team expanded the questionnaire to the full attorney-designed intake over four weeks. This was a significant increase in scope:
- Over 18 intake categories with conditional branching, where the questions Tara asks depend on the caller’s previous answers.
- Complex relational data: Vehicles (year, make, model, financing status, monthly payment per vehicle), real estate properties, individual debt line items, multiple employment and income sources, and prior bankruptcy filings.
- Rules-based lead sorting: Stretto applies attorney-defined rules to each lead, and attorneys make the final decision. Because a voice agent collects richer, conditional data than a static web form, it gives Stretto more flexibility to apply those rules and qualify leads accurately.
- Lead routing: Qualified leads are routed to bankruptcy practitioners, while callers who do not meet the qualification criteria are directed to alternative resources.
The Amazon Aurora schema expanded to a full relational data model supporting one-to-many relationships. A single caller record might include four vehicles, two properties, and dozens of individual debt line items.
Measuring results and optimizing
The final phase focused on collecting production data and tuning the system based on real caller behavior. The team tracked key performance indicators including call volume, average duration, intake completion rate, profile completeness, conversion rate, and drop-off points.
Insights from production data drove several optimizations: reordering questions to reduce early drop-offs, adjusting conditional branching to collect high-value fields earlier in the conversation, and modifying qualification thresholds based on attorney feedback. The following table shows two key production metrics.
| Average call duration (completed calls) | ~8 min | 
| Data extraction accuracy | ~96% | 
Testing for quality and compliance
Deploying a voice agent that handles sensitive financial data requires more than functional testing. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center (GenAIIC) advisory team guided the development of a comprehensive testing framework spanning four categories:
- Happy path testing: Complete end-to-end intake interviews with cooperative callers across the full questionnaire. These calls confirm that the over 18 categories collect accurate structured data and that the qualification rules produce correct results.
- Adversarial testing: Callers who provide contradictory information, change answers mid-conversation, refuse to answer certain questions, or attempt to manipulate the qualification outcome. The agent needs to handle the ambiguity and keep the conversation coherent.
- Compliance testing: Consent collection, disclosure delivery, and data handling workflows. The team verified that the agent delivers disclosures accurately and collects consent before proceeding, because bankruptcy intake involves sensitive financial information.
- Barge-in scenario testing: Callers interrupting at various points in the conversation, including during disclosures, mid-question, and during the agent’s responses. Tara should recover without losing context or asking the caller to repeat information.
Responsible AI controls in production
The team treated responsible AI as a production control, not only a testing step. Amazon Nova 2 Sonic includes built-in safety protections, described in the AWS AI Service Card for Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. On top of those, the solution keeps consequential decisions out of the model: lead sorting runs on explicit attorney-defined rules after the call, and attorneys make the final decision. Consent and disclosures are delivered and logged before intake begins, and the adversarial test suite checks that attempts to manipulate the conversation don’t change lead outcomes. Beyond model inference, the solution uses the Amazon Bedrock bidirectional streaming API for real-time audio, tool use for structured data capture during the interview, and private connectivity to Amazon Bedrock through VPC endpoints.
The GenAIIC advisory team also provided guidance on prompt engineering best practices for voice-specific applications, including techniques for managing conversational state across session continuation boundaries and structuring system prompts that maintain consistent agent personality across long interviews.
Results
After roughly three months in production, Stretto reported the following results:
- Per-lead value: Fully qualified leads with complete intake data are significantly more valuable to bankruptcy attorneys than web form leads, which capture only a few basic fields.
- Lead conversion: Stretto’s early production results show a 20 percent relative increase in conversion rate compared with the web form, even before the solution has been rolled out broadly across additional districts.
- Data quality and call length: Stretto reports that Tara extracts structured fields at approximately 96 percent accuracy in its testing, and completed calls average about 8 minutes.
- Voice solution cost: Stretto reports a 95 percent reduction in per-minute voice cost compared to its previous solution.
        “I’m incredibly grateful to the AWS GenAI Innovation Center team. Their expertise helped bring our voice agent, Tara, to life, driving a 20 percent increase in our lead conversion rate.”
— Danya Gordin, Principal AI Architect, Stretto
        “As one of the partners in the AWS Generative AI Partner Innovation Alliance, we can confirm that the GenAIIC program is a true catalyst, bringing customers and partners together to solve real problems and deliver business impact. With Stretto, that meant taking a voice agent to production in a matter of weeks and transform the bankruptcy intake process”
— Marcelo Wzorek, Executive Manager, CI&T
Conclusion
Stretto’s journey from web form leads to AI-assisted intake interviews illustrates what becomes possible when voice AI reaches the quality bar for sensitive use cases. By combining the speech-to-speech capabilities of Amazon Nova 2 Sonic with a well-designed architecture on AWS, the team built a voice agent that is natural enough for callers discussing personal financial hardship and cost-effective enough to deliver meaningful savings at scale.
The phased approach, validating voice quality first, deploying a minimal intake to production, then expanding scope based on real-world data, reduced risk at each step. The team built on validated assumptions rather than projections.
If you are exploring AI voice agents for your own use case, here are some resources to get started:
- Learn about Amazon Nova 2 Sonic and speech-to-speech capabilities.
- Get started with Amazon Bedrock to access foundation models including Amazon Nova 2 Sonic.
- Explore AWS Fargate for serverless compute for containers.
- Learn about the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center for advisory support on your generative AI initiatives.
If you are weighing voice AI for a sensitive, high-value intake process, your AWS account team and the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center can help you scope and build it.

articles.title: Bulgaria’s first unicorn Payhawk raises €255.14 million at €1.82 billion valuation in Goldman Sachs-led Series C round | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Payhawk, a London-based AI-native spend management platform, today announced a €255.14 million ($280 million) Series C round, valuing the business at €1.82 billion ($2 billion) as it builds the global finance operating system (OS) for the AI era.
The round was led by Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives. All existing investors, including QED, Greenoaks, Lightspeed, Hedosophia and Bek Ventures, participated in the round, alongside new investors Galdana Ventures, Cogito Capital, Inveready and Invus, and leading European entrepreneurs Tomas Okmanas and Didac Lee. This round brings the company’s total funding to more than $515 million.
Hristo Borisov, co-founder and CEO of Payhawk, said, “The role of the finance team is rapidly moving away from manual checks, lengthy reconciliations and labour-intensive work towards becoming more strategic. While most companies use AI to speed up existing processes, we built AI agents to fundamentally rethink how finance operates.”
Founded in 2018 in Sofia by Hristo Borisov, Boyko Karadzhov, and Konstantin Dzhengozov, Payhawk is an AI-native spend management platform that orchestrates global money across Bills, Cards, Expenses, Travel, and Procurement for maximum control, automation and savings.
The company plans to move beyond spend management to build an operating system (OS) where AI agents, payments, and enterprise controls run finance together.
“Through our technology, finance departments can benefit from ‘zero-touch finance’, where neither the finance professional nor the employee deals with any admin work. 77% of our customers use our agents daily across financial control, procurement, travel and reporting to save time and money for their businesses. But AI alone cannot deliver this transformation, it must be combined with a robust payment infrastructure and enterprise controls to truly unlock the potential of every enterprise in the new AI era,” added Borisov.
According to the company, ERP systems, banks, procurement platforms, treasury products, travel tools and spend platforms are all becoming more intelligent with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. But Payhawk argues that making each application smarter does not automatically create a smarter finance operation.
“Integrations connect systems. MCP makes information easier to access. But an operating system changes how the entire finance function works. As software moves from recommending actions to actually taking them, that distinction becomes much more important,” stated Borisov.
The company is building its finance OS around three interconnected layers: AI agents that perform financial work; payments infrastructure that lets agents safely interact with money; and enterprise controls that determine what agents can do and when human intervention is required.
Borisov revealed that Payhawk aims to build a global finance category built from Europe. “Europe does not need to build local versions of categories invented somewhere else. We should build categories the rest of the world follows as craftsmanship and innovation are strongly embedded cultural traits for Europeans. We want to build the infrastructure through which businesses around the world run their financial operations in the age of AI. Being born in Europe has exposed us to this complexity from day one. We know what it takes for our customers to stay in control with their businesses spread around the world while scaling and while trying to be efficient at the same time. The window to define that category is open now — and we are moving fast,” he commented.
Headquartered in London, Payhawk now operates across 33 countries and 12 offices, with a platform that spans multiple currencies, banking systems, payment rails, regulations and local practices.
Payhawk reports it achieved positive cash flow in Q3 and still holds 70% of the capital it raised in its 2022 funding round. In March 2022, it raised an additional €89 million and extended its funding to €191 million, making it Bulgaria’s first unicorn.
In November 2021, the company raised €99 million in Series B funding, valuing it at €505 million. It raised €16.5 million in Series A in April 2021 and €3 million in a Seed round in March 2020.
The company notes that its business model relies on predictable subscription pricing rather than card interchange, aligning growth with helping customers save money rather than incentivising them to spend more. The company says this independence also lets Payhawk develop AI-native finance products that work beyond its own cards. In the US, for example, its Financial Controller Agent works with customers’ existing business cards, eliminating the need to switch providers or reissue cards.
“Payhawk’s exceptional growth reflects the strength of its engineering DNA, global footprint and clear vision for the future of modern spend management systems. As payments, AI and enterprise software increasingly converge, we believe Payhawk is well positioned to emerge as a leader in this rapidly evolving market. We are excited to partner with the team as they continue to scale globally and enter their next phase of growth,” said James Hayward, Managing Director within Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, who is also joining Payhawk’s Board of Directors.

articles.title: Como desbloquear uma pessoa no TikTok • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Como desbloquear uma pessoa no TikTok
Se você desbloquear alguém no TikTok, a pessoa voltará a ter acesso ao seu perfil, enviar mensagens e interagir com seus vídeos
Se você mudou de ideia e quer desbloquear uma pessoa no TikTok, o processo pode ser feito pelo aplicativo no celular ou pela versão web. No app, basta acessar as configurações de privacidade para gerenciar as contas restritas, enquanto no PC é preciso localizar o perfil desejado para desfazer a restrição.
Após o desbloqueio no TikTok, o usuário recupera o acesso ao seu perfil, podendo visualizar seus vídeos e interagir novamente nas publicações abertas ao público. Vale lembrar que a plataforma não restabelece o vínculo de seguidores automaticamente, exigindo que ambos voltem a se seguir para retomar o contato antigo.
A seguir, o Tecnoblog te explica como desbloquear alguém no TikTok pelo celular e pelo PC.
Você consegue desbloquear uma pessoa no TikTok pelo aplicativo, acessando a lista de restrições nas configurações da conta. Veja o passo a passo no celular Android ou iPhone.
Abra o aplicativo do TikTok no seu smartphone e toque em “Perfil”, no canto inferior direito da tela.
Toque no botão de três riscos, no canto superior direito, e selecione a opção “Configurações e privacidade”.
Navegue até a seção “Visibilidade” e toque na opção “Contas bloqueadas”.
Encontre o usuário restrito na lista e toque no botão “Desbloquear”. Assim, ele poderá voltar a ver seu perfil nas buscas e seus vídeos publicados no TikTok.
Você pode desbloquear alguém no TikTok pelo PC acessando diretamente o perfil do contato restrito. Para isso, siga os seguintes passos:
Ao desbloquear alguém no TikTok, você remove imediatamente as restrições impostas anteriormente, mas a plataforma não restaura automaticamente o vínculo entre os perfis. Veja o que muda após essa ação:
Não, o usuário não volta a seguir você automaticamente após o desbloqueio. Como a ação de bloquear alguém no TikTok rompe o vínculo entre os perfis na base de dados da rede, é preciso clicar em “Seguir” novamente para restabelecer o contato.
Se o seu perfil no TikTok estiver configurado como uma conta privada, o usuário desbloqueado precisará enviar uma nova solicitação para acompanhar suas publicações. Nesse caso, o acesso ao seu conteúdo só será liberado após a sua aprovação manual nas notificações.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review
articles.text:
Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort.
This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI, a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple.
The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers.
Just another day in a thrilling life of crime.
Rockstar
Just another day in a thrilling life of crime.
Rockstar
The family that moves furniture together stays together.
Rockstar
The family that moves furniture together stays together.
Rockstar
Just another day in a thrilling life of crime.
Rockstar
The family that moves furniture together stays together.
Rockstar
But it’s the scenes between the over-the-top and somewhat repetitive action scenes that really make this Grand Theft Auto stand out. Almost every explosive gunfight or high-speed car chase is counterpointed by a sublimely dull, lightly interactive moment of mere routine existence: grilling burgers with pals by the water, playing fetch with a random dog, helping a neighbor tune up a car, or joking around over 18 holes of mini golf.
Taken together, the juxtaposition lends a sense of surreal hyperreality to the goings-on in Vice City and its environs. Each of the game’s two sides gives the other a chance to breathe, forming a series of emotional peaks and valleys that stretch across a truly gargantuan amount of detailed simulation and pure gaming content.
Grand Theft Auto VI never lets you get too settled with a budding life of crime or a budding family life. And it’s all the better for it.
The couple you love to love
A large part of why this works so well is Jason and Lucia, the dual protagonists whose relationship drives the story. While that relationship starts off a bit awkwardly—thanks chiefly to Lucia’s brief prison stint—it quickly develops into a true criminal and life partnership. Both sides of the relationship are driven by a mutual desire to move up in the criminal world and eventually settle down to a legit family life, if they can just earn enough from the next big score.
I can’t tell who’s in this screenshot because of the bandanas.
Rockstar
I can’t tell who’s in this screenshot because of the bandanas.
Rockstar
The love of a good woman makes the dull Jason downright tolerable.
Rockstar
The love of a good woman makes the dull Jason downright tolerable.
Rockstar
I can’t tell who’s in this screenshot because of the bandanas.
Rockstar
The love of a good woman makes the dull Jason downright tolerable.
Rockstar
Of the two, Jason is definitely the duller partner. An ex-military meathead with a ripped body and a dull, affect-free vocal delivery, a decent chunk of Jason’s lines essentially boil down to “Yeah, sure, that’s fine.” While the game struggles to expose a bit of a tender and thoughtful side hiding underneath Jason’s cool demeanor, the writing can’t quite break through the emotionless masculine facade that Jason wears as a semi-permanent mask.
Lucia is much more interesting as a vivacious and amiable Latina eager to grab any opportunity presented to her. The game takes some time to dig into the difficulties of Lucia’s underprivileged youth and highlight her strained relationship with an unreliable mother, helping to add some important depth to her chip-on-her-shoulder journey of self-improvement. And even the boring Jason seems that much more appealing seen through the lens of Lucia’s good-natured teasing and genuine affection.
While Jason and Lucia can and do operate independently—and the game lets you change between them frequently—it’s their moments of togetherness that really stand out. There’s an easy, rom-com comfort to their time together, whether they’re discussing their future on the couch (“I feel like I haven’t done anything normal in a minute”), taking some time for quick romance (the game cuts away before things get too hot and heavy), or laying down covering fire for each other during a firefight (the lack of a co-op mode for these missions feels truly baffling).
You jump, I jump, Jack. Er, Jason.
Rockstar
You jump, I jump, Jack. Er, Jason.
Rockstar
It’s important that your significant other be a good hang.
Rockstar
It’s important that your significant other be a good hang.
Rockstar
You jump, I jump, Jack. Er, Jason.
Rockstar
It’s important that your significant other be a good hang.
Rockstar
There’s a minor relationship simulation component to the game, with a simple “heart level” that can rise or fall based on some basic decisions. Don’t expect a lot of dating-sim style drama, though; as long as you make the completely obvious choices when they’re presented, it’s hard to let the relationship fall apart. That’s a good thing, too, because this is a relationship that’s easy to root for, even when the participants are literally getting away with murder.
Hitting and missing
In true Grand Theft Auto fashion, Jason and Lucia’s particular way of chasing The American Dream is through a life of crime. Their travels through the criminal underworld start off kind of slow, as Lucia’s begging gradually compels Jason to reluctantly introduce her to the two-bit operators with which he’s found himself involved.
For the first half of the game, the pair are constantly interacting with a rogues’ gallery of new criminal acquaintances, each more over-the-top than the last, and all of them having specific needs that somehow only Jason and Lucia can fulfill. Many of the missions these small-time crooks have on offer end up feeling like the criminal equivalent of errands—drive here, take that, lose the cops, repeat.
And while a few standout characters develop complex interpersonal relationships with Jason and Lucia over multiple missions, most of these early side characters feel like one-note caricatures that can be distilled to a few tropey traits.
It isn’t until the back half of the game that the main storyline really starts to focus on what it does best: integrating Jason and Lucia into a persistent ring of professional criminals working toward bigger and bigger scores. Here, the missions build on each other, with characters going undercover, casing targets, and learning new skills that eventually come together in some truly tense and bombastic heists. These missions also do the best job of showing off the dual protagonist system, frequently shifting the perspective between Jason and Lucia to highlight their different skills and views on how things are going down.
Ah, great, who are these yahoos…
Credit:
Rockstar
Ah, great, who are these yahoos…
Credit:
Rockstar
Outside of this core plot, though, many of the missions and side stories in GTA VI make Jason and Lucia feel like side characters in their own story. I found myself beginning to tune out during some of the many missions in which one or both protagonists serve as glorified security props or overpaid getaway drivers amid other characters’ contrived turf wars. And even dozens of hours into the game, there were still missions that felt like tutorials, seemingly built around the opportunity to introduce some new simulation system or control scheme.
Through it all, the game can’t seem to totally shake the style of sophomoric humor that feels a lot less “edgy” today than it did when Grand Theft Auto III hit back in 2001 (for players who are old enough to remember that release, at least). There are countless extended bits where the entire joke seems to boil down to “Man, kinky sex is weird, isn’t it?” or “Hey look, it’s a male penis (or something that looks similar to one).” And the game seems to take particular pleasure in forcing Jason into uncomfortable situations with plenty of T&A, much to Lucia’s good-natured bemusement.
A word of warning for parents: This is a game that definitely earns a hard “M for Mature” rating and shows how standards for that rating have shifted since GTA: San Andreasearned an AO re-rating for hiding a single sex scene amid its legacy code.
Grand Theft Auto VI gets a lot less safe for work than this, let me tell you (but not show you).
Credit:
Rockstar
Grand Theft Auto VI gets a lot less safe for work than this, let me tell you (but not show you).
Credit:
Rockstar
There are moments where GTA VI’s satire cuts a bit deeper. I especially liked a couple of side stories that skewered buzzword-spewing crypto bros and multi-level marketing schemes with some welcome over-the-top excess. Overall, though, the game’s warmed-over one-liner takes on “wokeness” felt about as fresh as jokes about mothers-in-law and TV dinners, without much in the way of thought-provoking statements on society as a whole in 2026.
What do you want to do?
Grand Theft Auto VI has a gift for finding excuses to lure you into an expertly designed space and then throwing together a reason for why you have to shoot/punch your way out. That might sound snarky, but I actually mean it more or less sincerely; I was frequently surprised by the scenarios the writers dreamed up to turn what seemed like a routine trip to some beautiful locale into a firefight with way more armed goons than seems strictly necessary.
The moment-to-moment shooting will feel very familiar to Grand Theft Auto fans, by which I mean it’s dead simple to hide behind convenient cover and pop up to pick off relatively stupid enemies one by one with a dizzying array of available weaponry. The rare enemies that do manage to flank you seem to have incredibly bad aim, even at close range, and both Jason and Lucia can take a whole lot more punishment than the average quick-to-crumble grunt.
*Making car engine revving noises with my lips* BRRRRRRRRRRRMMMMMM!
Rockstar
*Making car engine revving noises with my lips* BRRRRRRRRRRRMMMMMM!
Rockstar
Eyes on the road, Lucia!
Rockstar
Eyes on the road, Lucia!
Rockstar
*Making car engine revving noises with my lips* BRRRRRRRRRRRMMMMMM!
Rockstar
Eyes on the road, Lucia!
Rockstar
Driving around town is significantly more exciting—you’ll be darting between cars in heavy traffic to chase down antagonists, avoid the police, or simply get where you’re going faster. It’s still a blast to sample as many vehicles as you can, from zippy but easy-to-wreck sports cars to tank-like trucks that can plow through traffic, tiny motorbikes that can squeeze through tight spaces, and off-road vehicles that can explore off the beaten path.
Driving through the city also offers ample opportunities to get distracted from your main goals by dozens of side activities that dot the map. Even as I struggled to work through the story on deadline, I found myself getting sucked in for hours trying to master drone racing, chasing gold medals in countless mud-splattered rally races, or hunting for one of the many meditation spots hidden in out-of-the-way corners.
While most of these side activities offer money or improve character stats, some are simply there to be experienced. Completionists will have a bear of a time tracking down every single hidden collectible, rare car, robbable location, and beautiful landmark the developers have placed throughout the city. Grand Theft Auto VI seems set to be one of those games you can just load up to hang out in long after the main story missions are done.
A technical marvel
Even with a fast vehicle, much of that “hang out” time can be spent simply crossing the game’s massive map. Getting from the depths of the wilderness in the north to the tip of the keys in the south is a six-plus-mile trip (measured at an apparently real-world-accurate scale) that can take 10 minutes to weave your way across on a good traffic day. During these cross-city treks, the tenor of the city’s architecture morphs noticeably as you pass from rich gated communities through the glitzy skyscraper-laden downtown and on to downtrodden neighborhoods, backwoods swamps, and laid-back island beach communities.
As nice as Vice City’s outdoor architecture is, GTA VI’s interiors are where the game’s developers really show off. Practically every story mission seems to introduce a new cavernous indoor space that’s fully furnished and lovingly crafted to look naturally lived-in and also utterly unlike anything you’ve seen before. And while you can’t go into every one of the thousands of buildings you pass on the streets of Vice City, you can enter a surprisingly large number, each with its own distinct layout and decorations.
I dare you to try to count the number of people in this scene.
Credit:
Rockstar
I dare you to try to count the number of people in this scene.
Credit:
Rockstar
Another element that makes all these spaces feel lived-in is the game’s surprisingly detailed crowd system. Grand Theft Auto VI sometimes packs over a hundred non-player characters into a single space, with no two characters looking or acting alike in size, shape, dress, or animation. Working your way through these crowds can be integral to some of the game’s missions, but even when you’re just casually exploring, it’s fun to take advantage of eavesdropping opportunities, listening in on individual conversations that build into overlapping chatter (realistically muffled through walls and over distance).
Grand Theft Auto VI’s spaces also seem specifically designed to show off the game’s incredible lighting system, which really shines on a PS5 Pro. The effect is most apparent at night, when car headlights streaming through a window or the rotating blue-and-red of a cop car can cast the entire world in an otherworldly glow.
But even in “normal” lighting conditions, I’d occasionally find myself slack-jawed at the details: a laptop screen partially reflected in a character’s glasses, the way rotating pyrotechnic laser effects played across dancers in a crowded club, the fluttering shadows cast by a leafy tree near sunset, or the finger smudges visible on your cell phone in bright sunshine.
Dance Floor Jason is activated by purple light.
Rockstar
Dance Floor Jason is activated by purple light.
Rockstar
Just another day in paradise.
Rockstar
Just another day in paradise.
Rockstar
Look at that headlight halo. Just look at it!
Rockstar
Look at that headlight halo. Just look at it!
Rockstar
Just another day in paradise.
Rockstar
Look at that headlight halo. Just look at it!
Rockstar
I know we said we wanted to shoot your photograph in natural light, but maybe we could go somewhere different?
Rockstar
Check out those long shadows as the sun gets low.
Rockstar
I could watch these clouds crawl across the sky all day.
Rockstar
#nofilter
Rockstar
I could go on and on about the little “attention to detail” touches that add up to a more engaging world simulation. Characters who fall in the dirt get dust on only the specific parts of their clothes that hit the ground. Older characters look distinctly wrinkly, with veins that show through their thinning skin. Fabric and hair flow naturally in the wind and as characters move. Rain beads on car roofs and drips off overhangs during a storm.
Through it all, one moment really stood out to me. As I prepared for an upcoming firefight, I had Lucia start eating some chips to buff her health. Halfway through the bag, I had her pick up a nearby soda, too. At first, Lucia held the chip bag in one hand and used the other to pick out individual chips. But once that other hand was occupied with a soda, she started shaking the bag above her head to pour the chips directly into her mouth.
When I thought about the effort that went into coding and recording that specific animation for such a highly specific edge case, I thought about the millions of man-hours that went into making Grand Theft Auto VI the ultimate expression of this kind of urban crime/life sim. It might be a long time before we see this level of focused effort on a singular interactive vision again.
Kyle Orland has been the Senior Gaming Editor at Ars Technica since 2012, writing primarily about the business, tech, and culture behind video games. He has journalism and computer science degrees from University of Maryland. He once wrote a whole book about Minesweeper.
E.g. light gets distorted when it passes through the water in (some) drinking vessels, open glass doors show the reflection of things which are not currently visible to the player, hair looks and moves realistically, etc.
Lots and lots of ray tracing and complex physics, all running in realtime at 30ps on a six-year old platform with the (rough) equivalent of a 2-year old mid-range GPU bolted onto it.
View: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ULM2OIj5o0I
GTA6 may look like a high-end CGI rendering, but the breadth of what they're achieving within that game engine is impressive, and goes a long way to explaining both the time and cost needed to build GTA6.

articles.title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
articles.text:
AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
- Date:
- November 14, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.
- Share:
More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.
Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.
The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.
AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss
The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.
Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.
Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.
Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.
The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.
"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."
Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict
Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.
Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.
For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.
Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.
"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."
The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening
Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.
But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.
The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.
At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.
"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."
The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.
How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns
Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.
The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.
The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.
This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.
"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."
Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.
"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."
From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments
The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.
Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.
Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.
These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.
For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.
Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.
Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?
Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.
Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.
Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.
"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."
