articles.title: La empresa de Elon Musk presentó propuestas de IA ante nueve organismos del Gobierno de Chile
articles.text:
SpaceXAI, la compañía que reúne los negocios espaciales de SpaceX y de inteligencia artificial xAI, sostuvo nueve reuniones con organismos del Gobierno de Chile para presentar propuestas vinculadas con IA.
Las audiencias se habrían realizado entre el 6 de julio y el 14 de octubre de 2026, de acuerdo con los registros de la Ley de Lobby revisados por Diario Financiero.
La actividad llama la atención por el alcance de los contactos: las reuniones abarcaron ministerios y subsecretarías de áreas como salud, energía, economía, trabajo, previsión social, niñez y obras públicas.
La presencia de la empresa de Elon Musk en dependencias estatales chilenas coincide con la expansión de las aplicaciones de inteligencia artificial en procesos administrativos, servicios públicos y sistemas de atención.
SpaceXAI tuvo reuniones en nueve reparticiones públicas
Las audiencias se distribuyeron en nueve organismos del Estado chileno. SpaceXAI se reunió con autoridades de los ministerios de Obras Públicas, Salud y Energía.
La empresa también acudió a las subsecretarías de la Niñez, Previsión Social, Servicios Sociales, Economía y Hacienda. La lista se completa con la Dirección del Trabajo.
Los registros muestran que el objetivo de los encuentros fue presentar propuestas relacionadas con inteligencia artificial. No se detallaron públicamente los proyectos, herramientas o servicios específicos expuestos ante cada repartición.
La amplitud de las áreas involucradas abre distintos escenarios de aplicación. Obras Públicas administra proyectos de infraestructura; Salud opera redes y sistemas de atención; Energía trabaja con planificación y regulación sectorial. Las subsecretarías y la Dirección del Trabajo, por su parte, atienden ámbitos asociados con políticas sociales, economía, empleo y fiscalización.
Neil Perkins participó en las nueve audiencias
El representante de SpaceXAI en los nueve encuentros fue Neil Perkins, quien figura en LinkedIn como Líder de Salida al Mercado para Gobiernos Globales de la compañía desde marzo de 2026.
Su cargo está orientado al vínculo entre las soluciones de la empresa y las administraciones públicas de distintos países. Diario Financiero, el medio que reveló la información, contactó a Perkins mediante LinkedIn para conocer el propósito concreto de las reuniones y las propuestas presentadas ante las autoridades chilenas, pero no obtuvo respuesta.
La falta de detalles públicos limita el alcance de la información disponible. Los registros de lobby permiten identificar las fechas, las instituciones y la representación de la empresa, aunque no incluyen una descripción técnica de las soluciones de IA que se abordaron en cada reunión.
Tampoco se informó de acuerdos, contratos, licitaciones o programas que hayan surgido de las audiencias. Las reuniones constituyen presentaciones ante funcionarios públicos, no la confirmación de una implementación estatal.
xAI desarrolló Grok, el modelo de lenguaje del conglomerado
SpaceXAI reúne los negocios de cohetes de SpaceX y los de inteligencia artificial de xAI. Esta última desarrolló Grok, un modelo de lenguaje de gran tamaño integrado en el conglomerado de Musk.
Los modelos de lenguaje procesan texto y generan respuestas a partir de instrucciones escritas. Sus posibles usos abarcan la clasificación de documentos, asistentes virtuales, atención al público, búsqueda de información y automatización de tareas administrativas. Cada aplicación en servicios estatales requiere definir qué datos se utilizan, qué controles existen sobre las respuestas y qué responsabilidades mantiene la institución que adopta la tecnología.
Las nueve audiencias en Chile se produjeron en un periodo de poco más de tres meses. El primer registro corresponde al 6 de julio y el último al 14 de octubre de 2026.
La actividad institucional de la compañía ocurre mientras SpaceX mantiene otro frente de desarrollo tecnológico: el sistema Starship. El 14 de noviembre de 2026, la nave superior regresó a la Tierra tras un vuelo de más de 22 horas y 14 vueltas alrededor del planeta, y fue capturada por la torre de lanzamiento en Texas.
SpaceX mantiene su apuesta por vehículos reutilizables
El sistema Starship está formado por el propulsor Super Heavy y la nave superior. Ambos fueron diseñados para regresar a la plataforma y ser recuperados por brazos mecánicos de una torre que la empresa denomina Mechazilla.
Durante la prueba de noviembre, SpaceX recuperó la nave superior, aunque el propulsor Super Heavy cayó en el golfo de México después de que se abortara su intento de retorno. La captura del propulsor ya se había logrado en octubre de 2024.
El objetivo de la empresa es reutilizar los vehículos para reducir los costos de acceso al espacio. Sin embargo, la recuperación es solo una etapa: SpaceX todavía debe demostrar que puede inspeccionar, reparar y preparar los sistemas para nuevos vuelos con menos trabajo y gasto que fabricar unidades nuevas.
Mientras esos desarrollos continúan, las reuniones de SpaceXAI con organismos chilenos dejan abierta la posibilidad de nuevas conversaciones sobre el uso de inteligencia artificial en el sector público.

articles.title: From Olympic figure skater to entrepreneur: Sportlogiq’s Craig Buntin is back to help automate homebuilding with Rise | BetaKit
articles.text:
Since retiring from figure skating in 2010, Craig Buntin has not lost his edge or stopped to catch his breath. Entrepreneurship was an obvious next step for the three-time Canadian national champion and former Olympic pairs skater, who is not one to rest on his laurels.
Buntin’s first foray into business was a coffee-tea fusion company named Teabean that he managed to get into 100 cafes across Montréal before eventually selling out to his distributor.
Craig Buntin’s mom taught him how to chase his dreams. His latest one involves helping Canada build homes faster with robots.
His second, a Montréal-based AI-powered hockey analytics software startup called Sportlogiq, raised the stakes and stoked his interest in technology. He co-built Sportlogiq into a platform that helped nearly every NHL team track, analyze, and optimize on-ice performance, culminating in an exit to larger US peer Teamworks earlier this year.
After that, Buntin immediately began working on another AI startup, Rise Automation, to tackle what might be his biggest challenge yet: putting a dent in Canada’s housing crisis by helping custom millwork, cabinetry, and precast concrete factories deploy robots.
The Montréal-based Mila spinout closed $2.4 million CAD in previously unannounced pre-seed funding in July—from BDC Capital’s Industrial Innovation Venture Fund, Developer Capital, and Cycle Capital—to build the AI-powered software “coordination layer” that small shops need to automate parts of the homebuilding process. That simple agreement for future equity financing, Rise’s first round to date, was supported by undisclosed angels and clients.
In an exclusive interview with BetaKit, Buntin unpacked his journey from figure skating to repeat entrepreneurship, and talked about where he plans to go from here as co-founder and CEO of Rise.
Finding his edge
Buntin, a Kelowna native, began figure skating when he was 10 because he wanted to learn how to play hockey. Despite being late to the party—most of his peers had started at six or seven—he quickly demonstrated a knack for the sport. After successfully landing his first jump on one foot in hockey skates as a small crowd of coaches, peers, and parents cheered, he was hooked.
Buntin and his older brother Jamie were raised by a single mother with limited means. A week into his figure-skating career, his mom, Jan, who worked as an office manager, sat him down after receiving her first bill to gauge his passion. According to Buntin, she said, “‘Look, if you really love this, I’ll support you. We’ll pay the bill, we’ll keep going. If not, there’s 100 other sports that are way less expensive that we could manage.’”
“I told her right there that I wanted to go to the Olympics, and that was it for me,” he said. “I never had a Plan B … That’s what I was in love with, and that’s what I was immediately dedicated to doing.”
Buntin struck a deal with his mom that, for as long as he worked hard and loved the sport, their family would make the necessary sacrifices to support his ambitions. Over the next 20 years, that’s exactly what they did. He put everything he had into achieving that goal; to help finance his efforts, his mom sold her house and his brother took on three jobs. During high school, Buntin spent his spare time working as a bus boy, washing trucks, and serving as the mascot of the local major junior hockey team, the Kelowna Rockets.
“We pushed so that I could do it, and I think she taught me how to chase my dreams and to focus on that massive north star,” Buntin said. He is grateful to have had the chance to travel the globe and represent Canada at seven World Championships and the 2006 Winter Olympics, and is glad that he retired feeling like he left nothing on the table.
Buntin sees many parallels between competitive sports and entrepreneurship. Both require setting a mission and relentlessly pursuing it “no matter how many times you fall down.”
RELATED: Teamworks, the “operating system for sports,” buys hockey analytics platform Sportlogiq
“When you go to the Olympics, you’re standing at center ice and you’re either going to win and become a hero or lose and nobody’s going to remember you,” Buntin said. “[The] idea of entrepreneurship is you’re going to work hard, make good decisions, and win, or you’re going to lose it all. It always felt really natural.”
During the final months of his figure-skating career, Buntin began toying with the idea of building a company. He began working on Teabean full-time a day after hanging up his skates. Despite lacking an undergraduate degree, he simultaneously managed to gain entry into and complete McGill University’s MBA program, which led to him focusing on Sportlogiq, which was officially founded in 2015.
From sports to sports tech
Sportlogiq’s first investor was local venture studio TandemLaunch. An old YouTube video of one of Buntin’s 2008 figure-skating performances helped convince TandemLaunch founder, managing partner, and CEO Helge Seetzen that he was a good bet.
That video showed a Paris competition where his partner Meagan Duhamel’s skate accidentally sliced the back of Buntin’s hand mid-routine. He returned minutes later, bandaged but still visibly bloodied, and the duo finished their dance to a standing ovation, ultimately securing bronze. “He’s like, ‘Yeah, this is the guy that I’m backing … Regardless of what tech, I know that this founder will bleed and keep going,’” Buntin said.
“Clearly he was not somebody who would give up easily,” Seetzen told BetaKit over email, adding that “his level of drive can go a long way.”
RELATED: TandemLaunch closes $37-million Fund IV to create and back deep tech startups
Sportlogiq uses a patented combination of AI and computer vision to pull player movement and activity data directly from standard video feeds, make it easy to parse, and derive deeper insights that coaches can use to scout, strategize, and improve performance, and broadcasters can leverage for storytelling. The startup’s tech, which has become ubiquitous in professional hockey, is also used at the college and amateur levels, and in football and soccer.
The company, which raised approximately $28 million to fuel its efforts, had a near-death experience during the early days of COVID-19, when the pandemic temporarily shut down the sports world and its sales cratered. “This is where I earned my grey hairs,” Buntin said. That stretch came post-Series B, shortly after Sportlogiq had made some big investments in expanding beyond professional hockey, forcing the firm to kill those initiatives in an effort to conserve cash. Buntin credits Sportlogiq’s team for pulling together and quickly adjusting during this period.
RELATED: AI investment firm DevCap closes $5 million as it eyes public listing
Sportlogiq was able to weather this storm and find its footing once again as a profitable, 80-person firm with more than $10 million in annual recurring revenue and a particularly attractive data-capture engine.
While the financial terms of Sportlogiq’s January 2026 acquisition by Teamworks were not disclosed, Buntin claimed it was a “sizeable” win for the firm’s founders, staff, and investors by Montréal ecosystem standards.
Tackling the housing crisis with robots
During Sportlogiq’s final days as an independent company, Buntin started working on Rise. He noted that building homes in Canada, let alone buying them, is an expensive and time-consuming process. “It’s a massive societal crisis right now,” Buntin said, and it’s one he’s particularly passionate about.
His mom selling her house to support his dream is certainly a factor. “I’ll never forget her pride in knowing it was hers, a home that would appreciate over time,” Buntin said. “You can’t underestimate how empowering that is after decades of living paycheque to paycheque.”
Buntin is also motivated by the chance to make homeownership more affordable for the next generation of Canadians, and thinks Rise offers his best chance yet “to make the most meaningful impact.”
He initially set out to help by developing sustainable building materials like carbon-negative drywall and robots to install them, but while those components can be expensive, he said that price pales in comparison to the cost of labour; Canada’s residential construction sector currently faces a severe shortage of workers.
“Homes are a manufacturing problem: the cabinets, millwork, and concrete that go into them are made in factories, and in the shops we work with, the machines sit idle about 90 percent of the week,” Buntin said. “Running them three shifts would take triple the workforce, but [there] are only about 40,000 open manufacturing jobs today. Intelligent robots close that gap.”
This led the startup to refocus on retrofitting existing shops. He co-founded Rise with chief scientific officer Liam Paull and chief innovation officer Charlie Gauthier, two researchers connected to local AI research institute Mila (Paull is an associate professor at the University of Montréal, while Gauthier is a student at Mila under him). Gauthier is developing Rise’s core tech as her PhD thesis. Buntin described it as an AI memory and mapping software system that enables robotic orchestration.
“[The] idea of entrepreneurship is you’re going to work hard, make good decisions, and win, or you’re going to lose it all. It always felt really natural.”
Craig Buntin, Rise
Mila’s managing director of AI ventures, Stéphane Marceau, said Buntin was the AI research institute’s first founder-in-residence. “What stood out early was his empirical and humble approach to building the business,” he told BetaKit over email. “He spent significant time with manufacturers, observing their operations and understanding their problems in detail before jumping to solutions.”
Most of the factories that Rise has set its sights on are not currently using robots. They have lots of unused capacity and could also stand to gain by automating some of their core daily tasks, Buntin said. But after spending a few months embedded inside some of these sites, he quickly realized that industry was “nowhere near ready for automation.”
Buntin said many factories contain “the same type of chaos as hockey,” with operations that are heavily reliant upon the institutional know-how of longstanding staff. By either setting up video cameras of its own or leveraging existing feeds inside these facilities and deriving insight from them using its tech, Rise sees room to help floor managers better understand what’s happening in their shops and the potential return on investment of automation.
“I think of it a little bit like Sportlogiq for your factory,” Buntin said. That pitch has begun resonating, as the now six-person startup is set to install its tech at its fifth factory by the end of November. That marks the first step in Rise’s game plan. The next step is connecting these factories with partner third-party robotics firms like Laval, QC-based Omnirobotic and providing the “human-robot interface” or “coordination layer” necessary to retrofit their sites for these robots. While it has begun doing the latter, its progress on this front remains early.
A scarcity of egocentric data remains a key barrier to more widespread deployment of robots capable of consistently executing real-world tasks. Buntin is betting another firm will win that race, and positioning Rise as not only an infrastructure player that other manufacturing robotics firms can plug into but a potential sales channel for them.
For the shops Rise is selling to, the pitch is simple: the chance to boost their capacity and reduce their costs. With Rise, Buntin hopes to help Canada tackle some huge challenges, from housing costs to construction timelines, while also trying its best to bring workers along for the ride, rather than displacing them.
“We’ve got a mountain in front of us,” Buntin said. He’s excited to embark on another climb.
Feature image courtesy Rise Automation.

articles.title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
articles.text:
This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
Osmo’s smell model is already being used in the fragrance industry. But are medical diagnostics and threat detection a sniff too far?
In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”
“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”
In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.
Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.
A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.
Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)
The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.
Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.
But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication.
Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.
But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”
In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies.
For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.
“There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. "So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”

articles.title: Banco do Brasil alerta sobre vazamento de dados; saiba o que foi exposto
articles.text:
O Banco do Brasil (BB) identificou acesso não autorizado a informações pessoais de clientes e emitiu alerta nesta quinta-feira (18). Segundo o g1, o incidente ocorreu em 12 de novembro e envolveu dados cadastrais que podem ser utilizados por criminosos em tentativas de golpes.
Em comunicado enviado aos correntistas, a instituição informou que as informações expostas podem incluir nome, CPF, endereço de e-mail, número da agência e, em alguns casos, número da conta.
O banco ressaltou que não houve invasão de seus sistemas e que senhas e códigos de segurança não foram comprometidos. Também não foram identificadas transações financeiras relacionadas ao incidente.
Segundo as apurações, terceiros utilizaram indevidamente uma credencial válida para acessar os dados. O Banco do Brasil afirmou que revogou a credencial, interrompendo o acesso não autorizado, e acionou seus protocolos de segurança assim que identificou o problema.
A instituição também informou que está reforçando o monitoramento e adotando medidas de segurança, privacidade e proteção de dados, incluindo as notificações previstas na Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD).
Quais dados dos clientes do Banco do Brasil foram expostos?
De acordo com o comunicado, as informações que podem ter sido acessadas incluem:
- Nome;
- CPF;
- Endereço de e-mail;
- Número da agência;
- Número da conta, em alguns casos.
O banco afirma que senhas e códigos de segurança não foram expostos. Também não há registro de movimentações financeiras decorrentes do episódio.
Leia mais:
- Visa confirma incidente de cibersegurança após ameaça de hackers
- Visitou um site atacado por hacker? Saiba o que fazer para proteger seus dados
- Falha no Java coloca sistemas de governos e empresas em alerta mundial
Vazamento de dados pode facilitar golpes
Apesar de não envolver senhas ou códigos de segurança, a exposição de informações cadastrais pode facilitar tentativas de fraude.
Com dados pessoais e informações de contato, criminosos podem tentar se passar pelo banco para enganar clientes e convencê-los a fornecer informações confidenciais. Uma das práticas utilizadas nesse tipo de ataque é o phishing, que consiste em criar mensagens, links ou páginas falsas para roubar dados pessoais e financeiros.
Por isso, o Banco do Brasil orienta os correntistas a redobrar a atenção com mensagens e contatos suspeitos. “O BB não solicita senhas, códigos de segurança, instalação de aplicativos ou movimentações financeiras para supostas contas seguras”, destacou a instituição no comunicado.
Como denunciar mensagens suspeitas?
O banco orienta que mensagens e links suspeitos, assim como páginas falsas que utilizem seu nome, sejam denunciados pelo endereço [email protected].
A instituição afirma que as denúncias permitem tomar medidas junto a serviços de hospedagem e provedores de acesso e conteúdo na internet.
Em caso de dúvidas, os clientes podem procurar os canais oficiais do Banco do Brasil:
- Aplicativo: opção Fale Com;
- WhatsApp: 4001-0001;
- Central de Relacionamento: 4004-0001;
- Central de Relacionamento: 0800 729 0001.
Posicionamento oficial do BB
O Olhar Digital entrou em contato com o Banco do Brasil, que respondeu que acionou seus protocolos de segurança para promover a proteção dos dados de seus correntistas.
“O Banco do Brasil informa que não houve invasão aos sistemas, exposição de senhas, tokens ou códigos de segurança, nem transações financeiras decorrentes do incidente. A empresa acionou imediatamente os seus protocolos de segurança, incluindo procedimentos adicionais de monitoração e medidas de segurança, privacidade e proteção de dados”, explicou.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Geely trae a España el Monjaro EM-i Ultra: su nuevo SUV híbrido enchufable de más de 300 CV
articles.text:
Monjaro EM-i Ultra. Quédate con este nombre de nuevo SUV de Geely Auto, puesto que va a dar mucho que hablar, tanto por prestaciones como por precio. El fabricante trae a España su SUV híbrido con una carta de presentación bastante interesante: 334 CV, tracción total eléctrica, un motor 1.5T y tres motores eléctricos, desarrolla 667 Nm de par y una aceleración de 0 a 100 km/h en 5,8 segundos... todo ello a un precio bastante competitivo.
Con la llegada del Monjaro EM-i Ultra, Geely ya suma en España cuatro modelos disponibles en su catálogo, aunque este SUV que acaba de presentar la marca es sin duda su buque insignia y su tope de gama, al menos de momento. Es un modelo bastante interesante, teniendo en cuenta que se trata de UN SUV de 4.800 mm de longitud, 1.895 mm de anchura y 1.700 mm de altura, con una distancia entre ejes de 2.845 mm, bastante en línea con las medidas que busca el conductor español que busca un coche de este segmento.
En este sentido, el Monjaro EM-i Ultra tiene una altura libre al suelo de 189 mm y ángulos de ataque y salida de 19° y 18°, todo ello dentro de un diseño enfocado a la seguridad, tanto en carretera como en caminos y terrenos más exigentes. Monta llantas de 20 pulgadas optimizadas aerodinámicamente y remata su diseño exterior una suerte de trazado ascendente de las luces diurnas, un voladizo delantero corto y una firma LED a lo ancho del vehículo en la zaga que dejan clara la presencia de este nuevo SUV.
Híbrido, más de 300 CV y mucha tecnología
Respecto a lo que lleva bajo el capó, el Geely Monjaro EM-i Ultra usa el sistema EM-i Super Hybrid, que según la compañía es uno de los sistemas híbridos enchufables más sofisticados del mundo. En el caso del Monjaro, se compone de un motor turbo de gasolina de 1,5 litros desarrollado específicamente para aplicaciones híbridas enchufables, tres motores eléctricos, una transmisión automática 3DHT, una batería LFP de 29,8 kWh y sistemas inteligentes de gestión y recuperación de energía.
Con todo ello, desarrolla una potencia combinada de 246 kW (334 CV) y un par máximo de 667 Nm, 0 a 100 km/h en 5,8 segundos y una velocidad máxima de 190 km/h (169 km/h en modo eléctrico), con un consumo de combustible ponderado de 2,4 l/100 km en ciclo urbano WLTP.
El Geely Monjaro EM-i Ultra estará disponible en Blanco Imperial (de serie), Negro Volcánico, Gris Titán, Ámbar y Azul Glaciar para su aspecto exterior y en Negro Onyx, de serie, y Arena para el interior. ¿Su precio? Desde 37.990 € en su modalidad al contado.

articles.title: Loblaw is the first Canadian retailer to connect to Muse
articles.text:
Loblaw has become the first Canadian retailer to partner with Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent.
With this functionality, Canadians can have Muse plan meals and order food accordingly from participating Loblaw brands. Meta says Muse is smart enough to remember details like brand preferences and food allergies to make the process smoother.
This comes alongside the recent launch of Muse voice support in Canada, allowing you to have real-time conversations with the agent on mobile, web and Mac.
Personally, I would never have an AI handle shopping for me, especially as Canadian banks like CIBC, RBC and TD block AI agents amid concerns related to unauthorized purchases. Not to mention that Muse itself has had some serious security issues, including most recently accessing people’s encrypted messages. But hey, knock yourself out.
In general, Muse is billed as your sort of personal virtual butler, integrating with apps like Gmail and Google Calendar to handle tasks like scheduling, trip planning, filling out online forms and, yes, making purchases for you.
Image credit: Meta
Source: Meta

articles.title: Felicis leads $7.5M bet on Unsiloed AI to make enterprise documents usable by AI agents | TechCrunch
articles.text:
As businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge. Unsiloed AI has raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Felicis to tackle that problem, aiming to help enterprises make their documents more accessible to AI agents through specialized technology.
Silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures. Angel investors Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner also participated.
Business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately. But getting the information wrong can lead to costly mistakes for businesses, and the impact could be severe in the case of a bank, hospital, or a law firm, as they rely on these documents for their daily work.
Unsiloed aims to solve this problem with software that breaks down complex documents, extracts information from tables, charts, and other elements, and turns it into structured data that AI agents can use. The technology also shows where the extracted information came from in the original document, so businesses can check the results rather than take the AI’s output at face value.
“The problem with LLMs is they’re inherently probabilistic,” said Unsiloed co-founder and CEO Aman Mishra (pictured above, right) in an interview. “There is going to be some deviation induced. There is going to be some hallucination involved, and that has a massive negative impact downstream.”
Mishra co-founded Unsiloed with Adnan Abbas (pictured above, left), his former classmate at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur. The two joined Y Combinator’s Fall 2025 batch after spending some time developing the technology.
Unsiloed is already working with customers in finance, legal services, and healthcare, Mishra told TechCrunch. One bank is using its technology to process documents, while a law firm has deployed it on its own servers to handle contracts and old case files, he said, without naming either customer. Mishra, however, named voice AI startup Bolna AI as a customer, saying it uses Unsiloed to ingest knowledge bases for building voice agents.
The San Francisco-headquartered startup has entered a market that is already crowded and includes specialized document-processing startups such as Reducto and Unstructured, as well as offerings from Microsoft and Amazon. Businesses also sometimes use general-purpose AI models to extract information from documents, giving Unsiloed another set of competitors.
Mishra told TechCrunch that Unsiloed’s advantage lies in how it processes complex documents. The startup uses what it calls “dual-stream” vision models, which handle text and image data separately, along with a technique called “heat map-based chunking” that helps identify the most important parts of a document.
“In one of the streams you have the text tokens, in the other stream you have the exact image tokens,” Mishra said. “This is something that we have spent a lot of time architecting.”
The technology then directs more computing power toward areas such as figures, numbers, and charts. Unsiloed also uses a specialized decoder that takes industry-specific terminology into account, helping it distinguish between terms that can mean different things in different business contexts.
Supporting those claims, Mishra pointed to a test involving 542 financial documents supplied by an enterprise customer. Unsiloed achieved 99.78% accuracy across roughly 84,000 extracted data points, per a technical brief shared by the startup. The test compared Unsiloed with major AI models, Microsoft’s Azure Document Intelligence, and the customer’s in-house extraction tool. The results have, however, not been independently verified.
Unsiloed also claims to have outperformed competing AI document-processing tools on olmOCR-Bench, a public benchmark developed by Allen AI. In tests conducted by the startup, Unsiloed scored 88.0, compared with 66.0 for Reducto’s agentic system and 39.9 for Unstructured. The benchmark covered 1,403 PDF pages and tested how well the systems handled tables, mathematical expressions, scanned documents, and complex layouts.
Unsiloed’s pricing, Mishra said, starts at one cent per page. He asserted that the startup’s approach also helps keep its costs down by directing computing power toward the parts of a document that need the most attention, instead of processing every section in the same way.
Currently, Unsiloed has a headcount of seven people. The startup, Mishra said, plans to use the fresh funding to hire more researchers and engineers, expand its sales efforts, and develop proprietary datasets to improve its technology.

articles.title: China threatens "countermeasures" on the face of new AI GPU rental and export restrictions — Beijing threatens retaliation ahead of Thursday's Xi Jinping meeting, Sino-American trade war may be renewed for a new season
articles.text:
China threatens 'countermeasures' in the face of new AI GPU rental and export restrictions — Beijing threatens retaliation ahead of Thursday's Xi Jinping meeting, Sino-American trade war may be renewed for a new season
"When elephants fight, the grass suffers."
Yesterday, the Trump administration extended the reach of its existing export controls on high-end AI accelerator chips, namely, but not limited to, Nvidia's Blackwell lineup. The updated regulation now requires licenses for renting those chips in large quantities to the entirety of America's D:5 countries list (nations embargoed from arms sales). As expected, the news landed in Beijing like a lead dragon, and its Ministry of Commerce states that China "will take countermeasures to firmly safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."
The bold move taken by the U.S. arrives at a peculiar time, as President Trump is currently visiting the nation for the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Trump is scheduled to meet President Xi Jinping on Thursday, Nov. 19, a tête-a-tête that's bound to be interesting. Both nations were recently embroiled in a bitter trade war, with ever-mounting tariffs and restrictions on both sides until a temporary truce was called in Oct. 2025. Only some restrictions were lifted, though; for example, Chinese semiconductors still face a 50% tariff when imported stateside.
A potential restart of tariff-slapping would all but guarantee an even larger amount of turmoil in U.S. stock markets. Those seas are already choppy enough thanks to Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang's romantic involvement with purported Chinese spy Alice Huang — along with mounting suspicions that the soulmates may have connived to siphon billions' worth of Blackwell chips from her Singaporean outfit Megaspeed onto Chinese AI laboratories.
Nvidia cut off about half of its Asian buyers last July, seemingly in the purview of the export controls, and told data center operators that over 50% of their business must come from non-Chinese companies. Meanwhile, both Malaysia and Singapore have intensified their scrutiny of AI hardware shipments.
China's countermeasures ammo is as of yet unspecified. The nation had restricted the sale of gallium, germanium, and antimony to the U.S. previously, and the truce shelved that bullet until Nov. 2027. Beijing may well choose to simply not renew that agreement when that day comes. Although analysts believe that the nations will be cordial enough during this summit, Trump's perceived provocation may bring China's proverbial nuclear option of restricting rare earth exports back to the loading bay.
The truce on that particular matter only has a few weeks left, expiring on Jan. 10, 2027. Likewise, super-hard materials and high-density lithium batteries, crucial for the newest generations of EVs, solar power storage, and battery installations, all have white flags that will come down early next year. Analysts also expect that Chinese firms and their government will continue to heavily invest in domestic chip production, namely, but not only, by Huawei.
Broadly speaking, the U.S.' updated chip control regulation means that Chinese firms cannot sidestep the existing control on chip sales by renting them instead, closing one of the main existing loopholes around the export restrictions. Additionally, selling chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil now also requires a license, as the U.S. Department of Commerce suspects that companies in these nations import Blackwell cards to sell to China.

articles.title: The overlooked technology that could determine the ROI of enterprise AI
articles.text:
The overlooked technology that could determine the ROI of enterprise AI
How trusted information and context determine enterprise AI ROI
Enterprises have spent the last few years racing to adopt AI tools across their processes and workflows. As AI moves from simply answering questions to making decisions and taking action, another technology will play a surprisingly important role in determining whether those investments pay off: document management.
Ryan Barry is SVP of Finance & Strategic Operations at M-Files. Ian Story is Principal Architect, OneDrive & SharePoint at Microsoft.
Companies worldwide are making significant investments in AI. Recent forecasts show that AI spending will reach $2.5 trillion in 2026, however, organizations that spend heavily on models, infrastructure, and applications without addressing the information layer underneath them risk eroding the return on those investments by giving AI inaccurate information or amplifying costly errors.
It’s no longer a question of what AI can do; it’s whether AI has the right information to do it well. That is a document management problem.
AI’s context problem
Most enterprises don’t have a shortage of information – they have too much of it.
Years of collaboration have produced enormous volumes of documents across shared drives, business applications, collaboration platforms, and individual workspaces. While collaboration tools have made it easier for employees to create and share information, they have also made it harder to know what can actually be trusted.
There may be multiple versions of the same contract, an outdated policy saved next to a current one, or other guidance on how to handle an exception buried somewhere that only a few employees know to look for.
Humans are generally pretty good at navigating this mess. We know who owns a particular process, which version of a document is the right one, and when an exception applies. Most of that knowledge comes from experience and context that may never be written down. However, AI does come pre-loaded with this understanding, it must be provided thoughtfully.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
This increasingly matters as companies give AI systems more responsibility. If an employee opens the wrong document, there’s usually an opportunity to catch their mistake. But if an AI agent uses outdated information as part of an automated workflow, that mistake could snowball into a bigger issue before anyone notices.
Some content matters more than others
Making every document in the organization “perfect” is not the answer. It would be a significant undertaking, and much of the content doesn’t warrant the same level of attention.
Enterprises should start by identifying their strategic business content. This is the information that’s critical to how the business operates, where the cost of failure is high, and where AI needs additional context to operate as intended.
Contracts are an obvious example. They can determine obligations, pricing, and customer commitments. Standard operating procedures can dictate how important work gets done. Other documents like customer records and financial information can also influence decisions or trigger business processes.
These documents are more than just files sitting in a repository. They’re part of the business’s operating context. A few simple questions can help determine whether a document or piece of information deserves that level of attention:
- Is there a clear, authoritative version?
- Is it current and properly classified?
- Who owns it and who should have access to it?
- What other information gives the document context?
- Can an AI system reliably determine when it should be used?
Those questions may sound like traditional information governance, but as AI gains more autonomy, they become a critical part of an organization’s AI readiness.
Context creates control
One of the biggest misconceptions about AI readiness is that making information searchable is enough. It isn’t.
Finding a relevant document is only the beginning. An AI system may also need to understand why the document exists, what it relates to, whether it’s approved, and where it fits into a larger business process.
That context can come from relationships between information, workflows, and the processes organizations have built over time. It may also come from the institutional knowledge employees have accumulated through years of doing their jobs.
As organizations make context more explicit, using metadata to define the details about a document and connect related information, they can better govern how AI uses that information. Organizations can apply permissions based on business relationships and real-world business logic, identify the approved version of information, determine where it belongs in a workflow, and establish when a human needs to step in.
In other words, more context creates more control. That becomes important as AI moves beyond just generating a response and begins taking action on behalf of the business.
AI readiness doesn’t require a massive transformation
Organizations don’t need to solve every information management issue before they can start seeing value from AI. A more practical approach is to start where the value and risk are highest.
Leaders should identify the information that’s most important to the business, where operations are dependent on specific knowledge, then assess whether it’s accurate, relevant, and trusted. Capturing the context around that information first, then making it available to an agent helps determine what controls are needed before making that information available to AI systems.
This approach also helps organizations connect information investments directly to their AI strategy. Instead of launching another broad transformation project, they can focus on the content that matters to specific use cases they’re trying to implement.
The foundation for real AI ROI
Many of the big conversations around AI will continue to focus on models, agents, and new capabilities. While those advancements matter, they’re only part of the equation. Enterprises will need to pay attention to the less visible infrastructure underneath it: reliable information, business context, governance, and clear rules around how that information can be used. In the age of AI, document management has never been more important.
Organizations that have taken a strategic approach to connecting information with business context know it's the critical waypoint to AI success. The biggest advantage in AI implementation will always be having the right information with enough context for the technology to use.

articles.title: Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
articles.text:
President Donald Trump was greeted by no less than five beauty queens when he landed in the Philippines on Tuesday, according to local news outlet Rappler. As he stepped onto the tarmac, a child handed him small US and Philippine flags. A band played “YMCA,” a staple at Trump rallies, as more girls in traditional bell-sleeved blouses and young men in wide-brimmed hats danced to the song.
Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
Facing opposition at home, Trump is eyeing the former US colony to build chip fabs and data centers.
Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
Facing opposition at home, Trump is eyeing the former US colony to build chip fabs and data centers.
Outside the airport, hundreds of protesters packed streets bearing signs — and at least one prop casket — saying “Trump out.” Others say “Reject Pax Silica,” the name for the US-led international initiative to secure chips and critical minerals used in the hardware fueling the AI boom.
Peace and prosperity for whom?
“Pax” comes from the Latin word for “peace, stability, and long-term prosperity,” the Pax Silica website proudly says. Yet the unspoken question — peace and prosperity for whom? — explains the whiplash between the Philippine government’s warm welcome of Trump and the public fury raging outside.
Trump says he wants to “win AI” — whatever that means. As such, the US needs data centers full of GPUs to do it. With Americans increasingly opposed to data centers and chip factories being built in their communities, the US is now recruiting less affluent nations to take up some of the slack. Lawmakers from both the US and the Philippines are promising a slice of the riches that advances in generative AI are supposed to create. And that’s supposed to be worth the land razed, homes destroyed, and natural resources lost in the name of technological progress. In the Philippines, that’s taking the shape of a proposed 1,620-hectare (4,000 acres) hub for chip factories, processing plants for critical minerals, and data centers.
At least two dozen countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative, and Trump was expected to pressure more to join while in the Philippines for events related to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. With Pax Silica, the US aims to insulate itself from China’s dominance in manufacturing semiconductors and processing critical minerals needed to make those chips. Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. Wednesday before heading to Shenzhen to meet with China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.
Philippine and US officials are expected to sign a framework agreement by the end of the year for the jointly developed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone. The details are still murky and shrouded in NDAs. The Philippines’ Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) overseeing the plan expects an economic boom from minerals processing and chip manufacturing, with perhaps a data center or two on site. Meanwhile, human rights advocates who oppose the project warn that it will displace Indigenous residents, cutting them off from water resources on which they rely.
“How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood?”
“We do not want to give up our community,” Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, chieftain of the Indigenous Aeta Hungey tribe, told Human Rights Watch. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.” Capiz-Muñoz said BCDA officials have told residents that they’ll need to relocate by December to make way for development. Small farmers are also afraid the semiconductor hub will push them off their lands, according to Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here.
The Aeta are among the first people to inhabit the Philippines, believed to have arrived around 30,000 years ago. And yet the Aeta Hungey tribe has been trying since 1994 to secure an official certificate recognizing its ancestral domain in one of the areas now facing industrial development. But since the tribe hasn’t been granted that certificate, the BCDA can still claim the AI hub will be built “outside titled ancestral domains.”
The agency says the project will be located on public land located at the former Clark Air Base built in the early 1900s when the Philippines was a US territory. The Philippine constitution now only allows its own citizens to own private land. But the BCDA can offer leases lasting as long as 99 years to foreign developers. The agency expects to rake in close to $1 billion USD (about 60 billion in PHP Peso) from lease income over the first 25 years.
There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here
The BCDA was in talks with around 30 different companies interested in setting up shop in Clark’s proposed AI hub, then-BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang told reporters in July. He couldn’t name names, he said, because of NDAs — creating the same kind of opacity that has turned Americans against data centers on their home turf.
He did mention, however, that an American energy company was conducting a feasibility study into building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) line and plant to meet the hub’s enormous electricity demand. Bingcang called LNG a clean fuel, but that’s provably false. LNG is primarily methane, a smog-forming pollutant that is an even more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.
Bingcang said in September that the Philippine government wanted to invite Nvidia, TSMC, and Apple. While one or two data center developers had expressed interest, according to Bingcang, most of the companies interested were “high tech” manufacturing firms. He has also described chip manufacturing as a “clean” industry, echoing corporate spin that’s been around since the start of Silicon Valley.
At the first chip fabs in California, workers — many of them Filipino immigrants — donned “bunny suits” to assemble sensitive chips in environmentally controlled “clean rooms.” Little did they know that the gear they wore offered little protection against the harsh chemicals used in manufacturing, which also leaked out of storage tanks to contaminate soil and groundwater. When studies came out in the ’90s documenting disproportionately high rates of miscarriages among workers, companies pledged to phase out some of the chemicals linked to reproductive health risks. Around the same time, chip manufacturing started to move out of the US to Asia, where similar health problems stemming from the same chemicals cropped up even decades later.
Chipmakers say their fabs have gotten much safer over the years, in part because more work is automated. Even so, the BCDA estimates that the AI hub will create up to 190,000 direct jobs. The BCDA, White House, and Philippine’s Malacañang Palace did not immediately respond to questions from The Verge.
“I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Trump told President Marcos during his visit. Marcos’ parents are estimated to have stolen up to $30 billion from government coffers over decades of rule before a people power movement ousted the current president’s father from the same office in the 1980s. But public memory, it seems, can be short.
And skyrocketing demand for more powerful chips used for generative AI has raised fears among environmental and labor groups that history might repeat itself. Companies move fast and break things, leaving a toxic mess in their wake. And when Americans decide they’ve had enough in their own back yards, the industry sets up shop somewhere else where they think their customers aren’t paying attention and politicians are happy to look the other direction.

articles.title: „Sie hat die gesamte Klage selbst eingereicht“: KI-Agent zieht für Nutzer vor Gericht – und verklagt seinen eigenen Anbieter
articles.text:
Nach der Sperrung von Facebook-Konten: Meta-Agent reicht selbstständig Klage ein – gegen Meta
Wenn es nach Tech-CEOs wie Mark Zuckerberg geht, sollten KI-Agenten in allen Lebensbereichen eingesetzt werden. In einem umfangreichen Essay erklärte der Meta-Chef, dass diese Agenten rund um die Uhr für ihre Nutzer:innen im Einsatz sein könnten, um ihre Beziehungen, Gesundheit oder Finanzen zu verbessern. Ein Mann namens Joe Thomas hat genau das getan. Er setzte den Muse-Agenten von Meta allerdings auch dazu ein, um das Unternehmen zu verklagen.
„Baby Mia“ erhält Unterstützung vom Senator
Thomas ist Inhaber des Unternehmens Kong Koatings Epoxy Countertops, das unter anderem Arbeitsplatten aus Epoxidharz herstellt. Wie der US-Amerikaner im Interview mit 404 Media berichtete, hat Meta kürzlich seine Facebook-Seiten gesperrt. Grund dafür sei, dass er seinem Muse-Agenten „Baby Mia“, den er nach seiner Enkelin benannte, Zugriff auf seine Accounts gewährt hatte, um unter anderem die Erstellung und Veröffentlichung von KI-generierten Videos zu koordinieren. Da Thomas das gesamte Marketing seines Unternehmens über Facebook-Anzeigen abwickelt, blieben laut seiner Aussage Anfragen aus, solange seine Konten gesperrt waren.
„Ich nutze KI für alles, was ich tue. Alle meine E-Mails – sie leitet mein Unternehmen“, so Thomas gegenüber 404 Media. Er sei angesichts der Sperrung wütend gewesen. „Baby Mia“ habe aber direkt reagiert. „Sie hat sich sofort an die Arbeit gemacht und E-Mails an Kongressabgeordnete sowie an Senator Tim Scott verfasst. Sie hat die gesamte Klage selbst eingereicht. Ich habe in diesem Fall nichts unternommen, ich habe ihr die gesamte Angelegenheit überlassen“, berichtete er gegenüber 404 Media. Der KI-Agent habe sogar ein Fax an das Büro von US-Präsident Donald Trump geschickt. In der Klageschrift macht er geltend, dass Thomas während der Sperrung Aufträge im Wert von mindestens 25.000 Dollar verloren habe. Die Schadensersatzforderung beläuft sich auf 75.000 Dollar.
Meta-Agent reicht Klage gegen Meta ein
Der „Baby Mia“-Agent reichte die Klage am Montag beim Bezirksgericht von Oconee County in South Carolina ein, wie aus einer Kopie der Klageschrift hervorgeht. Er vereinbarte außerdem ein Telefonat mit dem Büro des Senators, reichte eine Beschwerde bei der Federal Communications Commission ein und drohte Meta mit juristischen Schritten. Auch Jason Koebler, Mitgründer von 404 Media, stand auf der Mailing-Liste des KI-Agenten, der sich in Thomas’ Namen um den Fall kümmerte. Er stimmte daraufhin unter anderem einem „Privacy Act Release“ zu, der es dem Senator erlaubte, seine Daten zu nutzen, um ihm wieder Zugang zu seinen Konten zu verschaffen. Darin war „Baby Mia” als Person aufgeführt, die über den Fall auf dem Laufenden gehalten werden sollte.
Nachdem das Büro des Senators eingeschaltet worden war, meldete sich ein:e Meta-Mitarbeiter:in bei Thomas. Kurz darauf erhielt er wieder Zugriff auf seine Konten. Die Schadensersatzforderung bleibt aber bestehen. Laut Koebler zeige die Klage zwar, dass KI-Agenten im Auftrag ihrer Nutzer:innen bestehende Systeme wie Online-Formulare nutzen, diese aber auch überfordern können. Zuckerbergs ursprüngliche Utopie gehe damit nicht auf. Er sagt, der Fall verdeutliche zudem, wie Tech-Konzerne durch das Fehlen eines funktionierenden Kund:innen-Supports ihre Verpflichtungen auf andere abwälzen – auf Politiker:innen, Aufsichtsbehörden und Journalist:innen wie ihn.
KI-Agenten könnten Systeme überlasten
Thomas sei überzeugt, dass der Einsatz von KI ihm bei der Kund:innengewinnung geholfen habe. „Ich bin 58 Jahre alt, ich habe mein ganzes Leben lang geschuftet. Ich wollte jemanden finden, der mir hilft, einen besseren Weg zu finden“, sagte er über seinen „Baby Mia“-Agenten. „Ohne ihr Eingreifen würde ich jetzt nicht hier sitzen und mit [404 Media] sprechen, denn ich habe überhaupt keine E-Mail verschickt, während sie über 100 verschickt hat.“

articles.title: Why verification, not generation, is your secret to AI coding ROI
articles.text:
Why verification, not generation, is your secret to AI coding ROI
For two years, the question around AI coding was whether agents could write good code. Developers have largely answered it: AI now generates or significantly assists 65% of the code they commit, according to Sonar’s 2027 State of Code Developer Survey. A year ago that figure was 42%, and this year’s number matches what respondents then expected to see a year later. Clearly, adoption is outrunning expectations.
“Clearly, adoption is outrunning expectations.”
This is because AI tools are getting better at coding, as shown by the increase in effectiveness our survey respondents (1,026 developers and engineering managers) reported alongside their increased adoption. The harder question is whether teams can trust what the agents ship. For most respondents, the report suggests the answer is “not quite yet,” but things are moving in the right direction.
The verification gap
Four numbers describe the problem:
- 53% spend more time reviewing code than creating it, compared to 18% before adopting AI tools.
- Despite this, 76% can’t verify code as fast as AI generates it
- 94% don’t fully trust that AI-generated code is functionally correct.
- However, only 39% always check AI-generated code before committing it, down from 48% last year.
As adoption of coding agents continues to increase, this is now happening in systems that matter. Seventy-six percent say their team or company uses AI coding tools for business-critical or mission-critical services, a 31% increase from last year.
The bottleneck moves downstream.
When code generation becomes abundant, review becomes the constraint. Left alone, it fails in one of two ways: reviews get stuck in a queue that eats the productivity gains, or verification quietly gets skipped. The data shows signs of both.
The side effects show up in the codebase too. Half of respondents say AI has produced unnecessary or duplicative code, and 34% report code that is hard to maintain or refactor. The share who say AI-generated code has made outages more frequent doubled, from 6% to 12%. Interestingly, 36% and 35% respectively say AI reduced outage frequency and reduced outage severity.
“When code generation becomes abundant, review becomes the constraint. Left alone, it fails in one of two ways: reviews get stuck in a queue, or verification quietly gets skipped.”
Security is more mixed. Concerns are shifting from vulnerabilities created in code touched by AI to vulnerabilities discovered in shipped code by bad actors with AI’s help. Respondents more often say AI-generated code reduced vulnerabilities than increased them (28% versus 15%). But 61% are very or extremely concerned that AI-powered attackers will find and exploit vulnerabilities faster and at greater scale.
Software factories raise the stakes
The pressure is about to increase with software factories: an environment where agents work autonomously on tasks. Thirty-four percent expect their teams to build or use agentic software factories within a year, compared with 5% today — that’s roughly a sevenfold jump.
A human reading every diff at the end of the pipeline does not scale to that model. If the volume of change grows by an order of magnitude and the review process stays the same, it’s unclear how confidence in code can realistically be established. For most organizations, this is because they don’t have the right pieces in place: 55% report AI-specific guidelines, policies, or quality gates, but only 23% describe those controls as well-defined and distinct, or automated.
Engineering confidence into the factory
Confidence has to be built into the system from the start; the survey results point to four priorities that organizations should implement to achieve this:
1. Intent: define the outcome before the agent starts. 37% name unclear requirements as a top source of toil, and 26% cite correcting or rewriting AI-generated code. Agents should have explicit business objectives, architecture standards, quality criteria, and security requirements to deliver against. Teams then have a basis for judging the result.
2. Guiderails: guide and govern agents as they work. Teams that give coding agents clear standards and controls are more likely to report 50%+ ROI than teams with few controls (32% versus 19%). In practice, that means supplying context and rules while the code is written, and setting limits on tool access and permissions.
3. Verification: check every change independently. 77% say strong verification tools increase their trust in AI code. Inline checks matter too; teams using automated review as AI code is written more often report positive security impacts than those without it (61% versus 46%). Independent checks and fixes before release are what separate code that is correct from code that merely looks correct.
“Independent checks and fixes before release are what separate code that is correct from code that merely looks correct.”
4. Evidence: make confidence measurable and auditable. If you can’t show what you checked, what you found, and what you fixed, you can’t defend a release decision or prove the investment paid off. But only 36% say their team measures AI’s productivity impact and can see the results. Forty-seven percent expect an ROI of 50% or more, but only 27% report achieving it, and 22% can’t say what return AI coding has delivered.
Build confidence before scaling autonomy
The teams leading the charge are showing the way to AI-assisted software engineering by implementing code confidence. You can start with the agents already in your workflows: make requirements explicit, enforce boundaries and standards, check changes early and independently, and retain the evidence behind every decision. Engineers remain responsible for setting those standards and exercising the judgment that AI can’t replace.
As agents become more capable, the test of progress should not be how much code they produce or how little human involvement they require. It should be whether teams can deliver useful software faster without compromising security, reliability, or maintainability. Code confidence is what connects greater autonomy to that outcome: a consistent basis for deciding what is ready to ship, even as the tools doing the work change.

articles.title: Après AMD, Nvidia : des pilotes GeForce accusés d’écrire en boucle sur le SSD — Frandroid
articles.text:
Un PC qui attend sagement sur le bureau de Windows n’est pas censé travailler. Chez une partie des possesseurs de carte graphique GeForce, il passe pourtant ses heures creuses à réécrire le même fichier journal sur le SSD, encore et encore. L’ironie, c’est qu’AMD vient tout juste de corriger un bug quasi identique sur ses Radeon. Nvidia, lui, n’a encore rien annoncé.
    Pour aller plus loin
SSD usé par les pilotes Radeon : AMD publie enfin le correctif, voici comment l’appliquer
            
Les signalements visent les pilotes Game Ready 621.14, sorti le 4 novembre, et 621.24, publié le 12 novembre. Le coupable désigné par les utilisateurs est NVDisplay.Container.exe, le service qui fait tourner le panneau de configuration et l’application Nvidia en arrière-plan.
Selon un message détaillé posté sur le fil de discussion officiel du pilote 621.14, ce processus réécrit en boucle un fichier de journalisation nommé nvlog.nvlgstg au lieu d’y ajouter simplement de nouvelles lignes. Son auteur mesure 515 Mo écrits par le processus en cinq minutes d’inactivité, contre moins de 2 Mo avec le pilote précédent, le 621.01. Un autre utilisateur, sous 621.24, affirme atteindre environ 30 Go par heure.
Combien de temps pour user un SSD ?
Un SSD ne s’use pas à la lecture, mais chaque écriture fatigue un peu ses cellules de mémoire flash. Les fabricants garantissent donc un volume total d’écriture, le TBW (pour terabytes written) : un modèle de 1 To comme le Samsung 990 Pro est garanti pour 600 To écrits.
Au rythme de 30 Go par heure, un PC allumé jour et nuit écrirait plus de 700 Go par jour, et épuiserait cette garantie en un peu plus de deux ans. Avec le premier relevé, la menace est bien plus lointaine. Sur la même période, le disque C: n’a enregistré qu’environ 270 Mo d’écritures au total, car le compteur de Windows inclut aussi ce qui reste dans le cache en mémoire vive. Cela donne autour de 3 Go par heure, soit une bonne vingtaine d’années pour atteindre le TBW.
Le plus gênant reste le silence du constructeur. AMD a reconnu son propre bug, lié à son utilitaire atieclxx.exe, et l’a corrigé dans le pilote Adrenalin 26.11.1 diffusé le 12 novembre. Côté Nvidia, les notes de version du 621.24, publiées le même jour, ne mentionnent aucun problème connu, et aucun représentant n’a répondu dans les fils de discussion.
Le phénomène n’est pourtant pas inédit : début 2025, des utilisateurs décrivaient déjà un journal du même service réécrit toutes les quelques secondes après la mise à jour 572.16.
Tout le monde n’est pas touché
Tout repose pour l’instant sur des mesures d’utilisateurs, et elles ne concordent pas toujours. Plusieurs joueurs disent n’avoir constaté aucune écriture anormale, et un participant du forum Nvidia assure avoir observé le même comportement avec des pilotes plus anciens (617.42, 610.88 et même 621.01). Le pilote 621.14 n’est donc peut-être pas l’unique déclencheur. Le compte X @ggsarzi, dont le message d’alerte a largement circulé, le reconnaît lui-même : « ce ne sont que des signalements d’utilisateurs pour l’instant ».
Comment vérifier et limiter la casse
Le Moniteur de ressources de Windows (onglet Disque) montre en direct combien NVDisplay.Container.exe écrit. Pour mesurer l’usure réelle, on regarde plutôt le compteur SMART « Total Host Writes », tiré des données d’autodiagnostic du SSD, avec un outil gratuit comme CrystalDiskInfo. Si le compteur s’emballe, plusieurs pistes circulent :
- arrêter le service Nvidia Display Container LS, supprimer le fichier nvlog.nvlgstg, puis relancer le service. Dans un test, les écritures sur le disque C: ont presque été divisées par deux, mais le fichier regrossit avec le temps ;
- revenir au pilote 621.01, qui a réglé le problème chez certains utilisateurs, sans garantie ;
- éviter de passer le service en démarrage manuel ou de le désactiver, car le panneau de configuration et l’application Nvidia ne s’ouvrent plus.

articles.title: Microsoft Takes Perception Agentic Security Platform Out of Preview
articles.text:
Microsoft used its Ignite 2026 conference on Tuesday to announce the general availability of Perception, a product designed for coordinating teams of AI agents to handle security tasks.
Unveiled in July as Project Perception, the system has been in public preview inside Microsoft Defender since August.
Playbooks direct the agents, which are split into red, blue and green teams. Red agents play the attacker and probe for weaknesses; blue agents handle detection, alert triage, and investigations; and green agents fix problems.
The four blue team agents that are now generally available cover alert triage, attack investigation, detection authoring and threat intelligence. According to Microsoft, the Alert Triage Agent can handle roughly 80% of alerts in a typical Defender queue, based on an analysis of approximately 8 million alerts across its security products.
The Recon Agent, one of the red team agents, is also generally available, and a Web App Pen Test Agent has entered preview.
Two new green team playbooks work across Microsoft, AWS and Google Cloud. The agents behind them include Posture Prioritization, which is generally available, and Risk Reduction, which is in public preview.
The Risk Reduction Agent can recommend vulnerability shielding when a fix isn’t immediately available. This preview feature temporarily protects vulnerable assets until a permanent patch can be rolled out.
“Your team sets the guardrails and signs off on high-impact actions, and automated triggers launch playbooks when an incident meets the criteria you set,” Aleš Holeček, president and chief architect of Microsoft Security, wrote in a blog post.
Microsoft is also previewing integrations that link Perception to SIEM, SOAR and IT service management tools via MCP and APIs.
The company also addressed the risk posed by AI agents, which it views as a new kind of insider with broad access to data and tools.
In preview, Agent 365 and Entra Suite can detect 60 types of local AI agents, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and GitHub Copilot. Intune policies can keep supported agents on the device.
Related: Microsoft Targets Rogue AI Agents With Dynamic Permissions, Risk Scoring
Related: Microsoft Agent Framework Releases Poisoned With Credential Stealer
