articles.title: French frugal AI infrastructure startup MountAIn raises €7.3 million to bring advanced AI to sub-€9 chips | EU-Startups
articles.text:
MountAIn, a Grenoble-based frugal AI infrastructure company, has raised €7.3 million in Seed funding to run advanced AI on microcontrollers costing less than €9.11 ($10).
The round was led by 360 Capital and Supernova Invest, with participation from Crédit Agricole Alpes Développement (C2AD) and additional support from Bpifrance.
“The next great leap in AI won’t happen only in data centres. It will happen mostly across the billions of devices operating in the physical world. That requires embedded AI that is both energy-efficient and affordable. MountAIn delivers exactly that, with a level of performance we haven’t seen anywhere else,” said François Tison, Partner at 360 Capital.
MountAIn was founded in 2025 by Vincent Huard, Olivier Montfort, and David Nahmani with a goal of making AI accessible on ultra-low-cost microcontrollers. The founders argue that the vast majority of the world’s physical equipment runs on microcontrollers that consume milliwatts of power, yet AI development tools are built primarily for GPUs.
With its MountainCore platform, the company addresses this mismatch by automatically adapting complete computer vision applications, the AI model, pre-processing, post-processing, and data movement, to run within the strict memory, compute, and power limits of low-cost embedded processors.
“AI models are designed for GPUs and data centres, yet most equipment in the real world could run on microcontrollers consuming just milliwatts of power,” said Huard, CEO and co-founder of MountAIn.
According to the company, MountainCore can reduce model memory requirements by up to threefold, improve use of on-chip AI accelerators and preserve model accuracy without retraining. It also compresses deployment timelines that previously stretched across months into a matter of hours.
MountAIn has built partnerships with Teledyne e2v, chip designer Alif Semiconductor, and computer vision platform Roboflow, which serves more than two million developers and 80,000 companies. Its IBEX autonomous vision sensor, which runs on solar power, connects via satellite and consumes under 100 milliwatts, is designed for use cases such as early wildfire detection and infrastructure monitoring without relying on constant cloud connectivity.
The company also runs an invite-only Early Adopter Program (EAP), which gives select engineering teams a structured path to test MountainCore against a defined model, hardware target and success condition, allowing participants to help with product development using evidence from real deployments.
“The AI model is only part of the equation. MountainCore enables the entire application to run on these tiny processors. What once took months of engineering now takes hours, and major industrial companies such as Teledyne are already putting the technology to work. This financing will help us turn that early success into large-scale commercial deployment,” added Huard.
The funding comes at a time when demand for on-device AI is growing sharply across industrial, infrastructure and remote monitoring sectors. While the demand is there, the tools remain optimised for data-centre-grade hardware, which is impractical at the edge, and MountAIn plans to use the new capital to close this gap.
MountAIn says it will use the new funding to accelerate MountainCore’s commercial rollout, expand its engineering team in Grenoble and strengthen the company’s footprint in both Europe and Silicon Valley. It is set to demonstrate MountainCore’s industrial capabilities at CES in January 2027, with target customers including semiconductor manufacturers, smart camera makers and industrial equipment companies.

articles.title: The leaked Lenovo Legion Go Beam could be the affordable handheld we need
articles.text:
For a while there, it seemed like Lenovo had given up on selling handheld gaming PCs, hiking the price of its Legion Go 2 and Legion Go S far higher than other RAM-starved competitors. A decent one can easily cost $1,000 if not $2,000 now. But it looks like Lenovo might be about to announce a relatively cheap handheld once again— the Legion Go Beam.
The leaked Lenovo Legion Go Beam could be the affordable handheld we need
It looks comparatively cheap — and that might be a good thing in this economy.
Windows Latest has leaked images of the handheld, and there’s no question it’s designed to be a value alternative to even the company’s least expensive Legion Go S variant. While it’s got the same big stippled grips and triggers for comfort, there’s only one USB-C port on the top instead of two, a comparatively cheap-looking D-pad, no touchpad, and only a single tiny intake and exhaust for its fan.
There’s no SteamOS logo where that would go, so it likely runs Windows instead… but then there’s that name, “Beam.” Perhaps you’ll “beam” your games to it because it’s a streaming and cloud gaming handheld, instead of one that primarily plays games on its own chip? Maybe that’s why it doesn’t need as much airflow as previous handhelds?
Perhaps there’s a partnership with Xbox Cloud Gaming specifically, and that’s why it’s all lit up in Xbox green?
But it might just be green because it looks nice with white, which has been the “value” color for handhelds so far (see: ROG Ally, Xbox Ally, and the Windows-based Legion Go S). And it might be “Beam” because there’s a literal beam of light on the bottom, even though the first thing I do with most handhelds is turn any and all distracting RGB lighting off. Or maybe it’s “Beam” just because it sounds like a friendly, fun, value-oriented name, instead of something “S” or “Pro.”
I won’t begin to speculate on the Legion Go Beam’s price, except to say that “cheap” may be relative. The Legion Go S was originally supposed to cost $499, but wound up costing far more except on the occasional sale. The Legion Go 2 was supposed to start at $1,099 but wound up costing $1,500 and up after RAMageddon. Streaming-first handhelds have been far cheaper, though, like the $249 Sony PlayStation Portal.
Lenovo has a history of announcing its new gaming devices at CES in January each year, including previous Legion Go handhelds, so I’m expecting to see an official announcement of the Lenovo Legion Go Beam then. Even if so, that doesn’t mean it’ll be available in January — there’s often a many-month lag.

articles.title: Tackling GPU Bottlenecks in Plane-Wave DFT with K-Point Batching and Mixed Precision | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Training a next-generation machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) requires ground truth: tens to hundreds of millions of density functional theory (DFT) calculations of energies, forces, and stresses across diverse structures and chemistries.
Plane-wave DFT, with VASP as its dominant implementation, is the gold standard for generating that data. It is accurate, well-validated across materials classes, and ubiquitous at the national labs and research institutions running these calculations at scale.
As MLIP training datasets have grown, so has the pressure to generate DFT data faster and cheaper. But the small unit cells and dense k-point grids common in MLIP data generation can leave significant GPU performance unused. VASP’s OpenACC implementation has delivered meaningful speedups, especially for large-system calculations. However, for smaller systems, sequential k-point processing limits GPU utilization. At the same time, AI workloads are reshaping GPU hardware development toward lower-precision data types, creating a growing gap between what modern NVIDIA GPUs can deliver and what FP64-only HPC codes are optimized for.
This post introduces two new NVIDIA capabilities that address these bottlenecks. The first, Daviator, resolves the small-system GPU performance problem through k-point and spin-batched GPU kernels. In particular, a batched Davidson solver delivers significant performance gains. The second, a new mixed precision execution layer, enables further performance gains, especially on inference-class GPUs with a high FP32:FP64 throughput ratio.
For a projected reference dataset workload, the results show up to 22x faster time-to-solution and up to 75% lower cost compared to CPU execution, depending on hardware and configuration.
The GPU bottleneck in plane-wave DFT
In periodic systems, electronic wavefunctions are parameterized by crystal momentum, a discrete set of k-points that samples the Brillouin zone. For periodic structures with small unit cells, hundreds to thousands of irreducible k-points are required to achieve well-converged results.
Each k-point solve is largely independent; for instance, no inter-k-point communication is required during the Davidson eigensolver step. Despite this independence, VASP’s OpenACC GPU port processes k-points sequentially. For large systems, the work per k-point can fully saturate a GPU, but for small systems with dense k-point grids, the hundreds of small GPU dispatches per step causes kernel launch overhead to dominate compute time. The result: a single-atom iron system with 752 k-points ran 8x slower on the more expensive GPU hardware than on CPU. Thus, researchers working at this scale were left with a manual routing decision based on the size of the job.
Additionally, plane-wave DFT traditionally runs in FP64, a conservative default that guarantees accuracy throughout the solver pipeline. But GPU hardware is no longer symmetric in this regard. On data center GPUs, FP64 throughput has held flat across NVIDIA Hopper, Blackwell, and Rubin GPUs, while FP32 throughput has continued to increase. Inference-class and workstation GPUs like the RTX PRO 6000 push this further, with a 64:1 FP32:FP64 ratio (Figure 1). As AI workloads drive hardware development toward lower-precision data types, the fraction of peak GPU throughput available to FP64-only codes is stagnating.
Daviator: Batching k-points for GPU saturation
Daviator is a library of GPU kernels developed by NVIDIA that replaces sequential per-k-point processing in plane-wave DFT inner loops with batched GPU operations. At the core of the transformation lies a batched Davidson eigensolver that replaces sequential loops that cause latency with batched FFTs, GEMMs, and custom kernels. This drops the number of GPU kernel launches drastically, enabling SM occupancy to go from a fraction of capacity to near saturation. Data stays resident in GPU memory throughout. VASP retains full ownership of the SCF loop, mixing, symmetry, and I/O; Daviator integrates at well-defined call boundaries over data already on device.
Running a calculation
Daviator will be available through the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice by setting LDAVIATOR=True in the INCAR. Existing VASP inputs work without modification. The POSCAR, INCAR, and KPOINTS below are a standard setup for a k-point-dense metallic system.
Daviator intercepts the Davidson solver internally (ALGO = Normal) and routes it through batched GPU operations.
POSCAR:
Fe1
1.0
   2.3017038599999999    0.0000000000000000   -0.8137751999999999
  -1.1508519300000000    1.9933340200000000   -0.8137751999999999
   0.0000000000000000    0.0000000000000000    2.4413256099999998
Fe
1
direct
   0.0000000000000000    0.0000000000000000    0.0000000000000000 Fe
INCAR:
ALGO = Normal
LDAVIATOR = True
EDIFF = 5e-05
IBRION = 2
ISIF = 3
ISMEAR = 1
ISPIN = 2
NBANDS = 12
NSIM = 6
LASPH = True
LMAXMIX = 4
LORBIT = 11
LREAL = False
LWAVE = False
MAGMOM = 1*5.0
NELM = 100
NSW = 3
PREC = Accurate
SIGMA = 0.05
KPAR = 1
KPOINTS:
Gamma-centred 30x30x30 mesh
0
Gamma
30 30 30
Some of Daviator’s GPU kernels are specialized for the batch sizes they meet and may trigger a compilation on first use.
Add these lines to your job script before launching VASP to ensure efficient caching:
export CUDA_CACHE_PATH=/tmp/cudacache   # fast storage, not $HOME
export CUDA_CACHE_DISABLE=0             # make sure caching is on
Finally, run as usual:
mpirun -np 1 vasp_std
For now, VASP with Daviator is limited to single-node execution. Multi-node support, coverage of systems with non-collinear spins (vasp_ncl) and explicit gamma-only runs (vasp_gam) is expected to be released at a later stage.
Results
The benchmarks below compare Daviator against VASP 6.6.0 CPU and OpenACC baselines on NVIDIA H100s/H200s and B200s.
Daviator overcomes the OpenACC port’s limitations; a single iron atom achieves over 2x speed-ups relative to the CPU baseline (Figure 2). The gains increase for higher-accuracy functionals: the 22x Davidson speedup on LiFePO4 r2SCAN enables higher accuracy meta-GGA runs at production scale.
For mid-size systems like a 64-atom Bi-doped GaAs structure, VASP with Daviator cut execution time by more than 85%. Even at 348 atoms with a single k-point, Daviator delivers a significant improvement over the OpenACC and CPU baselines. VASP with Daviator improves the previous state-of-the-art for all system sizes, eliminating the need to route jobs between CPU and GPU based on system size.
Going further with mixed precision
Daviator eliminates the k-point bottleneck, but currently relies on FP64 arithmetic and storage. GPU hardware is shifting toward lower-precision data types, and HPC codes that adapt to mixed precision stand to recapture substantial performance from hardware they already own.
Further increasing the throughput, especially on GPUs with a high FP32:FP64 ratio, requires leveraging the FP32 units, but developing a mixed-precision Davidson solver is non-trivial. Not every kernel in the Davidson pipeline is equally precision-sensitive, but simply running each in FP32 and comparing against FP64 only yields a pass/fail result.
Additionally, the failures can be insidious. Hard failures are obvious: a solver rejects an ill-conditioned input. Soft failures are not: energy drift, incorrect convergence, diverging MD trajectories that appear valid on casual inspection. Genuine mixed precision requires knowing exactly where the precision boundaries lie.
By using a generic floating-point type with configurable mantissa and exponent bits, we can identify the minimum required bit counts for each that still produce correct results. The following section describes a general workflow for a precision requirements analysis that can be adapted for other codes as well.
Knowing the exact precision requirements for each kernel informs whether to switch it to FP32, improve the implementation to bring it into FP32 range, or keep it as an FP64 island.
Implementing this approach depends heavily on the specific code, but always requires the following building blocks:
- An instrumented version of the code that uses a generic floating point type with a configurable mantissa and exponent bit count.
- A run script that executes the code with a specific precision setting and input.
- A compare script that checks the accuracy of the results against a reference.
- A screening script that runs the instrumented code multiple times for each kernel, first with decreasing mantissa bits until the comparison fails, and then with the smallest working mantissa size and decreasing exponent bits.
Once this setup is in place, re-run the screening after each code change to track precision requirements. Measured precision requirements for different implementations of a reduction kernel vary (Figure 3).
The results depend on the input and comparison threshold. Here, all kernels would pass a simple FP32 run (Figure 4) without providing an insight into the numerical properties. The baseline is likely to fail with either a slightly larger input or a stricter comparison. The algorithm choice may also come with additional constraints.
The code instrumentation can be performed at three levels:
- The library level: Some libraries offer configurable precision, though only to a limited extent. The emulated matrix multiplications in cuBLAS, for example, allow screening the precision requirements of GEMMs by explicitly setting the mantissa bit count.
- The language level: The native floating-point types can be replaced with a generic one. NVIDIA CCCL provides such a type, with both compile-time and runtime configuration of mantissa and exponent bits.
- The compiler level: A completely non-intrusive and mostly automatic instrumentation can be achieved by replacing floating-point operations with a software implementation during compilation. The Verificarlo project takes this approach with its VPREC backend, but is limited to CPU code.
A complete instrumentation also covers dependencies and standard math functions. The instrumented code will be much slower, but the runs can be largely parallelized across HPC resources.
To move from analysis to implementation, start by adding FP64↔FP32 conversion infrastructure around your application’s hot path or a subset of it. Then create type-configurable versions of the functions and kernels in that region. For an initial implementation, keep everything exceeding FP32 requirements as an FP64 island; each subsequent iteration can reduce the FP64 footprint further.
Following this workflow, the original analysis of the Davidson algorithm, based on Verificarlo, indicated that large parts of the code could run with FP32 arithmetic and storage. The FFTs, the application of the Hamiltonian, and the orbital updates run in FP32, while the subspace eigenproblem, the tall-skinny GEMMs behind the subspace matrices, as well as the energies and convergence measures remain in FP64.
The tall-skinny GEMMs in the Rayleigh-Ritz projection were the remaining FP64 bottleneck. Pure FP32 accumulation here is insufficient as the output feeds directly into a numerically sensitive eigenvalue solver. The split-k algorithm resolves this by breaking the dot products into FP32 chunks with a final FP64 accumulation step (Figure 5).
Results
In VASP, convergence is controlled by the EDIFF parameter, which specifies the threshold for the total energy change between electronic iterations within an ionic step. Below that threshold, convergence is reached.
The default is 10-4 eV, while some calculations go down to 10-6 eV or lower. For reference, FP32 provides around 7 significant decimal digits of precision. EDIFF is an absolute threshold that varies by system and typically scales with atom count, so there is no single best setting.
The mixed-precision Davidson implementation converges to an EDIFF of 10-4 to 10-6 eV depending on the input; continuing with FP64 allows the calculation to converge below the FP32 noise floor. On GaAsBi-64, FP32 enables a 2× speed-up at EDIFF = 10-5 eV, and the combined FP32→FP64 run is 1.5× faster than pure FP64 at EDIFF = 10⁻⁸ eV (Figure 6).
On H100 and H200, where FP64 Tensor Cores match FP32 throughput, mixed precision delivers only marginal end-to-end gains. The benefit is concentrated in hardware with a high FP32:FP64 ratio such as the RTX PRO 6000, where the FP32 Davidson solver runs 3x–7x faster, delivering roughly 2x end-to-end acceleration (Figure 7).
Enabling mixed precision
Daviator’s mixed precision can be enabled by setting LDAVIATOR_MIXED_PRECISION to 1 (0 is FP64). Within an ionic step, the calculation starts in mixed precision (with FP32 storage) until a configurable threshold DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 or a number of SCF steps DAVIATOR_SWITCH_TO_FP64_AFTER_STEP is reached. For most inputs LAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 works well from 10-4 to 10-5.
The following INCAR parameters are available to configure the use of mixed precision specifically for Daviator (Table 1).
| INCAR Parameter | Values | Description | 
|---|---|---|
| LDAVIATOR_MIXED_PRECISION | False = FP64 True = FP32 | Enable/Disable Mixed Precision (FP32 = mixed arithmetic and FP32 storage in Daviator) | 
| DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 | real number > 0 in eV | EDIFF threshold for FP32 | 
| DAVIATOR_SWITCH_TO_FP64_AFTER_STEP | Integer N >= 0, switch to FP64 after electronic step N (N=0 is FP64) -1 = FP32 only, i.e. converge to DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32, then stop -2 = dynamic. i.e. switch to FP64 after DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 convergence | Selects when an ionic step switches from reduced precision to FP64. | 
The INCAR for a run that uses FP32 until EDIFF = 5-5 eV and then switches to FP64 until EDIFF = 5-7 eV would look like this:
ALGO = Normal
EDIFF = 5e-07
[...]
LDAVIATOR = True
LDAVIATOR_MIXED_PRECISION = True
DAVIATOR_SWITCH_TO_FP64_AFTER_STEP = -2
DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 = 5e-05
Hardware requirements and availability
A VASP user license is required. Daviator and its mixed precision option will be available on any NVIDIA GPU through the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice; add the INCAR parameters above to activate it.
What both layers deliver at scale
The Open Materials 2024 (OMat24) inorganic materials dataset contains over 100 million VASP data points (total energy, forces, and stress) from molecular dynamics (“AIMD”), relaxation (“rattled-relax”), and static (“rattled”) calculations for MLIP training and validation.
To estimate the time and cost to compute this dataset, we extrapolated from a benchmarked sample of 13 representative inputs across the dataset’s system-size distribution. The individual benchmark runs were tuned to maximize resource utilisation and overall throughput, assuming multiple parallel runs per node. While OMat24 was generated with real-space projectors, the benchmarks and projections here use the more precise reciprocal-space projector setting in VASP (INCAR: LREAL=False).
On the same number of cloud instances, VASP + Daviator is up to 22x faster than VASP on CPU nodes, and up to 7x faster than VASP without Daviator on GPU (Figure 8). For a batch of eight small systems on one GPU, the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice raises throughput a further 3–5x.
To estimate the price of the data set generation, we applied a geometric mean of the on-demand prices of AWS, Azure, CoreWeave and Google. On datacenter GPUs, the existing OpenACC GPU support in VASP is more expensive than the corresponding CPU computation.
However, the combination with Daviator reduces the cost to roughly 35% of the CPU cost on H100/200 and B200, with mixed precision contributing up to $200,000 in additional savings. The overall lowest price-point—around 25% of the CPU cost—is achieved on RTX PRO 6000 using VASP with Daviator and FP32 (Figure 9).
What’s next for GPU-native DFT
For standard DFT, GPUs are now the clear choice for VASP. For teams building MLIP training pipelines at the scale of OMat24 and beyond, VASP + Daviator delivers a GPU-native workflow end-to-end with cost savings of 60–75% over CPU, or approximately $5–6M USD for a dataset the size of OMat24.
For teams running RTX PRO 6000 or other NVIDIA GPUs with a high FP32:FP64 ratio, mixed precision yields a 2x speedup over FP64, with benefits beyond dataset generation. Daviator also opens up workload classes that were previously impractical at GPU scale. Meta-GGA functionals like R²SCAN are now viable for production; the reported speed-ups for LiFePO₄ may bring higher-accuracy DFT within reach for battery, catalyst, and defect datasets.
Acknowledgments
The VASP development team and Akhilesh Mishra contributed to this post.

articles.title: GTA 6 affole complètement le marché du jeu vidéo avec des ventes qui atteignent un niveau exceptionnel
articles.text:
À quelques heures de sa sortie, GTA 6 cumule près de 16 millions de précommandes numériques et 1,54 milliard de dollars de recettes. Sur le papier, le jeu dépasse déjà des chiffres qui faisaient référence dans l'histoire du jeu vidéo.
Il n'est pas exagéré de dire que GTA 6 marquera l'année, et sans doute la décennie, tant il fait parler et tant il a déjà fait des adeptes. Les précommandes du jeu vidéo ont encore bondi ces dernières heures. Selon le dernier relevé publié par Sensor Tower, le titre de Rockstar Games approche des 16 millions de copies numériques réservées. GTA 6 aurait déjà généré plus de 1,54 milliard de dollars de recettes, dont les deux tiers sur PlayStation. À quelques heures de disponibilité du jeu, les illustre Cyberpunk 2077, Red Dead Redemption 2 et même GTA V voient déjà leurs records vaciller.
BenQ iScreenBar : la barre lumineuse qui s’accorde avec l’iMac
Des lignes en harmonie avec celles de l’ordinateur d’Apple, une conception rigoureuse, des matériaux sélectionnés, rien n’a été laissé au hasard, tout comme le service qu’elle rend une fois allumée !
Les précommandes de GTA 6 ont doublé en deux semaines
Le nombre de copies de GTA 6 précommandées sur PS5 et Xbox Series, remboursements déduits, est désormais estimé à 15,88 millions, pour 1,54 milliard de dollars de chiffres d'affaires. Imaginez, c'est comme si près de 23 % des Français avaient acheté le jeu avant même qu'il ne sorte, un score qui ferait rougir n'importe quel candidat à l'élection présidentielle dans quelques mois. Le 13 novembre, il y a moins d'une semaine donc, le compteur affichait encore 12,13 millions de copies et 1,18 milliard. Le 3 novembre, il n'en était qu'à 7,71 millions. Autrement dit, les réservations ont plus que doublé en deux semaines.
Si nous faisons les comptes, ces jours-ci le jeu a généré environ 90 millions de dollars par jour, contre moins de 30 millions début novembre. La répartition, elle, est extrêmement favorable à la PlayStation 5, qui pèse pour 75 % des ventes, avec 11,83 millions de copies et 1,15 milliard de dollars de recettes, contre 4,04 millions de copies et 390 millions sur Xbox, en rappelant que GTA 6 sera jouable sur la vieille Xbox One. Avec environ 97 dollars comme panier moyen, l'édition Ultime reste la reine des précommandes.
On rappelle qu'il ne s'agit ici que d'estimations, et que ces chiffres ne portent que sur les ventes numériques, sans les boîtes vendues en magasin, qui ne contiennent qu'un seul petit code d'ailleurs, et que ces données s'entendent avant la commission prélevée par les boutiques. Pour le moment, Take-Two, la maison mère de l'éditeur Rockstar Games, n'a pas commenté les chiffres, en se contentant d'évoquer un élan « sans précédent » pour le jeu.
GTA 6 bouscule déjà l'histoire du jeu vidéo
Jusqu'ici, le record de précommandes généralement cité appartenait à Cyberpunk 2077. 8 millions d'exemplaires furent annoncés par CD Projekt en 2020, PC compris. GTA 6 fait déjà presque deux fois mieux, sur consoles uniquement. Son aîné, l'increvable GTA V, avait totalisé 7 millions de précommandes en 2013, avant de générer la coquette somme de 800 millions de dollars dès son premier jour, puis le milliard en trois jours, plus vite que n'importe quel jeu ou film à l'époque.
Les aventures d'Arthur Morgan, avec Red Dead Redemption 2, avaient engrangé 725 millions de dollars lors de son premier week-end, en 2018. GTA 6 avait dépassé ce montant au plus tard début novembre, plus de deux semaines avant sa sortie, et ses seules précommandes numériques surpassent déjà le milliard de GTA V, boîtes comprises. Les méthodes de calcul diffèrent, entre chiffres officiels et estimations, mais l'écart est significatif.
Les joueurs Xbox vont même pouvoir, en principe, entrer à Vice City dès ce mercredi midi, grâce à l'astuce de la Nouvelle-Zélande, avant le lancement français dans la nuit de mercredi à jeudi, à minuit. D'ici là, gare aux pièges, puisque différentes acteurs de la cybersécurité repèrent des activités malveillantes autour du jeu, comme dernièrement un faux téléchargement du jeu qui cache un logiciel voleur de données. Rappelons enfin qu'aucune version PC n'existe, et que le jeu visera 30 FPS sur toutes les consoles.

articles.title: L'IA trouve les failles vraiment trop vite : Anthropic et Google sonnent la fin des 90 jours de grâce avant la divulgation
articles.text:
Depuis des années, le milieu de la sécurité informatique suit une règle tacite : un chercheur qui trouve une faille prévient discrètement l’éditeur, puis lui laisse 90 jours avant de la rendre publique. Ce délai de trois mois doit permettre au correctif d’arriver chez tout le monde avant que les pirates ne connaissent la faille, et s’en servent.
Or, dans un billet publié ce lundi 16 novembre, Anthropic, l’entreprise derrière l’intelligence artificielle Claude, a décidé de ramener ce délai à 30 jours pour les failles de gravité élevée ou critique, et à 45 jours pour les autres. Les nouvelles règles valent pour les signalements faits à partir du 1er janvier 2027.
Et la raison profonde de ce bouleversement dans les principes de divulgation coordonnée et responsable ? L’IA.
Une faille ne reste plus secrète trois mois, estime Anthropic
Anthropic justifie ce changement par les progrès rapides des modèles d’IA, devenus bien meilleurs pour dénicher des failles. Selon l’entreprise, une brèche repérée par une IA a de plus en plus de chances d’être retrouvée par une autre, bien avant le délai des 90 jours, ce qui augmente fortement le degré de risque en sécurité informatique.
Anthropic dit d’ailleurs constater déjà davantage de redécouvertes. Google part du même constat.
Le 13 novembre, Project Zero, l’équipe de chasseurs de failles de Google qui avait popularisé la règle des 90 jours, a annoncé passer à 60 jours le 2 février 2027, puis à 30 jours le 3 janvier 2028, que le correctif soit prêt ou non et quelle que soit la gravité de la faille. L’équipe supprime au passage les 30 jours supplémentaires qu’elle accordait depuis 2021 pour déployer un correctif.
Ce rythme pèse surtout sur les mainteneurs, qui entretiennent les logiciels libres, et Anthropic le reconnaît. Elle rappelle qu’elle joint déjà un correctif à ses signalements quand c’est possible. Elle propose aussi aux mainteneurs de projets libres critiques OSS Scanner, un service gratuit qui passe leur code au crible de ses modèles régulièrement.
En somme, l’entreprise dont les modèles accélèrent la chasse aux failles propose aussi de les mettre au service de ceux qui doivent les corriger. Les logiciels difficiles à mettre à jour, comme ceux des infrastructures critiques, auront un calendrier négocié au cas par cas.
Les failles déjà exploitées par des pirates gardent leur régime : elles restent soumises au même délai de sept jours qu’avant. Les nouveaux délais ne s’appliquent pas non plus aux trouvailles d’OSS Scanner qu’aucun humain n’a encore relues.

articles.title: Nvidia casi triplicó desde enero el valor de sus inversiones en empresas privadas, que ya llega a USD 65.500 millones
articles.text:
Nvidia reveló el 17 de noviembre que sus participaciones en empresas privadas valen USD 65.500 millones, casi el triple de los USD 22.000 millones que había informado en enero. Es la primera vez que presenta resultados desde que Jensen Huang, su cofundador, renunció tras 33 años al frente de la compañía.
El aumento combina inversiones nuevas con revalorizaciones de las empresas en las que ya tenía acciones, según TechCrunch. Solo en el último trimestre, el fabricante de chips destinó USD 16.000 millones a comprar acciones, y en los primeros nueve meses de su año fiscal sumó USD 58.000 millones.
La comparación con el año anterior muestra el cambio de ritmo. En noviembre de 2025, Nvidia había informado gastos por USD 5.000 millones en acciones durante el mismo período. La cifra actual incluye compras en empresas que cotizan en bolsa y en otras que no.
Nvidia dijo a fines de 2023 que invierte para ampliar el ecosistema de la inteligencia artificial y respaldar a compañías que considera capaces de abrir mercados. Desde entonces apoyó a casi 350 startups, según PitchBook, una firma que registra el capital de riesgo. Entre ellas figuran Anthropic y OpenAI.
Garantías por USD 118.000 millones
Las inversiones en acciones no son el único compromiso. Nvidia informó garantías financieras por USD 118.000 millones, de las cuales USD 105.000 millones corresponden al respaldo que dio a OpenAI para un centro de datos en Ohio, según TechCrunch. Una garantía implica que la empresa pagaría si el cliente no puede hacerlo.
El propio balance mide el avance de ese negocio. En el trimestre, la compañía facturó USD 115.800 millones, el 103% más que un año antes, según su comunicado. Para el cuarto trimestre proyectó ingresos de USD 130.000 millones, sin contar ventas de chips para centros de datos a China.
La directora ejecutiva interina, Colette Kress, también es la directora financiera. En la conferencia con analistas dijo que Nvidia seguirá dando asistencia financiera a clientes sólidos, pero que “a medida que el mercado madure” evaluará “rigurosamente” futuras inversiones, compromisos y garantías.
Kress agregó que la compañía pretende devolver a sus accionistas todo el flujo de caja libre sobrante, descontado lo que considere estratégico. Nvidia no precisó qué parte de ese dinero seguirá yendo a startups.
Los inversores prevén un freno
En el sector de capital de riesgo, donde los fondos financian empresas jóvenes, anticipan un recorte. Según TechCrunch, Nvidia participó en 105 rondas de financiación este año, a menudo como mayor inversor. Varios inversores consultados esperan inversiones más selectivas y cheques más chicos en las empresas que ya integran su cartera.
Umesh Padval, socio gerente de Seligman Ventures, describió el efecto de esa presencia: “Cuando Nvidia estaba en la lista de accionistas, todos se sentían seguros”. Sin ese respaldo, dijo, los fondos tradicionales podrían pensarlo dos veces antes de invertir, e incluso pausar acuerdos.
Maria Davidson, fundadora de Relational Capital, advirtió que un cambio de rumbo sería “un golpe grande” para muchas empresas jóvenes. Otros inversores esperan que Google, Amazon, Microsoft o AMD ocupen parte de ese lugar, aunque Dharmesh Thakker, del fondo Battery Ventures, dudó de que financien a empresas sin ingresos como lo hizo Nvidia.
En paralelo, según TechCrunch, la empresa compró este año Hugging Face, una plataforma de modelos de IA de código abierto, por unos USD 13.000 millones. La operación se completaría en 2027. En el comunicado de resultados, Nvidia mencionó el acuerdo de adquisición.
En septiembre, el directorio de Nvidia aprobó ampliar en USD 150.000 millones su autorización para recomprar acciones propias. Al cierre del trimestre, la compañía tenía unos USD 227.300 millones disponibles bajo esa autorización, y pagará su próximo dividendo trimestral de 0,25 dólares por acción el 23 de diciembre.

articles.title: The power of one, the progress of many: SheSparks 2027 set to spotlight the multiplier effect
articles.text:
The power of one, the progress of many: SheSparks 2027 set to spotlight the multiplier effect
YourStory’s flagship women-focused event returns to Delhi on February 19–20, with a focus on collective progress, entrepreneurship, and access to opportunities.
When one woman succeeds, the benefits can extend beyond her own career or business. The knowledge she shares, the connections she builds, and the opportunities she creates can help other women move forward.
This idea is at the heart of SheSparks 2027, YourStory’s flagship women-focused event, which returns to Delhi on February 19 and 20 at The Ashok Hotel.
With the theme ‘The Multiplier Effect’, the event will explore how women's individual achievements can drive collective progress through mentorship, shared knowledge, access to opportunities, and networks of support.
Since its inception in 2018, SheSparks has brought together women from business, arts, science, sports, public service, and other fields to exchange ideas, share experiences, and build connections. The 2027 edition will focus on how these relationships can help more women advance across business, technology, entrepreneurship, leadership, and society.
For the first time in its history, SheSparks will be held as a two-day programme. Across both days, the event will feature keynotes, panel discussions, fireside chats, and workshops covering ambition, identity, reinvention, the future of work, women in the AI age, financial independence, entrepreneurship, and leadership.
Conversations will also examine how mentorship, sponsorship, allyship, and professional networks can help address barriers to women's workforce participation and economic progress.
Beyond the discussions, SheSparks 2027 will offer several opportunities for women to connect with investors, employers, customers, and peers.
The Capital Room will connect women founders with investors based on investment fit, while the Returnship Fair will bring women looking to restart their careers in touch with employers and career guidance. The SheCommerce Bazaar will showcase women-led brands and businesses, helping them reach customers, markets, and potential partners.
A major highlight of the event will be SheSparks 100. Building on YourStory and HerStory’s Future Shapers: She Leads Change Awards, the initiative will recognise 100 women across entrepreneurship, business, technology, capital, policy, culture, and social impact. The focus will be on their achievements and the opportunities they have helped create for others.
Over the years, SheSparks has hosted leaders and changemakers, including Sudha Murty, Nivruti Rai, Soha Ali Khan, Vani Kola, Tessy Thomas, Chetna Gala Sinha, and Swati Bhargava.
The 2027 edition expects to bring together over 600 attendees, with an anticipated reach of more than five million women.
Through conversations, connections, and practical initiatives, SheSparks 2027 aims to demonstrate how individual achievements can create opportunities for others, helping more women participate and progress across industries.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.title: Jensen Huang rompe su silencio tras dimitir: “Sería un honor volver como CEO de NVIDIA”
articles.text:
Jensen Huang ha dicho que sería “un honor” volver a dirigir NVIDIA si el consejo se lo pide. Es su primera declaración pública desde que dimitió la semana pasada. Su salida llegó tras conocerse varias relaciones extramatrimoniales: una con una empleada y otra con Alice Huang, una mujer a la que la inteligencia estadounidense investiga como posible activo de China.
Qué ha dicho. El comunicado es breve, lo ha publicado en X y tiene dos partes:
- La disculpa. “No he estado a la altura de lo que se espera de todos en NVIDIA y he cometido errores graves en mi vida personal. He creado problemas al consejo que lamento profundamente”.
- El ofrecimiento. “Si el consejo decide que mi regreso es lo mejor para nuestros accionistas, nuestros empleados, la compañía y Estados Unidos, sería un honor atender estas llamadas y volver como CEO”.
Entre líneas. El último de la lista es Estados Unidos, y eso va por Donald Trump. El lunes, el presidente dijo que “no le importaría” ver a Huang de vuelta y que este “ha aprendido una gran lección”.
Huang se está apalancando en una presión que ya estaba ahí antes del comunicado. Hay una petición firmada por casi 200.000 empleados, la carta de un alto directivo al presidente del consejo, Harvey Jones; y el apoyo de Elon Musk. El mercado también lo ha notado: las acciones han recuperado lo que habían perdido en el día en cuanto el WSJ adelantó el comunicado.
Sí, pero. Según el WSJ y CNN, el consejo no está pensando en readmitirle. Va en dirección contraria: el martes creó un comité que vigilará la seguridad nacional y el cumplimiento de los controles de exportación. Colette Kress sigue como CEO interina mientras se buscan candidatos dentro y fuera de la empresa.
Y ahora qué. El 1 de diciembre, Huang declarará a puerta cerrada ante tres comités de la Cámara de Representantes, entre ellos el de Inteligencia. Al día siguiente lo hará el director jurídico de NVIDIA, Tim Teter. Las transcripciones podrán hacerse públicas más tarde y desde luego que por aquí las seguiremos con atención.
- Un detalle: el portavoz de NVIDIA ha dicho que esperan “reunirse con los presidentes de los comités el 2 de diciembre”. Solo ha citado la fecha de Teter, no la de Huang.

articles.title: 800 V et 660 km d'autonomie : la Leapmotor B05 fait un bond de géant… mais pas pour nous !
articles.text:
Fraîchement lancée chez nous, la Leapmotor B05 s’apprête déjà à recevoir des améliorations de circonstance en Chine. La marque a en effet confirmé l’arrivée d’une version optimisée de sa compacte électrique au Salon de l’Automobile de Guangzhou, qui se tiendra le 27 novembre prochain. Outre un équipement enrichi, c’est surtout la technique qui fait un bond de géant, avec l’adoption d’une plateforme 800 V.
Les temps de recharge seront donc logiquement revus à la baisse. Rappelons que le modèle actuel annonce un 10 à 80 % de batterie en 27 minutes grâce à une puissance de charge de 174 kW avec l’accumulateur de 67,1 kWh. Ce n’est déjà pas si mal, les autres modèles du groupe effectuant plutôt le 20 à 80 % en 30 minutes… Aucune information n’a cependant été communiquée sur les nouvelles performances à la borne.
Jusqu’à 660 km d’autonomie : un rayon d’action en nette hausse
On devrait probablement glisser sous les 25 minutes, ce qui renforcera encore l’attractivité du modèle. Passer moins de temps à recharger, c’est bien. Aller plus loin ensuite, c’est encore mieux ! Bonne nouvelle, l’autonomie progressera aussi, avec jusqu’à 660 km sur le cycle CLTC. Cela correspondrait à environ 500 km sur notre norme WLTP, ce qui reste supérieur aux 482 km d’autonomie du modèle actuel.
Côté équipement, cette B05 révisée gagne un affichage tête haute en réalité augmentée, un écran tactile agrandi à 17,3 pouces, des sièges zéro gravité et 14 haut-parleurs. L’habitacle est sinon identique à la version sortante, avec une planche de bord toujours aussi impersonnelle. Et de dehors aussi, la compacte ne change guère. Son design assez standard ne bascule pas outre mesure dans la folie.
Une arrivée en Europe déjà compromise par la stratégie de la marque
Sauf à prendre la version Ultra, qui n’est malheureusement pas disponible chez nous : celle-ci ajoute une lame avant, des jupes latérales, un diffuseur et un aileron plus généreux. La garde au sol a aussi été abaissée d’un petit centimètre. A défaut d’avoir la variante Ultra, avons-nous donc plus de chances de voir cette B05 améliorée arriver en Europe ? Pas vraiment pour des raisons d’ordre stratégique.
Il suffit de voir ce qui s’est passé avec le B10 pour anticiper le même scénario avec la B05. Des responsables voyaient mal remplacer aussi tôt un véhicule fraîchement commercialisé chez nous. Ils évoquent notamment une dynamique d’achat sensiblement différente entre la Chine et l’Europe, où les nouveaux modèles se présentent à intervalles réguliers. Nul doute donc qu’il faudra aussi attendre un cycle de quelques années pour espérer voir une B05 améliorée.

articles.title: DycoVue wants to make sure your hospital never loses your X-ray
articles.text:
If you’ve ever had a brain scan, the strange noises of the machine might be the first thing to scare you. Staying still while it makes its clanging noises is another challenge, but what really gets you is the anxiety of waiting for a radiologist to interpret the images and tell you what is happening inside your head. In Nigeria, where radiologists are in short supply, getting that report can be another hurdle.
During her five years as an advanced nurse practitioner in the United States, Kafilat Shobajo had encountered several cases where radiology reports missed fractures or other abnormalities she could identify from examining patients and reviewing their X-rays. In the two years before speaking to TechCabal in November, she said she had caught at least five errors that could have changed a patient’s diagnosis or treatment. The experiences made her question how much room there was for such oversights in a healthcare system that struggles with a shortage of specialists.
A 2025 study published in BMC Medical Education estimated that Nigeria had fewer than 700 radiologists, or roughly one for every 660,000 people. Shobajo’s own assessment of the facilities she spoke with revealed that some radiologists were working across at least three hospitals.
However, the shortage of specialists was only part of the problem. Before building a product, Shobajo mentioned that her team conducted a three-month pilot to understand the needs of diagnostic centres and clinics. They found that many facilities were not properly storing the medical images they produced.
“During our pilot, the majority of the facilities had their images stored on WhatsApp or Telegram,” Shobajo said.
She told TechCabal that her first instinct had been to build an artificial intelligence tool that could help radiologists and frontline clinicians interpret medical images. However, medical AI models are only as useful as the data they learn from, and Shobajo was concerned that models trained on images from other populations might not produce accurate results for African patients.
“Our tumours are larger, so chances are if they bring that model here, it’s not going to be accurate,” she said. “What DycoVue does is we build the infrastructure for clinics in digital imaging. So before you can start saying you’re going to use AI to help interpret your medical images, hospitals need to store their data first.”
This led her to build DycoVue, a healthtech startup developing software that helps healthcare facilities manage their medical imaging records, including storing, organising, retrieving and sharing the images with the healthcare professionals involved in a patient’s care, in 2025.
How DycoSuite works
The company’s main product is DycoSuite, an imaging management system built around a technology known as a Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS). PACS systems allow healthcare facilities to store, retrieve and share medical images digitally. DycoSuite is designed to replace the scattered films, CDs and images shared across messaging apps with a central system where a patient’s imaging records can be stored and retrieved when needed.
Shobajo says the system is designed to fit into a clinic’s existing imaging workflow, rather than requiring staff to manually upload every scan. When a diagnostic centre signs up, DycoVue’s engineers visit the facility to connect its imaging equipment to the platform. Once the connection is set up, images are transferred to the system as they are produced.
“It automatically goes to the cloud. We have engineers that can come and ensure that. If clinics are interested in using DycoVue, we would come to their clinic, do a demo for them to see the product, our engineers will make the connection, and that’s it,” Shobajo said.
The company also said it provides ongoing technical support after installation. Shobajo says this is important because deploying software is only useful if clinics can rely on it when they need it. Patients are shared a link that contains the images from the scan.
Once images are stored centrally, clinicians can retrieve earlier scans and compare them with newer ones. A patient who returns with the same complaint would not have to rely on a physical film or remember which facility holds an earlier image, as the doctor would be able to access the previous scan from the cloud. Shobajo said the platform also allows radiologists to review images remotely instead of being physically present at the diagnostic centre. Shobajo says DycoVue wants to reduce the time patients spend waiting for their results, with a target of delivering them within 15 minutes.
DycoSuite is also intended to bring imaging and laboratory information together under a patient’s record. Shobajo argues that diagnosing and monitoring a condition can involve several tests, and the results should be accessible together rather than scattered across different systems.
“Whatever they’re doing, whether it’s images or labs related to the same issue, the same patient information should be under one bucket,” she said.
DycoAtlas, the company’s second product, is a needs-assessment and mapping tool intended to help governments, healthcare planners and philanthropies understand where diagnostic facilities and equipment are located, what services they offer and what prevents them from operating effectively. So far, the team has surveyed 240 facilities across four states, according to Shobajo. The team also records facility coordinates because it found that some diagnostic centres it visited were not listed on Google Maps.
Building the infrastructure for AI-assisted imaging
DycoVue has been operating since 2025 and has so far funded its operations without external investment, according to Shobajo. The company currently has five team members, split between Nigeria and the United States. Shobajo said the startup recently signed its first paying user, a private diagnostic centre in Nigeria, where the team is deploying the product. She did not disclose how the company charges facilities.
According to the company, its pilot helped two facilities digitise more than 100,000 medical images covering about 600 patients, with records dating from 2023 to 2026.
Shobajo explained that DycoVue’s priority is to get the product into more facilities and demonstrate that clinics can use it to manage their imaging records. Shobajo says the company is considering raising capital in 2027 to improve its existing products and expand its reach. The company wants to connect DycoSuite to electronic medical record (EMR) systems already used by healthcare providers, creating a more connected record of patients’ diagnostic history.
That groundwork is also central to the company’s plans for AI-assisted medical imaging. Shobajo says DycoVue hopes to begin developing this capability in 2027. She argues that storing images over time is important for tracking how a patient’s condition changes and for building datasets that can support AI models.

articles.title: Alfonso, funcionario de la Seguridad Social: “Quien retrase un año su jubilación podrá recibir un pago de 8.500 euros”
articles.text:
Explica Alfonso Muñoz Cuenca que uno de los incentivos que tienen los trabajadores que deciden continuar trabajando tras alcanzar su edad ordinaria de retiro es el de poder acceder a un pago único de 8.000 o 8.500 euros. Es decir, se trata de un incentivo que puede pagarse si se retrasa un año la jubilación. Depende de la situación de cada trabajador.
Con la jubilación demorada, el trabajador puede optar por retrasar de manera voluntaria su acceso a la pensión a cambio de un complemento económico. Este complemento puede ser en forma de incremento de la pensión mensual o bien a tanto alzado. También puede haber una mezcla de ambos. En este caso sí que hace falta que se haya retrasado un mínimo de dos años completos. Es decir, que si solo se retrasa un año, no se puede pedir la opción de pago mixto.
Este pago se calcula de manera individual. Depende de la cantidad de la pensión y de los años cotizados que tenga el trabajador en el momento de alcanzar la edad ordinaria de jubilación. Por ello, en algunos casos, los 8.500 euros de los que habla Muñoz pueden ser superiores. De hecho, en algunos casos pueden llegar a ser superiores a los 10.000 euros por año de demora. En los ejemplos que pone el organismo ya se contempla esta posibilidad. Es el caso de las personas que tienen una carrera de cotización más larga y una pensión más alta.
Qué hay que decidir al solicitar la pensión
Esta elección solo hay que hacerla una vez. Es decir, en el momento de solicitar la pensión (cuando se adquiere el derecho al complemento). Una vez elegida la opción, no se puede cambiar (artículo 210.2 de la Ley General de la Seguridad Social). Como insiste Muñoz, el trabajador tiene estas opciones:
Es importante pensar si queremos recibir el dinero en un solo pago (al jubilarnos) o si preferimos que nos aumenten nuestra pensión mensual. Hay que saber que podemos trabajar y cobrar pensión si cumplimos los requisitos de compatibilidad y que tenemos estos incentivos por retrasar nuestro retiro.
También es relevante pensar en cómo afectará a nuestros impuestos. Este pago único se considera rendimiento del trabajo (por ello tributa en el impuesto sobre la renta de las personas físicas (IRPF)). La Agencia Tributaria contempla una reducción del 30 % en el caso de que se cumplan los requisitos. Hay que saber que el importe bruto del complemento no es necesariamente equivalente al importe neto.
Muñoz también apunta a que hay que pensar en otros aspectos. Por ejemplo, en nuestra salud. O en las características de nuestro puesto de trabajo. También es importante pensar en la calidad de vida.
Además, debemos tener en cuenta nuestros proyectos personales. Saber que existe este incentivo económico nos va a permitir tenerlo en cuenta en nuestra planificación de la jubilación. También hay que tener en cuenta aquellas circunstancias que hacen más o menos viable continuar trabajando.

articles.title: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
articles.text:
Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
- Date:
- November 11, 2026
- Source:
- ETH Zurich
- Summary:
- Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.
- Share:
A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.
Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.
By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.
The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.
Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers
The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.
Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.
The major difference lies in how that information is stored.
"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.
Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.
Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better
One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.
In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.
Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.
However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.
Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.
Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.
New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests
The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.
The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.
To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.
"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.
Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.
A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers
One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.
However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.
Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.
Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.
Story Source:
Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yu Yang, Igor Kladarić, Martynas Skrabulis, Michael Eichenberger, Stefano Marti, Simon Storz, Jonathan Esche, Raquel García Bellés, Max-Emanuel Kern, Andraz Omahen, Arianne Brooks, Marius Bild, Matteo Fadel, Yiwen Chu. Mechanical resonator–based quantum computing. Science, 2026; 392 (6801): 972 DOI: 10.1126/science.aef4139

articles.title: Microsoft Agent Framework Releases Poisoned With Credential Stealer
articles.text:
Hackers distributed two malicious versions of Microsoft’s Agent Framework Python package through PyPI in a November 17 supply chain attack, potentially exposing cloud and CI/CD credentials belonging to users who installed them.
Microsoft Agent Framework is designed for developing AI agents and multi-agent applications. The affected package, agent-framework, has approximately 190,000 downloads per month.
The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were released roughly 33 minutes apart. Both have since been quarantined on PyPI, where version 1.26.0 remains the latest clean release.
Microsoft has acknowledged the incident, with an Agent Framework maintainer confirming in a GitHub discussion that the compromised releases were removed from PyPI and that an investigation was underway.
The malicious distributions retained the legitimate framework components while introducing additional code that attempted to steal credentials. This allowed applications to continue functioning normally despite the compromise.
Researchers at OX Security, Wiz, Endor Labs, and SafeDep independently analyzed the malware, which exploits a Python startup mechanism to execute automatically in an affected environment.
The malware runs whenever the Python interpreter starts, even if the application doesn’t explicitly import the compromised package.
Its targets include secrets stored in environment variables and configuration files, as well as credentials belonging to other running processes. It also attempts to obtain Azure managed identity tokens and Azure DevOps authentication tokens that could provide access to cloud resources.
The second malicious release expanded the credential-stealing functionality to GitHub Actions.
The method used to publish the malicious packages remains unknown. Unlike legitimate releases, which included both built and source distributions, the malicious versions contained only built packages. Wiz also found no corresponding releases or malicious code in Microsoft’s main source repository, suggesting the packages may have been uploaded outside the normal release process.
SafeDep identified a PyPI maintainer account named vibiret, created on the day of the attack, with publishing permissions for the affected package and five related projects. However, the account’s involvement in the malicious uploads has not been confirmed.
Organizations are advised to check developer environments, CI/CD pipelines, and container images for the compromised versions, and replace affected installations with verified packages. They should also rotate potentially exposed credentials, investigate suspicious cloud activity, and rebuild affected environments.
Microsoft’s Agent Framework repository on GitHub is inaccessible at the time of writing. Several other Microsoft repositories, including ONNX Runtime projects, have similarly disappeared, but it is unclear whether the incidents are related.

articles.title: Meatable co-founder’s new firm Iconic raises €9.1 million to build AI operating system for large capital projects | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Iconic, an Amsterdam-based startup building an AI operating system for large capital projects, has raised €9.1 million ($10 million) in Seed funding to bring AI-powered intelligence to these projects, with five major clients already onboard.
Peak Capital, an early-stage venture capital fund based in Amsterdam, Berlin, and Munich, led the round, with participation from Bridford Group, Common Magic, Graduate Ventures, NP-Hard, and Tiny VC.
“Capital projects are among the largest undertakings in the physical economy, yet far too few land on time, on budget, and on scope. The bottleneck is decision quality, not effort. Iconic is the shift behind our Blue Collar Renaissance thesis made real: AI-native software reaching the built world. With exceptional founders and blue-chip customers from day one, we are proud to lead this round,” said Tea Elezi, Partner at Peak Capital.
Iconic was founded in mid-2025 by second-time founders Krijn de Nood (co-founder of Amsterdam-based Meatable) and Richard Stronkman (founder of PublicSonar). Before co-founding Meatable, de Nood led assurance reviews of megaprojects worth up to $15 billion at McKinsey. Stronkman founded and exited PublicSonar, an AI company specialising in extracting early-warning signals from unstructured data, the same core capability that underpins Iconic.
Iconic helps asset owners and contractors in energy, infrastructure, and AI to review documents, apply lessons learned and standards, and make better project decisions.
According to the company, companies invest an estimated $15 trillion in capital projects annually, yet fewer than 3% are delivered on time, on budget, and to plan. It argues that capital projects rarely fail because of engineering complexity, but because decisions are made without a complete understanding of the project, mostly because information is fragmented across documents and systems shared by owners, contractors, and engineering firms.
Iconic claims that its proprietary AI software connects design, engineering, commercial, and contract information to identify contradictions, missing information, design flaws, and constraints before they cause rework or claims.
“Software has always organised the documents, but it never understood the project. Capital projects fail in predictable ways, yet every new one is treated as unique, and what one team learns leaves with its people. We are building software that understands each project and remembers the ones before it,” said Krijn de Nood, Iconic’s CEO and co-founder.
The company reports that in one review, it found that the plot plan for a new industrial plant placed part of the facility inside the site’s safety boundary, where construction was prohibited. Since it was caught during design, it could be addressed before construction, avoiding redesign and months of delay.
Iconic is ISO 27001 certified, SOC 2 Type II compliant, and GDPR compliant. The Dutch startup also reveals that since its inception, it has signed five clients in energy, infrastructure, and AI infrastructure: a global energy major, a leading European utility, a major European airport, a European rail infrastructure owner, and a global contractor building semiconductor fabs and data centres. Each spends over $1 billion annually on capital projects.
It notes that client demand is growing faster than its team can serve it. Therefore, it plans to use this funding to expand its commercial and delivery teams in Amsterdam, support expansion into Germany, the UK, and the US, and extend the platform across the project lifecycle with blueprints for each project type, so every project improves the next.

articles.title: Online shoppers can save $65 in fees at Rogers, Fido right now
articles.text:
Rogers and flanker brand Fido are back to offering free shipping on phones as we head into the holiday shopping season. Moreover, Rogers is waiving its $40 device setup charge for online orders.
Previously, Rogers and Fido charged $25 for shipping. However, as of Nov. 17, both providers’ websites now list shipping costs as free. Further, a banner at the top of the websites notes that customers who buy online also skip the device setup fee.
It’s a notably change, both for the consumer savings as well as Rogers’ recent history with both these fees.
Rogers first launched the $25 shipping fee back in 2024 just ahead of that year’s iPhone launch. The fee stuck around for a while until it received some scrutiny from the CRTC earlier this year. Rogers briefly lowered the fee to $9 in July, only to increase it back to $25 in September.
The device setup fee, on the other hand, was a new charge Rogers introduced in response to the CRTC’s ban on junk fees. Rogers wasn’t the only one, with Bell also introducing a similar $40 device fee. The CRTC is still reviewing the fees to determine if the carriers violated the new rules.

articles.text:
PCIe and trust; rack-scale co-design; heterogeneous scaling; AI data center primer; on-device balancing; EU semi trends.
Cadence’s Rajesh Pamujula considers how to establish trust when sensitive data, proprietary models, cryptographic keys, and confidential workloads increasingly traverse PCIe links.
Synopsys’ Neeraj Paliwal argues that extreme co-design, where silicon, interface IP, memory, cooling, and power are designed together as one system, is needed for efficient racks that are capable of running increasingly demanding AI workloads.
Siemens’ Kevin Rinebold and Andras Vass-Varnai examine the evolving semiconductor design landscape shaped by the shift from monolithic scaling to heterogeneous architectures and consider how to navigate the complexities of AI-driven 3D-IC and chiplet technologies.
Keysight’s Linas Dauksa provides a primer on the technologies that power AI data centers, how they handle training and inference workloads, and why they’ve become the backbone of modern AI.
Arm’s Michael Gamble checks out how to enable gaze-based interactions in lightweight smart glasses by running fast, sensor-dependent AI on-device while larger workloads stay where more compute is available.
SEMI’s Sitong He chats with Patrick Vandenameele of imec about the trends reshaping the semiconductor industry, why collaboration matters more than ever, and the role Europe can play in global competitiveness.
Plus, check out blogs featured in the latest Low Power-High Performance newsletter:
Rambus’ Kushal Koolwal examines why longer contexts, higher concurrency, multimodal models, and AI agents will continue changing where memory pressure appears.
Siemens EDA’s Jim Shiely shows how to use evidence from silicon to improve the tools and decisions for next-gen hardware.
Synopsys’ Andrew Appleby observes that traditional voltage scaling is no longer sufficient to deliver real-time performance within tight energy and thermal limits.
Cadence’s Joe Chen demonstrates how to right-size the memory hierarchy around the device’s data streams, reuse patterns, latency requirements, and operating constraints.
Arm’s Siyu Mou explains the rationale behind 8-bit floating-point data formats, their ecosystem momentum, and hardware support.
