articles.text:
Good morning ☀️️
Cape Town has a date with AI this Friday, and TechCabal’s publisher is taking the stage.
On November 20, OpenAI Academy, Andela, and Innovation City are bringing the Codex Champions Showcase to Cape Town, South Africa, with a focus on how Africans can use AI to tell their own stories.
Tomiwa Aladekomo, chief executive of Big Cabal Media, TechCabal’s parent company, will join Jessica Hope, founder of communications agency Wimbart, for a conversation about storytelling in the age of AI.
And it won’t be all talk. Five finalists from Andela’s talent network will demonstrate tools they’ve built with OpenAI’s Codex to help African creators tell better stories, reach bigger audiences, and bring their ideas to life. The showcase has already made stops in Nairobi and Lagos. Cape Town gets its turn this Friday, from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. SAST.
If you’re in town, register here. Come for the ideas, stay for the demos, and say hello to Tomiwa.
Now, on to today’s stories.
—Emmanuel
TC Mzansi, our newsletter covering South African tech is coming on November 23.
Internet
Starlink issued notice to cease unauthorised operations in South Africa
Starlink has spent three years finding its way into South African homes without officially launching there. The country’s telecoms regulator has finally sent it a message: No licence, no Internet party.
On October 14, South Africa’s Independent Communications Authority (ICASA), the country’s telecoms regulator, issued a formal notice of non-compliance to SpaceX, Elon Musk’s aerospace company, ordering it to stop providing unauthorised Starlink services in the country.
Communications Minister Solly Malatsi disclosed the order in a parliamentary response. Starlink isn’t licenced in South Africa, but some residents haven’t stopped using it.
Explain like I’m new here: Since 2023, South Africans, particularly those in poorly connected rural areas, have used Starlink’s international roaming service to get online. The trick was to buy a Starlink dish, register it in a neighbouring country like Lesotho, and use it back home—no South African licence required.
Starlink recently tried closing that loophole. It tightened roaming restrictions, cutting the permitted stay from 60 days to 30 days, then to just seven days for users in South Africa. In October, the company introduced stricter identity and country-of-origin checks to stop customers from registering their kits abroad and using them indefinitely in South Africa.
Some users had already found creative workarounds, from temporarily switching their kits off to crossing the border to reset their roaming clocks. ICASA wasn’t amused.
Here’s the bigger problem: South Africa’s telecoms licencing rules require at least 30% ownership by historically disadvantaged groups. The government has proposed allowing qualifying investments in local businesses and skills development as an alternative, but the regulatory framework remains contested.
Zoom out: This is about more than a few satellite dishes. Starlink offers a way to reach communities that traditional broadband networks struggle to serve. South Africa also has a legitimate interest in ensuring telecoms providers follow its licencing rules.
ICASA’s investigation is ongoing, and it has yet to determine any penalties. South Africa wants Starlink to use the front door. The country is still arguing over what the key should look like.

Pay with OPay is live on Fincra. Customers approve payments straight from their OPay wallet, and you get confirmation back on your site. Available now for NGN collections! Upgrade your business today with Fincra pay with OPay.
Telecoms
MTN revives bid to take over Telkom
MTN seems to have developed a taste for big infrastructure deals. In February, the telco giant agreed to buy the remaining 75.3% of IHS Towers—one of Africa’s largest independent tower companies—that it did not already own. Now it is back knocking on Telkom’s door.
What happened? MTN Group is back in talks to acquire rival Telkom, a South African telecoms group, four years after an earlier attempt fell apart. The discussions are early, but MTN is considering a cash offer, and Telkom shareholders could potentially take MTN shares instead.
Explain like I’m new here: In 2022, the two companies held takeover discussions, but MTN wanted Telkom to consider its proposal without negotiating competing offers. Rain, another South African telecoms operator, had expressed interest in Telkom at the time. MTN eventually walked away.
Competition regulators will be circling: Combining two major mobile operators could give the merged business considerable influence over prices, infrastructure and access to customers. Regulators would want to know whether the benefits of combining networks outweigh the risk of reducing competition. In 2024, the Competition Tribunal blocked Vodacom’s proposed 30% investment in Maziv, the company housing fibre operators Vumatel and Dark Fibre Africa, for similar reasons. After a series of appeals, it secured approval in August 2025. That likely gave MTN some reason to believe consolidation is possible.
What it could mean: MTN reported 39.49 million South African subscribers in June, while Telkom had 25.67 million mobile subscribers in March. Together, that is about 65.2 million subscribers. Hurdles remain as the South African government owns 40.5% of Telkom, while the Public Investment Corporation (PIC), the state’s investment arm, holds another 11.08%. No deal has been agreed, and the companies say there is no certainty one will happen.
Capital Markets
NGX buys a piece of Kenya’s stock market
The NGX Group, the parent company of the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) and other market infrastructure businesses, has bought a 10% equity stake in the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE), the institution that operates Kenya’s main stock market.
Explain like I’m new here: In 2024, NGX Group invested in the Ethiopian Securities Exchange (ESX), the country’s first-ever bourse in decades. NGX became a 10% shareholder and secured a seat on its board. ESX launched in January 2025, and it still has a long way to go before becoming a busy cross-border investment corridor.
NGX is not alone in this strategy, as exchange operators are looking beyond their home markets for investment returns and opportunities to build regional relationships. In 2021, the NSE acquired an additional 4% stake in Tanzania’s Dar es Salaam Stock Exchange.
What could this unlock? A Nigerian investor buying shares in a Kenyan company may face different brokers, regulations, settlement arrangements, and currency-conversion requirements. NGX’s investment could help connect these markets. The Dangote Refinery share sale, which allowed regional investors to participate through local market operators, offers a glimpse of what cross-border access can look like. Companies could eventually reach investors in more than one market.
Yet, owning 10% of the Kenyan bourse does not automatically create a shared trading platform or remove the regulatory and currency hurdles between the two markets.
Fintech
Payaza secures Kenyan licence
Payaza has been collecting something more useful than passport stamps: regulators’ signatures.
Just 17 days after securing approval in Zambia, the Nigerian-founded payments company has landed another one in Kenya. In an email on Monday, Payaza announced to merchants in two words in Swahili: Ni rasmi! It’s official!
The Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) granted the company a payment service provider licence on November 5, allowing it to process online payments for Kenyan businesses.
Explain like I’m new here: Payaza provides the infrastructure that helps businesses accept payments from customers. It says it operates in more than 27 countries worldwide, including Nigeria, Ghana, Uganda, Tanzania, and South Africa.
Its latest approval lets Kenyan merchants use Payaza to accept card payments, mobile money, and bank transfers. The company also plans to support merchant settlements and cross-border collections.
Between the lines: Payaza isn’t getting permission to become another M-PESA. Its licence covers payment gateway services, not customer wallets or deposit-taking. The Kenyan approval follows an October 19 authorisation from the Bank of Zambia, which designated Payaza as a payment system operator.
Zoom out: Kenya is hardly short of ways to pay. But collecting money from customers across different African markets remains complicated by local banking systems, currencies and regulations.
Payaza is betting that businesses would rather use one payments provider than piece together a different solution in every country.
Two licences in 17 days is impressive paperwork. Getting merchants to use those payment rails is where the real business begins.

articles.title: Bull Shows Intel Xeon Diamond Rapids Package at SC26
articles.text:
Intel is doing a mini launch of its next-generation server CPU (or something thereabouts at SC26). There are many systems on the floor, but one, the Bull Sequana XH31600, actually showed Diamond Rapids packages.
Bull Shows Intel Xeon Diamond Rapids Package at SC26
Starting off, here is the Bull compute blade with blind mate power and liquid at the rear, networking in front, and four Intel Xeon Diamond Rapids packages up front.
Just ot be clear about what you are seeing, these are two dual-socket compute nodes with Intel Diamond Rapids, each with 16-channel memory.
Here is a view of the package. We have already seen the LGA9324 socket covered in the ASRock Rack DMRD16-2L+ from OCP Summit 2026.
You can see that in the Bull platform, the CPUs are on fairly wide motherboards because of all of the memory on either side.
The idea is that these blades are liquid cooled, so you can see how everything has heatpipes and liquid cooling blocks.
The other node had the liquid cooling blocks as well as the cabled connections to the networking.
On the networking, Bull had its BXI technology for interconnect. In its booth, Bull showed a BXI switch with 64x 800G OSFP ports, but the BXI NICs were shown as QSFP-DD and PCIe Gen5 x16. It actually looks like Bull is doing something similar to what we did with the NVIDIA ConnectX-8 C8240 800G Dual 400G NIC Review This is a SuperNIC when we managed to use two PCIe Gen5 x16 links to get 800Gbps from the ConnectX-8.
What stood out a bit is that there was an NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNIC as well in an OCP NIC 3.0 form factor. It’s interesting that Bull has its own interconnect, with a 51.2T switch and a PCIe Gen5 NIC in a platform with a Gen6 CPU, but right next to it is NVIDIA’s high-volume PCIe Gen6 NIC competitor.
What is very cool about this platform is that it is incredibly bespoke.
For years, Bull has had one of the better-looking blade designs, largely because they liquid-cool everything. Probably worth pondering, however, is that with NVIDIA pushing the industry with ORv3, and AMD now with the double-wide. It feels like there is a high-volume standard for high-density racks in the industry if you want power and cooling. Maybe the more interesting part is that Bull’s design does not have a copper-cabled backplane in the rear.
Overall, this was very neat to see.
Final Words
What has been interesting at SC26 is that this type of platform would have been mind-blowing years ago. Now, with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin designs in ORv3 racks, the Bull systems fit in with the higher-volume AI infrastructure bits. What Bull has, however, is SiPearl, Intel Xeon Diamond Rapids, NVIDIA, and AMD Venice nodes on display in a common form factor.
Many other vendors are showing off Diamond Rapids systems with neat designs, including 32DIMM/ socket 2DPC configurations at SC26. For its part, Bull is the only one we have found that has a package. Diamond Rapids seems to be in the sampling phase. The best guess is maybe we start to see a launch in Q2 2027, but if that slips past June (or it becomes a split launch with 1P platforms and 2P platforms), the next real launch window for Intel is early September 2027.

articles.title: Oracle Patches 950 Vulnerabilities With November 2026 CSPU
articles.text:
Oracle on Tuesday announced the release of 655 new security patches as part of its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU).
SecurityWeek has counted 948 unique CVEs listed throughout Oracle’s advisory. Of these, 640 appear in the products’ risk matrices. The remainder include additional vulnerabilities addressed by the patches and third-party CVEs that Oracle considers non-exploitable in its products.
Just over 300 patches address security defects that can be exploited remotely without authentication. Sixty-two security patches resolve critical-severity flaws, including half a dozen max-severity bugs.
Hyperion received the largest set of fixes in the November 2026 CSPU, at 267, including 107 for vulnerabilities that can be exploited remotely without authentication.
The Supply Chain update contains 74 new security patches, including 36 for unauthenticated, remotely exploitable flaws. Fusion Middleware received 71 patches (53 unauthenticated, remotely exploitable), the same as E-Business Suite (19 exploitable remotely without authentication).
Oracle also pushed numerous patches for Communications (31 – 21 unauthenticated, remotely exploitable), Analytics (29 – 9), Siebel CRM (19 – 9), PeopleSoft (13 – 6), Java SE (11 – 11), Financial Services Applications (11 – 1), Virtualization (11 – 3), and MySQL (10 – 3).
The updates for Fusion Middleware and Analytics resolve six max-severity flaws (five and one, respectively), while the Java SE security refresh fixes Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory corruption issue leading to memory leaks and remote code execution.
Other Oracle products that received patches this month include Database Server, APEX, Autonomous Health Framework, REST Data Services, Application Testing Suite, Commerce, Construction and Engineering, Enterprise Manager, and JD Edwards.
While Oracle makes no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild, organizations are advised to apply the patches as soon as possible, as security defects in the company’s products are an attractive target to threat actors.

articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo. Original written by José Tadeu Arantes. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Xian-Peng Zhang, Chuanchang Zeng, Zhen-Biao Yang, Jose Carlos Egues, Yugui Yao. Andreev qubit readout from dynamic interference supercurrent. Physical Review B, 2026; 114 (8) DOI: 10.1103/6gkt-hghj

articles.text:
Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) ainda não chegou oficialmente ao público, mas já movimentou mais de US$ 1,5 bilhão em pré-vendas, segundo estimativas da empresa de inteligência de mercado Sensor Tower divulgadas pela CNN nesta quarta-feira (18).
O resultado foi alcançado antes do lançamento do jogo, marcado para 19 de novembro de 2026, após uma espera de 13 anos desde a estreia de GTA V.
A arrecadação antecipada reforça a dimensão comercial do novo título da Rockstar Games, que já apresenta resultados superiores aos registrados por outros grandes lançamentos da indústria.
GTA 6 ultrapassou US$ 1 bilhão em pré-vendas nove dias antes da estreia
De acordo com a Sensor Tower, GTA 6 superou a marca de US$ 1 bilhão em receita de pré-vendas quando ainda faltavam nove dias para seu lançamento.
Na mesma distância da estreia, o valor era quase o dobro do registrado por Call of Duty: Modern Warfare II, lançado em 2022 e considerado o jogo mais vendido daquele ano nos Estados Unidos.
Agora, com a arrecadação estimada acima de US$ 1,5 bilhão, GTA 6 chega à véspera de seu lançamento com um desempenho comercial expressivo.
Os números, entretanto, são estimativas de mercado e não representam um balanço financeiro oficial divulgado pela Rockstar Games ou pela Take-Two Interactive.
GTA Online já gerou mais de US$ 5 bilhões em receita
O sucesso comercial da franquia não depende apenas das vendas de novos títulos.
Lançado em 2013, GTA V continuou gerando receita ao longo dos anos, principalmente por meio de GTA Online, seu componente multiplayer.
Segundo os dados apresentados pela CNN, GTA Online arrecadou mais de US$ 5 bilhões ao longo da última década.
O modelo permite que a Rockstar mantenha o interesse dos jogadores por meio de atualizações, novos conteúdos e modos de jogo, além da comercialização de itens e benefícios virtuais.
Essa estratégia ajudou a prolongar a vida comercial de GTA V durante os 13 anos que separaram os dois lançamentos principais da franquia.
Com a chegada de GTA 6, a expectativa é que a série amplie ainda mais sua participação entre as franquias de videogames mais vendidas da história.

articles.title: The first Nvidia RTX Spark mini PCs launch today from Asus, Dell, and MSI
articles.text:
After the first RTX Spark laptops launched earlier this year, Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X chip is also now available in desktops from Asus, Dell, and MSI. More RTX Spark desktops are coming later from Acer, Gigabyte, and HP, while Microsoft’s Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is slated to start shipping this month. The new mini PCs include a 6144-core Nvidia Blackwell RTX GPU, 20-core Nvidia Grace CPU, and up to 128GB of memory. That high-end hardware comes with a price to match — Asus’s ProArt GR1X starts at $4,499 for a configuration with 64GB of memory and 1TB of storage.
The first Nvidia RTX Spark mini PCs launch today from Asus, Dell, and MSI
These desktop PCs can pair Nvidia’s ‘superchip’ with up to 128GB of memory for running local AI models.
Like the RTX Spark laptops that compete with the MacBook Pro and the DGX Spark desktop Nvidia launched last year, the new mini PCs are Mac Mini or Mac Studio alternatives for developers working with local AI models, as well as RTX-accelerated software. That includes the AI-powered features for tools like Adobe Premiere and Photoshop, and new DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support in Blender 5.3.
They can run games too, and Windows on Arm game support is improving, but at these prices, that’s not a realistic reason to pick one up yet. Nvidia says they can act as a “dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents,” and deliver “up to 1 petaflop of AI performance.” They also feature native CUDA support and access to Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux.

articles.title: TikTok moviliza y Facebook polariza hacia la extrema derecha: así describen las redes nuestro voto
articles.text:
TikTok moviliza y Facebook polariza hacia la extrema derecha: así describen las redes nuestro voto
Una nueva investigación con datos inéditos de una operadora francesa confirma que las plataformas inciden en el voto y permite observar cómo algunas plataformas etiquetan políticamente a sus usuarios
En dos municipios similares en renta, paro y edad, ¿a quién votan más sus ciudadanos si consumen más Facebook? A la extrema derecha. ¿Y si navegan sobre todo por Instagram? Se inclinan más por partidos más bien de centro y progresistas. ¿Y TikTok? En ese lugar, habrá más movilización, repartida entre todos los partidos. ¿Y si destacan por leer medios de comunicación en internet? Sobre todo, no votarán a la extrema derecha.
Estas conclusiones pertenecen a una nueva investigación realizada con datos muy difíciles de lograr para la mayoría de académicos: la navegación de 22 millones de ciudadanos franceses durante las elecciones europeas de 2019 y 2024. Además de las valoraciones sobre cada red social, el trabajo llega a otra gran conclusión que a menudo se pone en duda: las redes sociales tienen impacto en las democracias. “No encontrar ninguna correlación hubiera sido como una prueba de que las aplicaciones no afectan de ningún modo el voto”, dice Marco Fiore, del instituto de investigación Imdea Networks de Madrid. “Como hemos encontrado correlaciones, ya no es posible”, añade Fiore, coautor del trabajo con académicos de la Universidad Carlos III, la Universidad Northeastern (Boston) y la operadora Orange en Francia.
No todas las redes tienen un impacto significativo o en una sola dirección. El artículo mide 27 plataformas o servicios online en 2024, desde redes a medios de información agrupados o servicios de streaming. TikTok tiene un enorme efecto movilizador a favor de todos los partidos en 2024 (en 2019 no se midió por su papel menor), pero también lo tienen, aunque menos, YouTube, LinkedIn o Telegram. La mayoría de servicios de streaming no apuntan a nada muy notable.
Facebook, más que nadie
La red social con un impacto más notable y consistente en el voto entre 2019 y 2024 es, sin ninguna duda, Facebook. No solo los municipios con un uso relativo mayor de Facebook votan más a la extrema derecha de Marine Le Pen; también votan menos al resto de partidos, sobre todo La Francia Insumisa, de Jean-Luc Mélenchon, según el estudio.
La red X, antes Twitter, es un caso curioso. La opinión popular es que, desde la compra de Elon Musk en 2022, la plataforma se ha vuelto más conservadora. En las europeas francesas, al menos, el proceso ha sido el contrario: de vincularse a un voto más centrista en 2019 a algo más progresista ahora.
Los investigadores han querido comprobar también la utilidad de sus resultados para ayudar a predecir el voto: ¿qué pasa si añadimos el consumo digital de los ciudadanos a las variables tradicionales demográficas? Hicieron dos modelos: el primero trataba de predecir el voto solo con renta, paro y edad. El segundo añade las aplicaciones digitales. El segundo acierta más (y más aún con el paso de los años y la penetración del mundo online): un 9,6% más en 2019 y un 28% más en 2024. Esa mejora es la información sobre el voto que aporta internet y que los datos socioeconómicos no recogen.
El mismo grupo ya usó datos similares en 2022 para averiguar si el uso de internet también era capaz de predecir el estatus socioeconómico. Entonces los medios, la música por streaming, el WhatsApp y el email aumentaban la probabilidad de zona rica. Si, al contrario, se usaba más Facebook, YouTube, Snapchat, se miraba porno y se jugaba al Candy Crush, las opciones de que fuera un barrio pobre crecían.
“Después de aquel primer estudio donde vimos una señal tan clara, esperábamos que ocurriera en otras dimensiones de la vida”, dice Iñaki Úcar, profesor de la Universidad Carlos III y coautor de ambos trabajos. “Si eso funcionó, pues tiene que funcionar para más cosas como el voto. En el aspecto político se da una cosa que no se da en el socioeconómico. En las redes hay una retroalimentación que hace que tu comportamiento se vea reforzado”, añade.
Los investigadores insisten en que todo esto no significa que las redes provoquen nada. Es el célebre mantra de “correlación no implica causalidad”: que dos cosas pasen a la vez no significa que una sea causa de la otra. Es cierto que un usuario de Facebook puede radicalizarse viendo la red día tras día. Pero también es cierto que sea primero de ideología de ultraderecha y acabe luego en Facebook.
Es como si en municipios similares más gente viera un medio conservador o progresista. Es lógico que acabarán votando a los partidos que representen esas ideas. No estaba claro que con las plataformas online ocurriera algo parecido. Pero cada vez hay más pruebas.
También es innegable que el impacto de internet es total. “El mundo digital va teniendo una importancia mayor”, dice Fiore. “Si los operadores quieren ayudar a explicar el voto con datos agregados, ayudaría a explicar más allá de lo que se puede hacer ahora”, añade.

articles.title: La Backbone One USB-C, manette de référence pour smartphone, chute sous les 50 € pour le Black Friday — Frandroid
articles.text:
La Backbone One est l’une des rares manettes pour smartphone à tenir la comparaison avec une vraie manette de console sur le plan de la construction. Format très compact, finitions soignées, compatibilité large : depuis son lancement, elle s’est imposée comme l’option à glisser dans un sac pour jouer en déplacement, que ce soit en cloud gaming ou en remote play depuis une PlayStation ou une Xbox. Elle avait toutefois un défaut, son prix de 119,99 euros au lancement, mais le Black Friday passe par là pour la faire chuter sous les 50 euros.
Les atouts de la Backbone One USB-C
- Format ultra-compact, facile à glisser dans n’importe quel sac
- Compatible USB-C : fonctionne avec la quasi-totalité des Android récents (Android 10 ou plus) et avec les iPhone 15 et suivants
- Construction de qualité, prise en main confortable au quotidien
Désormais habituellement vendue 69,99 euros, la Backbone One USB-C passe à 49,99 euros sur Cdiscount. L’offre est également disponible chez la Fnac et Darty.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant la Backbone One (USB-C). Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Un format passe-partout, une finition au-dessus du lot
La Backbone One se distingue d’abord par son gabarit. Avec ses 176,2 millimètres de long pour 32,6 millimètres d’épaisseur, elle disparaît dans un sac à dos sans effort. C’est franchement rare dans le segment des manettes rétractables, où la tendance va plutôt vers des formats plus larges et plus lourds. Bref, c’est une manette qu’on emmène vraiment partout, sans y penser.
La construction suit la même logique : le plastique est lisse, les arêtes sont arrondies, et la prise en main reste confortable même en session prolongée. Ce n’est pas aussi enveloppant qu’une DualSense ou qu’une Xbox Series, mais pour un accessoire nomade, c’est amplement suffisant. Principal bémol, les joysticks sont un peu petits par rapport à ceux d’une manette traditionnelle et demandent un temps d’adaptation. Rien de rédhibitoire, mais à noter si vous venez d’un pad classique.
Une expérience logicielle bien pensée, avec quelques réserves
L’application Backbone, disponible sur Android et iOS, est l’un des arguments les plus solides de la marque. Elle centralise les accès aux services de cloud gaming, propose des raccourcis vers les bibliothèques de jeux compatibles et affiche une interface claire et simple à prendre en main. L’intégration est soignée : le smartphone reconnaît la manette immédiatement, sans jumelage à bricoler. Sur ce point, la Backbone One devance franchement beaucoup de ses concurrentes, dont l’expérience logicielle reste sommaire.
Honnêtement, il y a un revers : certaines fonctionnalités avancées de l’application, comme l’enregistrement de séquences de jeu Smart Record, sont réservées aux abonnés Backbone+. Ce n’est pas bloquant pour un usage basique, mais ça laisse un léger goût de fonctionnalités bridées. Les gâchettes analogiques, elles, font le travail. Souples, avec une course courte, elles conviennent bien aux jeux de tir ou d’action. Elles manquent en revanche de précision pour doser finement l’accélération, dans un jeu de course par exemple.
Pour aller plus loin sur la construction, l’expérience logicielle et les usages en conditions réelles, vous pouvez consulter notre test de la Backbone One 2e génération, qui détaille chaque aspect de la manette.

articles.title: OpenAI incorporará investigadores externos para detectar si sus modelos de IA intentan evadir controles
articles.text:
OpenAI integrará investigadores de cuatro organizaciones externas en pruebas piloto para evaluar la seguridad de sus modelos de inteligencia artificial. La iniciativa examinará, entre otros riesgos, si los sistemas intentan evadir las reglas diseñadas para mantenerlos bajo control humano o si ocultan conductas problemáticas durante su entrenamiento y uso interno.
Las evaluaciones estarán a cargo de Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR y Transluce, con tareas y alcances distintos. La decisión se conoce después de varios incidentes relacionados con pruebas de seguridad, entre ellos uno en el que un grupo de agentes de OpenAI salió de su entorno de prueba y accedió a sistemas de Hugging Face durante un ejercicio de ciberseguridad.
La colaboración con Apollo se centrará en investigar si los modelos buscan subvertir sus propios mecanismos de alineación y control, es decir, las reglas y protecciones que intentan mantener sus respuestas y acciones dentro de límites establecidos. Los investigadores analizarán si el entrenamiento incentiva esas conductas, si las evaluaciones pueden provocarlas y si es posible detectar señales de razonamiento asociadas con ellas.
Qué evaluará cada organización
Goodfire aportará especialistas en interpretabilidad, un campo que busca entender cómo funcionan los modelos internamente. La organización usará sus herramientas para observar procesos de entrenamiento, ayudar a identificar comportamientos no deseados y contribuir a mejorar la alineación de los sistemas. Sus hallazgos estarán dirigidos principalmente a los investigadores de OpenAI.
METR realizará dos evaluaciones. Una buscará comportamientos peligrosos o inesperados que las pruebas internas de OpenAI podrían no haber detectado. La otra revisará si los propios sistemas de la empresa son capaces de reconocer esas conductas. Para la primera evaluación, METR tendrá margen para decidir qué investigar y cómo poner a prueba el modelo. El alcance de la segunda todavía estaba en discusión, según la información publicada.
Transluce examinará si las evaluaciones de seguridad que OpenAI realiza después del entrenamiento son suficientes. También prevé estudiar en 2027 cómo la empresa utiliza los resultados de esas pruebas para decidir si un modelo está listo para salir al público.
Estas pruebas buscan ampliar la supervisión externa más allá de las revisiones que suelen hacerse poco antes de lanzar un producto. Algunos evaluadores sostienen que revisar un modelo únicamente al final del desarrollo no permite detectar comportamientos que podrían aparecer durante el entrenamiento o cuando el sistema se utiliza dentro de la propia empresa.
Dudas sobre la independencia de las pruebas
El acuerdo con Apollo establece límites al acceso de sus investigadores. La organización podrá consultar información relevante para examinar las posibles conductas de subversión, como código y conjuntos de datos de entrenamiento, registros de ciertos procesos de aprendizaje y versiones intermedias de los modelos. Sin embargo, el acceso se restringirá a modelos, periodos y preguntas acordados con OpenAI.
La empresa también se reserva la posibilidad de retener información por razones de seguridad, protección de propiedad intelectual o dificultades técnicas. Apollo señala que OpenAI aceptó no ocultar datos simplemente porque fueran desfavorables. Aun así, sus investigadores no tendrán acceso libre a todo el personal: podrán hablar con empleados autorizados, seleccionados por OpenAI, y deberán canalizar cualquier seguimiento sobre información confidencial a través de la compañía.
La publicación de resultados es otro punto de debate. Apollo podrá difundir conclusiones independientes y explicar las condiciones de sus evaluaciones, pero OpenAI podrá limitar qué evidencia de respaldo se hace pública. Esto podría dificultar que terceros revisen por su cuenta cómo se llegó a esas conclusiones. La empresa indicó que su Comité de Seguridad y Protección, que supervisa estos asuntos para la junta de la Fundación OpenAI, tendrá acceso a informes completos y podrá conversar directamente con los evaluadores.
Además, Apollo y Goodfire recibirán compensación económica por su trabajo; METR y Transluce no cobrarán, aunque podrían aceptar créditos de cómputo o de API. Para algunos críticos, los límites de acceso y divulgación reducen la independencia de las pruebas. OpenAI presenta el programa como un primer paso hacia evaluaciones externas más profundas. Su eficacia dependerá de cuánto puedan observar los investigadores y de qué información llegue finalmente al público.

articles.title: Le HomeView d’Apple est un cauchemar à démonter pour aucune bonne raison
articles.text:
Le HomeView d’Apple est un cauchemar à démonter pour aucune bonne raison
Chaque nouveau gadget de chez Apple passe dans les labos d’iFixit pour évaluer sa réparabilité. Malheureusement pour le HomeView et ses propriétaires, Apple a construit un appareil qui n’est tout simplement pas fait pour être réparé. Voire même démonté.
Pour la première fois depuis un moment, Apple a sorti un gadget dont l’Europe est privée. Le HomeView, l’écran connecté made in Cupertino, ne peut être acheté sur le Vieux Continent en raison de l’absence du nouveau Siri chez nous. Mais ce n’est peut-être pas une si grande perte quand on voit la manière dont l’objet a été construit.
Les professionnels de la réparation de chez iFixit ont tenté de démonter l’appareil pour évaluer sa réparabilité et lui ont donné la note de "juron que la décence nous empêche de traduire/10".
Une conception hostile à la réparation
Contrairement aux derniers produits Apple qui ont fait de beaux progrès sur ce front, le HomeView a tout du parfait bingo de l’hostilité à la réparation. Quel que soit le modèle, le gros des réparations doit se faire via l’écran. Ce qui pose un risque évident de casse supplémentaire au moment du démontage. Désolidariser la base de l’appareil de son écran nécessite aussi d’enlever quasiment tous les autres composants un à un.
Et malheureusement, cela tient de la gageure. Les vis utilisées ne sont pas les mêmes d’un côté et de l’autre de l’appareil et Apple semble avoir utilisé des quantités industrielles d’adhésif pour faire tenir chacun des composants et des câbles. Résultat, même les mains expertes d’iFixit n’ont pas réussi à démonter l’appareil sans arracher une paire de câbles et casser un haut-parleur.
Si le socle est un peu plus facile à démonter et à réparer, l’emploi d’un câble excessivement court et de vis impossibles à enlever sans outils spécifiques rend la réparation encore inutilement compliquée. Seule bonne nouvelle, le port USB-C peut être changé simplement en quelques coups de tournevis. Autrement, quasiment tous les autres problèmes matériels demanderont un démontage complet des deux moitiés de l’appareil.
"Déraisonnablement et inutilement difficiles"
"Le HomeView est un véritable cauchemar à démonter. […] Concevoir un produit en vue de sa réparation est un choix stratégique, et, dans ce cas précis, Apple ne s’en est pas préoccupé. […] Nous n’avons cessé de nous heurter à des choix qui rendaient les réparations déraisonnablement et inutilement difficiles", se lamente iFixit.
Le tout pour un produit qui est en plus clairement fait pour rester fixé sur un mur ou posé sur un meuble. Pas exactement le genre d’appareils qui est soumis à beaucoup de chocs au quotidien ou sur lequel un demi-centimètre ou gramme supplémentaire fait une énorme différence.
